fix(op-node): bootstrap follow-mode ELSync sequencer from genesis

A follow-mode sequencer (SequencerEnabled + L2FollowSource, so
NeedInitialResetEngine) configured with --syncmode=execution-layer
deadlocks at genesis: it starts in syncStatusWillStartEL, so
IsEngineInitialELSyncing() stays true and the driver's SyncStep backs off
before reaching TryInitialResetEngineForSequencer. The only exit from
willStartEL is insertUnsafePayload receiving a peer payload — which never
arrives for the chain's sole producer at genesis. The chain never advances.

A follow-mode sequencer produces the chain rather than syncing it, so at
genesis it has nothing to initial-EL-sync to. Fix:

- SyncStep: attempt the follow-mode initial reset before the EL-sync
  backoff, so the engine gets seeded instead of waiting forever.
- TryInitialResetEngineForSequencer: after seeding an uninitialized engine,
  transition willStartEL -> finishedEL (mirroring insertUnsafePayload's
  existing "skip EL sync when a finalized block exists" transition) so the
  driver stops backing off and the sequencer can build. EL sync still
  engages later via forkchoice updates, which tolerate SYNCING in ELSync,
  if the follow source is ever ahead.

Scoped to follow-mode sequencers (NeedInitialResetEngine); verifiers and
non-follow nodes are unaffected. Generic (no-follow-source) ELSync sequencer
bootstrap from genesis remains unsolved and is tracked separately.

Refs #21119.

fix(op-node): reorg follow-mode sequencer onto upstream chain on divergence

A follow-mode sequencer (light op-node CL that produces unsafe blocks while
following a supernode's safe head) failed to adopt the supernode's deposits-only
invalid-message replacement: the invalid executing message persisted
(ethereum-optimism/optimism#21119).

Root cause: in EngineController.FollowSource, the divergence branch did a soft
followExternalRefs(true). That soft unsafe-head update was designed for pure
light-CL verifiers (#18571), which have no local block production. A follow-mode
sequencer keeps extending its own fork, so the soft update was clobbered by the
next sequencer block before the FCU landed, leaving head on the fork and safe on
the upstream chain. op-reth then rejected the FCU as inconsistent, the reset
re-selected the fork via the deny-list-unaware FindL2Heads, and the follower
oscillated indefinitely.

Fix: when the follower is also a sequencer (origin-selector resetter wired, i.e.
SequencerEnabled), reorg decisively onto the upstream refs with forceReset. This
cancels the in-flight fork build (ResetOrigins), aborts the sequencer, and FCUs
the engine onto the upstream chain in one shot (head==safe), after which the
sequencer rebuilds on the new head. Pure verifiers keep the proven soft path.

Adds unit guards TestFollowSource_SequencerDivergenceForcesReset and
TestFollowSource_VerifierDivergenceStaysSoft, plus cross-node convergence and
forward-progress assertions to the shared invalid-message replacement scenario.

fix(op-node): bootstrap follow-mode ELSync sequencer from genesis

A follow-mode sequencer (SequencerEnabled + L2FollowSource, so
NeedInitialResetEngine) configured with --syncmode=execution-layer
deadlocks at genesis: it starts in syncStatusWillStartEL, so
IsEngineInitialELSyncing() stays true and the driver's SyncStep backs off
before reaching TryInitialResetEngineForSequencer. The only exit from
willStartEL is insertUnsafePayload receiving a peer payload — which never
arrives for the chain's sole producer at genesis. The chain never advances.

A follow-mode sequencer produces the chain rather than syncing it, so at
genesis it has nothing to initial-EL-sync to. Fix:

- SyncStep: attempt the follow-mode initial reset before the EL-sync
  backoff, so the engine gets seeded instead of waiting forever.
- TryInitialResetEngineForSequencer: after seeding an uninitialized engine,
  transition willStartEL -> finishedEL (mirroring insertUnsafePayload's
  existing "skip EL sync when a finalized block exists" transition) so the
  driver stops backing off and the sequencer can build. EL sync still
  engages later via forkchoice updates, which tolerate SYNCING in ELSync,
  if the follow source is ever ahead.

Scoped to follow-mode sequencers (NeedInitialResetEngine); verifiers and
non-follow nodes are unaffected. Generic (no-follow-source) ELSync sequencer
bootstrap from genesis remains unsolved and is tracked separately.

Refs #21119.

fix(MultisigTask): tolerate negative per-call gas refund

`_execTransaction` guarded the simulated `execTransaction` with
`require(gasInfo.gasRefunded >= 0)`, assuming forge's `lastCallGas().gasRefunded`
is always non-negative. That assumption is wrong: `gasRefunded` is the per-call
EIP-3529 refund delta (an int64), not the tx-level counter (which floors at 0).
A call frame whose SSTORE refund removals outweigh its grants legitimately
reports a negative value — see paradigmxyz/revm-inspectors#267, which changed the
refund counter to i64 precisely "because this can go negative."

This surfaced on a heavy OPCM (U19) upgrade simulation, where the root-safe
`execTransaction` frame nets a negative refund and the task aborts with
"MultisigTask: negative gas refund is invalid" even though the transaction is
valid (on-chain the refund floors at 0, so nothing reverts).

Drop the require and clamp the value to 0 for the gas-cap accounting, which is
the only thing it feeds. Behavior is unchanged for non-negative refunds.

fix(op-node): bootstrap follow-mode ELSync sequencer from genesis

A follow-mode sequencer (SequencerEnabled + L2FollowSource, so
NeedInitialResetEngine) configured with --syncmode=execution-layer
deadlocks at genesis: it starts in syncStatusWillStartEL, so
IsEngineInitialELSyncing() stays true and the driver's SyncStep backs off
before reaching TryInitialResetEngineForSequencer. The only exit from
willStartEL is insertUnsafePayload receiving a peer payload — which never
arrives for the chain's sole producer at genesis. The chain never advances.

A follow-mode sequencer produces the chain rather than syncing it, so at
genesis it has nothing to initial-EL-sync to. Fix:

- SyncStep: attempt the follow-mode initial reset before the EL-sync
  backoff, so the engine gets seeded instead of waiting forever.
- TryInitialResetEngineForSequencer: after seeding an uninitialized engine,
  transition willStartEL -> finishedEL (mirroring insertUnsafePayload's
  existing "skip EL sync when a finalized block exists" transition) so the

  engages later via forkchoice updates, which tolerate SYNCING in ELSync,

fix(op-node): reorg follow-mode sequencer onto upstream chain on divergence

A follow-mode sequencer (light op-node CL that produces unsafe blocks while
following a supernode's safe head) failed to adopt the supernode's deposits-only
invalid-message replacement: the invalid executing message persisted
(ethereum-optimism/optimism#21119).

Root cause: in EngineController.FollowSource, the divergence branch did a soft
followExternalRefs(true). That soft unsafe-head update was designed for pure
light-CL verifiers (#18571), which have no local block production. A follow-mode
sequencer keeps extending its own fork, so the soft update was clobbered by the
next sequencer block before the FCU landed, leaving head on the fork and safe on
the upstream chain. op-reth then rejected the FCU as inconsistent, the reset
re-selected the fork via the deny-list-unaware FindL2Heads, and the follower
oscillated indefinitely.

Fix: when the follower is also a sequencer (origin-selector resetter wired, i.e.
SequencerEnabled), reorg decisively onto the upstream refs with forceReset. This
cancels the in-flight fork build (ResetOrigins), aborts the sequencer, and FCUs
the engine onto the upstream chain in one shot (head==safe), after which the
sequencer rebuilds on the new head. Pure verifiers keep the proven soft path.

Adds unit guards TestFollowSource_SequencerDivergenceForcesReset and
TestFollowSource_VerifierDivergenceStaysSoft, plus cross-node convergence and
forward-progress assertions to the shared invalid-message replacement scenario.

and on CI for both op-reth and op-geth. Replace it with an eventual-consistency

test(interop): gate post-reorg settle on cross-safe advancement

The settle-first convergence check used MatchedWithProgressFn at cross-safe,
which passes trivially while the follow-source is still oscillating: during
oscillation both the sequencer and supernode verifier are pinned at the
replacement height, so a cross-safe head match is satisfied immediately. The
test then transacted mid-oscillation, the tx landed in a fork block the
follow-source reorged away, and it was orphaned (AssertTxInBlock failed).

safe is monotonic and only advances once the supernode cross-validates the
sequencer's post-replacement blocks, i.e. the divergence is resolved and the
oscillation has stopped. Then assert the sequencer agrees with the supernode
verifier at cross-safe. Also trims the over-verbose comments in this file.

feat(op-conductor): reorg-recovery wedge hardening (demotion grace + reconnect-reconcile)

Closes the deep-reorg wedge demonstrated by the tight-health stress test
(~2% of reorg-reaching runs). All changes gated by --reorg-recovery.enabled;
with the flag off the grace is 0 and behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged.

Fix 1 — non-cancellable demotion-grace latch (leadership-race vector). A stale
leader (ErrSequencerNotHealthy) now keeps reporting healthy for a fixed 5s grace
so it can receive and commit the op-reth reorg notification before staleness
transfers leadership away. At grace expiry it is demoted UNCONDITIONALLY: a
healthy poll during the grace cannot cancel a pending demotion (a fresh
timestamp does not prove a correct chain), so a node oscillating onto a
fresh-but-wrong fork cannot evade failover. ErrSequencerConnectionDown and any
other error demote immediately. The latch is a pure state machine
(demotion_latch.go); the control loop owns the grace timer and applies the
unconditional demotion at expiry. The health check itself is untouched.

Fix 2 — reconnect-reconcile (WS-gap vector). reth_subscribeChainNotifications
has no replay, so a reorg during a WS disconnect is lost. Each successful
(re)subscribe now emits a synthetic ReorgEvent{Resync:true} so the leader
re-reads and commits its EL's current unsafe head, catching up any missed
reorg. Idempotent (no-op when EL head == FSM head), counted separately
(reorg_resyncs_count).

Fix 3 — subscriber reconnection test. Fake WS server exercises subscribe →
deliver → drop → reconnect → re-subscribe → resume, and asserts Commit frames
are read and ignored (kept alive, no spurious reconnect).

docs(op-conductor): document reorg-recovery demotion grace

Document the Phase 7 non-cancellable 5s demotion grace (and the reconnect
reconcile) added by --reorg-recovery.enabled: a stale leader is held healthy
long enough to commit a deep-reorg head before failing over, then demoted
unconditionally. Notes the operational trade-offs (≤5s added failover latency on
a stuck-but-connected sequencer; one guaranteed leadership handoff per deep
reorg; connection loss still fails over immediately; shallow reorgs unaffected;
grace is 0 when the flag is off) across README, RUNBOOK, and the public mdx.

perf(sdm): materialize canonical PostExec efficiently across flashblocks

Make the op-rbuilder canonical PostExec (0x7D) flashblock path both
O(1)-per-flashblock and consensus-identical to op-reth's single
whole-block pass.

Materialization without prior-tx replay:
- The per-flashblock canonical replay re-executed every prior tx from the
  parent state on each flashblock, making per-block cost O(N^2) in tx
  count. Replace it with materialize_post_exec, which seeds a throwaway
  State via with_bundle_prestate(real_bundle) and executes only the
  single PostExec system tx on top, then assembles the block from the
  already-accumulated execution info (the same prestate pattern op-reth's
  flashblocks worker uses). PostExec stays isolated in the throwaway
  state, so the main builder cache is never polluted. build_block is
  unified into one single-pass assembly path that optionally folds in the
  PostExec tx, deleting the duplicated canonical branch, the replay
  function, and the CanonicalPostExecExecution struct.

Block-scoped warming carry-forward across flashblock executors:
- SDM warming refunds are block-scoped, but op-rbuilder builds each
  flashblock with a fresh executor (fresh SDMWarmingInspector seeded
  empty), so warming provenance reset at every flashblock boundary and
  the produced refund set diverged from op-reth's single canonical pass
  (receipt root mismatch -> block rejected). Thread the inspector's
  block-scoped warming maps across flashblocks: expose WarmingState
  get/set on SDMWarmingInspector -> PostExecCompositeInspector ->
  OpEvm/PostExecEvm (+ factory hooks) -> PostExecExecutorExt, then capture
  the warming state after each flashblock (and the base block) and seed
  the next flashblock's executor. This makes per-flashblock accumulation
  identical to a single whole-block pass for every boundary alignment.
  Only warmed-set membership affects the consensus SDMGasEntry set; the
  carried provenance indices feed attribution events only. Adds inspector
  unit tests covering the carry.

Supporting changes:
- Implement the new warming_state/seed_warming_state methods for every
  external impl of the extended traits, which would otherwise be left
  unimplemented and break the Rust build: PostExecEvmFactoryHooks for
  FpvmOpEvmFactory (kona-client) and the UniEvmFactory test factory,
  PostExecEvm for the custom-node example's CustomEvm, and
  PostExecExecutorExt for its CustomBlockExecutor (whose bound is
  tightened from Evm to PostExecEvm to reach the carry methods).
- Route SDM activation checks through a shared helper.
- Satisfy clippy (or_fun_call) and rustfmt CI lints.

feat(op-reth): compute miner fee on pool tx in payload builder

Move the `effective_tip_per_gas` call in
`OpPayloadBuilderCtx::execute_best_transactions` to before
`into_consensus()`, so the miner fee is computed from the pool
transaction rather than the consensus transaction.

Semantically identical for vanilla op-reth users: for stock EIP-1559 /
legacy / deposit txs, `effective_tip_per_gas` returns the same value
on the pool or consensus form. The pool is queried with `block.basefee`,
so any tx returned from `best_txs` satisfies `max_fee_per_gas >= base_fee`.
The existing `expect` invariant still holds (I made the message more
explicit).

This unblocks a cleanup in Celo's reth implementation. On Celo,
`max_fee_per_gas` on the consensus tx can be denominated in an ERC-20
fee currency instead of native wei (CIP-64). The pool validator converts
to native equivalents and exposes the correct tip via the pool tx's
`effective_tip_per_gas` impl, but op-reth currently discards that view
via `into_consensus()` before reading the tip. Without this change, the
Celo fork needs a `SignedTx` newtype that stashes native-equivalent fees
on the consensus tx solely to thread them through this one call site
(~600 lines in celo-kona's `signed_tx.rs`, deletable once this lands).

See https://github.com/celo-org/celo-kona/issues/152

feat(op-interop-filter): correct + per-reason failsafe metrics & logs (#21115)

* fix(op-interop-filter): reflect auto-triggered failsafe in metric

The failsafe_enabled gauge was only updated on the manual SetFailsafeEnabled
path. Failsafe entered automatically via a chain ingester error or a
cross-validator error never updated the gauge, and reorg auto-recovery
clearing an error did not either. The metric tracked only the manual override
flag, not the effective FailsafeEnabled() state, so a node in failsafe could
report failsafe_enabled=0.

Wire an onFailsafeChange callback into the ingester (SetError/ClearError) and
cross-validator (setError). The backend registers a callback that records the
recomputed FailsafeEnabled() so the gauge stays correct when multiple chains or
the cross-validator can independently hold failsafe on (e.g. clearing one chain
while another still errors keeps the gauge at 1).

The cross-validator invokes the callback after releasing errMu to avoid
re-acquiring the RWMutex via Error().

Add tests covering the automatic paths and the RPC/manual path.

* feat(op-interop-filter): expose per-reason failsafe metric and logs

Failsafe can be on for several reasons at once: manual override, one or
more chain ingester errors (each with its own reason: reorg, conflict,
data_corruption, invalid_log), and a cross-validator error. The single
failsafe_enabled boolean collapsed all of that.

Add failsafe_reason_active{reason} gauge so each active reason is visible
independently (multiple series read 1 simultaneously), and a consolidated
'Failsafe active' log that enumerates all active reasons with per-chain
detail, emitted only when the reason set changes.

Funnel all failsafe observability through a single refreshFailsafe method,
serialized by failsafeMu so concurrent error transitions cannot latch a
stale gauge value (last writer observes all completed state changes) or
interleave log lines. This also replaces the duplicated record call in
SetFailsafeEnabled.

Add a multi-reason test; drop the unused failsafeWrites test field.

* chore(op-interop-filter): address review feedback on failsafe metrics

- Sort chain IDs numerically via eth.SortChainID (was lexicographic, which
  misordered high chain numbers in the log summary).
- Document that the cross-validator has no error-clear path today and that any
  future recovery path must fire onFailsafeChange.
- Minor formatting in the test helper.

* feat(op-interop-filter): periodically log failsafe reason while active

The transition log fires only once (deduped on the reason set), so a
long-lived failsafe (e.g. a reorg awaiting recovery) stops appearing in

fix(MultisigTask): skip address-code check on packed storage slots

The `_checkStateDiff` else-branch reinterpreted the low 160 bits of any
non-address-shaped slot value as a candidate address and asserted it had
no code. For SystemConfig slot 0x6c — which packs `superchainConfig`

pushes the value above `uint160.max`, and the truncated low bits do
point at deployed code, so the assertion fires.

are skipped. Unblocks U19 stacked simulation on Sepolia.

fix(MultisigTask): tolerate negative per-call gas refund (#1443)

`_execTransaction` guarded the simulated `execTransaction` with
`require(gasInfo.gasRefunded >= 0)`, assuming forge's `lastCallGas().gasRefunded`
is always non-negative. That assumption is wrong: `gasRefunded` is the per-call
EIP-3529 refund delta (an int64), not the tx-level counter (which floors at 0).
A call frame whose SSTORE refund removals outweigh its grants legitimately
reports a negative value — see paradigmxyz/revm-inspectors#267, which changed the
refund counter to i64 precisely "because this can go negative."

This surfaced on a heavy OPCM (U19) upgrade simulation, where the root-safe
`execTransaction` frame nets a negative refund and the task aborts with
"MultisigTask: negative gas refund is invalid" even though the transaction is
valid (on-chain the refund floors at 0, so nothing reverts).

Drop the require and clamp the value to 0 for the gas-cap accounting, which is
the only thing it feeds. Behavior is unchanged for non-negative refunds.

fix(op-node): reorg follow-mode sequencer onto upstream chain on divergence

A follow-mode sequencer (light op-node CL that produces unsafe blocks while
following a supernode's safe head) failed to adopt the supernode's deposits-only
invalid-message replacement: the invalid executing message persisted
(ethereum-optimism/optimism#21119).

Root cause: in EngineController.FollowSource, the divergence branch did a soft
followExternalRefs(true). That soft unsafe-head update was designed for pure
light-CL verifiers (#18571), which have no local block production. A follow-mode
sequencer keeps extending its own fork, so the soft update was clobbered by the
next sequencer block before the FCU landed, leaving head on the fork and safe on
the upstream chain. op-reth then rejected the FCU as inconsistent, the reset
re-selected the fork via the deny-list-unaware FindL2Heads, and the follower
oscillated indefinitely.

Fix: when the follower is also a sequencer (origin-selector resetter wired, i.e.
SequencerEnabled), reorg decisively onto the upstream refs with forceReset. This
cancels the in-flight fork build (ResetOrigins), aborts the sequencer, and FCUs
the engine onto the upstream chain in one shot (head==safe), after which the
sequencer rebuilds on the new head. Pure verifiers keep the proven soft path.

Adds unit guards TestFollowSource_SequencerDivergenceForcesReset (regression
guard for the reorg-reset) and TestFollowSource_VerifierDivergenceStaysSoft
(confirms the verifier soft path is unchanged).

feat(op-reth/txpool): expose `OpPool::inner` accessor `OpPool

` wraps an inner pool but only delegates the `TransactionPool` *trait* surface. Inherent accessors on the wrapped type — most notably `reth_transaction_pool::Pool::validator` — are unreachable from outside the crate because the `inner` field is private and has no accessor. This was incidental rather than intentional: `OpPool` was introduced in #20001 to layer interop-reorg filtering on `add_external_transactions`, and the lost accessibility wasn't part of the change's scope. The practical consequence for downstream consumers (e.g. flashblocks-style pool wrappers that want to pre-validate transactions before dispatching them to a more expensive path) is that they now have to reconstruct a parallel validator with the same configuration as the one `OpPoolBuilder::build_pool` already built — at runtime cost (extra validation task executor) and at maintenance cost (the parameter list has to be kept in sync by hand). Add a `pub const fn inner(&self) -> &P` so consumers can opt in to the inherent surface of the wrapped pool when they need it. The wrapper's public contract is otherwise unchanged.

fix(op-supernode): dial interop engine controller lazily

The interop engine controller uses a separate EL connection from the
virtual node and was set up inside the VN restart loop. A healthy VN
keeps running and reconnects its own EL client without restarting, so if
the engine-controller connection failed at startup c.engine stayed nil
forever and interop kept failing with ErrNoEngineClient.

Dial the engine controller lazily and set it up once in the chain
container constructor. Lazy dialing never touches the network at setup,
so the controller is usable immediately and connects (and reconnects) on
demand once the EL is reachable -- no VN restart required. Lazy is
applied to a copy of the L2 endpoint config so the virtual node, which
shares vncfg.L2, keeps its eager-dial behavior. Setting the engine up
once in the constructor also makes c.engine write-once, removing the
need for the previous in-loop retry and any locking.

A fatal engine-controller setup error now aborts chain-container
construction instead of being logged and ignored, so a chain that can
never reach its engine does not start.

Fixes #21136

time to install and start a new VirtualNode before IsRPCReady() flips

post-Resume points. Wait polls IsRPCReady() at the same 25ms cadence as
the router gate, with a 60s safety bound. Compile-time conformance
assertions (`var _ InteropChain = ...`) force every implementer to
provide it.

fix(op-node): reorg follow-mode sequencer onto upstream chain on divergence (#21155)

A follow-mode sequencer (light op-node CL that produces unsafe blocks while
following a supernode's safe head) failed to adopt the supernode's deposits-only
invalid-message replacement: the invalid executing message persisted
(ethereum-optimism/optimism#21119).

Root cause: in EngineController.FollowSource, the divergence branch did a soft
followExternalRefs(true). That soft unsafe-head update was designed for pure
light-CL verifiers (#18571), which have no local block production. A follow-mode
sequencer keeps extending its own fork, so the soft update was clobbered by the
next sequencer block before the FCU landed, leaving head on the fork and safe on
the upstream chain. op-reth then rejected the FCU as inconsistent, the reset
re-selected the fork via the deny-list-unaware FindL2Heads, and the follower
oscillated indefinitely.

Fix: when the follower is also a sequencer (origin-selector resetter wired, i.e.
SequencerEnabled), reorg decisively onto the upstream refs with forceReset. This
cancels the in-flight fork build (ResetOrigins), aborts the sequencer, and FCUs
the engine onto the upstream chain in one shot (head==safe), after which the
sequencer rebuilds on the new head. Pure verifiers keep the proven soft path.

Adds unit guards TestFollowSource_SequencerDivergenceForcesReset (regression
guard for the reorg-reset) and TestFollowSource_VerifierDivergenceStaysSoft
(confirms the verifier soft path is unchanged).

fix(op-supernode): dial interop engine controller lazily (#21152)

The interop engine controller uses a separate EL connection from the
virtual node and was set up inside the VN restart loop. A healthy VN
keeps running and reconnects its own EL client without restarting, so if
the engine-controller connection failed at startup c.engine stayed nil
forever and interop kept failing with ErrNoEngineClient.

Dial the engine controller lazily and set it up once in the chain
container constructor. Lazy dialing never touches the network at setup,
so the controller is usable immediately and connects (and reconnects) on
demand once the EL is reachable -- no VN restart required. Lazy is
applied to a copy of the L2 endpoint config so the virtual node, which
shares vncfg.L2, keeps its eager-dial behavior. Setting the engine up
once in the constructor also makes c.engine write-once, removing the
need for the previous in-loop retry and any locking.

A fatal engine-controller setup error now aborts chain-container
construction instead of being logged and ignored, so a chain that can
never reach its engine does not start.

Fixes #21136

* perf(sdm): materialize canonical PostExec efficiently across flashblocks

Make the op-rbuilder canonical PostExec (0x7D) flashblock path both
O(1)-per-flashblock and consensus-identical to op-reth's single
whole-block pass.

Materialization without prior-tx replay:
- The per-flashblock canonical replay re-executed every prior tx from the
  parent state on each flashblock, making per-block cost O(N^2) in tx
  count. Replace it with materialize_post_exec, which seeds a throwaway
  State via with_bundle_prestate(real_bundle) and executes only the
  single PostExec system tx on top, then assembles the block from the
  already-accumulated execution info (the same prestate pattern op-reth's
  flashblocks worker uses). PostExec stays isolated in the throwaway
  state, so the main builder cache is never polluted. build_block is
  unified into one single-pass assembly path that optionally folds in the
  PostExec tx, deleting the duplicated canonical branch, the replay
  function, and the CanonicalPostExecExecution struct.

Block-scoped warming carry-forward across flashblock executors:
- SDM warming refunds are block-scoped, but op-rbuilder builds each
  flashblock with a fresh executor (fresh SDMWarmingInspector seeded
  empty), so warming provenance reset at every flashblock boundary and
  the produced refund set diverged from op-reth's single canonical pass
  (receipt root mismatch -> block rejected). Thread the inspector's
  block-scoped warming maps across flashblocks: expose WarmingState
  get/set on SDMWarmingInspector -> PostExecCompositeInspector ->
  OpEvm/PostExecEvm (+ factory hooks) -> PostExecExecutorExt, then capture
  the warming state after each flashblock (and the base block) and seed
  the next flashblock's executor. This makes per-flashblock accumulation
  identical to a single whole-block pass for every boundary alignment.
  Only warmed-set membership affects the consensus SDMGasEntry set; the
  carried provenance indices feed attribution events only. Adds inspector
  unit tests covering the carry.

Supporting changes:
- Implement the new warming_state/seed_warming_state methods for every
  external impl of the extended traits, which would otherwise be left
  unimplemented and break the Rust build: PostExecEvmFactoryHooks for
  FpvmOpEvmFactory (kona-client) and the UniEvmFactory test factory,
  PostExecEvm for the custom-node example's CustomEvm, and
  PostExecExecutorExt for its CustomBlockExecutor (whose bound is
  tightened from Evm to PostExecEvm to reach the carry methods).
- Route SDM activation checks through a shared helper.
- Satisfy clippy (or_fun_call) and rustfmt CI lints.

feat(proxyd): add agreement interop validation strategy

Add an additive `agreement` interop-validation strategy that fans each
checkAccessList out to all configured supervisor urls concurrently and
decides once `min_responses` definitive verdicts arrive, without awaiting
slower endpoints.

A definitive verdict is a successful validation or a known supervisor
rejection; transport errors, timeouts, 5xx, failsafe (-32602/503) and
cancellations (499) are non-responses and never count. All-valid accepts,
all-invalid rejects with the real error, a mix logs and rejects, and fewer
than `min_responses` definitive verdicts fails closed. `MinResponses`
defaults to len(urls) (unanimity) and is validated to 1..len(urls) in Start.

Existing first-supervisor / multicall / health-aware strategies are
untouched and `performCheckAccessListOp` is reused unchanged.
feat(proxyd): add agreement interop validation strategy

feat(proxyd): make interop failsafe a hard short-circuit rejection

Failsafe enabled on any reachable endpoint now rejects the message
immediately, bypassing the quorum entirely. Previously failsafe
(ErrFailsafeEnabled, HTTP 503) was treated as an excluded non-response, so
a min=2-of-3 config could accept while a third endpoint was in failsafe.

Add isFailsafeError (the only 503 in the interop error map) and classify it
in each verdict goroutine before isDefinitiveInteropRejection. The receive
loop short-circuits on the first failsafe verdict, cancels in-flight
requests, and returns the failsafe error. Add a reject_failsafe metric
outcome.
feat(proxyd): make interop failsafe a hard short-circuit rejection

feat(proxyd): detect interop failsafe by dedicated code -320602

Switch failsafe detection from the overloaded HTTP 503 (derived from message
matching against ErrFailsafeEnabled) to the dedicated supervisor failsafe
code -320602 that op-interop-filter now emits.

- ParseInteropError gains a code-keyed fast path: a body with code -320602
  returns a failsafe RPCErr directly, immune to message wording.
- interopRPCErrorMap maps ErrFailsafeEnabled to -320602 (was -32602).
- isFailsafeError keys on Code == -320602 rather than HTTP 503.
- The definitive-rejection set excludes -320602 so failsafe is never a
  definitive verdict.

Because a failsafe assertion can arrive from any endpoint, including a slow
one, an accept now waits for all endpoints to be observed before returning;
failsafe still short-circuits the wait. This trades the slow-endpoint latency
skip on the accept path for failsafe-on-any-endpoint correctness, and makes
disagreement detection complete.

Hard cutover: relies on op-interop-filter emitting -320602, which must deploy
first.
feat(proxyd): detect interop failsafe by dedicated code -320602

feat(proxyd): fast-accept with failsafe priority among received verdicts

Revert the accept-waits-for-all-endpoints behaviour. The agreement strategy
again fast-accepts at the minimum: it decides as soon as minResponses
definitive verdicts arrive and never awaits slow or unresponded endpoints.

Failsafe still takes priority: a failsafe verdict read in the main loop
short-circuits to a reject, and before returning an accept the strategy does
a non-blocking drain of any verdicts already buffered so a failsafe that has
already arrived beats a met quorum. It never blocks on an endpoint that has
not yet responded. Disagreement detection returns to best-effort, as expected
with fast-accept.

Tests: restore TestAgreement_IgnoresSlowBackend (slow non-failsafe endpoint
must not delay accept); make TestAgreement_FailsafeOnAnyEndpoint_HardRejects
deterministic by gating the valid endpoints behind the failsafe response so
the failsafe is always observed. Agreement + failsafe tests pass under
-race -count=20.
feat(proxyd): fast-accept with failsafe priority among received verdicts

feat(proxyd): count any filter rejection as a definitive invalid verdict

A definitive INVALID verdict is ANY filter JSON-RPC rejection, not just the
known supervisor codes. The filter rejects a malformed/fabricated access list
with the generic -32602 ("failed to parse access entry"); previously that was
treated as a non-response, so an all-rejecting set fell through to
QuorumNotReached instead of a clean reject_agreed. This matches op-reth, which
caught the same latent gap via an acceptance test.

- ParseInteropError now reads the filter's actual JSON-RPC code via
  rpc.Error.ErrorCode() when the error implements it. A JSON-RPC error over
  HTTP 200 is an rpc.Error (not an rpc.HTTPError), so it previously collapsed
  to the -32000/500 fallback and the real code was lost.
- isDefinitiveInteropRejection broadens to "any *RPCErr filter rejection that
  isn't failsafe or a non-verdict failure": it excludes only failsafe
  (-320602, handled by isFailsafeError first), JSON-RPC internal (-32603 and
  proxyd's -32000 fallback), cancellation (HTTP 499), and transport/5xx. So
  -32602 and the -3204xx..-3215xx codes all count as definitive INVALID.

Fail-closed safety is unchanged (the tx is rejected either way); this produces
the correct reject reason/metric. Failsafe and accept-path behaviour are
untouched.

feat(op-reth): multi-endpoint quorum validation for interop filter

Fan out interop_checkAccessList to multiple interop-filter endpoints
concurrently inside InteropFilterClient and combine by quorum agreement:
a definitive verdict (valid, or a known SuperchainDAError rejection) counts
toward quorum; transport errors and timeouts do not. The aggregator decides
once min_responses verdicts arrive and does not await slower endpoints.
Accept iff all collected verdicts are valid; all-invalid surfaces the real
reason; a mix logs and rejects (Disagreement); too few definitive verdicts
fail closed (QuorumNotReached). A failsafe reported by any endpoint is a hard
short-circuit rejection regardless of quorum.

query_failsafe ORs admin_getFailsafeEnabled across endpoints, short-circuiting
on the first true so a slow endpoint cannot delay the failsafe poll.

CLI: --rollup.interop-http is now repeatable and --rollup.interop-min-responses
sets the quorum (defaults to the endpoint count, i.e. unanimity / fail-closed).
Single-endpoint configs behave as before. Updates OpPoolBuilder and the
op-rbuilder callers for the new with_interop signature.
feat(op-reth): multi-endpoint quorum validation for interop filter

feat(op-reth): detect interop failsafe by dedicated RPC code -320602

Switch failsafe detection in from_json_rpc from matching the error message
to the dedicated JSON-RPC error code -320602 the op-interop-filter server
emits, replacing the previously overloaded -32602. Detection is now by code
only, never by message text. The query_failsafe OR poll and the
check_access_list hard short-circuit on any-endpoint failsafe are unchanged.

This is a hard cutover: detection requires the filter to emit -320602, a
prerequisite server change that must deploy first.

feat(op-reth): a received failsafe beats a met quorum, deterministically

When the valid+invalid quorum is reached, non-blocking-drain the endpoint
futures that are already ready before returning Ok, and reject if any is
FailsafeEnabled. This makes "a failsafe that has arrived rejects even when the
minimum valids are in hand" deterministic instead of arrival-order dependent.
Endpoints that have not responded are still never awaited (fast-accept is
preserved); dropping the futures cancels them.

Make failsafe_on_any_endpoint_hard_rejects deterministic by requiring all
endpoints to resolve before the decision, and add a test proving a slow
non-failsafe endpoint does not delay accept.

refactor(alloy-op-hardforks): split lagoon/interop accessors

Addresses ajsutton's review comment on PR #21105.

Before this change, is_interop_active_at_timestamp was the only
hardfork accessor in the OpHardforks trait whose name disagreed
with the OpHardfork variant it checked (Lagoon). Every other
fork has a matching is_<fork>_active_at_timestamp method; Lagoon
was missing one because the rename left the old interop name
doing double duty.

  matching the is_karst_active_at_timestamp / is_jovian_*
  pattern. Checks OpHardfork::Lagoon directly.

  doc explains they are currently equivalent because Lagoon

  toggle diverge from the hard fork accessor if interop is ever
  decoupled from Lagoon.

Keeping is_interop_active_at_timestamp preserves backwards
compatibility for the trait's downstream consumers.

hard fork -> OpSpecId mapping, so the hard fork accessor is the

The two op-reth call sites (txpool validator and node startup)
continue to call is_interop_active_at_timestamp — they are
feature gates, not hard fork checks, so the feature toggle is
the right tool there.

ci(acceptance): fan out memory-all jobs to parallelism 32 on xlarge.gen2

Rebalance the three op-acceptance-tests memory-all-* jobs from
parallelism:2 x ACCEPTANCE_TEST_JOBS:8 on 2xlarge+.gen2 to
parallelism:32 x ACCEPTANCE_TEST_JOBS:32 on xlarge.gen2.

These jobs are the main-workflow critical path (~18m p50 / 22m p95).
The justfile timing-splits 182 tests across CIRCLE_NODE_TOTAL, so 32-way
fan-out gives ~6 tests/container, driving wall-clock toward the floor of
per-container overhead + longest single test. Spreading across more,

feat(op-reth): seed slot-preimage DB during state-dump import (#21108)

reth's V2 storage layout (`--storage.v2`, default-on) stores state in
hashed tables and, for pre-Cancun blocks, relies on an auxiliary MDBX DB
at `<datadir>/db/preimage` mapping `keccak256(slot) -> slot` so the
Execution stage can resolve plain storage keys when a SELFDESTRUCT wipes
a contract. That DB is populated only while executing blocks.

The OP Mainnet bedrock bootstrap (`init-state --without-ovm`) imports a
state dump straight into hashed storage and never populates the preimage
DB. A later pre-Ecotone selfdestruct of an imported contract then crashes
the Execution stage with "missing slot preimage for 0x... (addr=0x...)",
aborting backfill sync.

Close the gap on the op-reth side: after `init_from_state_dump`, when
storage is v2, re-read the dump (which carries plain slot keys) and seed
`keccak256(slot) -> slot` into the same env reth's execution stage reads.
Streaming parse with batched, sorted inserts keeps memory bounded; skip-
if-present makes it idempotent and crash-safe. No-op on v1, and reth
deletes the preimage DB once Ecotone activates.

The MDBX env open/insert is replicated from reth's private
`SlotPreimages::open`/`insert_preimages` at rev 81c0261 and must stay
byte-compatible; documented in-code. The durable fix belongs upstream
(a seeding helper in `reth-db-common` so importers can't bypass it).

feat(proxyd): halt CL consensus on unresolvable output root split

Each consensus cycle the CL poller queries optimism_outputAtBlock at the
group's safe block on every candidate and compares roots. A backend whose
root disagrees with a strict majority is banned. If there is no majority -
a tie (1v1, 2-2) or an N-way split - the disagreement is unresolvable and
consensus HALTS instead of guessing:

  - the served block height and cached optimism_syncStatus body freeze at
    the last-agreed value, so clients keep seeing the previous response;
  - the served consensus group is emptied, so general RPCs fail closed
    (ErrNoBackends) rather than routing to a backend on an uncertain fork.

Backends are not persistently banned during a halt - they are still polled
and re-verified every cycle - so consensus auto-recovers as soon as a
majority returns. A halt signals a potential chain split / derivation
divergence and is surfaced via the consensus_cl_halted gauge (alert target)
and the consensus_cl_halt_total counter.

Any backend count is now permitted, including even/2-node cross-client
groups (e.g. op-node + kona-node): the odd-backend startup guard is removed
since ties now halt rather than needing a majority to resolve.

Tests: unit decision cases (1v1 / 3-way / 2-2-1 tie -> halt; 2v1 majority,
unanimous, all-errored -> no halt), an end-to-end freeze + auto-recover
test, and a CL integration test asserting the all-disagree group fails closed.

feat(proxyd): add agreement interop validation strategy (#640)

* feat(proxyd): add agreement interop validation strategy

Add an additive `agreement` interop-validation strategy that fans each
checkAccessList out to all configured supervisor urls concurrently and
decides once `min_responses` definitive verdicts arrive, without awaiting
slower endpoints.

A definitive verdict is a successful validation or a known supervisor
rejection; transport errors, timeouts, 5xx, failsafe (-32602/503) and
cancellations (499) are non-responses and never count. All-valid accepts,
all-invalid rejects with the real error, a mix logs and rejects, and fewer
than `min_responses` definitive verdicts fails closed. `MinResponses`
defaults to len(urls) (unanimity) and is validated to 1..len(urls) in Start.

Existing first-supervisor / multicall / health-aware strategies are
untouched and `performCheckAccessListOp` is reused unchanged.

* feat(proxyd): make interop failsafe a hard short-circuit rejection

Failsafe enabled on any reachable endpoint now rejects the message
immediately, bypassing the quorum entirely. Previously failsafe
(ErrFailsafeEnabled, HTTP 503) was treated as an excluded non-response, so
a min=2-of-3 config could accept while a third endpoint was in failsafe.

Add isFailsafeError (the only 503 in the interop error map) and classify it
in each verdict goroutine before isDefinitiveInteropRejection. The receive
loop short-circuits on the first failsafe verdict, cancels in-flight
requests, and returns the failsafe error. Add a reject_failsafe metric
outcome.

* feat(proxyd): detect interop failsafe by dedicated code -320602

Switch failsafe detection from the overloaded HTTP 503 (derived from message
matching against ErrFailsafeEnabled) to the dedicated supervisor failsafe
code -320602 that op-interop-filter now emits.

- ParseInteropError gains a code-keyed fast path: a body with code -320602
  returns a failsafe RPCErr directly, immune to message wording.
- interopRPCErrorMap maps ErrFailsafeEnabled to -320602 (was -32602).
- isFailsafeError keys on Code == -320602 rather than HTTP 503.
- The definitive-rejection set excludes -320602 so failsafe is never a
  definitive verdict.

Because a failsafe assertion can arrive from any endpoint, including a slow
one, an accept now waits for all endpoints to be observed before returning;
failsafe still short-circuits the wait. This trades the slow-endpoint latency
skip on the accept path for failsafe-on-any-endpoint correctness, and makes
disagreement detection complete.

Hard cutover: relies on op-interop-filter emitting -320602, which must deploy
first.

* feat(proxyd): fast-accept with failsafe priority among received verdicts

Revert the accept-waits-for-all-endpoints behaviour. The agreement strategy
again fast-accepts at the minimum: it decides as soon as minResponses
definitive verdicts arrive and never awaits slow or unresponded endpoints.

Failsafe still takes priority: a failsafe verdict read in the main loop
short-circuits to a reject, and before returning an accept the strategy does
a non-blocking drain of any verdicts already buffered so a failsafe that has
already arrived beats a met quorum. It never blocks on an endpoint that has
not yet responded. Disagreement detection returns to best-effort, as expected
with fast-accept.

Tests: restore TestAgreement_IgnoresSlowBackend (slow non-failsafe endpoint
must not delay accept); make TestAgreement_FailsafeOnAnyEndpoint_HardRejects
deterministic by gating the valid endpoints behind the failsafe response so
the failsafe is always observed. Agreement + failsafe tests pass under
-race -count=20.

* feat(proxyd): count any filter rejection as a definitive invalid verdict

A definitive INVALID verdict is ANY filter JSON-RPC rejection, not just the
known supervisor codes. The filter rejects a malformed/fabricated access list
with the generic -32602 ("failed to parse access entry"); previously that was
treated as a non-response, so an all-rejecting set fell through to
QuorumNotReached instead of a clean reject_agreed. This matches op-reth, which
caught the same latent gap via an acceptance test.

- ParseInteropError now reads the filter's actual JSON-RPC code via
  rpc.Error.ErrorCode() when the error implements it. A JSON-RPC error over
  HTTP 200 is an rpc.Error (not an rpc.HTTPError), so it previously collapsed
  to the -32000/500 fallback and the real code was lost.
- isDefinitiveInteropRejection broadens to "any *RPCErr filter rejection that
  isn't failsafe or a non-verdict failure": it excludes only failsafe
  (-320602, handled by isFailsafeError first), JSON-RPC internal (-32603 and
  proxyd's -32000 fallback), cancellation (HTTP 499), and transport/5xx. So
  -32602 and the -3204xx..-3215xx codes all count as definitive INVALID.

Fail-closed safety is unchanged (the tx is rejected either way); this produces
the correct reject reason/metric. Failsafe and accept-path behaviour are
untouched.

* feat(proxyd): treat out-of-sync filter codes as soft non-responses

fix(ci): correct BASE_REVISION typo (devlop -> develop)

prepare-continuation-config set BASE_REVISION: devlop. collect-params.sh
computes the changed-file set with git diff --name-only "origin/${BASE_REVISION}...HEAD"
and, on failure, silently falls back to git diff HEAD~1 HEAD. Because

value; the fix is verified by ref resolution above.

feat(op-reth-test-engine): one-shot OP block execution (newPayload import + attrs-less FCU)

Phase 2 of the library-first OP test engine. Adds the import path that turns a
complete execution payload into a committed canonical block, plus attrs-less
forkchoice.

Insertion uses reth's in-memory canonical state (the engine-tree path), not a DB
write: execute against the parent overlay, verify the post-state root, build an
ExecutedBlock, then update_chain(Commit) + set_canonical_head. `latest()` then
yields a MemoryOverlayStateProvider so the next block executes on correct chained
state. Nothing past genesis touches MDBX.

- `exec::import_payload`: reuse OpExecutionPayloadValidator::ensure_well_formed_payload
  for structural validation + payload->block, execute via OpEvmConfig/BasicBlockExecutor,
  verify state root (INVALID on mismatch), commit. SYNCING on unknown parent.
- `TestEngine::{new_payload, forkchoice_updated}`. Attrs-less FCU advances the
  canonical/safe/finalized pointers: unknown head -> SYNCING (never silent VALID),
  unknown non-zero safe/finalized -> Error::UnknownForkchoiceBlock (resolved before
  any pointer moves). FCU with attributes returns Unsupported until the builder lands.
- `EphemeralChain`: store the chain spec; add state_at / commit_block /
  advance_forkchoice (+ test-only tip_header/latest_state).

fcu_unknown_safe cover the forkchoice paths. L1-fee *receipt* fields are an RPC-layer

op-reth(debug): add OP_RETH_STATE_TRIE_OVERLAY_THREADS knob to reproduce overlay deadlock

Adds an env-gated override for the state-trie-overlay worker-pool thread count
(reth's `RayonConfig::state_trie_overlay_worker_threads`). When
`OP_RETH_STATE_TRIE_OVERLAY_THREADS` is set to a positive integer, the op-reth
CLI builds its runtime with that many overlay-pool threads instead of the
default 4; when unset, behavior is identical to `CliRunner::try_default_runtime()`.

The overlay pool's 4-thread headroom normally masks the
`StateTrieOverlayManager::get_overlay` shard-lock-vs-worker-pool deadlock (the
suspected Ink sequencer-halt root cause). Shrinking the pool (e.g. to 1) removes
that headroom so the race surfaces readily on a devnet, which lets us reproduce
the halt and validate the fix. Pure debugging aid; default behavior unchanged.

fix(op-e2e): lazily generate genesis allocs per alloc type

The op-e2e/config init() unconditionally ran a full op-deployer genesis
pipeline for all 4 alloc types across 9 hardfork modes (36 pipelines) at
test-binary startup, costing minutes of CPU before any test ran. The
op-e2e-fuzz job runs three concurrent `go test -fuzz ./opgeth` processes;
each paid this full cost, oversubscribing CPU on the CI box. Under load the
combined startup exceeded the 15m no-output timeout, killing the job with
zero output from all three targets (including the pure-Go FuzzFastLzCgo,
which shares the binary and was blocked behind the same init).

Generate each alloc type lazily and once, so a binary only pays for the
alloc types its tests request. The opgeth fuzz binary uses only
DefaultAllocType, cutting its work from 4 alloc types to 1, and the two
FastLz targets need none, so they now start and stream output in seconds.

Refs ethereum-optimism/optimism#21191

fix(rollup-boost): ship the real binary from the Docker build

The rollup-boost Docker image was shipping a ~435KB cargo-chef stub
(an empty `fn main(){}`) instead of the real ~15.5MB binary, so the
container exited 0 immediately and devnets using it (e.g. anton-sdm)
lost their sequencer engine.

Root cause: `rust/rollup-boost/.dockerignore` excluded `**/Cargo.lock`,
so the lock never entered the build context. With `--locked` (enabled
in #21225), `cargo build` then fails ("cannot update the lock file ...
because --locked was passed") because there is no committed lock to
honor. The builder joined the build and the `cp` with `;` instead of
`&&`, so the failed build still copied cargo-chef's leftover dummy
binary out of `target/`, and the image build "succeeded" with a stub.
op-reth and op-rbuilder don't ignore Cargo.lock, so they were fine.

Fixes:
- Stop ignoring Cargo.lock so `--locked` has the committed lock.
- Use `&&` so a failed build fails the image instead of cp-ing a stale
  binary, and assert the built binary has a working CLI.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

ci(rust): share the Rust dependency cache across all jobs

The crate-download cache (.cargo/registry, .cargo/git, .cargo/bin,
.rustup) was keyed on the per-job prefix, so each of the ~18 Rust CI
jobs maintained its own copy even though the downloaded crate set is
identical for a given Cargo.lock — independent of job, profile, and
features. On any cold cache every job downloaded the full dependency
set from crates.io in parallel and CircleCI stored a separate multi-GB
copy per job.

Key this cache on a single shared 'rust-deps' prefix (still per-workspace
via the Cargo.lock checksum) so the dependencies are fetched and stored
once and reused by every job. The per-job target/ cache is unchanged.

No fallback key is used on purpose: a Cargo.lock change fully refreshes
the dependency cache rather than accreting old crate versions on top of
the existing set, bounding cache size. Lock changes are infrequent.
ci(rust): share the Rust dependency cache across all jobs

ci(rust): cache the Rust toolchain separately from dependencies

.rustup and the cargo-installed binaries (.cargo/bin) were stored in the
dependency cache keyed on Cargo.lock, so every dependency bump threw away
and re-downloaded the entire Rust toolchain — even though the toolchain
is pinned by mise.toml and rust/rust-toolchain.toml, not Cargo.lock.

Split them into a dedicated 'rust-toolchain' cache keyed on those pin
files. The toolchain is now refreshed only when the pins change, while
the dependency cache holds just the downloaded crate sources (registry +
git). Both remain shared across all jobs.

test(devstack): un-skip #21164 light-sequencer interop tests via VN-handoff bootstrap

A follow-mode ELSync light sequencer cannot bootstrap a chain from genesis: as
the sole block producer it has no peer payload to initial-EL-sync from, so it
deadlocks in willStartEL (#21164). This left two interop tests skipped. Bootstrap
them instead by sequencing on the supernode VN first, then handing off to the
light sequencers, and un-skip:
- TestLightSequencerSupernodeDerivesSafeChain
- TestSupernodeLightSequencerInteropInvalidMessageReplacement (op-reth only)

Preset / runtime
- WithSupernodeVNSequencerForBootstrap: the supernode VN sequences and the light
  follow-mode ELSync sequencers start stopped (l2CLNodeStartConfig.SequencerStopped
  -> driver.Config.SequencerStopped). The VN produces + gossips so the light seqs
  leave willStartEL via initial EL-sync.
- BootstrapLightSequencersViaVNHandoff helper: peers light<->VN, waits for the
  light seqs to EL-sync out of willStartEL, then stops sequencing on the VN and
  starts it on the light CLs.
- Batcher follows the VN during bootstrap, not the (stopped, EL-syncing) light
  seqs. Batching the light seqs leaves a gap at the handoff boundary that wedges
  L1 derivation ("dropping future span batch" forever) so the safe head never
  advances and interop verification stalls. The VN produces during bootstrap and
  tracks the light seqs via gossip after handoff, keeping a gap-free batch stream.
- Expose the supernode VN's EL per chain as L2ASupernodeEL / L2BSupernodeEL (a
  distinct node from L2ELA/L2ELB in light-sequencer mode; aliases them in
  virtual-sequencer mode).

invalid-message scenario
- Settle on cross-safe BEFORE asserting the invalid tx is gone. The unsafe head
  oscillates during recovery (#21119) and can reorg back onto an invalid-containing
  fork after the replacement validates; reading the block by number off the unsafe
  tip caught that transient. Once cross-safe advances past the block it is
  irreversible, so the read is stable.
- Anchor the post-recovery new-tx check on the supernode VN's L1-derived safe
  chain (the canonical source of truth): follow the tx by hash until it lands at or
  below the supernode's safe head, then assert it is present on BOTH the light
  sequencer's EL and the supernode VN's EL. This proves producer and verifier
  converge on one canonical chain, instead of trusting the producer's oscillating
  tip via a block-number comparison.
- MarkFlaky(#21125) for the residual reorg-recovery flake (a tx sent mid-storm can
  be orphaned even though the chain recovers). MarkFlaky only downgrades failures
  on the testingT it is called on, and DSL node assertions route through each
  node's own testingT, so it is applied to every node exercised in recovery, not
  just the test-body t.

feat(op-conductor): reorg-recovery wedge hardening (demotion grace + reconnect-reconcile)

Closes the deep-reorg wedge demonstrated by the tight-health stress test
(~2% of reorg-reaching runs). All changes gated by --reorg-recovery.enabled;
with the flag off the grace is 0 and behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged.

Fix 1 — non-cancellable demotion-grace latch (leadership-race vector). A stale
leader (ErrSequencerNotHealthy) now keeps reporting healthy for a fixed 5s grace
so it can receive and commit the op-reth reorg notification before staleness
transfers leadership away. At grace expiry it is demoted UNCONDITIONALLY: a
healthy poll during the grace cannot cancel a pending demotion (a fresh
timestamp does not prove a correct chain), so a node oscillating onto a
fresh-but-wrong fork cannot evade failover. ErrSequencerConnectionDown and any
other error demote immediately. The latch is a pure state machine
(demotion_latch.go); the control loop owns the grace timer and applies the
unconditional demotion at expiry. The health check itself is untouched.

Fix 2 — reconnect-reconcile (WS-gap vector). reth_subscribeChainNotifications
has no replay, so a reorg during a WS disconnect is lost. Each successful
(re)subscribe now emits a synthetic ReorgEvent{Resync:true} so the leader
re-reads and commits its EL's current unsafe head, catching up any missed
reorg. Idempotent (no-op when EL head == FSM head), counted separately
(reorg_resyncs_count).

Fix 3 — subscriber reconnection test. Fake WS server exercises subscribe →
deliver → drop → reconnect → re-subscribe → resume, and asserts Commit frames
are read and ignored (kept alive, no spurious reconnect).

docs(op-conductor): document reorg-recovery demotion grace

Document the Phase 7 non-cancellable 5s demotion grace (and the reconnect
reconcile) added by --reorg-recovery.enabled: a stale leader is held healthy
long enough to commit a deep-reorg head before failing over, then demoted
unconditionally. Notes the operational trade-offs (≤5s added failover latency on
a stuck-but-connected sequencer; one guaranteed leadership handoff per deep
reorg; connection loss still fails over immediately; shallow reorgs unaffected;
grace is 0 when the flag is off) across README, RUNBOOK, and the public mdx.

test(devstack): un-skip #21164 light-sequencer interop tests via VN-handoff bootstrap

A follow-mode ELSync light sequencer cannot bootstrap a chain from genesis: as
the sole block producer it has no peer payload to initial-EL-sync from, so it
deadlocks in willStartEL (#21164). This left two interop tests skipped. Bootstrap
them instead by sequencing on the supernode VN first, then handing off to the
light sequencers, and un-skip:
- TestLightSequencerSupernodeDerivesSafeChain
- TestSupernodeLightSequencerInteropInvalidMessageReplacement (op-reth only)

Preset / runtime
- WithSupernodeVNSequencerForBootstrap: the supernode VN sequences and the light
  follow-mode ELSync sequencers start stopped (l2CLNodeStartConfig.SequencerStopped
  -> driver.Config.SequencerStopped). The VN produces + gossips so the light seqs
  leave willStartEL via initial EL-sync.
- BootstrapLightSequencersViaVNHandoff helper: peers light<->VN, waits for the
  light seqs to EL-sync out of willStartEL, then stops sequencing on the VN and
  starts it on the light CLs.
- Batcher follows the VN during bootstrap, not the (stopped, EL-syncing) light
  seqs. Batching the light seqs leaves a gap at the handoff boundary that wedges
  L1 derivation ("dropping future span batch" forever) so the safe head never
  advances and interop verification stalls. The VN produces during bootstrap and
  tracks the light seqs via gossip after handoff, keeping a gap-free batch stream.
- Expose the supernode VN's EL per chain as L2ASupernodeEL / L2BSupernodeEL (a
  distinct node from L2ELA/L2ELB in light-sequencer mode; aliases them in
  virtual-sequencer mode).

invalid-message scenario
- Settle on cross-safe BEFORE asserting the invalid tx is gone. The unsafe head
  oscillates during recovery (#21119) and can reorg back onto an invalid-containing
  fork after the replacement validates; reading the block by number off the unsafe
  tip caught that transient. Once cross-safe advances past the block it is
  irreversible, so the read is stable.
- Anchor the post-recovery new-tx check on the supernode VN's L1-derived safe
  chain (the canonical source of truth): follow the tx by hash until it lands at or
  below the supernode's safe head, then assert it is present on BOTH the light
  sequencer's EL and the supernode VN's EL. This proves producer and verifier
  converge on one canonical chain, instead of trusting the producer's oscillating
  tip via a block-number comparison.
- MarkFlaky(#21125) for the residual reorg-recovery flake (a tx sent mid-storm can
  be orphaned even though the chain recovers). MarkFlaky only downgrades failures
  on the testingT it is called on, and DSL node assertions route through each
  node's own testingT, so it is applied to every node exercised in recovery, not
  just the test-body t.

yet" -- never a lookup error. A transient "could not get payload: not found" that
the op-node engine returns for a label while it is mid-reset during a reorg then
hard-fails the test, even though the chain recovers a moment later.

headBlockRef/HeadBlockRef pair on L2CLNode) and route ReachedFn/AdvancedFn through
it, returning lookup errors to the retry loop. AdvancedFn now captures its baseline
on the first successful read so a transient on the baseline is retried too. Switch
L2CLNode.AdvancedFn's baseline from the infallible HeadBlockRef to the fallible
headBlockRef with retry (its ReachedFn already tolerates). BlockRefByLabel stays as
a requiring wrapper for one-shot callers.

and restored /go/pkg/mod, but the Go module cache on the CI image lives
at ~/go/pkg/mod. The saved archive was therefore empty (16 B), so every

feat(op-reth): multi-endpoint quorum validation for interop filter

Fan out interop_checkAccessList to multiple interop-filter endpoints
concurrently inside InteropFilterClient and combine by quorum agreement:
a definitive verdict (valid, or a known SuperchainDAError rejection) counts
toward quorum; transport errors and timeouts do not. The aggregator decides
once min_responses verdicts arrive and does not await slower endpoints.
Accept iff all collected verdicts are valid; all-invalid surfaces the real
reason; a mix logs and rejects (Disagreement); too few definitive verdicts
fail closed (QuorumNotReached). A failsafe reported by any endpoint is a hard
short-circuit rejection regardless of quorum.

on the first true so a slow endpoint cannot delay the failsafe poll.

fix(op-reth): classify filter verdicts — definitive rejections vs soft out-of-sync

Two related classification fixes for the multi-endpoint interop aggregator.

Definitive rejections: a fabricated access list entry is rejected by the filter
with a generic -32602 "failed to parse access entry" (not a SuperchainDAError
code). is_definitive_invalid only counted InvalidEntry, so this legitimate
rejection was mis-classified as a non-response — with a single endpoint (min=1)
the aggregator collected 0 definitive verdicts and returned QuorumNotReached
instead of the filter's real rejection, regressing
TestInteropFilter_IngressRejectsInvalid. Now any JSON-RPC error response from
the filter is a definitive verdict (new Rejected { code, message } variant,
preserving the real reason) except the JSON-RPC internal error -32603, which
stays a non-response.

Soft out-of-sync failures: codes meaning "this node does not have the data yet"
— FutureData (-321401) and Uninitialized (-320400) — are soft, non-response
failures (new DataUnavailable variant; neither definitive_invalid nor failsafe).
A single out-of-sync node is ignored as long as the quorum is met by other
nodes; if every node is out of sync the aggregator fails closed
(QuorumNotReached). FutureData is a SuperchainDAError variant, so the soft check
precedes the SuperchainDAError mapping.

Classification order in from_json_rpc: no error response → Other (transport);
-320602 → FailsafeEnabled; (-321401|-320400) → DataUnavailable; SuperchainDAError
→ InvalidEntry; -32603 → Other; else → Rejected.

op-acceptance-tests: raise L1 base fee for EIP-7825 deposit-bypass test

The deposit check submits an L1 tx to OptimismPortal.depositTransaction,
which burns L1 gas inversely proportional to the L1 base fee. On an osaka
L1 the submission tx is itself capped at EIP-7825's MaxTxGas, so a low L1
base fee makes the burn exceed the cap and the deposit reverts (status=0),
which is what failed in CI.

The test tried to raise the base fee first, but it spammed L2 and waited
on the L2 base fee with an inverted predicate, so the wait returned
immediately and the L1 base fee stayed at its 1 gwei genesis value. Spam
L1 instead and wait until the L1 base fee is comfortably above the 1 gwei
deposit base fee before submitting.

Generalize loadtest.FundEOAs to accept either an L1 or L2 EL node so the
existing spam machinery can be reused on L1.

fix(rollup-boost): ship the real binary from the Docker build (#21233)

The rollup-boost Docker image was shipping a ~435KB cargo-chef stub
(an empty `fn main(){}`) instead of the real ~15.5MB binary, so the
container exited 0 immediately and devnets using it (e.g. anton-sdm)
lost their sequencer engine.

Root cause: `rust/rollup-boost/.dockerignore` excluded `**/Cargo.lock`,
so the lock never entered the build context. With `--locked` (enabled
in #21225), `cargo build` then fails ("cannot update the lock file ...
because --locked was passed") because there is no committed lock to
honor. The builder joined the build and the `cp` with `;` instead of
`&&`, so the failed build still copied cargo-chef's leftover dummy
binary out of `target/`, and the image build "succeeded" with a stub.
op-reth and op-rbuilder don't ignore Cargo.lock, so they were fine.

Fixes:
- Stop ignoring Cargo.lock so `--locked` has the committed lock.
- Use `&&` so a failed build fails the image instead of cp-ing a stale
  binary, and assert the built binary has a working CLI.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(op-e2e): bound fuzz RPC calls and stream parallel output (#21203)

FuzzFjordCostFunction made RPC/engine calls with unbounded contexts
(nil bind.CallOpts.Context defaults to context.Background, and
AddL2Block was passed context.Background). If any call wedges, the
test hangs until CircleCI's 15m no_output_timeout kills the whole
op-e2e-fuzz step with zero diagnostic output. Bound each call so a
stuck call fails fast with a clear error: setup calls share the
existing 60s ctx; the per-iteration GetL1Fee gets a fresh 30s
deadline since the fuzzing phase outlives the setup ctx.

Add --line-buffer to the parallel invocation so go test's periodic
"fuzz: elapsed:" progress lines stream to CI in real time instead of
being buffered (parallel's default --group) until each job completes.
This makes the no-output timeout reflect genuine progress gaps and
keeps the last progress line visible for diagnosing any future hang.

The precise trigger of the original intermittent hang is not
identified; this ensures the next occurrence is a bounded, diagnosable
failure rather than a silent 15m kill.

ci: share one Go module cache, downloaded once per pipeline (#21213)

* fix(ci): use shared go cache commands for acceptance tests

The op-acceptance-tests job hand-rolled its own go-mod cache that saved
and restored /go/pkg/mod, but the Go module cache on the CI image lives
at ~/go/pkg/mod. The saved archive was therefore empty (16 B), so every
run restored nothing and re-downloaded all modules from proxy.golang.org
with no retry — leaving the job exposed to transient proxy errors.

Switch to the shared go-restore-cache/go-save-cache commands, which cache
the correct paths (~/.cache/go-build and ~/go/pkg/mod) with proper key
fallbacks, matching every other Go job in the pipeline.

* ci: share one Go module cache, downloaded once per pipeline

Every Go job downloaded the module set independently, so each was its own
chance to hit a transient proxy.golang.org failure. There is a single Go
module in the repo, so that download is identical everywhere.

- Split the bundled go cache into a shared module cache (keyed on go.sum,
  paths ~/go/pkg/mod) and a per-namespace build cache (~/.cache/go-build).
  go-restore-cache/go-save-cache keep their interface, so existing callers
  are unchanged.
- Add a prep-go-modules job that downloads modules once and saves the shared
  cache; Go jobs require it (within main and develop-fault-proofs) so the
  cache is warm in-pipeline, and restore it read-only everywhere else.
- Replace the remaining hand-rolled Go caches (go-tests-v2, the save-only
  golang-build-cache in the contracts jobs) with the shared commands, and
  add caching to jobs that had none (go-lint, go-tests-with-fault-proof-deps,
  sanitize-op-program, cannon-stf-verify, analyze-op-program-client,
  check-nut-locks).
- Extract the cache helpers into helpers.yml so they are defined once and
  merged into every continuation config instead of duplicated.

Validated with circleci config validate against the merged config.

* ci: drop vestigial module/version params from go cache helpers

There is a single Go module in the repo, so the module cache is always the
root go.sum and the `module` parameter could only ever be `.`. The `version`
parameter just shadowed the global c-go-cache-version pipeline parameter that
no caller overrides. Drop both: key the shared module cache and per-namespace
build cache directly on go.sum and the inlined cache-buster, so every job
provably reuses the one module cache.

* ci: key Go build cache on branch+revision so it stays fresh

The build cache (~/.cache/go-build) tracks source, but it was keyed only on
go.sum. CircleCI cache keys are immutable, so the first commit for a given
go.sum froze the build cache and every later commit restored an increasingly
stale copy that save_cache could never refresh. Key it on branch+revision and
save fresh per commit, with restore falling back from this exact commit, to
the latest on the branch, to the latest overall for the namespace.

* ci: address caching review findings

- Gate the contracts-feature-tests workflow on prep-go-modules so its many
  concurrent go-ffi builds restore a warm shared module cache instead of each
  cold-downloading.
- Add Go caching to jobs that had none: cannon-go-lint-and-test,
  check-generated-mocks-op-node/-op-service, contracts-bedrock-coverage.
- Give golangci-lint and svm/solc caches a prefix fallback so a config change
  reuses the prior cache instead of a full cold start, and save the golangci
  cache with when: always so a failing lint run still warms it.
- Drop the now-redundant `go mod download` in op-acceptance-tests; the shared
  module cache already provides the modules.
- Remove a stale comment in rust-e2e.yml.

Out of scope (filed separately): the duplicate rust-build override
(ethereum-optimism/optimism#21219).

* ci: restore Go cache in contracts-bedrock-build

contracts-bedrock-build requires prep-go-modules but had no restore step, so
its `go run ... mktar` (in copy-contract-artifacts) still hit proxy.golang.org
— the requires added critical-path latency without the flake protection. Add
go-restore-cache/go-save-cache so the warmed shared module cache is used.
mktar is a root-module package (op-deployer has no own go.mod), so the cache
seeded by prep-go-modules covers its dependencies.

feat(op-reth): compute miner fee on pool tx in payload builder (#20382)

* feat(op-reth): compute miner fee on pool tx in payload builder

Move the `effective_tip_per_gas` call in
`OpPayloadBuilderCtx::execute_best_transactions` to before
`into_consensus()`, so the miner fee is computed from the pool
transaction rather than the consensus transaction.

Semantically identical for vanilla op-reth users: for stock EIP-1559 /
legacy / deposit txs, `effective_tip_per_gas` returns the same value
on the pool or consensus form. The pool is queried with `block.basefee`,
so any tx returned from `best_txs` satisfies `max_fee_per_gas >= base_fee`.
The existing `expect` invariant still holds (I made the message more
explicit).

This unblocks a cleanup in Celo's reth implementation. On Celo,
`max_fee_per_gas` on the consensus tx can be denominated in an ERC-20
fee currency instead of native wei (CIP-64). The pool validator converts
to native equivalents and exposes the correct tip via the pool tx's
`effective_tip_per_gas` impl, but op-reth currently discards that view
via `into_consensus()` before reading the tip. Without this change, the
Celo fork needs a `SignedTx` newtype that stashes native-equivalent fees
on the consensus tx solely to thread them through this one call site
(~600 lines in celo-kona's `signed_tx.rs`, deletable once this lands).

See https://github.com/celo-org/celo-kona/issues/152

Adds a regression test for the ordering of `effective_tip_per_gas()` and
`into_consensus()` in the payload builder loop. The test uses a pool-tx
wrapper whose `effective_tip_per_gas()` deliberately differs from its
inner consensus tx and asserts that `info.total_fees` uses the
wrapper-provided value. If a future change moves the read back behind
`into_consensus()`, the tip would come from the unwrapped consensus tx
and the test fails.

test(devstack): make Reached/AdvancedFn tolerate transient block-ref lookups (#21218)

ReachedFn and AdvancedFn wrap their reads in retry.Do0, but read via the
infallible BlockRefByLabel/HeadBlockRef getters, which call require.NoError.
require aborts the test goroutine (FailNow -> Goexit) on the first error instead
of returning it to the retry loop, so the retry can only ever handle "not reached
yet" -- never a lookup error. A transient "could not get payload: not found" that
the op-node engine returns for a label while it is mid-reset during a reorg then
hard-fails the test, even though the chain recovers a moment later.

Add an unexported fallible blockRefByLabel on L2ELNode (mirroring the existing
headBlockRef/HeadBlockRef pair on L2CLNode) and route ReachedFn/AdvancedFn through
it, returning lookup errors to the retry loop. AdvancedFn now captures its baseline
on the first successful read so a transient on the baseline is retried too. Switch
L2CLNode.AdvancedFn's baseline from the infallible HeadBlockRef to the fallible
headBlockRef with retry (its ReachedFn already tolerates). BlockRefByLabel stays as
a requiring wrapper for one-shot callers.

feat(proxyd): halt CL consensus on unresolvable output root split (#646)

* feat(proxyd): halt CL consensus on unresolvable output root split

Each consensus cycle the CL poller queries optimism_outputAtBlock at the
group's safe block on every candidate and compares roots. A backend whose
root disagrees with a strict majority is banned. If there is no majority -
a tie (1v1, 2-2) or an N-way split - the disagreement is unresolvable and
consensus HALTS instead of guessing:

  - the served block height and cached optimism_syncStatus body freeze at
    the last-agreed value, so clients keep seeing the previous response;
  - the served consensus group is emptied, so general RPCs fail closed
    (ErrNoBackends) rather than routing to a backend on an uncertain fork.

Backends are not persistently banned during a halt - they are still polled
and re-verified every cycle - so consensus auto-recovers as soon as a
majority returns. A halt signals a potential chain split / derivation
divergence and is surfaced via the consensus_cl_halted gauge (alert target)
and the consensus_cl_halt_total counter.

Any backend count is now permitted, including even/2-node cross-client
groups (e.g. op-node + kona-node): the odd-backend startup guard is removed
since ties now halt rather than needing a majority to resolve.

Tests: unit decision cases (1v1 / 3-way / 2-2-1 tie -> halt; 2v1 majority,
unanimous, all-errored -> no halt), an end-to-end freeze + auto-recover
test, and a CL integration test asserting the all-disagree group fails closed.

* test(proxyd): assert 2-1-1-1 plurality halts CL consensus

Document the reviewer's scenario from PR #646: a top root with a
plurality (2 votes) but no strict majority of 5 responders must halt
rather than advance. Passes against the current strict-majority logic;
guards against regressing to a plurality-wins policy.

* test(proxyd): cover 3-1-1 majority resolve and timeout-excluded responder count

- 3-1-1 (5 responders): strict majority resolves and bans BOTH minorities,

- partial timeouts: errored backends are excluded from the responder count,

`gameImpls[CANNON_KONA]` and `gameArgs[CANNON_KONA]` but left

    when the on-chain bond is non-zero (idempotent otherwise).

feat(op-chain-ops): add check-interop smoke-test CLI

A small CLI under op-chain-ops/cmd/check-interop for smoke-testing interop
cross-chain messaging against a running pair of L2 chains.

Subcommands:
- roundtrip: bridges ETH A->B and B->A via the SuperchainETHBridge predeploy,
  relaying each message itself through L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger.relayMessage,
  and asserts the recipient is credited the exact amount on each destination
  chain. No contract deploys — it uses the predeploys that already exist.
- failsafe: verifies the op-interop-filter failsafe lifecycle via the filter
  admin RPC — a bridge succeeds, its relay is rejected while failsafe is
  enabled, and succeeds again once disabled.

Flags can be supplied via CLI, CHECK_INTEROP_* env vars, or a TOML config file
(--config); CLI and env values override the file. Endpoints can be any reachable
RPC URL (e.g. a devnet's direct ingress), so no port-forward is required.

fix(op-acceptance-tests): fix flaky TestNotTruncateDatabaseOnRestartWithExistingDatabase

The test captured its no-truncation baseline from the live safe head
(`SafeL2BlockRef().Number`), which advances continuously and can be sampled
mid-L1-block. The safe head db only resolves at per-L1-block granularity, and
after the initial EL-sync reset its oldest retained entry is the *final* safe
head reached at that L1 origin. When the live sample lands strictly inside the
range of L2 blocks sharing the oldest retained L1 origin, the invariant
`db floor <= baseline` is unsatisfiable even though nothing is wrong:

    op-devstack/dsl/safedb.go:25
      Error: "8" is not less than or equal to "7"
      Messages: safe head db did not go back far enough

Capture the baseline from the db's own floor (oldest recorded safe head)
instead. The floor is aligned to per-L1-block granularity and only changes when
the db is reset/truncated, so re-checking it after restart remains a sound
no-truncation assertion while removing the race.

feat(sdm): enforce MAX_GAS_LIMIT on pre-refund EVM gas

SDM (post-exec) refunds let canonical, post-refund gas fall arbitrarily
below the real work performed, so the operational block-gas-limit rate
limit no longer bounds real compute once refunds appear. Cap the
pre-refund sum of evm_gas_used per block at MAX_GAS_LIMIT (500M, mirroring
SystemConfig.MAX_GAS_LIMIT) so a sequencer can never make a block prove
more computation than the system is designed to prove, even at 100%
refund.

Layer 1 (consensus, alloy-op-evm OpBlockExecutor): accumulate pre-refund
evm_gas_used and reject a tx whose declared gas limit would push the sum
past the ceiling, mirroring the existing block-gas-limit admission check.
This single change covers op-reth verifier replicas and the kona fault
proof, both of which verify through OpBlockExecutor.

Layer 2 (producers): op-rbuilder and the op-reth standard builder
self-limit before feeding txs to the executor, so honest blocks always
verify. The binding cumulative persists across flashblocks (each
flashblock gets a fresh executor whose internal accumulator resets).

re-added here with a real consumer. Producers read it through the new
PreRefundGasUsed trait since the generic BlockExecutor::Result associated
type is otherwise opaque.

Tracking: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/20709
