fix(derive): keep Karst upgrade gas on the activation block only

The one-time upgrade gas added to a NUT-bundle fork's activation block
(introduced with Karst) was sticking. SystemConfigByL2Hash /
to_system_config reconstruct the parent's system config gas limit from the
parent block header, which at the activation block already includes the
upgrade gas. The next block read that inflated limit back as its base, so the
elevated gas limit persisted on every block after the activation block.

By default the upgrade gas is subtracted again at the block right after the
activation block, reverting the gas limit. A new rollup-config bool
KeepKarstUpgradeGas / keep_karst_upgrade_gas (default false) lets chains that
already activated Karst with the leak baked into their history opt out: the
inflated limit is kept (so their history still validates) and the operator
clears it themselves with a setGasLimit whenever they choose.

The subtraction runs during system-config reconstruction (PayloadToSystemConfig
/ to_system_config), before the L1 receipts update in the caller, so a
setGasLimit in the same block's L1 origin takes precedence (the L1 update sets
the gas limit absolutely and overwrites the stripped value).

op-node: Config.StripsKarstUpgradeGas gates the subtraction; UpgradeGas helper.
kona: RollupConfig::strips_karst_upgrade_gas gates it in to_system_config (an
exact mirror), enabled by the preceding commit moving Predeploys out of
kona-protocol so it can depend on kona-hardforks for the upgrade gas value.

Also migrates the op-node derive test ptr helper to op-service/ptr.New (noted
in docs/ai/go-dev.md).

Tests: op-node + kona unit tests for both the default (strip) and opt-out
(keep) paths, and a post-activation gas-limit assertion in the kona action
test (TestActivationBlockNUTBundle, verified end-to-end under kona-host).
Documents how to run the Go + kona action tests in docs/ai/fault-proofs.md.

fix(alloy-op-evm): exclude a tx's own sender/to/created address from warming rebates

EIP-2929 pre-warms a transaction's own sender, call target, and (for CREATE)
the created-contract address: the tx is billed the warm access cost for them
and never the cold cost, so no cold->warm surcharge is ever paid and no SDM
warming rebate is owed. The inspector excluded the beneficiary, precompiles,
access list, and 7702 authorities from rebates but not the sender/to/created
address, and observed them with refunds enabled. A later tx whose sender or
`to` (or a CREATE whose created address) was warmed by an earlier tx in the
block therefore claimed a spurious 2500-gas warm-account rebate.

Fix: mark `caller` and the Call `target` intrinsically warm in
collect_intrinsic_warmth, and the top-level CREATE created address in the
`create` hook. They remain recorded in `warmed_accounts`, so a *different*
later tx that touches them via a normal opcode (genuinely cold for that tx)
still earns its legitimate rebate.

This is an over-refund / mis-metering fix, not a supply-inflation fix: the
refund<=evm_gas_used bound and settlement conservation already prevented an
ETH mint; this stops value leaking from the fee recipients to the sender for
surcharges never incurred.

Tests (executor-level, real EVM execution through ensure_top_level_initialized):
- test_intrinsic_warm_to_address_is_not_rebated
- test_intrinsic_warm_sender_is_not_rebated
- test_intrinsic_warm_created_address_is_not_rebated

fix(alloy-op-evm): stop rebating fee-vault settlement touches

The per-tx fee-vault settlement write in OpEvm::transact_raw notes the
L1/base-fee/operator-fee recipients via note_account_touch, which used
allow_refund=true. That is a protocol-level state write, not a user EIP-2929
opcode access — the tx is never charged a cold account-access for it, so no
cold->warm surcharge is paid and no warming rebate is owed. A second
non-deposit tx therefore wrongly claimed a 2500-gas WarmAccount rebate per
fee vault (settled as a debit to those same vaults — the fee-vault drain in
Immunefi report #81847's impact).

Fix: note_account_touch now observes with allow_refund=false. The account is
still recorded in warmed_accounts, so a *later* tx that genuinely accesses a
vault via an opcode (a real cold access) still earns its legitimate rebate;
only the settlement touch's own spurious claim is removed.

fix(proxyd): tighten interop access-list descriptor timestamp

proxyd validated interop executing-message txs with an ExecutingDescriptor
of {Timestamp: now+1000, Timeout: 0}. The inflated timestamp made the
filter's lower-bound invariant (init < inclusion) a near-no-op, accepting
references up to 1000s in the future, and the only expiry margin came from
that same inflated timestamp.

Pass Timestamp = now+30s (clock-skew tolerance) so it stays a tight
near-future lower bound while still admitting references to the chain's
current head, and Timeout = 7200 to match op-reth's
CHECK_ACCESS_LIST_TIMEOUT_SECS for the expiry-window margin.

fix(MultisigTask): don't bump the executor's nonce when broadcasting

The empty-signatures branch of executeTaskStep self-approves the safe tx
and increments each owner's nonce to mirror the approveHash side effect.
That is only correct during simulation. On a real `just execute` with the
default empty SIGNATURES, for a 1/1 safe whose sole owner is also the
executing sender, it bumps the sender's EOA nonce, so forge broadcasts the
execTransaction at nonce+1 — a gap that leaves the tx queued/pending forever
until the missing nonce is filled.

Guard the increment with !_isBroadcastContext(). Simulation is unchanged;
broadcast no longer desyncs the nonce. The execTransaction still succeeds
on-chain via the prevalidated signature (owner == msg.sender).

feat(op-reth): gate payload builder on interop failsafe

The payload builder never read the supervisor interop failsafe, so it kept
sealing interop txs into unsafe blocks during a failsafe window until async
pool eviction caught up, and it never excluded interop txs that bypassed the
filter (e.g. private or locally-submitted txs).

Thread a shared InteropFailsafe handle (Arc<AtomicBool>, mirroring
SdmPostExecOptIn) from the txpool interop filter client (writer) through node
setup into OpBuilderConfig (reader). When the failsafe is active, the build
loop now excludes every interop tx, detected intrinsically via its
CrossL2Inbox access list rather than the pool's interop-deadline marker, so
unfiltered interop txs are caught too.

test(op-reth): assert interop tx re-includes after failsafe clears

Thread one shared InteropFailsafe handle through three builds (off, on,
off) so the test proves the gate is re-evaluated per build and the
mark_invalid an excluded interop tx triggers does not persist once the
failsafe clears.
test(op-reth): assert interop tx re-includes after failsafe clears

fix(op-reth): revalidate non-propagatable interop txs (RETH-4)

The interop revalidation/eviction sweep iterated `pool.pooled_transactions()`,
which filters out `propagate=false` transactions. Non-propagatable interop txs
(`Private` origin, e.g. from `eth_sendRawTransactionConditional`) were therefore
never revalidated or evicted, yet the builder still selects them via
`best_transactions()` (no propagate filter) — a permanent eviction blind spot.

Scan `pool.all_transactions()` (pending/basefee/queued, no propagate filter) at
the three interop sites: the failsafe eviction in `maintain_transaction_pool_interop`,
the stale scan in `revalidate_stale_interop_txs`, and the eviction in `poll_failsafe`.

Adds a regression test that admits a `Private`-origin interop tx and asserts the
sweep evicts it on a definitive invalid verdict (fails on baseline).

fix(op-reth): evict all interop txs on reorg (RETH-5)

The interop txpool maintenance loop handled only `Commit` notifications and
silently dropped `Reorg`. A local-chain reorg can invalidate the initiating
message a pooled cross-chain executing tx depends on (and source-chain reorgs
are not observable here at all), leaving the dependent tx pooled and buildable.

Handle `Reorg` by evicting all interop txs from the pool. Extract the
scan-and-remove logic into `evict_all_interop_txs`, shared by the reorg arm,
the failsafe path, and `poll_failsafe`.

The OpPool reorg-window admission filter is kept: it suppresses re-admission of
interop txs via gossip or block reinjection while the chain settles.

fix(derive): keep Karst upgrade gas on the activation block only

The one-time upgrade gas added to a NUT-bundle fork's activation block
(introduced with Karst) was sticking. SystemConfigByL2Hash /
to_system_config reconstruct the parent's system config gas limit from the
parent block header, which at the activation block already includes the
upgrade gas. The next block read that inflated limit back as its base, so the
elevated gas limit persisted on every block after the activation block.

By default the upgrade gas is subtracted again at the block right after the
activation block, reverting the gas limit. A new rollup-config bool
KeepKarstUpgradeGas / keep_karst_upgrade_gas (default false) lets chains that
already activated Karst with the leak baked into their history opt out: the
inflated limit is kept (so their history still validates) and the operator
clears it themselves with a setGasLimit whenever they choose.

The subtraction runs during system-config reconstruction (PayloadToSystemConfig
/ to_system_config), before the L1 receipts update in the caller, so a
setGasLimit in the post-activation block's L1 origin takes precedence (the L1
update sets the gas limit absolutely and overwrites the stripped value).

op-node: Config.StripsKarstUpgradeGas gates the subtraction; UpgradeGas helper.
kona: RollupConfig::strips_karst_upgrade_gas gates it in to_system_config (an
exact mirror), enabled by the preceding commit moving Predeploys out of
kona-protocol so it can depend on kona-hardforks for the upgrade gas value.

Also migrates the op-node derive test ptr helper to op-service/ptr.New (noted
in docs/ai/go-dev.md).

Tests: op-node + kona unit tests for both the default (strip) and opt-out
(keep) paths, an op-node precedence test composing the real strip with a real
setGasLimit ConfigUpdate, and a post-activation gas-limit assertion in the kona
action test (TestActivationBlockNUTBundle, verified end-to-end under
kona-host). Documents how to run the Go + kona action tests in
docs/ai/fault-proofs.md.

fix(alloy-op-evm): roll back SDM block-warming for declined op-rbuilder candidates (#21359)

SDM block-warming refunds are recorded by an inspector during EVM execution —
before the commit decision — and are not journaled, so discarding a tx's changes
does not roll them back. The op-rbuilder payload builder selects txs via
execute_transaction_with_commit_condition and declines candidates
(CommitChanges::No) that exceed a builder gas/DA/address limit or are
reverted-and-excluded; those declined candidates still warmed the maps, so a
later committed tx could claim a block-warming refund attributed to a tx that
never entered the block. Commit-only paths (block import, debug_replaySDMBlock
derivation) never observe that warmth, so the producer's payload diverged from
derivation. With Osaka active (#21337) this surfaced as
TestFlashblocksSDMMaterializesPostExecBlock failing, so the test was skipped.

Fix: override execute_transaction_with_commit_condition on OpBlockExecutor to
snapshot the block-scoped warming state before execution and restore it whenever
the tx is not committed. The snapshot (a clone of the warming maps) is taken only
in Producing mode, so there is no clone cost when SDM is off or verifying.

- alloy-op-evm: the override plus a unit test for the declined-candidate rollback.
- op-rbuilder: comment at the decline site noting the rollback dependency.
- flashblocks_sdm_phantom_test.go: TestFlashblocksSDMPhantomWarmingDivergence
  drives a persistently-declined poisoner alongside committed victims and, per
  victim block, compares the producer-baked SDM payload against the commit-only
  derivation. FAILS pre-fix (divergent_blocks=6, refund 18400 vs 0), PASSES after.
- flashblocks_sdm_test.go: re-enable TestFlashblocksSDMMaterializesPostExecBlock
  (remove the t.Skip) and match the streamed flashblock to the sealed block by
  canonical hash instead of a "final flashblock" guess, fixing the 9-vs-15 flake.

Fixes: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/21354

ops: add keep_karst_upgrade_gas hardfork flag

Add a keep_karst_upgrade_gas boolean to the Hardforks config. When true, a
chain opts out of the Karst upgrade-gas fix, keeping the inflated gas limit
that Karst's activation block introduced because the chain already activated

future don't silently inherit it. Enabled on the chains that need it — OP,
Ink, Soneium, Mode, Metal, Zora, and Unichain — on both sepolia and mainnet.
CopyHardforks skips non-pointer fields so the bool doesn't break the
reflection-based time copy, and does not propagate the flag: each chain keeps
whatever it sets.

(kona) and Config.KeepKarstUpgradeGas (op-node).

fix(derive): keep upgrade gas on a NUT-bundle fork's activation block only

The one-time upgrade gas added to a NUT-bundle fork's activation block
(introduced with Karst) was sticking. SystemConfigByL2Hash /
to_system_config reconstruct the parent's system config gas limit from the
parent block header, which at the activation block already includes the
upgrade gas. The next block read that inflated limit back as its base, so the
elevated gas limit persisted on every block after the activation block.

By default the upgrade gas is subtracted again at the block right after the
activation block, reverting the gas limit. This applies to every NUT-bundle
fork from Karst onward (forks.From(forks.Karst) in Go, OpHardfork::Karst
.forks_from() in Rust), so future forks (Lagoon, ...) are covered
automatically — each strips its own fork's upgrade gas at its activation block.

A new rollup-config bool KeepKarstUpgradeGas / keep_karst_upgrade_gas (default
false) lets chains that already activated Karst with the leak baked into their
history opt out of the Karst subtraction only: the inflated limit is kept (so
their history still validates) and the operator clears it themselves with a
setGasLimit whenever they choose. Later forks have no opt-out.

The subtraction runs during system-config reconstruction (PayloadToSystemConfig
/ to_system_config), before the L1 receipts update in the caller, so a
setGasLimit in the post-activation block's L1 origin takes precedence (the L1
update sets the gas limit absolutely and overwrites the stripped value).

op-node: upgradeGasToStrip gates the subtraction in PayloadToSystemConfig.
kona: upgrade_gas_to_strip gates it in to_system_config (an exact mirror),
enabled by the preceding commit moving Predeploys out of kona-protocol so it
can depend on kona-hardforks for the upgrade gas value.

Also migrates the op-node derive test ptr helper to op-service/ptr.New (noted
in docs/ai/go-dev.md).

Tests: op-node + kona unit tests for the default (strip), opt-out (keep), and
generalized (Karst + Lagoon) paths, an op-node precedence test composing the
real strip with a real setGasLimit ConfigUpdate, and a post-activation
gas-limit assertion in the kona action test (TestActivationBlockNUTBundle,
verified end-to-end under kona-host). Documents how to run the Go + kona action
tests in docs/ai/fault-proofs.md.

fix(op-rbuilder): append trailing SDM PostExec tx in the standard builder

The standard builder threaded the post-exec mode into its ctx — so in
Produce mode the executor applied SDM refund settlement to state and
post-refund gas to receipts — but never materialized the trailing
PostExec (0x7D) tx carrying the refund entries. A verifier re-executes
the block with the mode derived from its transactions, finds no 0x7D,
runs with SDM disabled, and computes a different state root: every
block built by an opted-in standard-mode builder was consensus-invalid.

produce-side rules as op-reth's try_include_post_exec_tx and the
flashblocks builder's materialize_post_exec (shared via the new
context::build_current_post_exec_tx): empty entries produce no tx, the
sender is the zero address, and the tx is appended last. Derived
blocks (no_tx_pool) never append — they must reproduce exactly the
attribute transactions.

Interop (Lagoon) at genesis and pins the operator opt-in contract:
no PostExec tx without the opt-in, exactly one trailing anchored
PostExec tx with non-empty entries under a repeated-slot workload with
it, and none again after opting out. The driver round-trips every
payload through newPayload, so the missing-append bug fails it with a
state-root mismatch (verified against the unfixed builder). The test
framework now registers SdmAdminExt like the production launcher and

op-reth: generate superchain-configs.tar via build.rs, decommit it

Port op-reth's superchain-config archive generation from the bash
fetch_superchain_config.sh to a Rust build.rs that reads the superchain-registry
submodule with pinned, deterministic crates (toml/serde_json for TOML->JSON, zstd
to decode the dictionary-compressed genesis, miniz_oxide for zlib). The large
binary tar is now gitignored; only res/superchain-configs.tar.sha256 is committed.

build.rs semantics mirror kona's KONA_SYNC_SUPERCHAIN: env unset uses the
gitignored res/tar as-is, regenerating from the submodule only if it is absent;
OP_RETH_SYNC_SUPERCHAIN=1 (run by `just sync-superchain-rust`) always regenerates
the tar, its .sha256, and chain_specs.rs. The build.rs is git-free (finds the
submodule by relative path) so it works without a .git dir.

committed .sha256 + chain_specs.rs; the op-reth-building job templates init the
submodule so default builds can regenerate res/tar on demand.

feat(op-supernode): add HTTP-backed remote interop nodes

Introduce a "remote node": a participant in the interop set that the supernode
does not drive. Instead of running a consensus client, the supernode polls a
remote HTTP endpoint for that chain's FINALIZED initiating messages and seals
them into the chain's LogsDB, so driven chains can reference them as executing
messages, exactly as they reference messages from driven chains.

The wire protocol is the plugin boundary — point a remote node at any server,
in any language, that serves it:

  GET {url}/finalized?after={N}
  -> {"blockTime": <secs>, "block": <FinalizedBlock>|null}

- op-supernode/supernode/remote: the Adapter seam, the FinalizedBlock /
  InitiatingMessage wire types (normalized initiating messages), and HTTPAdapter,
  the production client.
- interop.remoteNode + Interop.AddRemoteNode: polls an adapter and seals finalized
  blocks into the per-chain LogsDB (mirrors processBlockLogs; finalized-only, no
  reorg handling). Ingesters launch in Start.
- verifyExecutingMessage resolves the initiating chain's block time from either a
  driven chain or a remote node.
- --interop.remote-nodes <chainID>=<url> configures remote nodes; the supernode
  builds an HTTPAdapter per entry. Only a real HTTP client ships in the binary.
- remote/remotetest: a deterministic HTTP server implementing the protocol, for
  tests (a real HTTPAdapter is pointed at an httptest.Server) — no mock in the binary.

Engine-level e2e (remote_engine_test.go): a driven chain emits a real CrossL2Inbox
executing-message log referencing a remote-node-served initiating message; the log is
sealed through the production processBlockLogs path (real decode) and validated by the
real verifyInteropMessages engine — accepted when valid, rejected when the reference is
tampered.

fix(op-reth): evict definitively-invalid interop txs on revalidation

The interop txpool revalidation sweep gated eviction on reth's
`is_bad_transaction()`, which is true only for `CrossChainTxPreInterop`
and false for `ValidationError(_)`. A definitive invalid verdict from the
interop filter (`InvalidEntry`/`Rejected`) therefore stayed buildable
until its ~2h cached deadline expired.

`is_bad_transaction()` answers reth's peer-penalization question, a
different concern from "is this tx now invalid and must be evicted". Add a
dedicated `InvalidCrossTx::is_now_invalid()` predicate and use it in the
revalidation sweep: evict on a decisive invalid verdict, retain on
transient/non-decisive outcomes (quorum miss, timeout, data-unavailable,
disagreement) so a flapping or unreachable interop filter cannot drain the
pool. Failsafe stays handled by the whole-pool eviction. reth's
peer-penalization predicate is left unchanged.
fix(op-reth): evict definitively-invalid interop txs on revalidation

fix(op-reth): revalidate non-propagatable interop txs (RETH-4)

The interop revalidation/eviction sweep iterated `pool.pooled_transactions()`,
which filters out `propagate=false` transactions. Non-propagatable interop txs
(`Private` origin, e.g. from `eth_sendRawTransactionConditional`) were therefore
never revalidated or evicted, yet the builder still selects them via
`best_transactions()` (no propagate filter) — a permanent eviction blind spot.

Scan `pool.all_transactions()` (pending/basefee/queued, no propagate filter) at
the three interop sites: the failsafe eviction in `maintain_transaction_pool_interop`,
the stale scan in `revalidate_stale_interop_txs`, and the eviction in `poll_failsafe`.

Adds a regression test that admits a `Private`-origin interop tx and asserts the
sweep evicts it on a definitive invalid verdict (fails on baseline).

fix(op-reth): evict all interop txs on reorg (RETH-5)

The interop txpool maintenance loop handled only `Commit` notifications and
silently dropped `Reorg`. A local-chain reorg can invalidate the initiating
message a pooled cross-chain executing tx depends on (and source-chain reorgs
are not observable here at all), leaving the dependent tx pooled and buildable.

Handle `Reorg` by evicting all interop txs from the pool. Extract the

fix(ci): stop fuzz jobs from oversubscribing the CPU

Each fuzz recipe runs N targets concurrently via `parallel`, and each
`go test -fuzz` defaults to GOMAXPROCS workers — N×N worker processes on
an N-core CI box. A starved worker can miss the `-fuzztime` deadline and
fail the target with a bare `context deadline exceeded` (not a real crash).

Pass `-parallel=1` so each target uses a single fuzz worker, leaving the
only parallelism across targets. Fixed in the shared `go_fuzz` helper
(op-node, op-batcher, op-chain-ops, op-service, op-challenger) and the two
bespoke recipes (cannon, op-e2e). Duration `-fuzztime` budgets are
unchanged, so CI wall-time is unaffected.

feat(op-alloy): cap PostExec gas_refund_entries length

Add MAX_GAS_REFUND_ENTRIES (8192) and reject any 0x7D PostExec payload
exceeding it in PostExecPayload::decode_checked — the single chokepoint
every decoder (Decodable2718 typed/fallback, Decodable, from_rlp_bytes)
routes through, so every node (op-reth verifier, kona, followers, p2p)
reaches the same verdict.

A valid block already bounds entries to <= the normal-tx count (each
entry must target a distinct, consumed, non-deposit/non-post-exec tx),
so this is defense-in-depth: it rejects a malformed oversized payload at
decode time, before a verifier executes the whole block only to fail the
unconsumed-entries check. The cap is unconditional (safe: 0x7D itself is
Lagoon-gated, so an over-cap payload can only exist post-activation and
no honest producer emits one). Bound the `arbitrary` impl with the same
cap so RLP-roundtrip property tests stay decodable.

fix(kona/protocol): bump brotli-decompressor to 5.0.1

Pulls in dropbox/rust-brotli-decompressor#44, which fixes a missing
`break` that let RFC 7932 §9.2 PADDING_2 errors (non-zero padding bits in
the final byte) be silently overwritten with SUCCESS — so corrupt brotli
streams decoded as `Ok`. Go (andybalholm/brotli, used by op-node) and the
C reference (libbrotlidec) both reject these, so 5.0.0 was a Go-vs-Rust
derivation divergence vector: op-node rejects the channel while kona
would have accepted it.

With 5.0.1 the decoder returns `ResultFailure` with zero bytes written,
which `decompress_brotli`'s existing `written == 0` arm already surfaces
as an error — no wrapper change needed. Adds a regression test using the
upstream PR's vectors; it fails on 5.0.0 (corrupt data accepted) and
passes on 5.0.1.

Closes #21181

fix(op-reth): evict definitively-invalid interop txs on revalidation

The interop txpool revalidation sweep gated eviction on reth's
`is_bad_transaction()`, which is true only for `CrossChainTxPreInterop`
and false for `ValidationError(_)`. A definitive invalid verdict from the
interop filter (`InvalidEntry`/`Rejected`) therefore stayed buildable
until its ~2h cached deadline expired.

`is_bad_transaction()` answers reth's peer-penalization question, a
different concern from "is this tx now invalid and must be evicted". Add a
dedicated `InvalidCrossTx::is_now_invalid()` predicate and use it in the
revalidation sweep: evict on a decisive invalid verdict, retain on
transient/non-decisive outcomes (quorum miss, timeout, data-unavailable,
disagreement) so a flapping or unreachable interop filter cannot drain the
pool. Failsafe stays handled by the whole-pool eviction. reth's
peer-penalization predicate is left unchanged.
fix(op-reth): evict definitively-invalid interop txs on revalidation

fix(op-reth): revalidate non-propagatable interop txs (RETH-4)

The interop revalidation/eviction sweep iterated `pool.pooled_transactions()`,
which filters out `propagate=false` transactions. Non-propagatable interop txs
(`Private` origin, e.g. from `eth_sendRawTransactionConditional`) were therefore
never revalidated or evicted, yet the builder still selects them via
`best_transactions()` (no propagate filter) — a permanent eviction blind spot.

Scan `pool.all_transactions()` (pending/basefee/queued, no propagate filter) at
the three interop sites: the failsafe eviction in `maintain_transaction_pool_interop`,
the stale scan in `revalidate_stale_interop_txs`, and the eviction in `poll_failsafe`.

Adds a regression test that admits a `Private`-origin interop tx and asserts the
sweep evicts it on a definitive invalid verdict (fails on baseline).

fix(op-reth): evict all interop txs on reorg (RETH-5)

The interop txpool maintenance loop handled only `Commit` notifications and
silently dropped `Reorg`. A local-chain reorg can invalidate the initiating
message a pooled cross-chain executing tx depends on (and source-chain reorgs
are not observable here at all), leaving the dependent tx pooled and buildable.

Handle `Reorg` by evicting all interop txs from the pool. Extract the
scan-and-remove logic into `evict_all_interop_txs`, shared by the reorg arm,
the failsafe path, and `poll_failsafe`.

The OpPool reorg-window admission filter is kept: it suppresses re-admission of
interop txs via gossip or block reinjection while the chain settles.

fix(derive): keep upgrade gas on a NUT-bundle fork's activation block only

Karst introduced "upgrade gas": extra gas added to a NUT-bundle fork's
activation block gas limit so the network-upgrade transactions fit. It is meant
to apply only to the activation block, but it stuck to every later block — the
SystemConfig gas limit is reconstructed from the parent header (op-node
PayloadToSystemConfig / kona to_system_config), so the inflated activation-block
limit was read back as the steady-state limit indefinitely. op-node and kona
shared the bug, so they agreed but were both wrong.

Subtract the upgrade gas again at the block right after the activation block,
for every NUT-bundle fork from Karst onward (forks.From(forks.Karst) in Go,
OpHardfork::Karst.forks_from() in Rust), so future forks are covered
automatically. A new rollup-config bool KeepKarstUpgradeGas /
keep_karst_upgrade_gas (default false) lets chains that already activated Karst
with the leak baked into their history opt out of the Karst subtraction only, so
their history still validates; the operator clears it later with setGasLimit.
The strip runs during system-config reconstruction, before
UpdateSystemConfigWithL1Receipts / update_with_receipts, so a setGasLimit in the
post-activation block's L1 origin still takes precedence.

Also syncs the superchain-registry submodule to the companion change
(ethereum-optimism/superchain-registry#1259), which enables
keep_karst_upgrade_gas per-chain for the affected sepolia and mainnet chains,
and regenerates the Go + Rust embeddings via `just sync-superchain`. Migrates the
op-node derive test `ptr` helper to the shared op-service/ptr.New.

* fix(kona/protocol): bump brotli-decompressor to 5.0.1

Pulls in dropbox/rust-brotli-decompressor#44, which fixes a missing
`break` that let RFC 7932 §9.2 PADDING_2 errors (non-zero padding bits in
the final byte) be silently overwritten with SUCCESS — so corrupt brotli
streams decoded as `Ok`. Go (andybalholm/brotli, used by op-node) and the
C reference (libbrotlidec) both reject these, so 5.0.0 was a Go-vs-Rust
derivation divergence vector: op-node rejects the channel while kona
would have accepted it.

With 5.0.1 the decoder returns `ResultFailure` with zero bytes written,
which `decompress_brotli`'s existing `written == 0` arm already surfaces
as an error — no wrapper change needed. Adds a regression test using the
upstream PR's vectors; it fails on 5.0.0 (corrupt data accepted) and
passes on 5.0.1.

Closes #21181

fix(ci): make op-reth-compact-codec resilient to a superchain-registry bump

The op-reth-compact-codec job builds op-reth on develop (to write compact
vectors) and then on the PR branch (to read them). `git checkout` switches the
tracked files between base and PR but leaves both the superchain-registry
submodule working tree and the gitignored res/superchain-configs.tar at the
other side's content. reth-optimism-chainspec's build.rs (superchain-configs is
a hard, unconditional dep of the op-reth bin) regenerates/validates that tar
against the committed .sha256, so on a PR that bumps the submodule it panics on
a base-vs-PR mismatch.

After each checkout, re-sync the submodule to the checked-out pin
(`just update-superchain-registry-submodule`) and drop the stale gitignored tar
so build.rs regenerates it from the now-current submodule.

op-conp2p: P2P gossip sidecar for the opql consensus nodes + delegated validator hook

Add op-conp2p, a thin P2P sidecar that reuses op-node's gossip stack to join the
OP network and receive unsafe ExecutionPayloadEnvelopes, delegating the per-block
signature verdict back to a consensus node (op-con-node / op-con-ex-node) over
JSON-RPC admin_verifyUnsafePayload. The node owns the signer truth and returns
accept/reject/ignore; the sidecar maps that onto the gossipsub validator result
(the relay decision) and holds no signer state.

op-node/p2p hook (minimal, upstreamable): add the optional
DelegatedBlockSignatureValidator interface; when the GossipRuntimeConfig passed
to the gossip layer implements it, verifyBlockSignature routes the signature
decision there instead of the built-in recover-and-compare. verifyBlockSignature
gains a ctx + blockVersion so the delegate can honor the validation timeout and
report the payload version. Built-in path and tests unchanged
(TestVerifyBlockSignature passes).

The sidecar sends a superset request serving both node kinds: executionPayload +
parentBeaconBlockRoot + signature + payloadHash (op-con-node JSON path) and
version + raw signature-prefixed payload bytes (op-con-ex-node op-alloy path). On
any transport/decode error it returns ValidationIgnore (never Reject) so honest
peers are not penalized.

derive: fix sticky upgrade gas for Karst (but keep it for select chains) (#21441)

* fix(derive): keep upgrade gas on a NUT-bundle fork's activation block only

Karst introduced "upgrade gas": extra gas added to a NUT-bundle fork's
activation block gas limit so the network-upgrade transactions fit. It is meant
to apply only to the activation block, but it stuck to every later block — the
SystemConfig gas limit is reconstructed from the parent header (op-node
PayloadToSystemConfig / kona to_system_config), so the inflated activation-block
limit was read back as the steady-state limit indefinitely. op-node and kona
shared the bug, so they agreed but were both wrong.

Subtract the upgrade gas again at the block right after the activation block,
for every NUT-bundle fork from Karst onward (forks.From(forks.Karst) in Go,
OpHardfork::Karst.forks_from() in Rust), so future forks are covered
automatically. A new rollup-config bool KeepKarstUpgradeGas /
keep_karst_upgrade_gas (default false) lets chains that already activated Karst
with the leak baked into their history opt out of the Karst subtraction only, so
their history still validates; the operator clears it later with setGasLimit.
The strip runs during system-config reconstruction, before
UpdateSystemConfigWithL1Receipts / update_with_receipts, so a setGasLimit in the
post-activation block's L1 origin still takes precedence.

Also syncs the superchain-registry submodule to the companion change
(ethereum-optimism/superchain-registry#1259), which enables
keep_karst_upgrade_gas per-chain for the affected sepolia and mainnet chains,
and regenerates the Go + Rust embeddings via `just sync-superchain`. Migrates the
op-node derive test `ptr` helper to the shared op-service/ptr.New.

fix(op-reth): evict definitively-invalid interop txs on revalidation (#21447)

* fix(op-reth): evict definitively-invalid interop txs on revalidation

The interop txpool revalidation sweep gated eviction on reth's
`is_bad_transaction()`, which is true only for `CrossChainTxPreInterop`
and false for `ValidationError(_)`. A definitive invalid verdict from the
interop filter (`InvalidEntry`/`Rejected`) therefore stayed buildable
until its ~2h cached deadline expired.

`is_bad_transaction()` answers reth's peer-penalization question, a
different concern from "is this tx now invalid and must be evicted". Add a
dedicated `InvalidCrossTx::is_now_invalid()` predicate and use it in the
revalidation sweep: evict on a decisive invalid verdict, retain on
transient/non-decisive outcomes (quorum miss, timeout, data-unavailable,
disagreement) so a flapping or unreachable interop filter cannot drain the
pool. Failsafe stays handled by the whole-pool eviction. reth's
peer-penalization predicate is left unchanged.

* fix(op-reth): revalidate non-propagatable interop txs (RETH-4)

The interop revalidation/eviction sweep iterated `pool.pooled_transactions()`,
which filters out `propagate=false` transactions. Non-propagatable interop txs
(`Private` origin, e.g. from `eth_sendRawTransactionConditional`) were therefore
never revalidated or evicted, yet the builder still selects them via
`best_transactions()` (no propagate filter) — a permanent eviction blind spot.

Scan `pool.all_transactions()` (pending/basefee/queued, no propagate filter) at
the three interop sites: the failsafe eviction in `maintain_transaction_pool_interop`,
the stale scan in `revalidate_stale_interop_txs`, and the eviction in `poll_failsafe`.

Adds a regression test that admits a `Private`-origin interop tx and asserts the
sweep evicts it on a definitive invalid verdict (fails on baseline).

* fix(op-reth): evict all interop txs on reorg (RETH-5)

The interop txpool maintenance loop handled only `Commit` notifications and
silently dropped `Reorg`. A local-chain reorg can invalidate the initiating
message a pooled cross-chain executing tx depends on (and source-chain reorgs
are not observable here at all), leaving the dependent tx pooled and buildable.

Handle `Reorg` by evicting all interop txs from the pool. Extract the
scan-and-remove logic into `evict_all_interop_txs`, shared by the reorg arm,
the failsafe path, and `poll_failsafe`.

The OpPool reorg-window admission filter is kept: it suppresses re-admission of
interop txs via gossip or block reinjection while the chain settles.

heads by ceil(offset / block_time) blocks (default 12h) so derivation

fix(op-reth/txpool): reserve L1-info deposit gas in tx-pool gas limit

Every OP block contains a system-injected L1-info deposit as its first
transaction, which always consumes some gas, so a non-deposit transaction can
never use the full block gas limit. op-geth accounts for this in tx-pool
admission via `EffectiveGasLimit` (`core/txpool/validation.go`), capping a tx at
`block_gas_limit - l1InfoGasOverhead`.

`OpTransactionValidator` only inherited the generic `EthTransactionValidator`
cap (the full `block_gas_limit`), so it admitted transactions in
`(block_gas_limit - overhead, block_gas_limit]` that can never be included; they
sit in the pool until they expire instead of being rejected at submission.

Reserve `L1_INFO_GAS_OVERHEAD` (70_000, matching op-geth) in
`validate_one_with_state` before delegating to the inner validator, rejecting
over-limit transactions with `ExceedsGasLimit`. Adds a `block_gas_limit()`
accessor on `OpTransactionValidator` and a regression test.

Closes #21546

Earlier the skip blamed an op-con-node L1-reorg re-derivation bug. Instrumenting
op-con-node's L1 source disproved that: it correctly follows the canonical L1
chain (contiguous tip advancement, fetched parent always matching tip, no

limitation — it cannot inject a *deep, winning* L1 reorg: ts.Next builds on the
canonical head, the safe block's L1 origin sits far below the L1 head (safe lags
L1 by ~the seq window during catch-up), so a short fork at that deep height loses
the fork choice to the longer canonical chain and op-con-node never sees a lasting
reorg. Re-enabling needs a harness that builds the fork longer than the pre-reorg
chain (e.g. repeated ts.New on the fork tip).

reverted.

fix(op-reth): set tx_gas_limit_cap for Osaka so eth_estimateGas works under Karst

EIP-7825 (Osaka) caps a single transaction's gas at 2^24, and the OP Stack
inherits this cap from Karst onward (KARST/INTEROP -> OSAKA eth base). The OP
EVM-env builder never populated `cfg_env.tx_gas_limit_cap`, so reth's
`estimate.rs` fell back to the block gas limit (e.g. 30-60M) as the trial upper
bound for `eth_estimateGas`. The Osaka EVM then rejected that trial with
"intrinsic gas too high", breaking any contract-call estimate that omitted an
explicit `gas <= 2^24`. This is the OP-side dual of reth PR #25612.

Set the cap in `evm_env_for_op` (the chokepoint for the block, next-block, and
payload env constructors), mirroring alloy-evm's `for_eth_block`. This is
forward-compatible: once reth is bumped past #25612 the field-set becomes
harmless belt-and-suspenders.

Add a chronology-driven unit guard in alloy-op-evm asserting the cap is set
exactly for Osaka+ forks, plus an op-reth integration test that drives a real
`eth_estimateGas` RPC end-to-end on a Karst-active chain.

superchain: load keep_karst_upgrade_gas from registry into op-node

op-node's superchain-registry decoder dropped keep_karst_upgrade_gas: the
Go HardforkConfig struct had no field for it (BurntSushi/toml silently
ignores unknown keys) and applyHardforks never copied it. So an op-node
started with --network=op-sepolia (or op-mainnet) loaded the flag as false
even though the registry sets keep_karst_upgrade_gas = true, and would
subtract the Karst upgrade gas at the post-activation block and diverge from
canonical history. Operators had to pass --override.keep-karst-upgrade-gas
by hand.

PR #21441 wired the flag into kona (its HardForkConfig reads it from the
embedded registry) and added the op-node rollup.Config field plus the CLI
override, but never extended the Go SCR-loading path. This closes that gap:

- Add KeepKarstUpgradeGas to superchain.HardforkConfig so the TOML key is
  decoded.
- Copy it in applyHardforks alongside the fork-time fields.

Tested first: asserting KeepKarstUpgradeGas == true for the SCR-loaded
sepolia and mainnet configs in TestGetRollupConfig fails on the baseline
(expected true, actual false) and passes after the fix. The reflection-based
TestApplyHardforks is updated to handle the new non-pointer bool field.

The `_calculateTokenAddress` helper predicted the child token address using
`type(OptimismMintableERC20).creationCode`. Because the test's compilation unit
imports dispute-restricted contracts, that embedded subobject is compiled under
the "dispute" optimizer profile (5000 runs), while L2 genesis etches the factory
predeploy from the default-profile artifact (999999 runs). The two creation codes
differ, so the predicted CREATE2 address no longer matched the address the factory
actually deploys, breaking the `vm.expectEmit` checks in the three
`*_validParams_succeeds` fuzz tests.

Use `DeployUtils.getCode("OptimismMintableERC20")`, which pins the default-profile
artifact (the same code genesis uses), matching the pattern already used in

fix(kona): graceful OOG on precompile gas overspend in fpvm provider

The fpvm precompile provider's hand-rolled `run` panicked via
`assert!(underflow, "Gas underflow is not possible")` if a precompile
reported `gas_used > gas_limit`. revm v40's `EthPrecompiles::run` (which
op-revm inherits by delegation) instead gracefully out-of-gases this case
(`spend_all` + `PrecompileOOG`).

The branch is unreachable for the registered precompile set — each checks
cost <= gas_limit before returning `Ok` — so there is no consensus impact.
But matching upstream keeps the FPVM and op-reth aligned by construction
rather than by audit, and removes a foot-gun where a future precompile
that omits the check would halt the fault-proof program instead of
deterministically OOG-ing.

test(contracts): fix OptimismMintableERC20Factory CREATE2 prediction across compiler profiles (#21592)

The `_calculateTokenAddress` helper predicted the child token address using
`type(OptimismMintableERC20).creationCode`. Because the test's compilation unit
imports dispute-restricted contracts, that embedded subobject is compiled under
the "dispute" optimizer profile (5000 runs), while L2 genesis etches the factory
predeploy from the default-profile artifact (999999 runs). The two creation codes
differ, so the predicted CREATE2 address no longer matched the address the factory
actually deploys, breaking the `vm.expectEmit` checks in the three
`*_validParams_succeeds` fuzz tests.

Use `DeployUtils.getCode("OptimismMintableERC20")`, which pins the default-profile
artifact (the same code genesis uses), matching the pattern already used in
OptimismMintableERC721Factory.t.sol.

fix(op-reth): set tx_gas_limit_cap for Osaka so eth_estimateGas works under Karst (#21574)

* fix(op-reth): set tx_gas_limit_cap for Osaka so eth_estimateGas works under Karst

EIP-7825 (Osaka) caps a single transaction's gas at 2^24, and the OP Stack
inherits this cap from Karst onward (KARST/INTEROP -> OSAKA eth base). The OP
EVM-env builder never populated `cfg_env.tx_gas_limit_cap`, so reth's
`estimate.rs` fell back to the block gas limit (e.g. 30-60M) as the trial upper
bound for `eth_estimateGas`. The Osaka EVM then rejected that trial with
"intrinsic gas too high", breaking any contract-call estimate that omitted an
explicit `gas <= 2^24`. This is the OP-side dual of reth PR #25612.

Set the cap in `evm_env_for_op` (the chokepoint for the block, next-block, and
payload env constructors), mirroring alloy-evm's `for_eth_block`. This is
forward-compatible: once reth is bumped past #25612 the field-set becomes
harmless belt-and-suspenders.

Add a chronology-driven unit guard in alloy-op-evm asserting the cap is set
exactly for Osaka+ forks, plus an op-reth integration test that drives a real
`eth_estimateGas` RPC end-to-end on a Karst-active chain.

fix(op-reth): install default rustls CryptoProvider for flashblocks TLS

rustls 0.23 no longer auto-selects a process-level CryptoProvider when
multiple provider features are present in the dependency graph, so op-reth
panics on startup when it opens the flashblocks wss connection:

    Could not automatically determine the process-level CryptoProvider
    from Rustls crate features.

This kills the flashblocks service, so pre-confirmation RPCs such as
eth_sendRawTransactionSync never receive flashblocks and time out (~30s)
even though the transaction is mined normally.

Install the aws-lc-rs default provider in main() before any TLS is used,
matching reth's default provider selection.

feat(op-reth/txpool): reserve the Isthmus operator fee in pool balance check

`OpTransactionValidator::apply_op_checks` reserved only the L1 data fee
(`l1_tx_data_fee`) when checking that a sender can afford a transaction, not the
Isthmus operator fee. On a post-Isthmus OP chain a sender covering
`L2 gas + value + L1 data fee` — but not the operator fee — was admitted to the
pool and then failed at execution. op-geth already charges the operator fee in
its txpool balance check (`NewOperatorCostFunc`/`NewTotalRollupCostFunc`,
`core/types/rollup_cost.go`), so op-reth was behind op-geth here.

Add `operator_fee_addition()` and fold it into `cost_addition`. It is guarded on
Isthmus activation (via the spec resolved from chain spec + timestamp) AND the
presence of both operator fee params — `L1BlockInfo::operator_fee_charge`
`.expect()`s the scalar and constant, so it would panic when they are unset —
so it returns zero (no panic) before Isthmus. Uses the tx gas limit (worst-case
spend), matching op-geth's `tx.Gas()`. Pool-admission only: no block-validation
/ state-root / execution change.

Sibling of the L1-info gas-limit reservation (#21546 / #21548).

proxyd: parallelize EL consensus-poller RPCs in UpdateBackend

UpdateBackend previously issued eth_syncing, eth_getBlockByNumber("latest"),
("safe"), and ("finalized") sequentially against the same backend, so one
poll cycle cost the sum of four round trips. On Worldchain prod this measured
at ~690ms/poll even with consensus_poller_interval set to 250ms, since the
call chain itself exceeded the configured interval and became the real
bottleneck (see INFRA-6716).

Fire the four RPCs concurrently instead; a cycle now costs roughly one round
trip. Error/zero-value precedence on failure is unchanged from the sequential
version (sync error > latest > safe > finalized), just evaluated after all
four results are in rather than short-circuiting between calls.

Also fixes MockBackend.wrappedHandler in the integration test harness, which
held its mutex across the full handler invocation and serialized concurrent
requests to the same mock backend — harmless for the old sequential poller,
but it caused the new concurrent calls to queue behind each other and time
out in tests that simulate a slow backend. The lock now only guards the
shared request log and handler reference, not handler execution, matching
how a real backend actually behaves under concurrent load.

feat(kona-protocol): construct L2BlockInfo from a sealed header and raw first tx

Add L2BlockInfo::from_header_and_first_tx, a constructor for callers
that hold a sealed header and the raw EIP-2718-encoded transactions of
a block rather than a fully decoded OpBlock. Compared to
from_block_and_genesis it:

- takes the block hash from the seal instead of recomputing it with
  hash_slow(); the caller must guarantee that the seal is the header's
  true hash (debug-asserted),
- decodes at most the first transaction -- the L1-info deposit -- and
  classifies it by its EIP-2718 type byte first, so a typed non-deposit
  first tx is reported as FirstTxNonDeposit without being decoded,
- uses strict decode_2718_exact, rejecting trailing bytes,
- skips the first transaction entirely at the genesis block, matching
  from_block_and_genesis, which never inspects transactions there.

The L1-origin and sequence-number extraction is shared with
from_block_and_genesis through a private from_block_info_and_first_tx
core, so the two constructors cannot drift apart.

perf(kona-driver): decode only the L1-info deposit when computing L2BlockInfo

After executing a payload, advance_to_target re-decoded every
transaction in the derived block -- bytes the executor had already
decoded and validated -- only to assemble a throwaway OpBlock from
which from_block_and_genesis read transactions[0] and re-hashed the
header.

Use L2BlockInfo::from_header_and_first_tx instead, feeding it the
executor's sealed header and attributes.transactions.first(). The O(n)
envelope decode, the OpBlock/BlockBody construction, and the redundant
header keccak all disappear from the per-block hot loop of the fault
proof program.

Document the (pre-existing) contract on Executor::execute_payload that
the returned header's seal must be its true hash: the driver now relies
on it for the derived L2BlockInfo as well as for the safe-head cursor.

As a side effect, chains whose extended transaction envelopes are not
OpTxEnvelope-decodable (e.g. Celo's CIP-64) can use kona-driver
unmodified, since only the first (deposit) transaction is decoded.

* ci: pin fork test block daily instead of weekly

The pinned block is the forked-state cache key, floored to the start of the period. fix(kona): graceful OOG on precompile gas overspend in fpvm provider (#21582)

The fpvm precompile provider's hand-rolled `run` panicked via
`assert!(underflow, "Gas underflow is not possible")` if a precompile
reported `gas_used > gas_limit`. revm v40's `EthPrecompiles::run` (which
op-revm inherits by delegation) instead gracefully out-of-gases this case
(`spend_all` + `PrecompileOOG`).

The branch is unreachable for the registered precompile set — each checks
cost <= gas_limit before returning `Ok` — so there is no consensus impact.
But matching upstream keeps the FPVM and op-reth aligned by construction
rather than by audit, and removes a foot-gun where a future precompile
that omits the check would halt the fault-proof program instead of
deterministically OOG-ing.

The spec states the top-most two bits of each field element must be 0 on

this for every field element except the first, which is special-cased for the

strictly bijective there; the encoder always writes them as 0.

refactor(kona-sp1): dedup advance_to_target onto kona-driver (#18494)

kona-sp1 carried a near-verbatim copy of kona_driver's advance_to_target
loop solely to emit SP1 cycle-tracker markers around the derivation and
execution phases. Copying consensus-critical derivation logic risks silent
drift from the canonical loop.

Replace the copy with the canonical kona_driver::Driver::advance_to_target
via an optional, prover-agnostic metric-collector interface:

- kona-driver: add DriverMetrics (phase_start/phase_end, default no-ops),
  DriverPhase, and NoopDriverMetrics. advance_to_target becomes a thin
  wrapper over a generic advance_to_target_with_metrics that reports each
  phase. The default path uses NoopDriverMetrics and compiles away, so the
  canonical derivation pays nothing and kona stays free of prover concepts.
- kona-sp1: delete the copied loop; add CycleTrackerDriverMetrics that emits
  the same cycle-tracker keys (payload-derivation, block-execution) the host
  reads, so the per-phase cost breakdown is preserved. The witness executor
  drives advance_to_target_with_metrics with that collector.

The GHSA-5jh4-3p33-85xc post-check and the outer block-execution-and-derivation
span are unchanged.

Verified: kona-driver + kona-sp1-client-utils build and clippy clean; unit
tests pass; guest ELF rebuilt for riscv64im-succinct-zkvm-elf; the

superchain: reject unknown keys when decoding registry configs

The BurntSushi/toml decoder silently drops keys the config structs don't model.
That is how keep_karst_upgrade_gas could be added to the registry yet never reach
op-node's rollup.Config until #21566 added the missing struct field by hand: the
value was read from the embedded TOML and thrown away with no error.

Add jsonutil.DecodeTOMLStrict, a shared strict TOML decode that rejects any source
key no struct field captures (an allowUnknown predicate lets callers tolerate
specific keys). Decode the embedded chain and superchain configs through it. Chain
configs allow nothing — ChainConfig models every field, which
TestAllEmbeddedConfigsDecodeStrictly enforces across all embedded chains — so a
registry bump that adds a field now fails to load until the struct is updated to
consume it. The superchain path allow-lists only the deliberately-unmodeled legacy
protocol_versions_addr.

Also extract the registry -> rollup.Config conversion into rollupConfigFromRegistry,
separate from the registry lookup, and add TestRollupConfigFromRegistry_AllFieldsSet:
it reflects over the converted Config and fails if any field is left zero, so a new
registry-derived field forgotten in the conversion is caught.

test(op-service/eth): relax FuzzDetectNonBijectivity for non-encoded blob[0] bits

The two high bits of blob[0] are not part of the encoding: FromData writes
them as 0 (x & 0b0011_1111) and ToData masks them off in reassembleBytes, so
flipping them decodes to identical data. FuzzDetectNonBijectivity's
sha256-derived flip could land there and fail require.NotEqual even though
nothing is wrong (flaky test #21539).

Relax the invariant to assert equality when the flip targets those two bits,
add a corpus seed that deterministically hits the case, and add
TestBlobNonEncodedHighBits asserting a no-op decode there. Test-only; no
production behavior change.

op-acceptance-tests: fix bug that incorrectly sets fork schedule

op-deployer merges user configs with defaults, potentially overwriting
the user's configs in some cases.

The intentbuilder.WithForkAtOffset would incorrectly *delete* a key in
its hardfork mapping when the caller wanted to deactivate a fork. When
merged with op-deployer's default config, the default would take
precedence because there is no explicit override.

The fix in the intentbuilder is twofold:

1. Explicitly set the deactivated hardfork to `nil` in the
   intentbuilder's mapping.
2. Set all subsequent forks to `nil` in the intentbuilder's mapping,
   so caller's don't need to remember to do that themselves.

The op-e2e/config/init.go file has a similar bug, except the json mangling
is done by hand rather than through the intenbuilder abstraction. This
commit fixes both cases and introduce a shared function
ForkOverridesAtGenesis to limit duplicated code.

This bug unfortunately was causing some acceptance tests to pass when
they should have failed. Fortunately, none of those failures look serious.
The other changes in this commit address those test failures.

The confusing op-deployer configuration handling is worth cleaning
up at some point, but would snowball this PR.

superchain: reject unknown keys when decoding registry configs (#21648)

* superchain: reject unknown keys when decoding registry configs

The BurntSushi/toml decoder silently drops keys the config structs don't model.
That is how keep_karst_upgrade_gas could be added to the registry yet never reach
op-node's rollup.Config until #21566 added the missing struct field by hand: the
value was read from the embedded TOML and thrown away with no error.

Add jsonutil.DecodeTOMLStrict, a shared strict TOML decode that rejects any source
key no struct field captures (an allowUnknown predicate lets callers tolerate
specific keys). Decode the embedded chain and superchain configs through it. Chain
configs allow nothing — ChainConfig models every field, which
TestAllEmbeddedConfigsDecodeStrictly enforces across all embedded chains — so a
registry bump that adds a field now fails to load until the struct is updated to
consume it. The superchain path allow-lists only the deliberately-unmodeled legacy
protocol_versions_addr.

Also extract the registry -> rollup.Config conversion into rollupConfigFromRegistry,
separate from the registry lookup, and add TestRollupConfigFromRegistry_AllFieldsSet:
it reflects over the converted Config and fails if any field is left zero, so a new
registry-derived field forgotten in the conversion is caught.

test(op-service/eth): relax FuzzDetectNonBijectivity for non-encoded blob[0] bits (#21647)

The two high bits of blob[0] are not part of the encoding: FromData writes
them as 0 (x & 0b0011_1111) and ToData masks them off in reassembleBytes, so
flipping them decodes to identical data. FuzzDetectNonBijectivity's
sha256-derived flip could land there and fail require.NotEqual even though
nothing is wrong (flaky test #21539).

Relax the invariant to assert equality when the flip targets those two bits,
add a corpus seed that deterministically hits the case, and add
TestBlobNonEncodedHighBits asserting a no-op decode there. Test-only; no
production behavior change.

so it falls back to the root .dockerignore. That file did not exclude .git,

the op-stack-go images pass git metadata via GIT_COMMIT/GIT_DATE build args (and
have their own allowlist ignore file), and the prestate build never COPYs it, so

The pool's transaction ordering (CoinbaseTipOrdering) and validator were
fixed at construction, so downstream builders had no way to substitute a
custom ordering or wrap the validator without reimplementing build_pool.

Add two defaulted, general-purpose seams to OpPoolBuilder: an ordering
generic (O = CoinbaseTipOrdering<T>) and a validator-wrapper generic
(W = IdentityValidatorWrapper) with with_ordering / with_validator_wrapper
methods. The defaults reproduce the standard pool exactly, so the default

validator-wrapper seams, organized under a custom_pool/ test module:

- ordering: a custom gas-descending ordering reorders block composition
  versus the default tip ordering, proving the ordering seam drives
  selection end-to-end.
- validator: a custom gas-limit-filtering wrapper rejects an oversized
  transaction at ingress so it never reaches a block, while the default
  wrapper admits it — proving the wrapper gates admission.

Each seam pairs a default-build test with a custom-build test through a

is a no-op, so the standard build path is unchanged.

kona-sp1 carried a near-verbatim copy of kona_driver's advance_to_target
loop solely to emit SP1 cycle-tracker markers around the derivation and
execution phases. Copying consensus-critical derivation logic risks silent
drift from the canonical loop.

via an optional, prover-agnostic metric-collector interface:

  canonical derivation pays nothing and kona stays free of prover concepts.

  the same cycle-tracker keys (payload-derivation, block-execution) the host
  reads, so the per-phase cost breakdown is preserved. The witness executor
  drives advance_to_target_with_metrics with that collector.

span are unchanged.

op-node: ignore stale sequencer action after Stop

A sequencer-action timer armed by the driver before Stop() can still fire
once after the sequencer is deactivated: Stop() clears nextActionOK so the
driver schedules no further actions, but it cannot retract a timer already
armed in the driver's select loop, and the loop only re-evaluates
planSequencerAction() on its next iteration.

When that stale action fires, onSequencerAction() built a new block on the
sequencer's cached latestHead and issued a forkchoice update reasserting it.
If an external actor (the op-test-sequencer, via op-node's own CommitBlock)
had just committed a conflicting block at that height, this silently reorged
the EL back onto the original chain — undoing a reorg that had already been
made canonical.

Guard onSequencerAction() on d.active, mirroring the intent of Stop() wiping
the in-flight building state, so a stopped sequencer performs no more work.

This is the shared root cause behind the stop-then-commit-conflicting-block
acceptance-test flakes, where each test has otherwise had to hand-roll a
SyncStatus quiescence wait.

Fixes #20198

op-node: ignore stale sequencer action after Stop (#21690)

A sequencer-action timer armed by the driver before Stop() can still fire
once after the sequencer is deactivated: Stop() clears nextActionOK so the
driver schedules no further actions, but it cannot retract a timer already
armed in the driver's select loop, and the loop only re-evaluates
planSequencerAction() on its next iteration.

When that stale action fires, onSequencerAction() built a new block on the
sequencer's cached latestHead and issued a forkchoice update reasserting it.
If an external actor (the op-test-sequencer, via op-node's own CommitBlock)
had just committed a conflicting block at that height, this silently reorged
the EL back onto the original chain — undoing a reorg that had already been
made canonical.

Guard onSequencerAction() on d.active, mirroring the intent of Stop() wiping
the in-flight building state, so a stopped sequencer performs no more work.

This is the shared root cause behind the stop-then-commit-conflicting-block
acceptance-test flakes, where each test has otherwise had to hand-roll a
SyncStatus quiescence wait.

Fixes #20198
Fixes #20943

The kona reproducible-prestate build (cannon-repro.dockerfile) uses the
monorepo root as its build context and has no dedicated Dockerfile.dockerignore,
so it falls back to the root .dockerignore. That file did not exclude .git,
meaning the ~2GB .git tree (with submodules) was scanned and transferred into
the build context on every prestate build even though no COPY references it.

the op-stack-go images pass git metadata via GIT_COMMIT/GIT_DATE build args (and
have their own allowlist ignore file), and the prestate build never COPYs it, so

fix(kona,security): reject truncated span-batch bitlist to match op-node

SpanBatchBits::decode previously silently zero-padded truncated input,
while op-node's decodeSpanBatchBits (rollup/derive/span_batch_util.go)
returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF for the same input via io.ReadFull.

This asymmetry caused Kona to derive a different L2 state than op-node
for the same L1 calldata: a truncated protected_bits field for a legacy
transaction flipped the EIP-155 protection flag from true to false in
Kona while op-node rejected the batch entirely. Under CANNON_KONA
respected fault-proof program (Karst upgrade, 2026-06-17), Kona-in-Cannon
is authoritative for dispute resolution, so the divergent state could
finalize on-chain.

Fix: add SpanBatchError::BitfieldTooShort and return it when b.len() <
buffer_len, matching op-node's rejection semantics.

Regression tests cover: empty input at bit_length=1, and 1-byte input
at bit_length=16.

fix(kona,security): bound gossipsub snappy pre-alloc by MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE

compute_message_id (registered as gossipsub message_id_fn) called
snap::raw::Decoder::decompress_vec on every inbound PUBLISH before any
signature or application-level validation. decompress_vec pre-allocates
a Vec<u8> whose size is read from the snappy frame header — an
attacker-controlled field bounded only by u32::MAX (~4 GiB).

A 7-byte snappy frame declaring u32::MAX decompressed length forces a
~4 GiB heap allocation. Amplification: 613,566,756x. On resource-limited
hosts the process aborts via handle_alloc_error; on Linux overcommit the
OOM killer fires. Attacker reconnects with fresh peer ID and re-publishes;
persistent restart-loop. Gossipsub mesh (mesh_D=8) fans out to every peer.

Op-node's parallel BuildMsgIdFn in op-node/p2p/gossip.go performs the
correct pre-check via snappy.DecodedLen(pmsg.Data) bounded to
maxGossipSize. This commit adds the same guard to Kona.

Regression test covers the exact 7-byte bomb payload and asserts that
compute_message_id returns the invalid-snappy hash branch without
allocating.

feat(kona-protocol): construct L2BlockInfo from a sealed header and raw first tx

Add L2BlockInfo::from_header_and_first_tx, a constructor for callers
that hold a sealed header and the raw EIP-2718-encoded transactions of
a block rather than a fully decoded OpBlock. Compared to
from_block_and_genesis it:

- takes the block hash from the seal instead of recomputing it with
  hash_slow(); the caller must guarantee that the seal is the header's
  true hash (debug-asserted),
- decodes at most the first transaction -- the L1-info deposit -- and
  classifies it by its EIP-2718 type byte first, so a typed non-deposit
  first tx is reported as FirstTxNonDeposit without being decoded,
- uses strict decode_2718_exact, rejecting trailing bytes,
- skips the first transaction entirely at the genesis block, matching
  from_block_and_genesis, which never inspects transactions there.

The L1-origin and sequence-number extraction is shared with
from_block_and_genesis through a private from_block_info_and_first_tx
core, so the two constructors cannot drift apart.

proof program.

the returned header's seal must be its true hash: the driver now relies
on it for the derived L2BlockInfo as well as for the safe-head cursor.

As a side effect, chains whose extended transaction envelopes are not
OpTxEnvelope-decodable (e.g. Celo's CIP-64) can use kona-driver
unmodified, since only the first (deposit) transaction is decoded.

ops/docker: pre-install solc versions serially before forge build

The op-deployer-contracts stage runs forge build with a cold /root/.svm
cache, so forge's parallel compile jobs lazily install the required solc
versions concurrently. svm-rs's install path is not fully atomic under
concurrency, which intermittently fails the docker build with:

(open upstream issue: foundry-rs/foundry#4736)

mise) and pre-install each required solc version one at a time before
invoking forge, so forge never triggers a lazy concurrent install. The
version list matches the install-solc-compilers command in CircleCI.

refactor(kona): dedup derivation prologue into kona-proof (#21658)

The sync-start prologue (resolve safe head, reject a claim behind it,
short-circuit a zero-step trace extension, build the pipeline cursor) was
duplicated between the native fault-proof program (bin/client single.rs) and
kona-sp1 (get_inputs_for_pipeline). This is consensus-critical validation, so
a fix applied to one path could silently miss the other, the same drift risk
#18494 fixed for the derivation loop.

Extract it into kona_proof::sync::prepare_derivation, the single source of
truth for the claim-validation and trace-extension logic:

- Returns DerivationInputs (TraceExtension | Derive{cursor,l1,l2}) so the
  callers stay agnostic to how derivation proceeds.
- Returns SyncStartError, which each caller maps onto its own error type:
  single.rs matches the claim-validation variants to its existing InvalidClaim
  (preserving its structured error logs) and lets Oracle errors flow through
  its From impl; get_inputs_for_pipeline maps via `?` onto anyhow.
- The "Trace extension detected" info log now lives once in the helper.

Behavior is preserved: the validation order and the zero-step
agreed==claimed check are identical to both originals. One minor diagnostic
change: single.rs's "Failed to create pipeline cursor" wrapper log is dropped
(the cursor error still surfaces as OracleProviderError); the shared helper
cannot distinguish which oracle op failed.

prepare_derivation branch tests and the existing sp1 get_inputs tests); guest

op-deployer: estimate broadcast gas against the target chain

op-deployer sizes each broadcast transaction's gas limit from the gas used
by its in-process script simulator, which runs a fixed Cancun-era gas
schedule (op-chain-ops/script). On a post-Glamsterdam L1, EIP-8037 raises
the contract code-deposit cost from 200 to 1530 gas/byte (~8x), so the
simulated estimate is far too low and any transaction that deploys contract
code fails with "contract creation code storage out of gas".

This affects every deploy flow: bootstrap superchain/implementations
(direct CREATE/CREATE2) and apply / manage migrate (a CALL to OPCM that
CREATEs the chain's contracts internally).

Size each broadcast's gas limit as max(live eth_estimateGas, simulated),
clamped to the block gas limit, for all broadcast types, falling back to
the simulated estimate on estimation error. The live estimate reflects the
chain's actual gas rules; keeping the simulated value as a floor means a
broadcast that depends on an earlier, not-yet-mined bundle tx (whose live
estimate may fail or read low) is never worse than before. The estimation
CallMsg leaves Gas unset so the node bounds its search by the block gas
limit rather than the 2^24 per-tx cap, which large post-Amsterdam deploys
exceed.

op-devstack: pin L1 geth subprocess gas limit to genesis

The fake-PoS L1 builder bumps a reorg block's gas limit by +100 to force a distinct block hash (op-test-sequencer builders/fakepos/job.go). The previously-default in-process L1 geth ran with Miner.GasCeil=0, so its gas limit stepped down each block and that +100 stayed within the +/-parentGasLimit/1024 adjustment bound. The geth subprocess (now the default) uses geth's default 60M ceiling, so the gas limit steps up by ~delta each block; the extra +100 then exceeds the bound and geth rejects the reorg block as a bad block, killing the L1 node.

Pin --miner.gaslimit to the genesis gas limit so the L1 gas limit stays constant, keeping the reorg +100 well within bounds. Fixes the elsync/reorg (TestUnsafeGapFillAfterSafeReorg, TestUnsafeGapFillAfterUnsafeReorg_RestartCLP2P) and follow_l2 (TestFollowL2_ReorgRecovery) acceptance tests under the subprocess L1 EL.

op-devstack: cap L1 geth subprocess cache to avoid CI OOM

Making the geth subprocess the default L1 EL surfaced OOM kills in the memory-all-* acceptance lanes: a lane's container was SIGTERM'd mid-run ("Recipe acceptance-test was terminated by signal 15", "Build was canceled") with every executed test passing and no artifacts uploaded.

Root cause: the subprocess geth ran with geth's default cache (ethconfig defaults to a 2 GiB database cache alone), while the removed in-process node left the cache fields unset (near-zero). Acceptance tests run up to ~12 devstacks concurrently per CI container (2xlarge+, 40 GB RAM), each now with its own L1 geth subprocess, so ~24 GB of L1 cache alone pushed peak memory past the container limit and the job was OOM-killed. It is probabilistic across the parallel-split containers, so one lane died while its sibling (running the same code) passed.

Pass --cache 128 to the L1 geth subprocess. The fake L1 is a few dozen blocks and needs almost no cache; this restores the in-process memory footprint.

feat(op-supernode): generate cross-chain executing messages

Every block plants a plain init log at log index 0 that other chains can
reference as an initiating message. After all chains are built, the
manager wires one executing message into each verifiable block on every
chain, referencing the init log of a strictly earlier block on another
chain; Origin and PayloadHash are derived from the actual log via the
same LogToMessagePayload/Keccak path the seal-side LogToLogHash uses, so
the logsDB Contains lookup matches by construction.

verification, so they are never sealed and a reference to them could
never resolve. Strictly-earlier timestamps keep this first cut off the
same-timestamp frontier and cycle-detection paths. With a single chain no
edges are planted.

fix(op-revm): discard journal after non-deposit tx errors

OpHandler::catch_error only reset the journal on the deposit error path, so a
non-deposit tx that failed validation left its sender EIP-2929-warm in the
shared journal. On the SDM Produce block-building path a later committed tx
could then be billed a warm access attributed to a tx that never entered the
block, diverging from a validator that never executed the failed tx — a
builder-vs-validator gas mismatch that rejects the block.

Add the missing else branch calling journal.discard_tx() on non-deposit
errors, matching upstream revm's EthHandler::catch_error and mirroring Base's
base/base#3806.

Add regression coverage in the alloy-op-evm block-executor tests (ported from
optimism-private#567): a builder-vs-validator divergence test for both the
NonceTooLow and EIP-3607 skipped-tx triggers, plus a guard that the
SDM-disabled path is unaffected.

test(op-rbuilder): warm-leak regression for skipped failed candidate

Pin the SDM warm-set leak at the layer that ships in the sequencer. In
PostExecMode::Produce, op-rbuilder's execute_best_transactions loop attempts a
candidate, sees it rejected, and skips it (continue) while building the rest
of the block on the same EVM. Before the op-revm catch_error fix, the skipped
tx left its sender EIP-2929-warm, so a later included tx was billed a warm
access for a tx that never entered the block — diverging from a validator that
never ran the skipped tx.

Two variants cover the validation errors that reproduce it, mirroring the
alloy-op-evm suite: NonceTooLow and EIP-3607 (contract sender). Each injects
[A (fails, skipped), B] via PayloadTransactionsFixed (the tx pool would
pre-filter the invalid A), where B does a BALANCE on A's sender, and asserts
the block's pre-refund EVM gas is identical with and without the skipped A.
Both verified red (2500-gas divergence) against an op-revm that does not
discard the journal on non-deposit errors, green once it does.

fix(op-reth): reserve Isthmus operator fee in tx-pool balance check

The tx-pool validator's OP balance check (apply_op_checks) reserved only
the L1 data fee on top of the intrinsic tx cost. Post-Isthmus, execution
also charges the operator fee up front based on the tx gas limit
(L1BlockInfo::tx_cost), so a sender whose balance covers gas + value +
L1 data fee but not the operator fee was admitted to the pool and
propagated, yet could never be included in a block.

Reserve the operator fee at pool admission when Isthmus is active and
the operator fee params have been tracked, deriving the spec from the
block timestamp so the Jovian formula change is picked up automatically.
The params-present guard is required because operator_fee_charge panics
on unset params, which is the state before the first post-Isthmus
L1-info block is tracked.

This matches op-geth's pool admission behavior (NewOperatorCostFunc /
TotalTxCost in core/txpool/validation.go). Gas limit is used as the
worst-case charge, same as op-geth's tx.Gas() and execution's upfront
deduction. Pool-admission only; no block-validation or execution change.

The sibling admission gap (missing EffectiveGasLimit / l1InfoGasOverhead
reservation) is tracked separately in #21546 and intentionally not
bundled here.

fix(devstack): funder sends each tx once (no resubmitter) to avoid over-funding

FunderEOA funded through txinclude's Persistent includer wrapped in a full
reliable EL (Monitor + Resubmitter). After a funding tx was mined, the
Resubmitter's next resubmit returned "nonce too low", which Persistent treats as
"advance the nonce and re-send" — re-sending the value transfer and over-funding
the recipient (observed: a single 0.1 ETH Fund delivering 2.7 ETH across 27 txs).
The exact-equality WaitForBalance then never matched and timed out. It was
timing-dependent (worse on slower L1 blocks vs the 1s poll cadence), which is why
it surfaced in the interop fault-proof tests on L1 but not in faster L2 funds.

Build the funder's includer with a Monitor (reliable receipt polling, including
the op-reth "indexing is in progress" retry) but a plain sender and no
resubmitter, mirroring loadtest's invalid-msg spammer. Each funding tx is sent
exactly once, so funding amounts are exact while concurrent funding stays
nonce-safe via the includer's nonce manager.

feat: document and enforce config field lifecycle (immutable/append-only/mutable)

Chain config TOMLs mix values that are fixed at genesis and can never change
(e.g. chain_id, block_time, the genesis block) with values that evolve over
time (hardfork activations, role rotations, contract upgrades). Nothing told a
reader — or CI — which is which.

This change makes the distinction explicit and enforced:

- Each Chain field carries a `lifecycle` struct tag (immutable / append-only /
  mutable) with a doc comment explaining the contract and how to classify new
  fields. This is the source of truth.
- superchain/configs/README.md gains a "Field lifecycle" table documenting the
  contract for humans.
- config.CheckImmutableFields compares an old and new config, driven by the
  tags: immutable fields must be unchanged; hardfork activations are
  append-only with a time rule — a not-yet-active activation may be added or
  re-scheduled, but one already in the past is frozen (it is on-chain history).
- TestImmutableFieldsUnchanged (ops/internal/manage) enforces this in CI by
  diffing every changed superchain/configs/*.toml against the merge-base,
  mirroring the existing codegen check.

op-node: move follow-source requests off the driver event loop

followUpstream currently performs its upstream status request and up to
four sequential L1 lookups directly in the driver's main select loop.
Slow or unresponsive RPCs therefore prevent the loop from servicing
sequencer actions and can delay block production - see the regression
test added in the previous commit.

Run the existing follow-source request sequence in a background
goroutine, keeping at most one fetch in flight (ticks arriving while a
fetch is active are coalesced), and deliver validated status snapshots
back to the driver loop, which applies all side effects (L1 status
event, success metric, engine FollowSource reconciliation) in the
original order. The request order, validation checks, failure metrics,
and RPC client timeouts are unchanged; no caching or request
deduplication is introduced.

The split contract: followUpstream returns nil on any failure and
performs no side effects; a non-nil status has passed every check.
startFollowUpstreamFetch always delivers exactly one result (nil on
failure), which the event loop relies on to clear its single-flight
flag - unit tests pin both the async delivery and this liveness
contract.

Also remove Driver.syncConfig, which became a write-only field once the
FollowSourceEnabled guard moved to eventLoop (the ticker channel is nil
unless follow-source is enabled, so followUpstream is unreachable
otherwise).

fix(kona,security): reject truncated span-batch bitlist to match op-node

SpanBatchBits::decode previously silently zero-padded truncated input,
while op-node's decodeSpanBatchBits (rollup/derive/span_batch_util.go)
returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF for the same input via io.ReadFull.

This asymmetry caused Kona to derive a different L2 state than op-node
for the same L1 calldata: a truncated protected_bits field for a legacy
transaction flipped the EIP-155 protection flag from true to false in
Kona while op-node rejected the batch entirely. Under CANNON_KONA
respected fault-proof program (Karst upgrade, 2026-06-17), Kona-in-Cannon
is authoritative for dispute resolution, so the divergent state could
finalize on-chain.

Fix: add SpanBatchError::BitfieldTooShort and return it when b.len() <
buffer_len, matching op-node's rejection semantics.

Regression tests cover: empty input at bit_length=1, and 1-byte input
at bit_length=16.
