fix(kona,security): bound gossipsub snappy pre-alloc by MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE

compute_message_id (registered as gossipsub message_id_fn) called
snap::raw::Decoder::decompress_vec on every inbound PUBLISH before any
signature or application-level validation. decompress_vec pre-allocates
a Vec<u8> whose size is read from the snappy frame header — an
attacker-controlled field bounded only by u32::MAX (~4 GiB).

A 7-byte snappy frame declaring u32::MAX decompressed length forces a
~4 GiB heap allocation. Amplification: 613,566,756x. On resource-limited
hosts the process aborts via handle_alloc_error; on Linux overcommit the
OOM killer fires. Attacker reconnects with fresh peer ID and re-publishes;
persistent restart-loop. Gossipsub mesh (mesh_D=8) fans out to every peer.

Op-node's parallel BuildMsgIdFn in op-node/p2p/gossip.go performs the
correct pre-check via snappy.DecodedLen(pmsg.Data) bounded to
maxGossipSize. This commit adds the same guard to Kona.

Regression test covers the exact 7-byte bomb payload and asserts that
compute_message_id returns the invalid-snappy hash branch without
allocating.

fix(kona,security): bound gossip payload decode path against snappy bomb

The B2 fix bounded snappy pre-allocation only in `compute_message_id`
(the gossipsub `message_id_fn`). But that function only computes an id;
every inbound gossip message is then decoded via
`OpNetworkPayloadEnvelope::decode_v*`, which calls `decompress_vec` with
no bound. The identical tiny snappy frame declaring a huge decompressed
length still OOM-kills the node at that second, unbounded site.

Extract `snappy_decompressed_len_within_bound` and apply it in the block
handler before `decode_v*`, mirroring op-node, which bounds
`DecodedLen <= maxGossipSize` in both its `message_id_fn` and its gossip
topic validator.

Make the regression tests sound. The previous bomb test passed even
against unbounded code (`vec![0; u32::MAX]` is a lazily-committed calloc
under overcommit, so it never faulted 4 GiB). Add a test that a frame
which *validly* decompresses to more than `MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE` takes the
invalid-snappy domain — this fails against an unbounded implementation —
plus direct tests of the guard predicate.

spike: Rust fork-mode core (ForkUnderlay + AlloyDB base state + diff write-log)

Fork DB core for the op-script-engine, the analog of op-chain-ops/script/forking:

- ForkUnderlay: a fixed-typed swappable underlay { Empty(EmptyDB), Fork(AlloyDB) }
  beneath the CacheDB overlay, so a fork installs at runtime without dropping the cache
  (the analog of Go ForkableState.SubstituteBaseState). Empty preserves today's
  CacheDB<EmptyDB> semantics exactly.
- script_createSelectFork(url, block?): the engine dials the L1 archive directly (Option
  A, unidirectional), pins state by BLOCK HASH (reorg-safe, matching Go RPCSource), swaps
  the underlay, and pre-inserts the persistent/excluded set (deployer/console/script
  infra) into the local overlay so cold reads never hit the fork. Block env stays
  spawn-time (Go swaps state only). One fork per process, before any run; a second install
  or an install after execution errors loudly. stateDump-while-forked errors.
- ForkDiff: an ExportDiff-shaped write-log folded from each execution's finalized touched
  set (NOT scraped from CacheDB). A touched account is kept only when it actually changed
  (created/selfdestructed, changed storage slot, or nonce/balance/codeHash != the
  pre-commit fork-loaded base) — revm's "touched" is broader than geth's "dirty" (fires on
  reads, 0-reward coinbase), so the base comparison matches geth's dirty semantics.
  Serialized in the exact forking.ExportDiff JSON shape (uint256 balance as a DECIMAL
  string, code map base64) for the Round-2 A/B gate.
- Async->sync bridge: WrapDatabaseAsync::with_handle on the engine's multi-thread tokio
  runtime handle, threaded through HostConfig; cold DB misses block_on the alloy HTTP
  future from the non-tokio worker thread.
- The *Fork Solidity cheat family stays a loud-revert (unused by the forked op-deployer
  paths). Go client gains CreateSelectFork/ForkDiff.

reliable EL (Monitor + Resubmitter). After a funding tx was mined, the

the recipient (observed: a single 0.1 ETH Fund delivering 2.7 ETH across 27 txs).

resubmitter, mirroring loadtest's invalid-msg spammer. Each funding tx is sent
exactly once, so funding amounts are exact while concurrent funding stays

fix(txinclude): don't resend an already-mined tx on ErrNonceTooLow

Persistent treated ErrNonceTooLow from the (re)submit path as "advance the nonce
and retry". But once our own tx is mined, a resubmit of the identical tx returns
ErrNonceTooLow (the account nonce has advanced past it) — so this blindly
resubmitted an already-included tx at the next nonce, duplicating it. For value
transfers that means over-sending (a single Fund delivered many multiples), and
it raced the receipt monitor so it was timing-dependent.

On ErrNonceTooLow, look up our own tx's receipt (bounded by
WithIncludedLookupTimeout, default 12s) to disambiguate:
  - receipt found  -> our tx was mined; return it as included (no resend).
  - not found      -> the nonce was consumed by a gap/other sender; advance.
The bound only needs to cover receipt-indexing lag (ErrNonceTooLow guarantees the
consuming block is committed) and is paid only on genuine gaps, which don't occur
when the includer is the account's sole sender.

Adds TestPersistentDoesNotResendMinedTx; TestPersistentFixesNonceTooLow keeps
covering the genuine-gap advance path (with a short lookup timeout).

op-acceptance-tests: make intentbuilder deactivate forks correctly

op-deployer merges user configs with defaults, potentially overwriting
the user's configs in some cases.

The intentbuilder.WithForkAtOffset would incorrectly *delete* a key in
its hardfork mapping when the caller wanted to deactivate a fork. When
merged with op-deployer's default config, the default would take
precedence because there is no explicit override.

The fix in the intentbuilder is twofold:

1. Explicitly set the deactivated hardfork to `nil` in the
   intentbuilder's mapping.
2. Set all subsequent forks to `nil` in the intentbuilder's mapping,
   so caller's don't need to remember to do that themselves.

This bug unfortunately was causing some acceptance tests to pass when
they should have failed. Fortunately, none of those failures look serious.
The changes to singlechain_runtime.go--together with new helpers in
forks.go and rollup/types.go--resolve those test failures.

feat(kona/node): implement syncmode.offset-el-safe for op-node parity

After execution-layer sync completes, retract the safe and finalized L2
heads by ceil(offset / block_time) blocks (default 12h) so derivation
re-derives the most recent window before it is considered safe, rather
than trusting the optimistically-synced tip. Ports op-node #21033.

- Add `duration_to_blocks` / `offset_block_num` helpers (ceil division,
  genesis clamp), mirroring op-node's DurationToBlocks / OffsetBlockNum.
- Add `L2ForkchoiceState::for_el_sync`: unsafe stays at the tip, safe and
  finalized retract to the offset head but are never moved below the EL's
  currently-reported safe/finalized heads. On the initial sync those are
  genesis (kona advances them only via derivation, never during EL sync),
  so the offset applies in full; on a later restart the EL already holds
  the committed heads, so nothing is re-derived.
- Thread `offset_el_safe: Option<Duration>` through `Engine::reset`,
  applied only on the post-EL-sync reset; all other resets keep the
  standard sync-start search.
- Add the `--syncmode.offset-el-safe` CLI flag (env
  KONA_NODE_SYNCMODE_OFFSET_EL_SAFE, default 12h) wired through
  EngineConfig and the engine actor.

Closes #21243

refactor(kona): dedup derivation prologue into kona-proof (#21658) (#21730)

* refactor(kona): dedup derivation prologue into kona-proof (#21658)

The sync-start prologue (resolve safe head, reject a claim behind it,
short-circuit a zero-step trace extension, build the pipeline cursor) was
duplicated between the native fault-proof program (bin/client single.rs) and
kona-sp1 (get_inputs_for_pipeline). This is consensus-critical validation, so
a fix applied to one path could silently miss the other, the same drift risk
#18494 fixed for the derivation loop.

Extract it into kona_proof::sync::prepare_derivation, the single source of
truth for the claim-validation and trace-extension logic:

- Returns DerivationInputs (TraceExtension | Derive{cursor,l1,l2}) so the
  callers stay agnostic to how derivation proceeds.
- Returns SyncStartError, which each caller maps onto its own error type:
  single.rs matches the claim-validation variants to its existing InvalidClaim
  (preserving its structured error logs) and lets Oracle errors flow through
  its From impl; get_inputs_for_pipeline maps via `?` onto anyhow.
- The "Trace extension detected" info log now lives once in the helper.

Behavior is preserved: the validation order and the zero-step
agreed==claimed check are identical to both originals. One minor diagnostic
change: single.rs's "Failed to create pipeline cursor" wrapper log is dropped
(the cursor error still surfaces as OracleProviderError); the shared helper
cannot distinguish which oracle op failed.

Verified: kona-proof, kona-client, kona-sp1-client-utils build and clippy
clean; fmt clean on both workspaces; 127 unit tests pass (incl. 3 new native
prepare_derivation branch tests and the existing sp1 get_inputs tests); guest
ELF rebuilt for riscv64im-succinct-zkvm-elf; TestSP1RangeSimpleEmptyChain
(honest + junk claim) passes through the real guest.

* refactor(kona): carry mismatched roots in SyncStartError::ClaimedRootMismatch

The variant only carried the safe-head number, so the kona-sp1 path (which
surfaces the error via its Display string) lost the claimed/agreed output
roots that the pre-refactor message included. Add both roots to the variant
so the error is self-describing and the message matches the original
"Claimed output root {claimed} does not match agreed output root {agreed} at
safe head {safe}" for every caller.

No behavior change beyond restoring that diagnostic text.

* docs(kona): drop redundant explicit link in fetch_safe_head_hash doc

The prologue refactor pulled `BootInfo` into sync.rs's imports, so the
`[`BootInfo`](crate::BootInfo)` intra-doc link is now resolvable by label
alone and rustdoc's redundant-explicit-links lint (denied under
RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings) fails the docs build. Use the bare `[`BootInfo`]`
form.

ops/docker: pre-install solc versions serially to fix "Text file busy" build flakes (#21734)

* ops/docker: pre-install solc versions serially before forge build

The op-deployer-contracts stage runs forge build with a cold /root/.svm
cache, so forge's parallel compile jobs lazily install the required solc
versions concurrently. svm-rs's install path is not fully atomic under
concurrency, which intermittently fails the docker build with:

  Error: "/root/.svm/0.8.15/solc-0.8.15": Text file busy (os error 26)

(open upstream issue: foundry-rs/foundry#4736)

Install svm (pinned + checksum-verified, same tool CI already uses via
mise) and pre-install each required solc version one at a time before
invoking forge, so forge never triggers a lazy concurrent install. The
version list matches the install-solc-compilers command in CircleCI.

* ci: retrigger after unrelated go mod download flake

* ops/docker: use forge itself to pre-install solc versions

Reviewer feedback: downloading a separate svm binary to warm the solc
cache added a new dependency and a lot of download/checksum plumbing.
forge already provides the same install path: `forge build --use
<version>` pins a single solc version and installs exactly that version
via svm's find_or_install before compiling anything, so looping over the
required versions installs them one at a time (serially) with no extra
tooling. Run it in an empty temp dir so nothing is actually compiled --
with zero sources forge prints "Nothing to compile" and exits in ~30ms
once the version is cached, so each iteration's cost is just the solc
download.

perf(kona-driver): decode only the L1-info deposit when computing L2BlockInfo (recreate #21347) (#21737)

* feat(kona-protocol): construct L2BlockInfo from a sealed header and raw first tx

Add L2BlockInfo::from_header_and_first_tx, a constructor for callers
that hold a sealed header and the raw EIP-2718-encoded transactions of
a block rather than a fully decoded OpBlock. Compared to
from_block_and_genesis it:

- takes the block hash from the seal instead of recomputing it with
  hash_slow(); the caller must guarantee that the seal is the header's
  true hash (debug-asserted),
- decodes at most the first transaction -- the L1-info deposit -- and
  classifies it by its EIP-2718 type byte first, so a typed non-deposit
  first tx is reported as FirstTxNonDeposit without being decoded,
- uses strict decode_2718_exact, rejecting trailing bytes,
- skips the first transaction entirely at the genesis block, matching
  from_block_and_genesis, which never inspects transactions there.

The L1-origin and sequence-number extraction is shared with
from_block_and_genesis through a private from_block_info_and_first_tx
core, so the two constructors cannot drift apart.

* perf(kona-driver): decode only the L1-info deposit when computing L2BlockInfo

After executing a payload, advance_to_target re-decoded every
transaction in the derived block -- bytes the executor had already
decoded and validated -- only to assemble a throwaway OpBlock from
which from_block_and_genesis read transactions[0] and re-hashed the
header.

Use L2BlockInfo::from_header_and_first_tx instead, feeding it the
executor's sealed header and attributes.transactions.first(). The O(n)
envelope decode, the OpBlock/BlockBody construction, and the redundant
header keccak all disappear from the per-block hot loop of the fault
proof program.

Document the (pre-existing) contract on Executor::execute_payload that
the returned header's seal must be its true hash: the driver now relies
on it for the derived L2BlockInfo as well as for the safe-head cursor.

As a side effect, chains whose extended transaction envelopes are not
OpTxEnvelope-decodable (e.g. Celo's CIP-64) can use kona-driver
unmodified, since only the first (deposit) transaction is decoded.

* chore(kona-driver)!: remove dead DriverError::Rlp variant

The driver no longer RLP-decodes transactions, so the variant is
unconstructable. Drop it together with the now-unused alloy-rlp
dependency.

This is a breaking change for code matching exhaustively on
DriverError.

* refactor(kona-protocol): decode first tx unconditionally in from_header_and_first_tx

The type-byte short-circuit only avoided fully decoding the first
transaction in the invalid case where it isn't a deposit, which
from_block_info_and_first_tx already rejects downstream. On a valid
chain the first tx is always the L1-info deposit, so the check never
helped. Drop it and decode unconditionally.

* chore(kona-sp1): refresh guest lockfile after kona-driver dep change

kona-driver no longer depends on alloy-rlp. The SP1 guest program
workspace path-depends on kona-driver and carries its own lockfile, so
`just check-sp1-guest-lock` fails until it is regenerated.

config: classify [optimism] and interop as immutable

Per review: the [optimism] EIP-1559 params and the interop dependency set are
consensus parameters, not freely-editable registry state. They are written once
at chain creation from the genesis deploy config and never refreshed by codegen;
the live values change only via network-synchronized mechanisms (an L1
SystemConfig event or a timestamped hardfork). No chain's eip1559 params have
ever changed in registry history.

We don't yet have a process for intentional changes to these, so for now mark
them immutable to warn against accidental edits (the check is advisory, so a
future intentional change surfaces a warning a reviewer acknowledges rather than
a hard block). Refined the immutable doc/README wording to explain this, and
added test cases for both.

test(op-acceptance): settle light-seq cross-safe before EL safe assert

TestSupernodeLightSequencerInteropInvalidMessageReplacement flakes (~2.4%
on memory-all-opn-op-reth) because the light sequencer is both a sequencer
and a follow-source follower: after the invalid-message reorg the fresh tx
re-diverges its unsafe head from the supernode upstream, and FollowSource's
forceReset (the #21119/#21155 fix) is clobbered by the next sequencer build
before the FCU lands. Recovery ratchets forward at ~1 block per two poll
cycles, so a losing shard can leave the light EL's safe pointer short of the
target when the final Reached(eth.Safe, ...) budget expires.

Settle on the light CL's cross-safe reaching settledBlock before polling the
EL: the EL's safe forkchoice pointer only advances once the CL emits the FCU
for that cross-safe head, so gating on the CL first removes the race without
masking a genuine stall (convergence is bounded — the sibling chain converges
in the same run).

fix(alloy-op-evm): discard SDM warming on rejected-candidate validation errors

A block producer in SDM Produce mode executes every candidate tx, including
ones it drops. When a candidate fails state validation (nonce-too-low,
insufficient-funds, sender-has-code), `OpEvm::transact_raw` still runs its
post-tx SDM bookkeeping on the error path, recording the fee-vault accounts in
the block-scoped warming map at the failed tx's index. A later committed tx
that touches a fee vault was then handed a phantom warming rebate that a block
built without the dropped tx never produces — leaking fee-vault value, making
block contents depend on a tx that isn't in the block, and risking a
PostExecSettlementUnderflow if the vault is underfunded.

`execute_transaction_with_commit_condition` already snapshots the warming map
before execution and restores it on the executed-then-declined path
(CommitChanges::No). Restore it on the validation-error path too, so a rejected
candidate leaves no warming behind: both non-inclusion paths now fall through
to a single restore site, and only the commit path skips it.

Adds regression coverage in block/tests.rs (mod sdm):
- test_dropped_state_invalid_tx_must_not_change_produced_block (the fix)
- plus contrast/scope-bounding tests for dropped-tx handling and the
  inspected-vs-plain execution paths.

a truncated channel, which the strict-decompression rule can act on. Context in

kona: reject leading 0x00 span-batch tx-type byte

read_tx_data treated a span-batch tx element with a leading 0x00 byte as a
legacy transaction: 0x00 <= EIP2718_MAX_TX_TYPE, so the byte was consumed as a
type prefix, and OpTxType::try_from(0x00) = Legacy then caused the remaining
bytes to be decoded as a legacy tx. op-node instead keeps the 0x00 and rejects
it as an unsupported typed-tx envelope, so the two derivation implementations
disagreed on the same L1 bytes.

Reject a consumed type prefix that resolves to Legacy (i.e. a leading 0x00): a
legacy tx carries no prefix, so its first byte is always an RLP list header
(> 0x7F). Genuine prefixless legacy txs are unaffected. Adds the shared
[00 c1 05] conformance vector to both the kona and op-node decoders.

  decodes as a valid legacy tx on both sides, so the leading 0x00 is the only

test(op-devstack): funder waits for balance >= target, not exact

`Funder.Fund` / `FundAtLeast` waited for the EOA balance to become
*exactly* the expected post-funding value (`WaitForBalance`, `==`). This
hangs forever when the wallet is over-funded, which happens under faucet
retries.

`dsl.Faucet.Fund` retries `RequestETH` up to 3x. When the target chain's
sequencer stalls long enough for the client-side request to exceed its
deadline, the in-flight funding tx stays in the mempool while the retry
issues a *new* faucet tx at the next nonce. Once the sequencer recovers,
both the original and the retry tx are included, so the EOA receives the
funding amount twice. The exact-match wait can then never be satisfied
and the test fails with "Condition never satisfied: awaiting balance to
be updated" after TransactionTimeout.

Observed in CI on `TestPreNoInbox` (memory-all-opn-op-reth): faucet
account dev-faucet-902 published nonce 0 (03f306) and, after a ~22s
op-reth "Cannot seal block, payload ID is unknown" stall tripped the
faucet client deadline, nonce 1 (e915bb). Block 81 sealed with txs=2 —
both transfers landed — funding the EOA 0.02 ETH while the test waited
for exactly 0.01 ETH.

- Add `EOA.WaitForBalanceAtLeast` (lower-bound wait). Keep exact-match
  `WaitForBalance` for sender-side callers whose expected balance is
  below the starting balance (a >= wait would return immediately).
- `Fund` / `FundAtLeast` now use the lower-bound wait: a funder only
  cares that the wallet has enough.
- Drop the redundant exact `WaitForBalance` in RunOperatorFeeTest that
  followed `NewFundedEOA` and re-introduced the same hang.

op-e2e/actions: emulate EL-sync p2p for the reth backend

The EL-sync tests rely on the sequencer and verifier engines peering over
devp2p so the verifier snap-syncs the chain from a single unsafe head. The
ephemeral reth engines are out-of-process subprocesses with no networking,
so Enode/AddPeers/PeerCount panicked 'not yet wired'.

Wire them against an in-process stand-in: a registry resolves a synthetic
enode back to the reth engine it identifies, peering is symmetric so both
PeerCount reads pass, and each peering starts a sync pump. The pump watches
optest_syncTarget (the head a forkchoice update reported SYNCING for) and,
while one is set, backfills the missing blocks from the peer engine one
validated optest_importBlock at a time — never moving safe/finalized, which
reproduces exactly the state op-geth reaches after backfilling under a
SYNCING forkchoice. It activates only once the engine has actually reported
SYNCING (which op-node triggers only during genuine EL sync, not for a
CL-mode gapped payload), so it fires exactly when a real EL would snap-sync.

The 'Forkchoice requested sync to new head' log the tests assert on is
emitted synchronously by the geth engine API inside forkchoiceUpdated, so
an async pump log would race the assertion. elSyncLogRPC wraps op-node's
engine RPC and reproduces it in op-node's own call path: it caches each

fix(kona,security): reject truncated span-batch bitlist to match op-node

SpanBatchBits::decode previously silently zero-padded truncated input,
while op-node's decodeSpanBatchBits (rollup/derive/span_batch_util.go)
returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF for the same input via io.ReadFull.

This asymmetry caused Kona to derive a different L2 state than op-node
for the same L1 calldata: a truncated protected_bits field for a legacy
transaction flipped the EIP-155 protection flag from true to false in
Kona while op-node rejected the batch entirely. Under CANNON_KONA
respected fault-proof program (Karst upgrade, 2026-06-17), Kona-in-Cannon
is authoritative for dispute resolution, so the divergent state could
finalize on-chain.

Fix: add SpanBatchError::BitfieldTooShort and return it when b.len() <
buffer_len, matching op-node's rejection semantics.

Regression tests cover: empty input at bit_length=1, and 1-byte input
at bit_length=16.

fix(kona,security): bound gossipsub snappy pre-alloc by MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE

compute_message_id (registered as gossipsub message_id_fn) called
snap::raw::Decoder::decompress_vec on every inbound PUBLISH before any
signature or application-level validation. decompress_vec pre-allocates
a Vec<u8> whose size is read from the snappy frame header — an
attacker-controlled field bounded only by u32::MAX (~4 GiB).

A 7-byte snappy frame declaring u32::MAX decompressed length forces a
~4 GiB heap allocation. Amplification: 613,566,756x. On resource-limited
hosts the process aborts via handle_alloc_error; on Linux overcommit the
OOM killer fires. Attacker reconnects with fresh peer ID and re-publishes;
persistent restart-loop. Gossipsub mesh (mesh_D=8) fans out to every peer.

Op-node's parallel BuildMsgIdFn in op-node/p2p/gossip.go performs the
correct pre-check via snappy.DecodedLen(pmsg.Data) bounded to
maxGossipSize. This commit adds the same guard to Kona.

Regression test covers the exact 7-byte bomb payload and asserts that
compute_message_id returns the invalid-snappy hash branch without
allocating.

fix(kona,security): bound gossip payload decode path against snappy bomb

The B2 fix bounded snappy pre-allocation only in `compute_message_id`
(the gossipsub `message_id_fn`). But that function only computes an id;
every inbound gossip message is then decoded via
`OpNetworkPayloadEnvelope::decode_v*`, which calls `decompress_vec` with
no bound. The identical tiny snappy frame declaring a huge decompressed
length still OOM-kills the node at that second, unbounded site.

Extract `snappy_decompressed_len_within_bound` and apply it in the block
handler before `decode_v*`, mirroring op-node, which bounds
`DecodedLen <= maxGossipSize` in both its `message_id_fn` and its gossip
topic validator.

Make the regression tests sound. The previous bomb test passed even
against unbounded code (`vec![0; u32::MAX]` is a lazily-committed calloc

fix(kona,security): revert postUnsafePayload gate & bind default; wire admin in devstack

`admin_postUnsafePayload` is node-level unsafe-head injection, not sequencer
control — op-node exposes it on any admin-enabled node, and its handler here
does not even use the sequencer client. Gating it on sequencer mode diverged
from op-node with no security gain, since `--rpc.enable-admin` already gates
the whole admin namespace. Revert it.

Keep `--rpc.addr` defaulting to `0.0.0.0` (revert the change to `127.0.0.1`):
the node ships as a Docker image, where `127.0.0.1` is unreachable from outside
the container. Accidental exposure of privileged methods is prevented by the
admin API being opt-in via `--rpc.enable-admin`, not by the bind address.
Ref ethereum-optimism/optimism#16487.

Gating the admin module on `--rpc.enable-admin` removes the admin RPC the
acceptance suite drives (StartSequencer/StopSequencer/SequencerActive). The
kona devstack runtime never enabled it, so the required `memory-all-kona-op-reth`
gate would fail. Set `KONA_NODE_RPC_ENABLE_ADMIN=true` there, mirroring op-node.

Add regression tests: the admin API is off by default, `--rpc.addr` defaults to
`0.0.0.0`, and the admin namespace is registered only when enabled (via an
extracted `merge_admin_module`).

op-acceptance-tests: make intentbuilder deactivate forks correctly

op-deployer merges user configs with defaults, potentially overwriting
the user's configs in some cases.

The intentbuilder.WithForkAtOffset would incorrectly *delete* a key in
its hardfork mapping when the caller wanted to deactivate a fork. When
merged with op-deployer's default config, the default would take
precedence because there is no explicit override.

The fix in the intentbuilder is twofold:

1. Explicitly set the deactivated hardfork to `nil` in the
   intentbuilder's mapping.
2. Set all subsequent forks to `nil` in the intentbuilder's mapping,
   so caller's don't need to remember to do that themselves.

This bug unfortunately was causing some acceptance tests to pass when
they should have failed. Fortunately, none of those failures look serious.
The changes to singlechain_runtime.go--together with new helpers in
forks.go and rollup/types.go--resolve those test failures.

feat(op-reth-test-engine): one-shot OP block execution (newPayload import + attrs-less FCU)

Phase 2 of the library-first OP test engine. Adds the import path that turns a
complete execution payload into a committed canonical block, plus attrs-less
forkchoice.

Insertion uses reth's in-memory canonical state (the engine-tree path), not a DB
write: execute against the parent overlay, verify the post-state root, build an
ExecutedBlock, then update_chain(Commit) + set_canonical_head. `latest()` then
yields a MemoryOverlayStateProvider so the next block executes on correct chained
state. Nothing past genesis touches MDBX.

- `exec::import_payload`: reuse OpExecutionPayloadValidator::ensure_well_formed_payload
  for structural validation + payload->block, execute via OpEvmConfig/BasicBlockExecutor,
  verify state root (INVALID on mismatch), commit. SYNCING on unknown parent.
- `TestEngine::{new_payload, forkchoice_updated}`. Attrs-less FCU advances the
  canonical/safe/finalized pointers: unknown head -> SYNCING (never silent VALID),
  unknown non-zero safe/finalized -> Error::UnknownForkchoiceBlock (resolved before
  any pointer moves). FCU with attributes returns Unsupported until the builder lands.
- `EphemeralChain`: store the chain spec; add state_at / commit_block /
  advance_forkchoice (+ test-only tip_header/latest_state).

Tests (all green, state-root INVALID path verified red/green) run on OP Mainnet with
Karst active: import_block_with_deposit asserts deposit (0x7E) receipt fields and that
the sender is charged gas *plus* a non-zero L1 data fee; import_invalid_block asserts a
bad state root yields INVALID with the parent as latestValidHash; fcu_unknown_head and
fcu_unknown_safe cover the forkchoice paths. L1-fee *receipt* fields are an RPC-layer
mapping; the consensus OpReceipt does not carry them.

Stacked on PR1 (seb/feat/op-reth-test-engine).

op-reth-test-engine: stateful in-flight payload builder

Add the sequencer-flow block builder on top of the one-shot import path:
forkchoice_updated-with-attributes opens a payload (deposits applied and
validated, payload id derived via the production OpPayloadBuilderAttributes /
BuildNextEnv path), include_tx executes and appends a pool tx (with the op-geth
engine API's gas-limit and force-empty semantics), and get_payload seals it into
OpExecutionData that round-trips back through new_payload.

reth's block builder ties the executor, EVM state, and parent to a single
borrowed lifetime, so it can't be parked across calls; the in-flight payload
instead keeps the ordered tx list and re-runs a deterministic one-shot assembly
on demand.

Tests drive the full sequencer flow (FCU+attrs -> include_tx -> get_payload ->
new_payload -> FCU) into a valid two-block chain, plus gas-limit rejection,
force-empty skipping, and remaining-gas accounting.

op-acceptance-tests,op-e2e: fix two bug related to op-deployer setup in tests (#21642)

* op-acceptance-tests: make intentbuilder deactivate forks correctly

op-deployer merges user configs with defaults, potentially overwriting
the user's configs in some cases.

The intentbuilder.WithForkAtOffset would incorrectly *delete* a key in
its hardfork mapping when the caller wanted to deactivate a fork. When
merged with op-deployer's default config, the default would take
precedence because there is no explicit override.

The fix in the intentbuilder is twofold:

1. Explicitly set the deactivated hardfork to `nil` in the
   intentbuilder's mapping.
2. Set all subsequent forks to `nil` in the intentbuilder's mapping,
   so caller's don't need to remember to do that themselves.

This bug unfortunately was causing some acceptance tests to pass when
they should have failed. Fortunately, none of those failures look serious.
The changes to singlechain_runtime.go--together with new helpers in
forks.go and rollup/types.go--resolve those test failures.

* op-e2e: deactivate future forks correctly

The op-e2e/config/init.go file has a similar bug as the previous commit,
except the mappings are configured by hand instead of the intenbuilder
abstraction. This bug caused most if not all of the op-e2e tests to fail
when attempting to bump op-deployer's default genesis fork to Karst.

* op-chain-ops: make fork offset lookup safe

deps: bump andybalholm/brotli to v1.2.2 (#21799)

Upgrades the brotli decoder used by op-node derivation (BatchReader,
rollup/derive/channel.go) from v1.1.0. andybalholm v1.2.0 fixed its handling of
truncated streams: it now returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF instead of a clean io.EOF
when input ends before the last meta-block completes, matching the C reference
(libbrotlidec) and RFC 7932 §9.3.

This bump is behaviorally inert for derivation on its own: op-node's
ChannelInReader.NextBatch collapses io.EOF and io.ErrUnexpectedEOF into the same
NextChannel + NotEnoughData outcome, and rlp.Stream already surfaces
ErrUnexpectedEOF for a mid-item EOF. Verified with a differential over the real
BatchReader (fixed channel decoded at v1.1.0 vs v1.2.2, full stream + all
truncation offsets + sampled corruptions): byte-identical batch output.

Its value is as an enabler for strict channel decompression
(ethereum-optimism/protocol-team#84): it gives op-node the signal to distinguish
a truncated channel, which the strict-decompression rule can act on. Context in
#21793.

test(op-devstack): funder waits for balance >= target, not exact (#21790)

* test(op-devstack): funder waits for balance >= target, not exact

`Funder.Fund` / `FundAtLeast` waited for the EOA balance to become
*exactly* the expected post-funding value (`WaitForBalance`, `==`). This
hangs forever when the wallet is over-funded, which happens under faucet
retries.

`dsl.Faucet.Fund` retries `RequestETH` up to 3x. When the target chain's
sequencer stalls long enough for the client-side request to exceed its
deadline, the in-flight funding tx stays in the mempool while the retry
issues a *new* faucet tx at the next nonce. Once the sequencer recovers,
both the original and the retry tx are included, so the EOA receives the
funding amount twice. The exact-match wait can then never be satisfied
and the test fails with "Condition never satisfied: awaiting balance to
be updated" after TransactionTimeout.

Observed in CI on `TestPreNoInbox` (memory-all-opn-op-reth): faucet
account dev-faucet-902 published nonce 0 (03f306) and, after a ~22s
op-reth "Cannot seal block, payload ID is unknown" stall tripped the
faucet client deadline, nonce 1 (e915bb). Block 81 sealed with txs=2 —
both transfers landed — funding the EOA 0.02 ETH while the test waited
for exactly 0.01 ETH.

- Add `EOA.WaitForBalanceAtLeast` (lower-bound wait). Keep exact-match
  `WaitForBalance` for sender-side callers whose expected balance is
  below the starting balance (a >= wait would return immediately).
- `Fund` / `FundAtLeast` now use the lower-bound wait: a funder only
  cares that the wallet has enough.
- Drop the redundant exact `WaitForBalance` in RunOperatorFeeTest that
  followed `NewFundedEOA` and re-introduced the same hang.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(deposit): drop redundant exact WaitForBalance after NewFundedEOA

`NewFundedEOA` already waits for the balance (now via the lower-bound
`WaitForBalanceAtLeast`), so the immediately following
`alice.WaitForBalance(fundingAmount)` was redundant and re-introduced
the exact-match hang under a double-funding faucet retry. Drop it;
`initialBalance := alice.GetBalance()` already reads the real balance
and the deposit math derives everything from it, so it stays correct
even if the wallet is over-funded.

The other two WaitForBalance calls are left exact on purpose: the L2
post-deposit credit is a legitimate exact assertion, and the L1
post-deposit balance is a decreasing balance where an at-least wait
would return immediately and defeat the check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(faucet): wait for balance >= funded amount, not exact

TestFaucetFund funds via FundNoWait, which calls dsl.Faucet.Fund
directly — the retry-up-to-3x path that double-submits under a
sequencer stall. Both waits target recipient (increasing) balances
(initial + fundAmount), so an exact wait hangs forever if the faucet
retry delivers the amount twice. Switch to WaitForBalanceAtLeast: the
test only needs to assert the funds arrived, and >= is safe here because
the balance starts below the target.

fix(kona,security): close three unauthenticated kona attack surfaces (#21753)

* fix(kona,security): reject truncated span-batch bitlist to match op-node

SpanBatchBits::decode previously silently zero-padded truncated input,
while op-node's decodeSpanBatchBits (rollup/derive/span_batch_util.go)
returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF for the same input via io.ReadFull.

This asymmetry caused Kona to derive a different L2 state than op-node
for the same L1 calldata: a truncated protected_bits field for a legacy
transaction flipped the EIP-155 protection flag from true to false in
Kona while op-node rejected the batch entirely. Under CANNON_KONA
respected fault-proof program (Karst upgrade, 2026-06-17), Kona-in-Cannon
is authoritative for dispute resolution, so the divergent state could
finalize on-chain.

Fix: add SpanBatchError::BitfieldTooShort and return it when b.len() <
buffer_len, matching op-node's rejection semantics.

Regression tests cover: empty input at bit_length=1, and 1-byte input
at bit_length=16.

* fix(kona,security): bound gossipsub snappy pre-alloc by MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE

compute_message_id (registered as gossipsub message_id_fn) called
snap::raw::Decoder::decompress_vec on every inbound PUBLISH before any
signature or application-level validation. decompress_vec pre-allocates
a Vec<u8> whose size is read from the snappy frame header — an
attacker-controlled field bounded only by u32::MAX (~4 GiB).

A 7-byte snappy frame declaring u32::MAX decompressed length forces a
~4 GiB heap allocation. Amplification: 613,566,756x. On resource-limited
hosts the process aborts via handle_alloc_error; on Linux overcommit the
OOM killer fires. Attacker reconnects with fresh peer ID and re-publishes;
persistent restart-loop. Gossipsub mesh (mesh_D=8) fans out to every peer.

Op-node's parallel BuildMsgIdFn in op-node/p2p/gossip.go performs the
correct pre-check via snappy.DecodedLen(pmsg.Data) bounded to
maxGossipSize. This commit adds the same guard to Kona.

Regression test covers the exact 7-byte bomb payload and asserts that
compute_message_id returns the invalid-snappy hash branch without
allocating.

* fix(kona,security): gate admin RPC on --rpc.enable-admin; default bind to 127.0.0.1

Three related fixes to close an unauthenticated admin-RPC exposure:

1. rust/kona/crates/node/service/src/service/node.rs — gate the
   AdminRpc module merge on config.enable_admin(). Previously the admin
   namespace was registered unconditionally on every Kona node, on the
   default 0.0.0.0 listener, with no authentication middleware. The
   --rpc.enable-admin CLI flag was parsed but never consulted at the
   registration site.

2. rust/kona/bin/node/src/flags/rpc.rs — change default --rpc.addr from
   0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) to 127.0.0.1 (localhost). Operators who need
   remote RPC access must opt in explicitly. Matches op-geth's default
   posture.

3. rust/kona/crates/node/rpc/src/admin.rs — add the same
   sequencer_admin_client.is_some() gate to admin_post_unsafe_payload
   that every other admin method already has. Previously,
   admin_post_unsafe_payload was reachable on non-sequencer nodes,
   allowing a forged execution payload to be injected as the local
   unsafe head without going through P2P validation.

4. rust/kona/crates/node/rpc/src/config.rs — add the RpcBuilder::
   enable_admin() accessor used by (1).

Reference: op-node's admin API is opt-in via the same
--rpc.enable-admin flag and defaults to 127.0.0.1.

* fix(kona,security): bound gossip payload decode path against snappy bomb

The B2 fix bounded snappy pre-allocation only in `compute_message_id`
(the gossipsub `message_id_fn`). But that function only computes an id;
every inbound gossip message is then decoded via
`OpNetworkPayloadEnvelope::decode_v*`, which calls `decompress_vec` with
no bound. The identical tiny snappy frame declaring a huge decompressed
length still OOM-kills the node at that second, unbounded site.

Extract `snappy_decompressed_len_within_bound` and apply it in the block
handler before `decode_v*`, mirroring op-node, which bounds
`DecodedLen <= maxGossipSize` in both its `message_id_fn` and its gossip
topic validator.

Make the regression tests sound. The previous bomb test passed even
against unbounded code (`vec![0; u32::MAX]` is a lazily-committed calloc
under overcommit, so it never faulted 4 GiB). Add a test that a frame
which *validly* decompresses to more than `MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE` takes the
invalid-snappy domain — this fails against an unbounded implementation —
plus direct tests of the guard predicate.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(kona,security): revert postUnsafePayload gate & bind default; wire admin in devstack

`admin_postUnsafePayload` is node-level unsafe-head injection, not sequencer
control — op-node exposes it on any admin-enabled node, and its handler here
does not even use the sequencer client. Gating it on sequencer mode diverged
from op-node with no security gain, since `--rpc.enable-admin` already gates
the whole admin namespace. Revert it.

Keep `--rpc.addr` defaulting to `0.0.0.0` (revert the change to `127.0.0.1`):
the node ships as a Docker image, where `127.0.0.1` is unreachable from outside
the container. Accidental exposure of privileged methods is prevented by the
admin API being opt-in via `--rpc.enable-admin`, not by the bind address.
Ref ethereum-optimism/optimism#16487.

Gating the admin module on `--rpc.enable-admin` removes the admin RPC the
acceptance suite drives (StartSequencer/StopSequencer/SequencerActive). The
kona devstack runtime never enabled it, so the required `memory-all-kona-op-reth`
gate would fail. Set `KONA_NODE_RPC_ENABLE_ADMIN=true` there, mirroring op-node.

Add regression tests: the admin API is off by default, `--rpc.addr` defaults to
`0.0.0.0`, and the admin namespace is registered only when enabled (via an
extracted `merge_admin_module`).

kona: defer invalid span-batch tx types to the typed decoder

Builds on the prefix-preservation fix. read_tx_data no longer rejects Deposit
(0x7E) inline: like a leading 0x00, a physically-present Deposit prefix is kept
and rejected once by the typed decoder (SpanBatchTransactionData::decode)
downstream, matching op-node's ReadTxData -> decodeTyped deferral. Only a byte
that maps to no OpTxType at all is still rejected at the reader, since it cannot
be represented in the returned type.

This removes the inconsistency where a leading 0x00 was preserved-and-deferred
while Deposit was rejected inline; both are now handled the same way. Adds tests
for the deferred Deposit and the inline-rejected unknown bytes, and corrects the
EIP2718_MAX_TX_TYPE doc/test wording about which high bytes fail where.

ci: fix rust shared-cache poisoning

After every Cargo.lock change, whichever rust job finished first won the
immutable shared dep-cache key. Fast lint jobs that never download crates
(typos, fmt, zepter, cargo-deny) or only fetch a single package's subset
(compact-codec, registry/superchain snapshots, Docker-built prestate
publish) could freeze an empty or partial registry that every later build
restored, re-downloading ~1100 crates per job until the next lockfile
change.

- Drop rust-save-build-cache from jobs that don't fully populate the
  cargo registry (restores kept).
- Bump the cache version 16 -> 18 to evict the poisoned keys (v17 was
  seeded with a partial registry by a since-removed single-package save).
- Add a pre-save guard that fails loudly if the registry is missing or
  empty; partial-registry protection remains structural (only
  full-workspace builds save).

fix(op-revm): discard journal after non-deposit tx errors (SDM warm-set leak) (#21723)

* fix(op-revm): discard journal after non-deposit tx errors

OpHandler::catch_error only reset the journal on the deposit error path, so a
non-deposit tx that failed validation left its sender EIP-2929-warm in the
shared journal. On the SDM Produce block-building path a later committed tx
could then be billed a warm access attributed to a tx that never entered the
block, diverging from a validator that never executed the failed tx — a
builder-vs-validator gas mismatch that rejects the block.

Add the missing else branch calling journal.discard_tx() on non-deposit
errors, matching upstream revm's EthHandler::catch_error and mirroring Base's
base/base#3806.

Add regression coverage in the alloy-op-evm block-executor tests (ported from
optimism-private#567): a builder-vs-validator divergence test for both the
NonceTooLow and EIP-3607 skipped-tx triggers, plus a guard that the
SDM-disabled path is unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(op-rbuilder): warm-leak regression for skipped failed candidate

Pin the SDM warm-set leak at the layer that ships in the sequencer. In
PostExecMode::Produce, op-rbuilder's execute_best_transactions loop attempts a
candidate, sees it rejected, and skips it (continue) while building the rest
of the block on the same EVM. Before the op-revm catch_error fix, the skipped
tx left its sender EIP-2929-warm, so a later included tx was billed a warm
access for a tx that never entered the block — diverging from a validator that
never ran the skipped tx.

Two variants cover the validation errors that reproduce it, mirroring the
alloy-op-evm suite: NonceTooLow and EIP-3607 (contract sender). Each injects
[A (fails, skipped), B] via PayloadTransactionsFixed (the tx pool would
pre-filter the invalid A), where B does a BALANCE on A's sender, and asserts
the block's pre-refund EVM gas is identical with and without the skipped A.
Both verified red (2500-gas divergence) against an op-revm that does not
discard the journal on non-deposit errors, green once it does.

Parameterizes the existing payload_builder_ctx test helper with post_exec_mode.

ci: fix rust shared-cache poisoning (#21832)

The shared rust dep-cache key is immutable, so after a Cargo.lock change
the first job to save wins. Fast jobs that download no crates (typos,
fmt, zepter, cargo-deny) or only one package's subset (compact-codec,
registry/superchain snapshots, Docker-built prestate publish) could
freeze an empty or partial registry that every later build restored.

- Drop rust-save-build-cache from jobs that don't populate the full
  cargo registry (restores kept); document the rule at the command.
- Bump the cache version 16 -> 18 to evict the poisoned keys.
- Add a pre-save guard that fails loudly on an empty registry.
- Remove the dead cache-key `prefix` parameter (unused since #21310)
  and its 18 call sites, which implied isolation that doesn't exist.

op-conp2p+op-devstack: publish op-con-node's signed unsafe blocks to gossip

Adds the PUBLISH direction to the op-conp2p sidecar, closing the sequencer
loop: a sequencing op-con-node signs each unsafe block it builds and serves
the signed envelopes on a websocket (opql_subscribeSignedUnsafePayloads);
the sidecar's new --signed-payload-ws flag subscribes to that feed and
publishes every envelope to the versioned /blocks gossip topic via
GossipOut.PublishSignedL2Payload — carrying the node's 65-byte signature
verbatim. The sidecar still holds zero signer state and never re-signs; the
"node owns the key, sidecar relays bytes" principle of the receive path now
holds in both directions.

- publish.go: raw jsonrpsee-protocol ws subscription client (gorilla/
  websocket; geth's rpc client cannot subscribe to jsonrpsee's explicit
  method names), reconnect with backoff, gap warnings on the best-effort
  feed, and a payload-hash fidelity guard: the SSZ re-encode of the payload
  must keccak to the node-signed payloadHash or the envelope is skipped
  loudly instead of gossiped as a block every verifier would reject. Also
  normalizes an Ethereum-legacy v byte (27/28) to the raw recovery id (0/1)
  the gossip wire requires — v is recovery metadata, not signed content.
- publish_test.go: round-trip tests — feed-shape decode → publish-encode →
  stock op-node receive decode (SSZ + OPStackP2PBlockAuthV1 signature
  verification against the expected signer), the fidelity guard on tampered
  payloads, v normalization, and notification framing.
- op-devstack: opConSequencerSigning extends the op-con-node sequencer
  launcher (--sequencer-signer-key/--sequencer-payload-ws-addr/
  --sequencer-stopped); StartOpConP2PSidecar gains options
  (WithSignedPayloadWS, WithFloodPublish); minimalFromRuntime tolerates a
  nil batcher; new preset NewSingleChainOpConSequencerP2PWithoutCheck /
  NewSingleChainOpConSequencerP2PRuntime: op-con-node sequencer (signing
  with the SequencerP2PRole key, launched stopped) + publishing sidecar
  static-peered to a STOCK op-node verifier, sequencing started via
  admin_startSequencer only once the verifier reports the sidecar as a
  connected peer (no batcher in the topology, so gossip gaps cannot heal
  from L1 — the first block must already have a live route).
- sequencer_p2p_test.go: TestOpConSequencerPublishesViaP2P — the mirror
  image of TestOpConVerifierViaP2P; the op-node verifier accepts and
  executes op-con-node's chain purely over gossip.

op-devstack: code-review fixes for op-con-node sequencer P2P tests

Review of the fan-out + wrong-signer + sidecar work surfaced one real test-logic
defect and some hardening:

- WrongSigner test was mislabeled/vacuous: it claimed the op-node verifier rejects
  the wrongly-signed block over gossip, but the op-conp2p publish sidecar delegates
  its gossipsub validator to the SEQUENCER's admin_verifyUnsafePayload, which
  go-libp2p-pubsub runs even on locally-published messages (PushLocal). The
  sequencer recognizes only the canonical (L1-derived SystemConfig) signer, so it
  rejects its own wrongly-signed block and the sidecar never propagates it — the
  op-node never receives one. The block cannot be forced through (the sequencer
  resolves the canonical signer from derivation regardless of the fallback env).
  Reframed the test + preset comments to assert the real, achievable property:
  the publish path refuses to gossip a non-canonically-signed block (rejection at
  the source), so no verifier receives it. Also replaced the test's time.Sleep
  sample loop with the sequencer's own advance as the clock (a positive DSL wait)
  per docs/ai/writing-acceptance-tests.md.

- Sidecar peer-id capture (GossipMultiaddr): only scan the sidecar's own
  "sidecar started" line (not any other peer_id= log), stop scanning once
  captured (was running ANSI-strip + regex on every stderr line for the process
  lifetime), and replace the buffered-channel put-back latch with a done-channel
  closed once — any number of callers, no re-send to remember.

- FanOut readiness: documented that awaitCLPeerCount(hub,2) does not directly
  observe the publish->receive-sidecar edge; a fully race-free gate needs op-conp2p
  to report its own topic-peer count (no such RPC today) — noted as a follow-up.

Green: WrongSigner (reframed) + FanOut + Publishes all pass.

op-conp2p: rely exclusively on the Direct Sync protocol suite

The sidecar's node-facing I/O now speaks Direct Sync end to end:

- CONSUME: cursor subscription (opql_subscribeUnsafePayloads {fromBlock})
  replaces the lossy live-forward feed. The sidecar tracks its last
  published block and resubscribes from the cursor on every reconnect; an
  in-stream gap forces a resubscribe so the producer's replay ring heals
  the hole. A below-horizon rejection (-32020) downgrades once to a live
  join (verifiers recover that range via req-resp or L1). Unsigned
  (cold-tier) messages are never gossiped.
- PUBLISH: the carrier's payload bytes are published VERBATIM via a new
  fork hook GossipOut.PublishRawSignedL2Payload (op-node/p2p/gossip.go) —
  the node signed + encoded once; no re-encode means byte fidelity by
  construction, retiring the SSZ fidelity guard. Legacy 27/28 recovery
  ids are still normalized defensively.
- VERIFY: buildVerifyRequest sends the UNIFIED {version, payload} shape —
  the canonical snappy(sig||ssz) bytes — one request for both node kinds
  (this also fixes the latent mismatch where the old superset carried
  UNCOMPRESSED bytes in the payload field).
- SERVE: the sidecar now passes a non-nil L2Chain to NewNodeP2P — P2P
  req-resp payloads-by-number is served from the node's
  opql_getUnsafePayload pull (ring-backed; absent heights → NotFound),

op-node: move follow-source requests off the driver loop (#21759)

* op-acceptance-tests: light sequencer must keep sequencing when its follow source stalls

Add a regression test for follow-source RPC latency leaking into the
op-node driver event loop. A stallable reverse proxy is interposed in
front of a light CL sequencer's follow-source endpoint and switched to
hold all requests without responding; the test then requires unsafe
block production to continue with no gap approaching the follow-source
client's 10s call timeout.

This test FAILS at this commit: followUpstream currently performs its
status request and L1 lookups synchronously in the driver's main select
loop, so a stalled endpoint freezes block production for the full call
timeout on every follow tick. The next commit moves those requests off
the driver loop and makes this test pass.

Test infra added:
- sysgo.StallableProxy / StallableFollowSourceProxies: a reverse proxy
  that can hold requests open on demand, wired via an L2CLOption that
  wraps any CL's follow-source URL; counts held requests so the test
  cannot pass vacuously
- the light-sequencer preset now accepts GlobalL2CLOptions (its runtime
  already plumbs them to the light sequencer CLs; only the option
  validation mask blocked them)
- dsl.L2ELNode.KeptAdvancing: requires a head to advance continuously,
  failing on any wall-clock gap beyond a bound - unlike Advanced, a
  stall followed by a catch-up burst is a failure

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* op-node: move follow-source requests off the driver event loop

followUpstream currently performs its upstream status request and up to
four sequential L1 lookups directly in the driver's main select loop.
Slow or unresponsive RPCs therefore prevent the loop from servicing
sequencer actions and can delay block production - see the regression
test added in the previous commit.

Run the existing follow-source request sequence in a background
goroutine, keeping at most one fetch in flight (ticks arriving while a
fetch is active are coalesced), and deliver validated status snapshots
back to the driver loop, which applies all side effects (L1 status
event, success metric, engine FollowSource reconciliation) in the
original order. The request order, validation checks, failure metrics,
and RPC client timeouts are unchanged; no caching or request
deduplication is introduced.

The split contract: followUpstream returns nil on any failure and
performs no side effects; a non-nil status has passed every check.
startFollowUpstreamFetch always delivers exactly one result (nil on
failure), which the event loop relies on to clear its single-flight
flag - unit tests pin both the async delivery and this liveness
contract.

Also remove Driver.syncConfig, which became a write-only field once the
FollowSourceEnabled guard moved to eventLoop (the ticker channel is nil
unless follow-source is enabled, so followUpstream is unreachable
otherwise).

fix(op-devstack): eliminate rollup-boost RPC port-bind race (#20938)

* fix(op-devstack): eliminate rollup-boost RPC port-bind race

The rollup-boost RPC port was pre-allocated by the Go harness
(net.Listen("127.0.0.1:0") -> Close() -> return port number), then
handed to the Rust subprocess via --rpc-port=N. The Rust binary had to
bind that port hundreds of milliseconds later (after Tokio init), during
which any other net.Listen(":0") in the test process could be handed
the same port by the kernel. Result: intermittent EADDRINUSE on
memory-all-opn-op-{reth,geth}, most visible on TestFlashblocksTransfer.

Adopt the same port-discovery pattern this binary already uses for its
flashblocks and debug ports:
  - rollup-boost (cli.rs) logs "RPC server listening on <addr>" after
    Server::build() returns, using the existing local_addr() API
    (already used at proxy.rs:210, 842).
  - op-devstack passes --rpc-port=0 and parses the bound address from
    the log stream, mirroring the existing flashblocks parser.

Pre-allocation is removed entirely; cfg.RPCPort > 0 still pins a
specific port for callers that need it.

Resolves the TODO at op-devstack/sysgo/rollup_boost.go:119-122.

Follow-up: op-devstack/sysgo/mixed_runtime.go:486 (kona-node
KONA_METRICS_PORT) uses the same pre-allocation pattern and should be
migrated separately once kona-node logs its bound metrics address.

* review: drop defer-close on log-parsing channels

The stdout parser callback is held by r.sub (via NewSubProcess) and can
fire after Start() returns. tasks.Await does not require channel
closure — it returns on first value or ctx done. The select-default
already drops duplicate emits while the channel is open, but if the
channel is closed first, a send would panic.

Drop the defers and document the lifecycle. No functional change for
the success path; eliminates a latent panic if a late/duplicate log
line ever races the deferred close.

op-reth: print a backtrace when an integration test dies on a signal

`p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently segfaults during teardown,
after its body has already passed (#20973). A binary killed by a signal produces
no Rust backtrace — `RUST_BACKTRACE` only covers panics — so five recurrences
over two months have yielded nothing beyond the signal number, and the crash has
never reproduced locally across 570+ attempts. Investigation is currently stalled
for want of a faulting stack.

Core dumps are not an option here: on the CircleCI Docker executor `/proc/sys` is
read-only so `core_pattern` cannot be set, and the host's pipe pattern makes the
kernel write the core outside the container. An in-process handler needs no
privileges, no artifacts and no CI configuration, and works locally too.

Install a handler for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS/SIGILL/SIGFPE that reports the faulting
thread's name and address, then its stack. The thread name alone discriminates
between the candidate causes: a database `atexit` destructor racing its own live
threads, background threads outliving process exit, or a runtime teardown race.

The stack is emitted in two stages, which matters:

  - `backtrace_symbols_fd` first. It writes straight to the fd and does not call
    malloc, so it is safe here. This is the guaranteed output.
  - `std::backtrace::Backtrace` second, for names and line numbers. Its
    symbolization allocates heavily and faults a second time when called from a
    handler — killing the process before anything is printed, since SIGSEGV is
    blocked inside its own handler. Attempting it only after the reliable frames
    are already on the wire means that failure costs nothing.

The handler re-raises with the default disposition, so the process still dies
with the original signal and nextest still records a crash. That composes with
the retry added in the parent commit: nextest prints a failed attempt's stderr
even when a later attempt passes, so a recurrence yields a stack while the job
stays green.

`libc` is already a workspace dependency; this adds it as a dev-dependency only.

Instrumentation only — no behavior change to any test, and no effect unless a
fatal signal fires.

rust: retry the eth69 teardown SIGSEGV flake

`reth-optimism-node::it p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently dies
with SIGSEGV after its body has already passed — the assertions succeed, nextest
prints `test result: ok`, and the binary then segfaults during teardown. The run
fails purely on the signal exit, which has repeatedly ejected unrelated PRs from
the merge queue.

Retrying is sound here specifically because the crash is teardown-only: every
assertion has already succeeded, and nextest reruns in a fresh process, so a pass
on retry re-establishes them from scratch rather than papering over a failure.
The run is still reported as FLAKY, and the failed attempt's stderr is still
printed, so recurrences stay visible and diagnosable.

This is the first nextest config for the `rust/` workspace, and it is the only one
CI reads. `rust/{op-reth,kona,op-alloy}` have no `Cargo.toml` at all and
`rust/alloy-op-evm/Cargo.toml` has no `[workspace]` table — all four are members of
`rust/Cargo.toml` — so their `.config/nextest.toml` files have never been loaded.
That is why op-reth's declared `retries = 2` never applied and this flake
hard-failed the merge queue instead of being retried.

No `[profile.default]` base block is added, so defaults are unchanged for every
other job.

Mitigation only — the crash mechanism is unresolved and tracked in #20973.

op-e2e/actions: emulate EL-sync p2p for the reth backend

The EL-sync tests rely on the sequencer and verifier engines peering over
devp2p so the verifier snap-syncs the chain from a single unsafe head. The
ephemeral reth engines are out-of-process subprocesses with no networking,
so Enode/AddPeers/PeerCount panicked 'not yet wired'.

Wire them against an in-process stand-in: a registry resolves a synthetic
enode back to the reth engine it identifies, peering is symmetric so both
PeerCount reads pass, and each peering starts a sync pump. The pump watches
optest_syncTarget (the head a forkchoice update reported SYNCING for) and,
while one is set, backfills the missing blocks from the peer engine one
validated optest_importBlock at a time — never moving safe/finalized, which
reproduces exactly the state op-geth reaches after backfilling under a
SYNCING forkchoice. It activates only once the engine has actually reported
SYNCING (which op-node triggers only during genuine EL sync, not for a
CL-mode gapped payload), so it fires exactly when a real EL would snap-sync.

The 'Forkchoice requested sync to new head' log the tests assert on is
emitted synchronously by the geth engine API inside forkchoiceUpdated, so
an async pump log would race the assertion. elSyncLogRPC wraps op-node's
engine RPC and reproduces it in op-node's own call path: it caches each
newPayload's block number and logs on a SYNCING forkchoice update to a head
it has seen.

* kona,gossip: bind message-id to topic, matching op-node

Address #21804 review (ajsutton). Two fixes:

  BuildMsgIdFn: sha256(domain || uint64_le(topic.len()) || topic ||
  payload)[..20]. Previously the id omitted the topic, so an unauthenticated
  peer could replay valid block bytes on the wrong block-version topic to
  produce the real message's id and suppress the real block via libp2p's
  cross-topic duplicate cache for up to 120s (block-propagation DoS).

  regression test.

fix(sdm): core/types: hash PostExecTx over its canonical encoding

PostExecTx.encode writes Data verbatim, so a post-exec tx's canonical EIP-2718
encoding is 0x7D || Data. But Transaction.Hash routed all non-legacy txs through
prefixedRlpHash(type, inner), which RLP-encodes the inner struct — giving
keccak256(0x7D || RLP([Data])), a hash preimage that does not match the wire
encoding. Every other typed tx (including DepositTx) has hash preimage == wire
encoding; PostExecTx was the sole outlier, so the hash op-geth exposed over RPC
and indexed receipts under diverged from op-reth (op-alloy TxPostExec::tx_hash,
which hashes the canonical encoding).

Special-case PostExecTx in Transaction.Hash to hash the canonical EIP-2718
encoding, keccak256(0x7D || Data), matching op-reth and the universal typed-tx
rule. The canonical encoding itself is unchanged, so transactions-root and block
hashes are unaffected — only the tx hash / receipt key changes.

op-alloy,op-acceptance-tests: pin post-exec tx-hash to the canonical rule

The post-exec (0x7D) tx hash must follow the universal typed-tx rule
keccak256(EIP-2718 canonical encoding) = keccak256(0x7D || Data). op-reth
(op-alloy TxPostExec::tx_hash) already does this — identically to TxDeposit,
and consistent with op-geth's DepositTx (whose encode preimage equals its hash
preimage).

op-geth's PostExecTx is the outlier: it overrides encode() to write Data raw
but still hashes via the generic inner-struct path, giving
keccak256(0x7D || RLP([Data])) — a hash preimage that does not match its own
wire encoding. That is an op-geth bug, to be fixed in op-geth and in the
op-service/sources codec (PR #21907, which currently reproduces op-geth's
value). op-reth needs no change.

Both clients agree on the canonical encoding, so the transactions-root and
block hashes are unaffected; the divergence is only in the RPC tx identifier /
receipt key. The SDM acceptance suite runs on a homogeneous op-reth stack and
reads the hash back from RPC, so it never exercised the rule — these tests pin
it:

  - op-alloy: golden vector asserting tx_hash() == keccak256(0x7D || Data),
    derived independently, with a guard against regressing to op-geth's buggy
    inner-struct value. Passes.
  - op-acceptance-tests/sdm: derive keccak256(0x7D || Data) from the served
    post-exec tx and assert (a) it equals the op-reth-served hash and (b)
    op-reth resolves the tx and receipt under it.

op-acceptance-tests: fund loadtest fee reserve on top of budget

FundEOAs reserved a fixed 2% of the budget for gas and let the funding
transfers' fee cap float with the base fee. All funding txs are pending
concurrently, so the mempool checks their cumulative worst-case cost
(gas * fee cap + value) against the funder's balance. Whenever a previous
load burst had escalated the base fee (e.g. between TestDAFootprint
subtests), that sum exceeded the funder's balance and the mempool
rejected the transfers with 'insufficient funds for gas * price + value',
failing the test.

Give every funding transfer a pinned gas limit and a fixed, generous fee
cap (10k gwei), and draw the cumulative worst-case funding fee from the
faucet on top of the budget. The funder's balance then equals the
cumulative worst-case pending cost of all concurrent funding txs, so the
mempool check passes by construction, independent of the current base
fee, and each account still receives exactly budget/numAccounts. Under
EIP-1559 only the actual base fee is charged, so the generous cap costs
nothing extra; it just has to outlast base-fee escalation while the txs
are pending, because txinclude does not bump fees yet (issue #16368).

op-batcher: load L2 blocks as execution payloads

The batcher's L2 block currency becomes eth.ExecutionPayload (#20264):
its opaque transactions are exactly what batch encoding needs, and they
round-trip OP Stack synthetic transactions (0x7E deposits, 0x7D
post-exec) without go-ethereum's typed decoding, which rejects them
under upstream go-ethereum.

- derive.PayloadToSingularBatch replaces BlockToSingularBatch (deleted):
  deposits are excluded by type byte and everything else — including
  post-exec txs — passes through verbatim; the L1-info deposit decodes
  via op-core/types. ChannelOut.AddBlock takes the payload.
- op-batcher's SizedBlock wraps the payload; DA estimation computes
  from the raw tx bytes (value-identical to the typed computation,
  pinned by TestSizedBlockParity).
- The driver fetches payloads (PayloadByNumber) via the dial providers,
  which now construct an op-service/sources client instead of dialing
  ethclient; L2EndpointProvider.EthClient becomes PayloadSource and
  dial.EthClientInterface is deleted. The RPC stays trusted, matching
  the previous ethclient fetching, which performed no verification
  either.
- derive.PayloadToBlockRef replaces the batcher's L2BlockToBlockRef use.
- op-e2e action helpers convert their typed blocks at the channel-out

op-reth: print a backtrace when an integration test dies on a signal

`p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently segfaults during teardown,
after its body has already passed (#20973). A binary killed by a signal produces
no Rust backtrace — `RUST_BACKTRACE` only covers panics — so five recurrences
over two months have yielded nothing beyond the signal number, and the crash has
never reproduced locally across 570+ attempts. Investigation is currently stalled
for want of a faulting stack.

Core dumps are not an option here: on the CircleCI Docker executor `/proc/sys` is
read-only so `core_pattern` cannot be set, and the host's pipe pattern makes the
kernel write the core outside the container. An in-process handler needs no
privileges, no artifacts and no CI configuration, and works locally too.

Install a handler for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS/SIGILL/SIGFPE that reports the faulting
thread's name and address, then its stack. The thread name alone discriminates
between the candidate causes: a database `atexit` destructor racing its own live
threads, background threads outliving process exit, or a runtime teardown race.

The stack is emitted in two stages, which matters:

  - `backtrace_symbols_fd` first. It writes straight to the fd and does not call
    malloc, so it is safe here. This is the guaranteed output.
  - `std::backtrace::Backtrace` second, for names and line numbers. Its
    symbolization allocates heavily and faults a second time when called from a
    handler — killing the process before anything is printed, since SIGSEGV is
    blocked inside its own handler. Attempting it only after the reliable frames
    are already on the wire means that failure costs nothing.

The handler re-raises with the default disposition, so the process still dies
with the original signal and nextest still records a crash. That composes with
the retry added in the parent commit: nextest prints a failed attempt's stderr
even when a later attempt passes, so a recurrence yields a stack while the job
stays green.

`libc` is already a workspace dependency; this adds it as a dev-dependency only.

Instrumentation only — no behavior change to any test, and no effect unless a
fatal signal fires.

rust: retry the eth69 teardown SIGSEGV flake, alert Slack on recurrence

`reth-optimism-node::it p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently dies
with SIGSEGV after its body has already passed — the assertions succeed, nextest
prints `test result: ok`, and the binary then segfaults during teardown. The run
fails purely on the signal exit, which has repeatedly ejected unrelated PRs from
the merge queue.

Retrying is sound here specifically because the crash is teardown-only: every
assertion has already succeeded, and nextest reruns in a fresh process, so a pass
on retry re-establishes them from scratch rather than papering over a failure.

But a retry turns the red job green, which would let recurrences pass unnoticed.
CircleCI does not parse nextest's `<flakyFailure>` element, so store_test_results
and Insights stay blind to a flaky-pass — so instead of relying on them, the
cargo-test job emits a JUnit report, greps it for `<flakyFailure>`, and on a hit
pings Slack. It alerts on every branch, not just develop — the crash has never
reproduced locally, so each occurrence is a rare chance at a stack, and one lost on
a PR run is a stack lost; fork PRs get no Slack token and self-skip. The step never
fails the job. The raw JUnit is also kept as an artifact, so the failed attempt's
captured stderr — including the crash backtrace added in the follow-up commit — is
retrievable.

Separately, the same JUnit report is uploaded via store_test_results, giving
CircleCI's Tests tab per-test pass/fail/timing for rust jobs — the first
test-results for rust CI, which previously had none. This is general visibility,
not the flake signal (CircleCI ignores the flaky shape, as above).

This is the first nextest config for the `rust/` workspace, and it is the only one
CI reads. `rust/{op-reth,kona,op-alloy}` have no `Cargo.toml` at all and
`rust/alloy-op-evm/Cargo.toml` has no `[workspace]` table — all are members of
`rust/Cargo.toml`, so their `.config/nextest.toml` files have never been loaded.
That is why op-reth's declared `retries = 2` never applied and this flake
hard-failed the merge queue instead of being retried.

No `[profile.default]` base block is added, so retry/timeout defaults are unchanged
for every other job. The retry filter uses `test(=exact)`: a `binary_id` predicate
would be more precise but nextest validates it against the whole-workspace binary
namespace, so a future crate/binary rename would hard-error every nextest run in
`rust/`; the exact-match test predicate degrades to a no-op instead.

Mitigation only — the crash mechanism is unresolved and tracked in #20973.

transaction/receipt JSON decoding, which under upstream go-ethereum
rejects OP synthetic txs (0x7E deposits, 0x7D post-exec) and silently
drops the OP receipt fee fields.

Blocks:
- RPCBlock keeps transactions as RawTransactions — canonical per-tx
  binary, JSON-(un)marshaled by class (OP classes via op-core/types,

  apis.EthExtendedClient: InfoAndUserTxsBy{Hash,Number} (synthetic
  classes excluded — decodes on upstream go-ethereum for any block),
  InfoAndDepositsBy{Hash,Number} and InfoAndFirstDepositBy{Hash,Number}

  demand — L1-safe, L2 only while go-ethereum resolves to op-geth.

- apis.ReceiptFetcher.TransactionReceipt returns *optypes.Receipt and
  apis.ReceiptsFetcher.FetchReceipts returns optypes.Receipts; the
  sources receipts providers decode the JSON methods straight into the

  consensus decode (JSON-only fee fields stay nil there, as before).

  deposit-receipt-aware (Canyon nonce+version hashing).

  canonical encoding; post-exec via its RLP-of-inner-struct rule)

op-devstack: make the conductor preset actually produce blocks

The MinimalWithConductors preset came up as a cluster whose chain never
advanced past genesis, which went unnoticed while the only conductor
acceptance test asserted Raft state alone (#21902). Three fixes turn it
into a live HA cluster:

- Seed sequencing when bootstrapping the cluster. A fresh Raft FSM
  holds no unsafe payload, so a conductor refuses to start a sequencer
  on its own (ErrNoUnsafeHead) and retried forever. Start the bootstrap
  node's sequencer manually — as an operator bootstraps a production HA
  cluster — and wait for the first block (whose commit seeds the FSM)
  before resuming the conductors.

- Recreate the p2p signer when an op-node restarts. The config held a
  PreparedSigner whose single signer instance is closed on node
  shutdown, so every restarted sequencer node (all conductor-managed
  nodes restart once during setup) failed to sign gossip with "signer
  is closed" and silently never published its blocks. This also fixes
  sequencer-restart scenarios outside the conductor preset.

- Mesh the nodes over CL p2p only. EL peering via admin_addPeer is
  flaky against op-reth subprocesses (#18570) and is not needed here:
  unsafe blocks reach follower ELs via CL gossip and the engine API.

op-devstack: Fix flaky super root readiness in acceptance tests

getSuperRoot polled superroot_atTimestamp for up to two minutes but
returned the first transient RPC error, so a single 10s per-call
BaseRPCClient deadline defeated the readiness window. Under constrained
CI the op-node driver event loop could not accept the BlockRefWithStatus
stateReq handshake within 10s, timing out one request and failing
TestSingleChainSuperFaultProofsFromOpNode with "context deadline
exceeded".

Treat individual RPC errors and nil data as not-ready within the outer
two-minute context, and reuse the successful poll response rather than
issuing an unprotected follow-up RPC that reopened the same race window.

Fixes ethereum-optimism/optimism#21952

op-supernode: drop unsafe payloads during invalidation recovery

A supernode VN that invalidates a block only enforces the deny list on the
derivation and sequencer build paths. Unsafe ingestion — the clsync queue and
the driver gap-fill — bypasses it entirely, so after an invalidation rewind
the VN re-adopts the denied branch: the denied block can arrive again by
gossip, and a far-ahead descendant handed to the EL triggers EL sync that
backfills and canonicalizes the denied ancestry. That undoes the deposits-only
replacement, re-triggers the same invalidation, and each cycle freezes every
chain's VN and forces a sequencing-window-deep local-safe walkback (observed
as a ~40k-block safe-head sawtooth on interop-reorg-2).

Unsafe ingestion is now gated while the highest denied height is above the
finalized head, i.e. from the moment of an invalidation until finality passes
it. Gated payloads are refused at queue entry (AddUnsafePayload) so none
survive the window to be gap-filled after it closes, and at insert
(insertUnsafePayload) covering the ELSync direct path. During the window the
chain advances via (deny-list-checked) derivation only. Finality is the
earliest provably-safe exit: while the denied branch can still be
canonicalized, a far-ahead FCU would push the EL into a sync ending in an
inconsistent forkchoice and a derivation reset. Outside the window the cost is
one local deny-list read per insert, and unsafe sync behaves byte-for-byte
stock. Plain op-nodes (no SuperAuthority) are unaffected.

Makes the previous commit's regression test pass.

op-supernode: drop unsafe payloads during invalidation recovery

A supernode VN that invalidates a block only enforces the deny list on the
derivation and sequencer build paths. Unsafe ingestion — the clsync queue and
the driver gap-fill — bypasses it entirely, so after an invalidation rewind
the VN re-adopts the denied branch: the denied block can arrive again by
gossip, and a far-ahead descendant handed to the EL triggers EL sync that
backfills and canonicalizes the denied ancestry. That undoes the deposits-only
replacement, re-triggers the same invalidation, and each cycle freezes every
chain's VN and forces a sequencing-window-deep local-safe walkback (observed
as a ~40k-block safe-head sawtooth on interop-reorg-2).

Unsafe ingestion is now gated while the highest denied height is above the
finalized head, i.e. from the moment of an invalidation until finality passes
it. Gated payloads are refused at queue entry (AddUnsafePayload) so none
survive the window to be gap-filled after it closes, and at insert
(insertUnsafePayload) covering the ELSync direct path. During the window the
chain advances via (deny-list-checked) derivation only. Finality is the
earliest provably-safe exit: while the denied branch can still be
canonicalized, a far-ahead FCU would push the EL into a sync ending in an
inconsistent forkchoice and a derivation reset. Outside the window the cost is
one local deny-list read per insert, and unsafe sync behaves byte-for-byte
stock. Plain op-nodes (no SuperAuthority) are unaffected.

Makes the previous commit's regression test pass.

ZKDisputeGame became a super-root game, but the challenger's ZK actor still

processed past the game's committed l1Head (ErrNotInSync, as the super game
does), so a node with a stale view does not over-challenge a valid proposal.

in this game; accept it with a warning rather than challenge. This diverges from
the super game to keep challenge decisions off the VerifiedRequiredL1 /
safe-head reverse index.

lifecycle over both op-node and op-supernode super-root sources.
