proxyd: add origin label to rpc_backend_http_response_codes_total

Distinguish client-originated backend requests from proxyd's own
consensus-poller requests on the backend response-code counter.

The counter is incremented in doForward, which is reached both by client
forwards (ForwardWithSource) and by the consensus poller (ForwardRPC),
so the metric conflated client traffic with internal polling. This adds
a new `origin` label (client|consensus) threaded through doForward.

origin is passed explicitly by each caller rather than inferred:
ForwardWithSource passes `client`, and ForwardRPC takes an `origin`
argument that the consensus poller supplies as `consensus`. ForwardRPC
is a generic single-RPC helper, so making origin a parameter avoids a
hidden assumption that every ForwardRPC caller is the poller.

origin is intentionally distinct from the transport `source` (http/ws):
consensus-poller calls are HTTP transport too, so a transport label
cannot separate them. Client-facing dashboards can filter origin="client"
while keeping the backend_name dimension.

kona-sp1-proposer: port op-succinct fault-proof proposer (create path)

Port succinctlabs/op-succinct's fault-proof proposer (fault-proof crate
at 13716c2c) into rust/kona/sp1/crates/proposer as the Rust proposer for
the super-root ZKDisputeGame (game type 10), covering game creation,
resolution, and bond claiming (#21414). The defend path (challenge
detection, proof requests, prove) follows in #21463. The Go op-proposer
is untouched and will be deprecated after the ZK upgrade.

The runtime skeleton (pinned-L1 sync, game DAG and canonical head
selection, task scheduler, backup, cursor walk) is a near-verbatim port;
adaptation is confined to the contract and data-source seams:

- Claims come from the supernode: superroot_atTimestamp supplies the
  super-root proof preimage, the root claim (keccak of the proof), and
  the safe/finalized timestamp views gating proposal cadence
  (PROPOSAL_SAFETY). The response type in super-range-executor gains the
  safe/finalized timestamp fields the Go server already serves.
- extraData is parentIndex (4B BE) || superRootProof; UUID-collision
  handling advances the timestamp with a fresh proof fetch, bounded by
  the safety limit.
- Discovered games are validated against the canonical super root; a
  timestamp that is not yet safe locally is pending (excluded from
  parent selection, re-validated each sync, persisted across restarts)
  rather than terminally dropped.
- Proposal cadence adds a catch-up rule: a head lagging by more than one
  interval proposes at the newest proposable timestamp instead of
  crawling across the gap (restart after downtime, devstack time warps).
- Identity collapses op-succinct's vkey triplet to the game's
  absolutePrestate (the super-aggregation program vkey) plus verifier.
- Bond claiming is two-phase for DelayedWETH: unlock once finalized,
  payout once the withdrawal delay elapses in L1 time (chain time, not
  wall time; the two diverge under devstack time travel).
- Not ported: the challenger (op-challenger owns that role), the prover
  and all proving config (defend path), sp1-cluster and GCP KMS
  dependencies, alt-DA features, and the anvil test harness (devstack
  supersedes it).

Devstack's ZK preset now starts the real proposer (first env-configured
sysgo service; JSON logs for the readiness matcher) unless
SkipHonestProposer, and acceptance tests drive the binary end to end:
root game creation, chaining, self-resolution, and two-phase bond
claiming. The four existing ZK lifecycle tests keep manual control via
WithoutHonestProposer. Salvaged from #21995: gameargs.ParseZK, the
ZKGameImpl parser cutover, and the WaitForZKGameCount DSL helper.

op-devstack,op-supernode: clear EL proxy upstream on stop, back off VN restarts

Fixes the two defects behind the TestSupernodeEngineControllerConnectsAfterELUnavailableAtStartup
flake (#22013):

1. sysgo left a stopped EL's tcpproxy upstream pointing at the dead
   process's freed OS-assigned port. When another chain's EL restarted
   and the OS reassigned it that port, the stale proxy silently piped
   the first chain's traffic to the wrong EL (observed as 'incorrect L2
   RPC chain id 901, expected 902'). OpReth/OpGeth now clear the proxy
   upstream on Stop/StopControlled, so a stopped EL's endpoints refuse
   connections until the owning process restarts and re-points them.

2. The supernode chain-container restart loop retried a fast-failing
   virtual node with no delay (~1000 init attempts/sec), flooding the
   EL it was mistakenly reaching with dials until its websocket
   acceptance returned 429s and starved healthy clients. The loop now
   applies capped exponential backoff to fast failures; a run past the
   threshold or a deliberate stop resets it.

op-deployer: bound forge subprocess waits, slow test broadcasts

A forge script broadcast can stall forever in its receipt-wait loop when a
tx enters the node's pool but is never mined (non-decrementing retry in
foundry v1.2.3). Tests invoked forge with context.Background() and no
cmd.WaitDelay, so one stuck broadcast burned the whole 90-minute go-tests
job until the CI watchdog killed it.

- forge.Client gains a per-invocation Timeout and always sets cmd.WaitDelay
  so a killed forge whose children hold the output pipes cannot wedge Wait.
- forge.Client gains SlowBroadcast, which adds --slow to broadcast script
  runs so txs are sent sequentially, removing the concurrent-broadcast
  nonce/pool race that leaves a tx unmined.
- Devnet tests construct their forge client via a shared testutil helper
  that enables both (10 minute timeout). Production paths are unchanged.

Fixes the hang signature tracked in #22010.

op-supernode: address review on unsafe-ingestion gating

Three review fixes on the deny-list gate, plus the comment dedupe.

Drain the unsafe queue when the gate is active. AddUnsafePayload only stops
new arrivals; payloads buffered before the invalidation stayed queued, because
forceReset doesn't touch the queue and DropInapplicableUnsafePayloads never
removes far-ahead entries. The driver's gap ticker peeks (never pops) such an
entry, so on the first tick after finality lifted the gate the stale
denied-branch payload was gap-filled into the engine and kicked off an EL-sync
attempt toward the invalidated branch — exactly the sequence the gate exists to
prevent, just bounded by finality. The lazy drain in insertUnsafePayload is
enough: the gap ticker reaches that path on every tick while such an entry is
queued.

Surface deny-list read errors. MaxDeniedHeight now returns an error instead of
folding a bbolt failure into "no denials". The gate still fails open — wedging
unsafe ingestion on a transient DB fault is worse than looping invalidation
until it heals — but it is logged rather than silent.

Log the gating state transition at Warn on both edges, with the max denied
height and finalized head, so an operator seeing the unsafe head sit still
during recovery has an explanation at default log level. Per-payload drops stay
Debug. Also refresh the payload-buffer gauge after draining so it doesn't read
stale for the whole window.

Collapse the two duplicated call-site comments to a pointer at
unsafeDenyGatingActive, and rename the shadowing `max` local.

Tests: a pre-invalidation queued payload is drained and never reaches the
engine after the gate lifts; a deny-list read error leaves ingestion stock.
Both verified red without the corresponding fix.

fix(proxyd): correct wholesale-failure and method_not_allowed metric attribution

Whole-branch review of the RPC call metrics found two design defects:

- The two batch-loop early exits in handleBatchRPC recorded per-element
  outcomes computed before the abort (cache hits, locally-answered elements,
  already-forwarded minibatches) as successes, even though the client only
  ever receives a single error envelope for the whole request set. A
  short-circuited 100-element batch could record ~30 successes and ~70
  failures instead of 100 failures. Add recordRPCCallsAll, which records
  every element at the fallback status regardless of any per-element result,
  and use it at both exits.

- eth_accounts is answered locally before the rpc_method_mappings lookup and
  so is never present in it, causing Server.metricMethodName to mislabel it
  as method_not_allowed with a 200 status — polluting the bucket operators
  use to find clients calling unsupported methods. WSProxier.metricMethodName
  had the mirror bug for the MethodUnknown/MethodNotAllowed sentinels passed
  in from clientPump's parse-failure path. Both now pass their respective
  sentinels through unchanged.

Also: move a stale comment in clientPump to the branch it actually describes,
correct a comment overstating writeRPCError's status code on the
single-request path, document why the WS drain rejection deliberately does
not increment httpResponseCodesTotal, and fix a require.NoError call inside a
mock WS backend's non-test-goroutine callback that could hang a test instead
of failing it.

Adds an integration test covering a mixed-outcome, multi-minibatch batch (the
exact shape the wholesale-failure defect lived in) and unit tests locking in
both metricMethodName fixes and recordRPCCallsAll.

fix(proxyd): stop client-supplied "unknown" method from evading method_not_allowed metric

WSProxier.metricMethodName passed MethodUnknown/MethodNotAllowed through
unchanged whenever the input equaled one of those sentinel strings. Since
the check was keyed on value, not on which code path produced the value,
a client could name its own method "unknown" in a WS frame and have it
recorded as method_name="unknown" instead of "method_not_allowed" -
letting any unauthenticated client evade the not-allowed bucket the prior
fix existed to make trustworthy.

Fix clientPump's prepareClientMsg-error branch to decide the metric label
from whether req is nil (prepareClientMsg's only two failure modes:
ParseRPCReq failed -> no req -> MethodUnknown; method didn't parse the
whitelist -> req != nil -> MethodNotAllowed), rather than from the raw
method string. The RecordRPCError call keeps using the raw method
deliberately - that's a different, higher-cardinality metric.

With the call site no longer needing a passthrough, delete the
value-equality sentinel check from metricMethodName entirely - a
passthrough keyed on a value a client can also send is a trap. Confirmed
the other two callers (the 429 branch and the relay fall-through) only
run when prepareClientMsg succeeded, so req.Method is always a real
whitelisted method there.

Adds integration tests pinning both sides: a WS frame naming its method
"unknown" now lands in method_not_allowed/403 and not in "unknown", and a
genuinely malformed frame still lands in "unknown".

fix(proxyd): address review findings on per-RPC-call metrics

Correctness fixes to the new per-call instrumentation, plus one pre-existing
bug the rollout plan made load-bearing.

- The deadline short-circuit recorded 504 unconditionally, but only the batch
  path maps context.DeadlineExceeded to ErrGatewayTimeout; the single-request
  path writes ErrInternal/500. The divergence now has one definition
  (deadlineShortCircuitStatus) and a test.

- A partially-overridden batch stamped the serving backend onto elements
  proxyd answered itself from consensus state or rejected via a block-tag
  rewrite. RPCRes carries an unexported servedLocally marker, set at the
  single merge point (OverrideResponses), so those elements attribute to
  proxyd. Also corrects the comment claiming servedBy == "" implies failure:
  it is also empty when every element was overridden.

- ErrTooManyBatchRequests had no HTTPErrorCode, so exceeding max_batch_size
  was written as HTTP 200. A client whose every batch was rejected failed
  100% of the time while both the HTTP and per-call metrics read healthy.
  Now 413, matching ErrRequestBodyTooLarge. This is a client-visible status
  change.

- WS notifications were counted before the client write and classified by
  id-absence alone, so an id-less error frame counted as a notification and a
  notification dropped on a disconnected client counted as delivered. Now
  gated on shape and recorded after a successful write.

- The WS relay increment moved after writeBackendConn, so "relayed" means
  actually relayed rather than attempted.

- Both WS error paths derive their metric status from the same response
  object sent to the client instead of an independently built copy.

- Corrected the statusCodeForRPCRes comment: doForward is not the only
  HTTPErrorCode writer. The interop filter's raw upstream status is copied
  through, so the status_code domain is partly sourced from a remote service
  and those calls carry backend_name="proxyd".

- WSProxier.metricMethodName documents that its collapsing branches are
  unreachable from clientPump today and why it is kept anyway, plus the
  ws_method_whitelist vs rpc_method_mappings divergence that makes
  sum by (method_name) non-comparable across the two rejection paths.

system-config: remove batchInbox getter and setGasConfig

The batch inbox address is defined in the rollup configuration, and nothing in the OP Stack read
it from the SystemConfig. Keeping the onchain copy meant OPCMv2's reinitialization could recompute
it with the new-chain addressing scheme, which is what rotated it for every pre-OPCM chain during
U19. `initialize` now clears the legacy slot instead of setting it.

`setGasConfig` goes too. It could only write version-0 scalars and did not update the
`basefeeScalar`/`blobbasefeeScalar` mirrors that OPCM reads, so calling it desynchronized
`scalar` from those mirrors and the next upgrade silently reverted the change. Removing it makes
the mirrors agree with `scalar` by construction. `overhead` is therefore immutable, which is
fine because op-node ignores it after Ecotone.

`startBlock` is unchanged — it is only written when unset, so reinitialization preserves it.

op-devstack: use mutual trusted EL peering to survive peer drops

ConnectP2P now registers the peering as trusted on both nodes instead of
a single untrusted admin_addPeer from the initiator. With discovery
disabled, a one-sided untrusted peering is unrecoverable once a session
drops: the inbound side has no dialable address to re-dial, so a single
hiccup permanently stalls EL sync. Trusted peers are never evicted and
are re-dialed indefinitely. DisconnectP2P drops the trusted status on
both sides so explicit disconnects still stick.

Also let net::session / net::peers log targets bypass the INFO level
filter on the op-reth stdout pipe, so disconnect reasons show up in
test logs.

Relates to #21041

`DebugNode` is implemented for `OpNode` alone, bounded on
`N: FullNodeComponents<Types = Self>`. A node that wraps `OpNode` but supplies
its own `NodeTypes` — as op-reth-premium's node types do — cannot satisfy that
bound, so it has to provide its own `DebugNode` impl to call
`launch_with_debug_capabilities()`.

That impl needs to return something implementing
`PayloadAttributesBuilder<OpPayloadAttrs>`, and `OpLocalPayloadAttributesBuilder`
is the only such type in the repo. It was private, so the only alternative was to
duplicate the dev-mode attribute logic, dummy `TX_SET_L1_BLOCK` system
transaction included — a copy that would silently drift from this one.

Makes the type public with a constructor (the field stays private), and derives
Debug/Clone to satisfy the workspace's `missing-debug-implementations` lint.
`lib.rs` already re-exports `node::*`, so no explicit re-export is needed.

constructor.

contracts-bedrock: remove SystemConfig batchInbox and setGasConfig

During U19, OPCMv2's reinit-everything path recomputed the batch inbox address via
`_chainIdToBatchInboxAddress` (the new-chain scheme) instead of preserving the existing value,
rotating it for every pre-OPCM chain. Nothing in the OP Stack reads it, since derivation takes the
batch inbox from the rollup config, so it was harmless, but it showed the onchain copy is a
redundant source of truth that can silently drift. Remove the copy rather than fix the reinit path.
Closes #21614.

`batchInbox()` and the `_batchInbox` initializer param are gone, and `initialize` clears the legacy
slot. OPCMv2 no longer computes a batch inbox, the migrator no longer reads and re-passes one, and
the now-unused `_chainIdToBatchInboxAddress` helper is removed.
`OPContractsManagerUtils.chainIdToBatchInboxAddress` stays because op-deployer still derives
new-chain batch inboxes with the same convention.

`setGasConfig` goes for the same reason. It could only write version-0 scalars and did not update
the `basefeeScalar`/`blobbasefeeScalar` mirrors that OPCMv2's `_loadFullConfig` reads, so calling it
desynchronized `scalar` from those mirrors and the next upgrade silently reverted the change.
Because `_setGasConfigEcotone` writes all three atomically, removing the only other writer makes
them agree by construction, so OPCM needs no change. `overhead` is therefore immutable, which is
fine because op-node zeroes it after Ecotone.

`startBlock` is deliberately kept: `_setStartBlock()` only writes when the slot is 0, so
reinitialization preserves it, unlike the batch inbox which was overwritten unconditionally. Two
new tests cover the difference. Keeping it also means `op-node genesis l2` needs no change, and
keeping `overhead` means no storage layout change.

Removes the `GPOParamsChange` action test, which drove a pre-Ecotone GPO change through
`setGasConfig`. Action tests deploy contracts from local source, so there is no longer a function to
call. The derivation path it covered keeps unit coverage in the `GasConfig` case of
op-node/rollup/derive/system_config_test.go.

contracts: add SuperchainERC20Factory wrap/unwrap predeploy

Adds a factory that wraps any existing ERC20 into a SuperchainERC20 so
it can move across the Superchain through the SuperchainTokenBridge.
New interop-gated predeploy at 0x4200...0026 (the slot freed by the old
OptimismSuperchainERC20Factory).

- deploy(chainId, token, name, symbol, decimals) CREATE2-deploys a
  SuperchainWrappedERC20 with salt = keccak256(chainId, token). The
  wrapped token's constructor takes no arguments and reads its
  parameters back from the factory, so the initcode is constant and the
  wrapped token address is identical on every chain, derived purely
  from the [chain_id, address] identity of the original token.
- On the original token's chain, metadata is read from the token itself
  (with a fallback to caller-supplied values for tokens without the
  metadata extension); on remote chains the deployer supplies it, or
  uses propagation:
- propagate(token, toChainId) sends the canonical wrapped metadata from
  the token's home chain to the factory on another chain via the
  L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger (the factory is the same predeploy address
  on every chain). relayDeploy requires the messenger, the factory
  itself as cross-domain sender, and message source chain == the
  token's claimed home chain, so remote chains receive authentic
  metadata without trusting any caller.
- wrap(token, amount) escrows original tokens in the factory and mints
  wrapped tokens 1:1 against the actually-received amount (so
  fee-on-transfer tokens cannot inflate supply beyond backing);
  unwrap(token, amount) burns and releases escrow. Both are only
  possible on the token's home chain; everywhere else supply moves
  exclusively through the SuperchainTokenBridge, so home-chain escrow
  always equals global wrapped supply.

interopsmoke: add chained-invalid-message smoke test

Verifies that interop invalidation is transitive. Chain A sends a
cross-domain message targeting an EventLogger on chain B; chain B relays
it with a corrupted identifier so the relay is invalid. The relay still
executes and calls emitLog, emitting a new initiating message that
exists only because the invalid relay ran. Chain A then executes that
message. When chain B's block is replaced, chain A's executing message
must be reorged out too.

A second dependent arm covers the block lineage: a plain log emitted on
a later chain B block, executed on chain A. That block is valid in
itself and is replaced only because its ancestor is, so a node that
invalidates dependencies on the invalid block but not on its descendants
fails. Both arms are independent, so one being refused at submission
does not stop the other from being asserted.

A control message that does not depend on the invalid block is asserted
to survive, so a node that discards a swathe of recent chain A blocks
does not pass.

rust: retry the eth69 teardown SIGSEGV flake, alert Slack on recurrence

`reth-optimism-node::it p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently dies
with SIGSEGV after its body has already passed — the assertions succeed, nextest
prints `test result: ok`, and the binary then segfaults during teardown. The run

the merge queue.

Retrying is sound here specifically because the crash is teardown-only: every
assertion has already succeeded, and nextest reruns in a fresh process, so a pass
on retry re-establishes them from scratch rather than papering over a failure.

But a retry turns the red job green, which would let recurrences pass unnoticed.
CircleCI does not parse nextest's `<flakyFailure>` element, so store_test_results
and Insights stay blind to a flaky-pass — so instead of relying on them, the
cargo-test job emits a JUnit report, greps it for `<flakyFailure>`, and on a hit
pings Slack. It alerts on every branch, not just develop — the crash has never
reproduced locally, so each occurrence is a rare chance at a stack, and one lost on
a PR run is a stack lost; fork PRs get no Slack token and self-skip. The step never
fails the job. The raw JUnit is also kept as an artifact, so the failed attempt's
captured stderr — including the crash backtrace added in the follow-up commit — is
retrievable.

Separately, the same JUnit report is uploaded via store_test_results, giving
CircleCI's Tests tab per-test pass/fail/timing for rust jobs — the first
test-results for rust CI, which previously had none. This is general visibility,
not the flake signal (CircleCI ignores the flaky shape, as above).

This is the first nextest config for the `rust/` workspace, and it is the only one
CI reads. `rust/{op-reth,kona,op-alloy}` have no `Cargo.toml` at all and
`rust/alloy-op-evm/Cargo.toml` has no `[workspace]` table — all are members of
`rust/Cargo.toml`, so their `.config/nextest.toml` files have never been loaded.
That is why op-reth's declared `retries = 2` never applied and this flake
hard-failed the merge queue instead of being retried.

No `[profile.default]` base block is added, so retry/timeout defaults are unchanged
for every other job. The retry filter uses `test(=exact)`: a `binary_id` predicate
would be more precise but nextest validates it against the whole-workspace binary
namespace, so a future crate/binary rename would hard-error every nextest run in
`rust/`; the exact-match test predicate degrades to a no-op instead.

The Slack token comes from a dedicated `slack` CircleCI context, so the two
cargo-test jobs get their own context list including it (not the shared
`*rust-ci-context`, which 20+ lint/build jobs use and should not hold a bot
token). The same gap silently disabled `rust-deny`'s own `@protocol-oncall`
develop-failure ping, so that job is moved onto the shared slack context too,
restoring the notification its comment already promises.

Mitigation only — the crash mechanism is unresolved and tracked in #20973.

op-acceptance-tests: fix SafeHeadProgression flake on post-resume EL stall

TestSupernodeInterop_SafeHeadProgression waited for cross-safe (CL) and the EL
safe label to reach a target with a fixed 15-attempt (30s) budget after
ResumeInterop. Under CI load the EL (op-reth) can be transiently starved and
halt block production for ~20s, which freezes every head — unsafe, local-safe
and cross-safe — in lockstep. The fixed budget is then exhausted before
cross-safe reaches the target, and the test fails with
"expected head to advance: safe". It is intermittent because it only triggers
when the stall lands in the post-resume window and lasts long enough; on an
unloaded machine cross-safe catches up in a few seconds.

Wait progress-aware instead. Add dsl ReachedWithProgressFn on L2CLNode and
L2ELNode (the "reach a target" analogue of the existing MatchedWithProgressFn):
keep a generous overall budget while the unsafe head keeps advancing, but fail
fast if it stops advancing entirely for a stall timeout. This tolerates a
self-recovering slowdown without masking a genuine hang — a permanently stuck
node still fails at the stall timeout, not the max wait.

Reproduced deterministically by SIGSTOPing op-reth during the post-resume
window: baseline 4/4 fail (exact symptom), fixed 0/3 fail; a never-released
freeze fails fast at the 40s stall timeout ("unsafe progress stalled ... for
40s"), not the 120s max wait.

ci: Stop using bash here-strings in a CircleCI command

CircleCI 2.1 treats a doubled left angle bracket as a parameter-tag
opener before any shell sees it, so the `mapfile`/`read` here-strings in
the publish step failed the whole continuation with "Unclosed tag". A
continuation that fails to compile emits no workflows at all, so every
check silently vanished from the PR rather than going red: pipeline
131138 ran `setup` and nothing else. `c-run_release` is true on branch
pushes, so the gated publish job is compiled on every PR.

Read the table via a temp file (keeps the exit status, unlike process
substitution, and keeps the variant stream off the loop body's stdin)
and split entries with plain expansion. kona-prestate-variants now
validates the whole table before printing anything, so a truncated read
cannot be mistaken for a valid short table.

Plain `circleci config validate` does not catch this: both callers of
the job sit behind `when:` gates, and processing skips them unless the
parameter is set. Verified with the private orb stubbed and all 23
`c-run_*` params true — compiles clean, and reproduces the failure on
the previous commit.

Also fixes a build-kona-client-elf comment the rename missed, and
documents both traps in docs/ai/ci-config-review.md item 9.
ci: Stop using bash here-strings in a CircleCI command

docs: Note that process substitution swallows the exit status

The CircleCI '<<' guidance suggested mapfile -t ARR < <(cmd) as the way
around the parameter-tag trap, which is the pattern rust-ci.yml
deliberately avoids: it trades an unclosed-tag failure for a silently
swallowed exit status. Show the temp-file form as the default and say
why, and note that a shell comment mentioning the token breaks
compilation too.

contracts-bedrock: resolve each proxy's own ProxyAdmin during upgrade

After an interop migration a chain set shares ETHLockbox, DisputeGameFactory,
AnchorStateRegistry, and DelayedWETH, all administered by the first chain's
ProxyAdmin. _apply previously routed every proxy upgrade through the calling
chain's ProxyAdmin, so upgrade() reverted on the shared contracts for any member
chain other than the first.

Resolve each proxy's administering ProxyAdmin per-target via _adminFor, reading
the target's self-reported admin (ProxyAdminOwnedBase) and falling back to the
calling chain's ProxyAdmin for not-yet-initialized proxies (initial deployment or
permitted proxy deployments). Shared contracts are re-upgraded idempotently on
every member's upgrade, relying on initializer idempotency.

Bump OPCM to 7.2.3. Ref: ethereum-optimism/optimism#21731
contracts-bedrock: resolve each proxy's own ProxyAdmin during upgrade

contracts-bedrock: Resolve each proxy's own SystemConfig during upgrade

The shared interop contracts are bound to the first member chain's SystemConfig:
migrate() initializes ETHLockbox and AnchorStateRegistry with
chainSystemConfigs[0] and reuses that chain's DelayedWETH. All three
initializers assign systemConfig unconditionally and _upgrade resets the
initialized slot, so once _adminFor let a non-first member reach them, that
member's upgrade() silently re-pointed all three at its own SystemConfig.

Add _systemConfigFor, symmetric with _adminFor: read the target's self-reported
systemConfig() and fall back to the caller's for a proxy that can't report one.
Apply it to the three shared initializers only. Per-chain contracts are resolved
from _cts.systemConfig in the first place, so routing them through the helper
would be a no-op that weakens upgrade-normalizes-state.

Move _adminFor into OPContractsManagerUtils.upgrade, which already receives both
the ProxyAdmin and the target and is where the admin is used. Resolving there
instead of at eleven OPContractsManagerV2 call sites keeps that contract under
the EIP-170 limit (24,522 of 24,576 bytes; it was 185 over) and extends the same
protection to the migrator. Callers are unaffected: every existing call site
already passes the target's own ProxyAdmin or a fresh proxy's deployer.

Bump OPCM to 7.2.4; develop already shipped 7.2.3.

op-reth: print a backtrace when an integration test dies on a signal

`p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently segfaults during teardown,
after its body has already passed (#20973). A binary killed by a signal produces
no Rust backtrace — `RUST_BACKTRACE` only covers panics — so five recurrences
over two months have yielded nothing beyond the signal number, and the crash has
never reproduced locally across 570+ attempts. Investigation is currently stalled
for want of a faulting stack.

Core dumps are not an option here: on the CircleCI Docker executor `/proc/sys` is
read-only so `core_pattern` cannot be set, and the host's pipe pattern makes the
kernel write the core outside the container. An in-process handler needs no
privileges, no artifacts and no CI configuration, and works locally too.

Install a handler for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS/SIGILL/SIGFPE that reports the faulting
thread's name and address, then its stack. The thread name alone discriminates
between the candidate causes: a database `atexit` destructor racing its own live
threads, background threads outliving process exit, or a runtime teardown race.

The stack is emitted in two stages, which matters:

  - `backtrace_symbols_fd` first. It writes straight to the fd and does not call
    malloc, so it is safe here. This is the guaranteed output.
  - `std::backtrace::Backtrace` second, for names and line numbers. Its
    symbolization allocates heavily and faults a second time when called from a
    handler — killing the process before anything is printed, since SIGSEGV is
    blocked inside its own handler. Attempting it only after the reliable frames
    are already on the wire means that failure costs nothing.

The handler re-raises with the default disposition, so the process still dies
with the original signal and nextest still records a crash. That composes with
the retry added in the parent commit: nextest prints a failed attempt's stderr
even when a later attempt passes, so a recurrence yields a stack while the job
stays green.

`libc` is already a workspace dependency; this adds it as a dev-dependency only.

Instrumentation only — no behavior change to any test, and no effect unless a
fatal signal fires.

fix(txinclude): don't resend an already-mined tx on ErrNonceTooLow

Persistent treated ErrNonceTooLow from the (re)submit path as "advance the nonce
and retry". But once our own tx is mined, a resubmit of the identical tx returns
ErrNonceTooLow (the account nonce has advanced past it) — so this blindly
resubmitted an already-included tx at the next nonce, duplicating it. For value
transfers that means over-sending (a single Fund delivered many multiples), and
it raced the receipt monitor so it was timing-dependent.

On ErrNonceTooLow, look up our own tx's receipt (bounded by
WithIncludedLookupTimeout, default 12s) to disambiguate:
  - receipt found  -> our tx was mined; return it as included (no resend).
  - not found      -> the nonce was consumed by a gap/other sender; advance.
The bound only needs to cover receipt-indexing lag (ErrNonceTooLow guarantees the
consuming block is committed) and is paid only on genuine gaps, which don't occur
when the includer is the account's sole sender.

Adds TestPersistentDoesNotResendMinedTx; TestPersistentFixesNonceTooLow keeps
covering the genuine-gap advance path (with a short lookup timeout).

op-rbuilder: build the pool from OpNode::standard_pool_builder

Both pool construction sites hand-copied the base pool configuration
(tx-conditional, interop endpoints and quorum) instead of starting from
`OpNode::standard_pool_builder`, which exists to be composed for exactly
this reason. Hand-copying means a base field added upstream is silently
dropped here — the pool keeps compiling with the old configuration.

Start from `standard_pool_builder` and override only what differs:
`enable_tx_conditional`, which additionally honors revert protection, and
the interop failsafe.

The failsafe override is load-bearing, not cosmetic. `BuilderConfig`
mints its own handle rather than adopting the node's, and the payload
builder reads the failsafe through `BuilderConfig` — so the pool must be
pointed back at that handle or the filter client and the builder would
observe different flags. A comment records this at both sites.

No behavior change: every value the previous code set is still set.

op-reth: remove unsupported --minimal option (breaking change)

--minimal configures maximum pruning, including pruning block bodies to
a fixed 10,064-block window. op-node reads the L1-info deposit
transaction from historical block bodies during derivation, so a
--minimal datadir breaks EL sync (l2 block is missing L1 info deposit
tx). The docs have long said not to use it; now the binary enforces it.

The flag lives in upstream reth arg structs that op-reth reuses, so it
cannot be removed at the type level. Instead the in-tree cli crate
grows a small deny-list (DENIED_ARGS) of (subcommand, arg id, error)
entries: denied args are hidden from all help output and rejected
after parsing with an error that points operators at the supported
pruning recipe and docs page. The shared parse entrypoints
(parse_args, try_parse_args_from, and the new parse_with_denied_args
used by the op-reth binary) all route through the deny-list, and
CliApp::run carries a backstop check so binaries that build their clap
command directly (the vendored op-rbuilder) reject --minimal at
startup too.

Nodes previously started with --minimal now exit at startup with the
guidance message; their datadirs were already unsupported and need a
resync regardless.

The CLI surface snapshot is updated to render --minimal with a
[hidden] marker, documenting the deny decision. The bin crate no
longer uses clap directly, so the dependency edge is dropped.

kona: gate PostExec transaction structure in batch validation

kona's batch validation enforced only PostExec activation: a 0x7D transaction
before Lagoon was dropped, but nothing checked how many there were, where in the
block it sat, or whether its payload was well-formed and anchored to the right
block. The execution layer rejects all of those — op-alloy's
parse_post_exec_payload_from_transactions, which kona's own proof executor calls,
plus PostExecState::new in alloy-op-evm.

op-node was just given these rules. Without the matching change a kona-node
follower and an op-node follower reach different verdicts on the same L1 data for
a batch carrying a malformed 0x7D: op-node drops the batch and lets the next one
supply the height, while kona-node accepts it, gets an EL rejection and takes the
deposits-only fallback. Two different safe chains, from a malicious batcher or
from a sequencer buggy at the Lagoon activation boundary.

Add check_post_exec_txs, called by both the singular and span paths, enforcing
activation, at-most-one, payload well-formedness, the payload's block-number
anchor, last-in-block, and the two entry rules PostExecState::new decides from the
payload alone: no zero-refund entry and no duplicate transaction index. Activation
moves into the shared function rather than staying duplicated in each caller's
classification match, so a future caller cannot bypass it. Rule precedence mirrors
op-alloy arm for arm, so a payload violating several rules yields the same reason
in both.

Four EL rules are deliberately left to the executor and documented as such: an
entry index out of range or targeting a deposit or the 0x7D itself, and
refund <= evm_gas_used. Entry indices are block-global — they count the deposits
the pipeline prepends — while a batch holds only the block's non-deposit
transactions, so those need the full transaction list; the ceiling needs
execution. This matches op-node's residual exactly, so the two cannot disagree.

Note the span path is defense in depth: it is only reached pre-Holocene, while SDM
activates at Lagoon, so on a real chain span batches are validated per block
through SingleBatch::check_batch. Enforcing the rules in both keeps them aligned.

op-node: gate PostExec transaction structure in derivation

Go derivation and the execution layer must reach the same verdict on block
validity. For PostExec (0x7D) transactions they did not, on both batch paths:
the span per-block validation loop had no 0x7D case at all, and
checkSequencerTxData on the singular path gated activation only. So 0x7D-not-last
and multiple-0x7D were accepted by derivation on both paths, pre-activation 0x7D
was accepted on the span path, and neither path looked at the payload.

This is not the permanent follower stall FM6 predicted. Post-Holocene an invalid
derived payload falls back to deposits-only attributes (build_invalid.go), so
followers make progress. It is worse than a stall for that height: the safe chain
commits a deposits-only block, discarding every user transaction the sequencer
included, and because the batch was accepted rather than dropped the batch queue
never tries a subsequent valid batch for the height. Reachable by a malicious
batcher and, more plausibly, by a buggy sequencer at the Lagoon activation
boundary.

Add a shared checkSequencerTxs, called by both paths so they cannot drift again,
enforcing every 0x7D rule decidable at batch-validation time: activation,
at-most-one, payload well-formedness, the payload's block-number anchor,
last-in-block, and — via checkPostExecPayloadEntries, mirroring
PostExecState::new — no zero-refund entry and no duplicate entry index. Four EL
rules remain unenforced for structural reasons rather than oversight: entry index
in range, entry not targeting a deposit or the 0x7D itself, and
refund <= evm_gas_used. The first three need the block's transaction list, since
SDMGasEntry.Index is block-global and derivation does not know the deposit count
at batch-validation time; the last needs execution. Both are documented at the
call site.

Position and count need no index adjustment: attributes.go prepends the l1-info,
deposit and upgrade transactions and attributes_queue.go appends the batch
transactions with nothing after, so last-in-batch is last-in-block.

testPostExecTx previously emitted {0xc2, 0x01, 0xc0} — valid RLP, but a
two-element list that cannot decode into the three-field payload. Every accept
row was therefore asserting that derivation accepts a 0x7D the EL rejects. It now
encodes a real payload anchored to the block under test, so those rows became
genuine parity assertions. Each drop row pins its log message so a batch dropped
for an unrelated reason cannot keep the row green while the rule regresses.

Note kona derivation still enforces activation only (batch/single.rs,
batch/span.rs) and needs the matching rules before Lagoon activates, or an
op-node and a kona-node follower disagree on the safe chain for a batch carrying
a malformed 0x7D.

alloy-op-evm: don't rebate inner CREATE warming

An inner (depth > 0) CREATE/CREATE2 claimed the 2500-gas SDM warm-account
rebate for the address it created, even though the creating transaction never
paid an EIP-2929 cold-account access for it: SDMWarmingInspector::create
suppressed the rebate only `if top_level`.

CREATE and CREATE2 are not EIP-2929-metered opcodes. The create path in
revm-interpreter-41.0.0 (src/instructions/contract.rs:23-110) charges
initcode_cost + create_cost/create2_cost + memory (+ EIP-8037 state gas) and
never a cold-account-access surcharge, so there is no cold->warm delta to
return at any depth. The rebate refunded a cost the EVM never levied,
over-debiting the fee vaults on legitimate CREATE2 factory traffic.

Insert the created address into intrinsic_warm_accounts unconditionally and
keep the observe_account_touch call, so the address is still recorded in the
block-warm set and a later tx that genuinely cold-accesses it still earns its
rebate. The change only ever adds to the per-tx suppression set, so it cannot
introduce an over-refund.

Also correct the created_address memoization comment, which had the revm
ordering backwards: inspect_frame_init dispatches Inspector::create through
frame_start before calling frame_init, so this hook seeds the OnceCell and revm
reuses our value rather than the reverse. The journal nonce read is
load-bearing, not a fallback. The CreateScheme match arms are enumerated so a
future nonce-dependent scheme cannot silently seed the cell with nonce 0.

alloy-op-evm: pin post-exec settlement conservation at arithmetic extremes

Closes the max-input saturation gap the SDM FMA flags as NON-BLOCKING under
FM2. Nothing pinned that the saturating arithmetic in post_exec_settlement_deltas
cannot silently truncate a settlement leg and break value conservation under
the widest inputs a hostile producer can reach.

Sweeps base_fee in {0, 1, 1e9, u64::MAX} x refund in {1, 21k, u64::MAX/2,
u64::MAX} x effective_gas_price in {basefee, basefee+1, u128::MAX}, asserting
each leg against its exact closed form as well as the conservation identity
sender == beneficiary + base_fee + operator_fee. Checking the legs individually
matters: the identity alone still holds if two legs clamp by offsetting
amounts. All of them hold exactly, so no saturation engages — the widest
product is ~2^192, well inside U256.

Only effective_gas_price >= basefee is exercised: below-basefee txs never reach
settlement (revm rejects them with GasPriceLessThanBasefee upstream), which is
the precondition the beneficiary_gas_price saturating_sub relies on.

This is coverage only; no behavior change.

contracts-bedrock: Resolve each proxy's own SystemConfig during upgrade

The shared interop contracts are bound to the first member chain's SystemConfig:
migrate() initializes ETHLockbox and AnchorStateRegistry with
chainSystemConfigs[0] and reuses that chain's DelayedWETH. All three
initializers assign systemConfig unconditionally and _upgrade resets the
initialized slot, so once _adminFor let a non-first member reach them, that
member's upgrade() silently re-pointed all three at its own SystemConfig.

Add _systemConfigFor, symmetric with _adminFor: read the target's self-reported
systemConfig() and fall back to the caller's for a proxy that can't report one.
Apply it to the three shared initializers only. Per-chain contracts are resolved
from _cts.systemConfig in the first place, so routing them through the helper
would be a no-op that weakens upgrade-normalizes-state.

Move _adminFor into OPContractsManagerUtils.upgrade, which already receives both
the ProxyAdmin and the target and is where the admin is used. Resolving there
instead of at eleven OPContractsManagerV2 call sites keeps that contract under
the EIP-170 limit (24,522 of 24,576 bytes; it was 185 over) and extends the same
protection to the migrator. Callers are unaffected: every existing call site
already passes the target's own ProxyAdmin or a fresh proxy's deployer.

Bump OPCM to 7.2.4; develop already shipped 7.2.3.

op-reth: print a backtrace when an integration test dies on a signal

`p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently segfaults during teardown,
after its body has already passed (#20973). A binary killed by a signal produces
no Rust backtrace — `RUST_BACKTRACE` only covers panics — so five recurrences
over two months have yielded nothing beyond the signal number, and the crash has
never reproduced locally across 570+ attempts. Investigation is currently stalled
for want of a faulting stack.

Core dumps are not an option here: on the CircleCI Docker executor `/proc/sys` is
read-only so `core_pattern` cannot be set, and the host's pipe pattern makes the
kernel write the core outside the container. An in-process handler needs no
privileges, no artifacts and no CI configuration, and works locally too.

Install a handler for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS/SIGILL/SIGFPE that reports the faulting
thread's name and address, then its stack. The thread name alone discriminates
between the candidate causes: a database `atexit` destructor racing its own live
threads, background threads outliving process exit, or a runtime teardown race.

The stack is emitted in two stages, which matters:

  - `backtrace_symbols_fd` first. It writes straight to the fd and does not call
    malloc, so it is safe here. This is the guaranteed output.
  - `std::backtrace::Backtrace` second, for names and line numbers. Its
    symbolization allocates heavily and faults a second time when called from a
    handler — killing the process before anything is printed, since SIGSEGV is
    blocked inside its own handler. Attempting it only after the reliable frames
    are already on the wire means that failure costs nothing.

The handler re-raises with the default disposition, so the process still dies
with the original signal and nextest still records a crash. That composes with
the retry added in the parent commit: nextest prints a failed attempt's stderr
even when a later attempt passes, so a recurrence yields a stack while the job
stays green.

`libc` is already a workspace dependency; this adds it as a dev-dependency only.

Instrumentation only — no behavior change to any test, and no effect unless a
fatal signal fires.

rust: retry the eth69 teardown SIGSEGV flake, alert Slack on recurrence

`reth-optimism-node::it p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently dies
with SIGSEGV after its body has already passed — the assertions succeed, nextest
prints `test result: ok`, and the binary then segfaults during teardown. The run
fails purely on the signal exit, which has repeatedly ejected unrelated PRs from
the merge queue.

Add a nextest retry scoped to that one test. Retrying is sound because the crash is
teardown-only: every assertion has already succeeded, and nextest reruns in a fresh
process, re-establishing them from scratch rather than papering over a failure. This
is a deliberate exception to the workspace's no-retries policy — a stopgap for an
unresolved crash tracked in #20973.

A retry turns the red job green, which would let recurrences pass unnoticed, and
CircleCI does not parse nextest's `<flakyFailure>` element (so store_test_results and
Insights stay blind to a flaky-pass). So the cargo-test job greps the JUnit report
for `<flakyFailure>` and pings Slack — on every branch, since the crash has never
reproduced locally and each occurrence is a rare chance at a stack. The step never
fails the job, and the JUnit is already kept as an artifact so the failed attempt's
stderr (the crash backtrace, once #21910 lands) is retrievable.

The Slack token comes from a dedicated `slack` CircleCI context, so the two
cargo-test jobs get a context list including it, not the shared `*rust-ci-context`
that 20+ lint/build jobs use and should not hold a bot token. The same gap silently
disabled `rust-deny`'s own `@protocol-oncall` develop-failure ping, so that job is
moved onto the slack context too, restoring the notification its comment promises.

Mitigation only — the crash mechanism is unresolved and tracked in #20973.

op-ufm: fix memory leaks in provider tx pool and RPC clients

Long-running op-ufm pods grow memory monotonically (see PR description).
Three sources:

1. TransactionPool entries were only removed on the "seen by every provider"
   success path. Receipt-retrieval timeouts and non-NotFound receipt errors
   returned without deleting, and any provider that never observed a tx
   permanently pinned it. Add a defer-based cleanup on the RoundTrip failure
   paths plus an age-based GC pass at the top of each Heartbeat as a safety
   net for the "success but never propagated" case.
2. iclients.Dial was called on every Heartbeat and RoundTrip interval and
   the returned ethclient.Client was never closed, leaking connections,
   file descriptors, and transport goroutines. Cache the client on Provider,
   dial lazily on first use, and Close() on Shutdown. Expose Close() on
   InstrumentedEthClient to delegate.
3. Same pattern for the signer client (recreated per RoundTrip). Upstream
   SignerClient has no Close in the pinned version, so we just cache and
   reuse a single instance.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

system-config: remove batchInbox getter and setGasConfig (#922)

* system-config: remove batchInbox getter and setGasConfig

The batch inbox address is defined in the rollup configuration, and nothing in the OP Stack read
it from the SystemConfig. Keeping the onchain copy meant OPCMv2's reinitialization could recompute
it with the new-chain addressing scheme, which is what rotated it for every pre-OPCM chain during
U19. `initialize` now clears the legacy slot instead of setting it.

`setGasConfig` goes too. It could only write version-0 scalars and did not update the
`basefeeScalar`/`blobbasefeeScalar` mirrors that OPCM reads, so calling it desynchronized
`scalar` from those mirrors and the next upgrade silently reverted the change. Removing it makes
the mirrors agree with `scalar` by construction. `overhead` is therefore immutable, which is
fine because op-node ignores it after Ecotone.

`startBlock` is unchanged — it is only written when unset, so reinitialization preserves it.

* system-config: keep removed functions as historical, clarify version markers

Per seb, the protocol specs keep historical information, so restore the
`batchInbox` and `setGasConfig` sections with their TOC entries rather than
deleting them, each marked `(-op-contracts/v8.0.0)` and noting removal in
`SystemConfig` v4.0.0. Split the `initialize` batch inbox MUST into a versioned
pair so the old behavior stays recorded next to the new one.

The existing `(+v4.1.0)` markers were ambiguous between an op-contracts release
and a contract semver. They mean the release: at `op-contracts/v4.1.0` the
feature-flag and optional-ETHLockbox pause work is present while SystemConfig is
at 3.7.0 and SuperchainConfig at 2.3.0, and no contract has ever been at 4.1.0.
Make that explicit with the full `op-contracts/vX.Y.Z` identifier, normalize the
existing markers in system-config.md and stage-1.md, and add a note to the
Function Specification section saying which scheme is which.

Also record what the monorepo PR actually changed about the overhead:
`ConfigUpdate` type 1 now always carries a zero in the `overhead` entry, and the
payload stays two words so its length is unchanged.

op-conductor: recover when leader falls behind consensus unsafe head

A leadership handover left the incoming leader wedged whenever its op-node was two
or more blocks behind the unsafe head consensus had committed. startSequencer only
posted the missing payload when the gap was exactly one block and bailed out
otherwise, and action's leader/healthy/inactive case re-queued that identical
failing start forever, so the cluster ran with no active sequencer at all until
something else moved leadership. In the sampled CI failure that pair of log lines
repeats 28 times, 29 mismatch warnings in all, with consensus_num=14 and
node_num=12 throughout, until the test gives up.

The gap opens because of a second defect. PostUnsafePayload hands the payload to
op-node asynchronously, but StartSequencer was called on the next line, and
op-node only starts sequencing at a head it has already adopted. Losing that race
costs a uniform 0-2s action retry backoff, and a sequencer that starts a second or
more behind the wall clock builds several blocks back to back to catch up, which
is exactly what strands the next leader two or more blocks behind.

Losing the race is not itself a variable: it was lost in 100% of sampled runs,
because a follower in this topology learns blocks only through L1 batch
derivation, which lags ~1.1s against a 1s block time. Two other draws make it
flaky. The backoff draw X decides when the second transfer lands, because
ensureOnlyOneLeader polls on a 1s grid, so T1 = T0 + ceil(X) seconds and
X >= 1000ms hands the next leader a gap of 2 and a wedge - 50% on its own. That is
multiplied by whether op-node's driver loop happens to wake during the interim
leader's active window (2s - X, mean 0.5s, against two or three wake sources of
period ~2s), roughly 0.6. Together ~30%, against ~34% measured on CI and ~20%
locally. The passing rerun bears out the second factor rather than the first:
sequencer2 was active for 887ms spanning block 11's due time, so it should have
built one block, but it built none and fired no sequencer action at all.

Every cluster member applies every committed payload, so the FSM now retains the
last 16 chained payloads, bounded by approximate size as well as by count, and
startSequencer replays whatever op-node is missing rather than relying on p2p
gossip or L1 derivation to deliver it. It then polls op-node's unsafe head and
only starts sequencing once adoption is observed, retrying op-node's own
head-mismatch rejection inside the same window. Catch-up and start share one
budget derived from shutdownCtx, so a whole attempt is bounded, cancellable, and
cannot hold the single action loop for two budgets in a row. A leader that is
already unhealthy, whose fallback is to hand leadership over anyway, uses a much
tighter budget.

A healthy leader that cannot bring its own op-node up to the committed head after
three attempts transfers leadership instead of retrying itself indefinitely. Only
that condition escalates: nothing committed to consensus yet, a degraded raft
barrier, a transient RPC failure, an op-node ahead of consensus, and this
conductor shutting down are all either transient or identical on every member, so
they are retried in place instead. op-node commits a sealed block to consensus
before it gossips it, which is why an op-node ahead of consensus cannot be one
member's problem alone. A transfer that fails is retried on the next action rather
than after another three failed starts.

Sequencing still only ever starts at the head consensus committed, and op-node
re-checks leadership on every start, so neither a double-active sequencer nor a
reorg of consensus-committed blocks is reachable.

A third defect is left for follow-up. planSequencerAction is only called at the
top of op-node's driver loop (op-node/rollup/driver/driver.go:299-317) and
forceStart sets nextActionOK and nextAction straight from the StartSequencer RPC
goroutine (op-node/rollup/sequencing/sequencer.go:745-750) without emitting an
event, so a freshly promoted sequencer does not begin building until some
unrelated event unblocks that select: an L1 head poll, the unsafe gap ticker at
2 * BlockTime, or a derivation step. It can idle up to ~2s past its first block
deadline and then burst. Both logs show it - the failing run took 243ms to fire
its first action, the passing run never fired one in 887ms - and it is a
production issue in its own right, but the flake is fixed without it.
op-conductor: recover when leader falls behind consensus unsafe head

op-conductor: bound raft shutdown

RaftConsensus.Shutdown waited on raft.Shutdown().Error() with no bound. That future
blocks in waitShutdown() until raft's internal goroutines have exited and carries no
deadline of its own, so a member that has lost quorum can leave it pending for as long
as the process lives. OpConductor.Stop shuts its components down in sequence, so
everything after consensus was stranded behind it.

That is what turned a single stuck test into a lost CI job: with sequencer1 gone and
sequencer2 unreachable, sequencer3 sat in the candidate loop and Shutdown blocked for
19 minutes until the package timeout killed the whole binary, taking the remaining
tests in it and the gotestsum rerun with it.

Wait a bounded time instead. raft closes the transport itself, but only after
waitShutdown returns, which is exactly what is stuck, so on giving up close it here:
that drops the listener and any in-flight peer connections raft's goroutines may be
waiting on, and gives raft a second bounded chance to unwind before Shutdown reports
that it did not.

Found while root-causing the TestSequencerFailover_ConductorRPC flake, whose primary
cause is fixed in the preceding commit. This half only contains the blast radius.

op-supernode: hold finalized instead of publishing activation anchor on zero FinalizedL1

A fresh virtual node has a zero-valued FinalizedL1 in its StatusTracker
until the first L1 finality poll fires. VerifiedBlockAtL1 treated that
zero ref as "nothing verified" and returned the interop activation
anchor cap, so the engine controller published the activation anchor as
the finalized head, poisoned the EL finalized label via FCU, and forced
a ~44k-block safe rewind on the next reset.

Two-part fix:
- VerifiedBlockAtL1 now returns an ErrNotStarted-wrapped error for a
  zero l1Block ("L1 finality view unknown"), so FinalizedL2Head holds
  the previous value via the existing HoldPrevious path instead of
  mapping to the activation-anchor cap.
- eth.PollBlockChanges now polls immediately on subscription instead of
  waiting a full interval (384s with op-node's default
  L1EpochPollInterval), closing the zero-FinalizedL1/SafeL1 window at
  the source.

Inverts the interop test subtest that asserted the old zero-ref
behavior, and adds a regression test for the priming poll.

Fixes #22127

op-node: guard super-authority anchor resolution against regressing EL heads

On a restart where the supernode's verifier state is lost (empty
verifiedDB while the chain is far past interop activation), the empty
verifier contributes the activation anchor and the engine controller
resolved it unconditionally: its downward protections
(superAuthorityFinalizedHead, crossSafeCache) are in-memory only and
empty on a fresh process, so the anchor seeded them instead of being
rejected, every FCU then published safe/finalized at the anchor, and
the next engine reset used those EL labels as its floor — a full
re-derivation from the anchor (observed on interop-reorg-4 as a reset
to genesis after a pod restart).

Harden the controller so a fresh process cannot be re-seeded below the
EL's own labels:
- initializeUnknowns checks localFinalizedHead instead of
  FinalizedHead(), so the super authority can no longer both skip the
  EL finalized-label load and pre-seed the cache with the anchor.
- The loaded EL finalized label seeds superAuthorityFinalizedHead, and
  the loaded EL safe label seeds the cross-safe cache: they are exactly
  the heads this node last published, so the existing monotonicity
  checks now hold across restarts.
- resolveAnchorAsSafe holds the cached cross-safe when the anchor is
  below it, mirroring applyFinalizedHeadCacheChecks on the finalized
  side.

A genuine bootstrap still resolves the anchor: the guards only refuse
downward movement relative to the labels the EL already has.

kona: match op-node span-batch uvarint decoding

kona decoded all six span-batch `uvarint` fields with
`unsigned_varint::decode::u64`, whose accept-set differs from op-node's
`binary.ReadUvarint` in both directions:

- Non-minimal encodings — `[0x81, 0x00]` (`1` with a redundant trailing
  zero) is a valid protobuf Base128 varint. op-node accepts it,
  `unsigned-varint` rejects it as `NotMinimal`.
- Ten-byte varints — a tenth byte terminating above `0x01` sets bits past
  63. op-node reports overflow, `unsigned-varint` returns `Ok` with the
  high bits silently discarded.

Either way a byzantine batcher can publish a span batch that one client
decodes and the other rejects, splitting derivation on identical L1 data.

All six fields (`rel_timestamp`, `l1_origin_num`, `block_count`,
`block_tx_count`, `tx_nonce`, `tx_gas`) now route through `read_uvarint`,
a port of `binary.ReadUvarint`. Encoding still uses
`unsigned_varint::encode::u64`, whose minimal output the new decoder
accepts in full.

Shared vectors pin the pair together: a field-level table on each side and
a whole span batch whose `block_count` is re-encoded non-minimally.

kona-sp1-proposer: port the op-succinct defend path

Port of upstream fault-proof (@ 13716c2c) defense: challenged games in the
owned set get a defense task (deadline-ascending, capped, per-game dedup)
that fetches the span's super roots, collects witnesses, obtains an SP1
super-aggregation proof bound to the signer, and submits prove(). The
existing resolution and claim tasks finish the game.

Departures from upstream, each forced by this repo's architecture:
- proving.rs replaces the single-chain host machinery with the super-root
  stack; the aggregation guest validates one shared l1Head, so the header
  chain walk is gone.
- Ownership is prestate-based (option A, #22111): prove, resolve, and claim
  are one set, keyed by loadable prestate artifacts. Sync loads every cached
  game's prestate so post-rotation games stay owned.
- Providers are Network (SPN request/poll, ported) and Mock (native-core,
  no ELFs, placeholder bytes; dev verifiers only). No cluster arm.
- Proving keys are per-prestate; setup verifies the aggregation vkey hashes
  to the on-chain prestate (the PR-1 deferred check). Poisoned prestates
  close the creation gate and heal only when artifacts change.
- Permanent unprovable verdicts are trust-gated on current_l1 so a stale
  mid-rewind supernode answer cannot burn an honest game's bond.
- Pre-submit re-check avoids guaranteed-revert prove() txs after long
  proving runs. No restart recovery, matching upstream.

Part of #21463. Fast finality is deliberately not ported (#22112).

op-reth: remove unsupported --minimal option (breaking change)

--minimal configures maximum pruning, including pruning block bodies to
a fixed 10,064-block window. op-node reads the L1-info deposit
transaction from historical block bodies during derivation, so a
--minimal datadir breaks EL sync (l2 block is missing L1 info deposit
tx). The docs have long said not to use it; now the binary enforces it.

The flag lives in upstream reth arg structs that op-reth reuses, so it
cannot be removed at the type level. Instead the in-tree cli crate
grows a small deny-list (DENIED_ARGS) of (subcommand, arg id, error)
entries: denied args are hidden from all help output and rejected
after parsing with an error that points operators at the supported
pruning recipe and docs page. The shared parse entrypoints
(parse_args, try_parse_args_from, and the new parse_with_denied_args
used by the op-reth binary) all route through the deny-list, and
CliApp::run carries a backstop check so binaries that build their clap
command directly (the vendored op-rbuilder) reject --minimal at
startup too.

Nodes previously started with --minimal now exit at startup with the
guidance message; their datadirs were already unsupported and need a
resync regardless.

The CLI surface snapshot is updated to render --minimal with a
[hidden] marker, documenting the deny decision. The bin crate no
longer uses clap directly, so the dependency edge is dropped.

op-core: move the PostExec payload decoder to op-core/types

The PostExec (0x7D) payload is a consensus wire format, but its only Go
definition lived in op-chain-ops/pkg/sdm, a chain-ops tooling package, while the
envelope carrying it (PostExecTx, PostExecTxType) lives in op-core/types. Move
PostExecPayload, SDMGasEntry, PostExecPayloadVersion and the decoder next to the
envelope and point the consumers at them, so the format lives in the package
that owns it rather than in the tooling that happened to need it first.

This is a move, not a de-duplication: one Go definition before, one after. What
is new is coverage. The decoder's strict framing (a single RLP value, no
trailing bytes, no short list) and its version check are now pinned by tests,
matching what op-alloy's PostExecPayload rejects at decode time.

No behaviour change. The decoder body is unchanged, and its consumers
(op-acceptance-tests, cmd/sdm-devnet) only read payload fields.

op-node: share the per-tx sequencer checks across batch types

checkSingularBatch delegated to checkSequencerTxData; checkSpanBatch carried its
own inline copy of the same rules. The copy had drifted: it never rejected
PostExec (0x7D) transactions before SDM activation, which checkSequencerTxData
has done since the type was introduced. It also shadowed the span's block index
with the transaction index inside the loop.

Extract checkSequencerTxs so both paths iterate a single implementation and drop
the inline copy. The span path now applies the PostExec activation gate too, so
the two batch types agree on which transaction types a sequencer may embed.

That behaviour change is unreachable in production, and it closes a divergence
rather than adding a rule. checkSpanBatch only runs pre-Holocene -- post-Holocene

activates at Lagoon, four forks after Holocene, so isSDM is always false here.
DeriveSpanBatch already rejects pre-SDM PostExec transactions when the span batch
is decoded.

row fails without this change.

between our lookup and the resend reaching a builder, making the resend
revert with GameAlreadyExists; clearing on that mistook an adoptable game
for a permanent failure and left the duplicate guard unarmed (sibling risk
in the sync-lag window).

A landed revert is final chain state with exactly two causes, so re-running
the lookup disambiguates: the uuid's game now exists (adopt it; games are
never deleted) or the cause is permanent (clear; a floating original would

kona-sp1-proposer: resolve in-flight creations by pool evidence, not resends

Adversarial review of the uuid-retry design found two defects: a resend
whose create would revert dies at fee estimation, which never yields the
landed-revert prefix, wedging the record forever (and the in-flight path
bypasses the parent-standing check); and pending-count nonces queue each
resend behind the stuck original, stacking same-uuid duplicates that all
revert once fees decay. Closing both properly required a parent
adjudication helper and pool checks, at which point the resend itself was
the complexity.

Drop the resend. The record still holds new proposals; each tick the
factory lookup adopts our landed game, and the record clears only when the
signer's pool drains (pending == latest), meaning nothing of ours can land
anymore. A visibly stuck transaction keeps holding; there is no time-based
clearing. Residual, documented: a transaction alive only in another node's
pool can land after the clear, re-creating the sibling case, which is
benign and self-healing (a valid own game whose bond the normal resolution
and claiming flow recovers).

op-reth: print a backtrace when an integration test dies on a signal

`p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` intermittently segfaults during teardown,
after its body has already passed (#20973). A binary killed by a signal produces
no Rust backtrace — `RUST_BACKTRACE` only covers panics — so five recurrences
over two months have yielded nothing beyond the signal number, and the crash has
never reproduced locally across 570+ attempts. Investigation is currently stalled
for want of a faulting stack.

Core dumps are not an option here: on the CircleCI Docker executor `/proc/sys` is
read-only so `core_pattern` cannot be set, and the host's pipe pattern makes the
kernel write the core outside the container. An in-process handler needs no
privileges, no artifacts and no CI configuration, and works locally too.

Install a handler for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS/SIGILL/SIGFPE/SIGABRT that reports the faulting
thread's name and address, then its stack. The thread name alone discriminates
between the candidate causes: a database `atexit` destructor racing its own live
threads, background threads outliving process exit, or a runtime teardown race.

The stack is emitted in two stages, which matters:

  - `backtrace_symbols_fd` first. It writes straight to the fd and does not call
    malloc, so it is safe here. This is the guaranteed output.
  - `std::backtrace::Backtrace` second, for names and line numbers. Its
    symbolization allocates heavily and faults a second time when called from a
    handler — killing the process before anything is printed, since SIGSEGV is
    blocked inside its own handler. Attempting it only after the reliable frames
    are already on the wire means that failure costs nothing.

The handler re-raises with the default disposition, so the process still dies
with the original signal and nextest still records a crash. That composes with
the retry added in the parent commit: nextest prints a failed attempt's stderr
even when a later attempt passes, so a recurrence yields a stack while the job
stays green.

`libc` is already a workspace dependency; this adds it as a dev-dependency only.

Instrumentation only — no behavior change to any test, and no effect unless a
fatal signal fires.

rejects OP synthetic txs (0x7E deposits, 0x7D post-exec) and silently
drops the OP receipt fee fields.

  demand — L1-safe, L2 only while go-ethereum resolves to op-geth.

  apis.ReceiptsFetcher.FetchReceipts returns optypes.Receipts; the

replica-healthcheck: switch providers to StaticJsonRpcProvider

Investigating a slow, linear memory leak (~5 MB/day per pod, ~85 B per
5s loop iteration) in the replica-healthcheck service. The signature
(perfectly linear growth, consistent across all pods, resets on pod
restart) points to a small per-RPC-call retention rather than a
metric-cardinality or buffer issue.

Non-Static JsonRpcProvider chains a detectNetwork() promise on every
send() call, which is the most plausible slow-retention source given
the code is otherwise stateless and holds no service-level references.
Switching to StaticJsonRpcProvider skips that path and lets us run
this replica as an A/B canary against the current fleet: if its line
goes flat while others keep climbing, root cause is confirmed.

Also fixes a latent null-deref: when getBlock(minBlock) returned null
the log line read `.number` off the null value, crashing the loop.

op-devstack: prevent one stalled dial from consuming ConnectP2P's whole budget

Root-causing the TestFollowSource_P2PSync flake (#22152): the peering
succeeded, but the admin_peers verification failed with
'dial tcp 127.0.0.1:40135: i/o timeout' after a websocket reconnect dial
was given the shared 30s wait.For context and the kernel never answered
that one loopback SYN. wait.For aborts on the first callback error, so a
single unanswered dial burned the entire budget even though the polled
condition became true ~5s in.

Fixes:
- tcpproxy: dial the upstream outside the proxy mutex so a slow upstream
  dial cannot stall other accepted connections, SetUpstream, or Close;
  bound each dial attempt with a context (net.Dial is not cancelled by
  the retry context); close the accepted conn when exiting on stop.
  Add tests for the package (none existed).
- ConnectP2P/DisconnectP2P: bound each admin_peers poll individually and
  retry only attempt timeouts within the unchanged 30s budget (a fresh
  attempt dials from a fresh source port); other errors still fail fast,
  and the last attempt error is surfaced on overall failure.

op-node: wake the driver loop when sequencer actions are armed

Sequencer.Start and Sequencer.Stop run on the admin RPC goroutine and set
nextAction/nextActionOK directly. The driver event loop only reads that
schedule at the top of an iteration, and is otherwise parked in its select,
so arming an action did not wake it. The newly promoted sequencer stayed idle
until an unrelated wakeup arrived (L1 head poll, unsafe-gap tick, derivation
step), then built its first block late. Stop had the mirror problem: the
armed timer survived, and fired a stale sequencer action afterwards.

The sequencer now signals a capacity-1 channel while holding the lock that
guards the schedule, and the event loop selects on it. The driver reads the
whole schedule on each iteration, so signals coalesce and a send is never
blocking.

planSequencerAction also forgets the deadline when it disarms, so re-arming
on the same instant still resets the timer.

Three defects in this PR's own hardening layers, found in a post-review
audit; upstream has no analog for any of them:

- response_trusted now requires current_l1 > verified_required_l1. The
  supernode API contract documents that data at current_l1 itself may
  still be incomplete (consumers gating on it must use strictly-greater),
  and this comparison gates PERMANENT GameUnprovable verdicts: at the old
  boundary a mid-reprocessing answer could condemn an honest game and
  forfeit its bond. Boundary case pinned in the unprovable-guard test.
- fetch_game classifies CHALLENGER_WINS games as terminally invalid at
  discovery (contract-terminal: children revert InvalidParentGame). An
  own game lost while held pending previously stayed pending forever,
  since owned pending entries are eviction-exempt, burning ~10 RPCs and
  a WARN per tick for the process lifetime.
- the creation gate no longer awaits SP1 key setup inline: the gate runs
  on the scheduler path (upstream-parity placement), so first network-mode
  use froze sync and defense scans for the whole setup. Setup now runs
  once per entry on a background task behind a one-shot latch; creation
  stays paused until the verdict lands, and a poisoned verdict still
  closes the gate until corrected artifacts are published.

op-node: reject unhandled payload statuses in CommitBlock

EngineController.CommitBlock switched on the engine's NewPayload status with
no default case, so it only stopped on INVALID and INVALID_BLOCK_HASH. Every
other status fell through to SetUnsafeHead + forkchoice update, meaning
INVALID_TERMINAL_BLOCK, and any status a future engine returns that this
version does not know about, silently became the node's unsafe head.

Invert the switch to an explicit accept-list and reject everything else.
VALID, SYNCING and ACCEPTED keep their current behaviour of proceeding to the
forkchoice update, matching insertUnsafePayload, so no status a conforming
engine returns on this path changes meaning.

The rejection message also formatted `err`, which is provably nil there: the
non-nil case returns a few lines earlier, so the error always read
"execution invalid: <nil>" and dropped the engine's validationError and
latestValidHash. Use eth.NewPayloadErr, which reports both.

replica-healthcheck: switch providers to StaticJsonRpcProvider (#694)

Investigating a slow, linear memory leak (~5 MB/day per pod, ~85 B per
5s loop iteration) in the replica-healthcheck service. The signature
(perfectly linear growth, consistent across all pods, resets on pod
restart) points to a small per-RPC-call retention rather than a
metric-cardinality or buffer issue.

Non-Static JsonRpcProvider chains a detectNetwork() promise on every
send() call, which is the most plausible slow-retention source given
the code is otherwise stateless and holds no service-level references.
Switching to StaticJsonRpcProvider skips that path and lets us run
this replica as an A/B canary against the current fleet: if its line
goes flat while others keep climbing, root cause is confirmed.

Also fixes a latent null-deref: when getBlock(minBlock) returned null
the log line read `.number` off the null value, crashing the loop.

op-node: Validate span batch overlap content against the safe chain in Holocene

The Holocene batch stage validates span batches with prefix checks only
(checkSpanBatchPrefix): for a batch overlapping the safe chain, the 20-byte
parent_check of the pre-overlap ancestor is verified, but the overlapping
elements' contents never are - unlike the legacy full checks (checkSpanBatch),
which fetch every overlapped payload and compare transactions and L1 origins.
Dropping that comparison was sound under a pre-interop invariant: the safe
chain was derived from this same batch data, so overlap content provably
agrees with it.

Interop deposits-only block replacement breaks that invariant: the canonical
block at a replaced height no longer matches the batch element it was
originally derived from, and the prefix checks never notice.
GetSingularBatches past-skips every element at or below the safe head without
inspection, the deny check only fires when a payload at the denied height is
proposed, and the channel flush is a side effect of that deny event - so a
walk anchored at the replacement silently splices the remainder of an
invalidated lineage onto the canonical chain. The derived chain ends up
depending on where the pipeline (re-)anchored relative to the replacement,
observed on devnet interop-reorg-5 as nodes deriving different chains from
identical L1 data.

Reinstate the full overlap content validation in the Holocene batch stage: a
prefix-accepted span batch that overlaps the safe chain has every overlapped
element compared against the canonical block at the same height (transactions
and L1 origin number), reusing the exact legacy comparison, now factored into
checkSpanBatchOverlap and shared by both the pre-Holocene and Holocene paths.
A mismatch drops the batch and flushes the channel, like any other invalid
batch under Holocene; a payload fetch failure is Undecided (retried).

This restores the invariant that a batch overlapping the safe chain must
agree with the safe chain, making derivation anchor-invariant across
replacement boundaries: re-deriving from any anchor yields the same chain.

Alternative to #22214, which gates the same comparison to deny-listed heights
to avoid consensus-visible changes on non-interop chains and payload fetches
on reset walk-backs; this version needs no deny list plumbing at all.
