The Holocene span batch prefix checks (checkSpanBatchPrefix) do not validate
the contents of batch elements that overlap the safe chain, unlike the legacy
full checks (checkSpanBatch). That is sound only while the safe chain is
guaranteed to agree with previously accepted batch data. An interop
deposits-only block replacement breaks that guarantee: the canonical block at
the replaced height no longer matches the batch element it was derived from.

Without this check, a span batch carrying a since-replaced block is silently
past-skipped over the replacement (GetSingularBatches drops elements at or
below the safe head without inspection), and the remainder of the invalidated
lineage is spliced onto the canonical chain. The deny-triggered
deposits-only replacement and channel flush only fire when the denied block is
re-proposed, so the derived chain ends up depending on where the pipeline
(re-)anchored relative to the replacement - observed on devnet
interop-reorg-5 as two nodes deriving different chains from identical L1 data.

Reinstate the legacy overlap content comparison, gated to heights that carry
deny list entries: an applied replacement is the only event that lets a
legitimate batch's overlap disagree with the safe chain, so the comparison is
restricted to those heights and is a no-op while the deny list is empty. A
mismatch drops the batch and flushes the channel, restoring
anchor-independence of derivation across replacement boundaries.

op-node: optionally continue the containing span after a block replacement

When a denied block is replaced with a deposits-only version, DepositsOnlyAttributes
flushes the channel the replaced block came from. That discards the remainder of
the span, so the lineage is handed to whichever channel comes next on L1.

A node that already held the following blocks locally re-applies them onto the
replacement and stays on the lineage the batcher continued. A node deriving the
same L1 data from scratch flushes, adopts the next channel, and dead-ends: no
batch on L1 ever chains onto its result, so it wedges permanently with no
recovery. On devnet interop-reorg-5 (chain 420120192, replaced block 13460)
three independent from-genesis syncs reproduced this.

--rollup.replacement-continues-span keeps the containing channel buffered so the
span tail re-applies onto the replacement. With it, a from-genesis supernode
derived the live chain: 13461=0xc476a12f (seq 4, origin 11391103), 13465=0x5d9e2aae,
13466=0x38e8ea21, 14245=0x12236ab4 — every value matching the live cluster,
where the same node without the flag produced channel B's 13461=0x67c34c2c and
wedged.

Off by default and hidden. Nodes running with and without it derive different
chains from identical L1 data, so making this the default is a spec-level
change, and the safety of retaining channel state across an invalidation still
needs review.
op-node: optionally continue the containing span after a block replac…

op-node: test the wedge when derivation anchors between two replacements

The live cluster survived its invalidation because its reset anchor landed
exactly ON a replacement: finality was pinned there, and a replacement is the
last block the pre- and post-invalidation branches share, so the denied block
was past-skipped and the containing span's tail re-applied.

An anchor between two replacements has no such protection. It re-proposes the
second denied block, the deny-triggered replacement flushes the containing
channel, and the next thing on L1 is a re-batch built on the other lineage,
which cannot chain onto the replacement. That wedges a node which never wiped
anything.

Pins all three legs: the re-propose, the re-batch dropping against the
replacement, and the span tail continuing when the channel is kept.

op-devstack: let acceptance suites select the sequencer EL binary

Adds an environment seam so a suite outside this repo can re-run these
acceptance tests against its own execution-layer build as the sequencer EL,
without forking any test bodies:

- DEVSTACK_L2EL_BINARY names a CLI-superset binary to launch instead of
  "op-reth", resolved through the existing rustbin overrides.
- DEVSTACK_L2EL_ARGS carries whitespace-separated extra CLI arguments for it.

Both unset leaves the option slice empty, so in-tree runs are unchanged. This
mirrors the existing DEVSTACK_L2CL_KIND / ResolveMixedL2CLKind pattern, which
exists so the kona suite can re-run these same tests against a different
consensus client.

The args variable is not cosmetic: a superset binary may bind a listener the
harness knows nothing about, and the harness can only randomize ports it knows
about. A fixed default port on an unknown listener collides as soon as a node
starts, since every node in a run shares one host.

Applied at sequencer EL start sites only — the default single-chain primary, the
single-chain interop runtime, the supernode runtimes including the
interop-filter variant, the sync-tester variant, and the SDM suite's explicit
node specs. Verifier and follow-node paths are deliberately untouched, so the
overridden binary builds while stock op-reth verifies; any block it produces
that stock op-reth rejects fails the run. Overriding both would let a
self-consistent divergence pass unnoticed.

Proofs history is disabled whenever a superset binary is named. The mixed
runtime enables it on every op-reth node, but a binary that replaces the payload
service cannot host op-reth's proof-history launcher, so the flag would be
either silently ignored or refused at startup.

op-devstack: gate EL override args behind the override binary

Renames the env seam to DEVSTACK_L2EL_OVERRIDE_BINARY / DEVSTACK_L2EL_OVERRIDE_ARGS
so it reads as an escape hatch rather than a general knob, and distinguishes it from
the pre-existing DEVSTACK_L2EL_KIND.

The args only ever qualify an override binary, so naming them without one is now
rejected instead of silently applied to stock op-reth — a stale value in the
environment would otherwise quietly alter an in-tree run. Same reasoning applies to
EL kinds with no op-reth analogue: op-geth and op-rbuilder now reject op-reth options
rather than dropping them, so an override can't look like it took effect on a node
that never saw it.

The env-parsing decision moves into a pure helper so the rejection path is directly
testable, and the precedence comment is corrected: option ordering only decides the
binary, since proofs-history disablement is one-way and extra args accumulate.

* fix(kona,security): close three unauthenticated kona attack surfaces (#21753)

* fix(kona,security): reject truncated span-batch bitlist to match op-node

SpanBatchBits::decode previously silently zero-padded truncated input,
while op-node's decodeSpanBatchBits (rollup/derive/span_batch_util.go)
returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF for the same input via io.ReadFull.

This asymmetry caused Kona to derive a different L2 state than op-node
for the same L1 calldata: a truncated protected_bits field for a legacy
transaction flipped the EIP-155 protection flag from true to false in
Kona while op-node rejected the batch entirely. Under CANNON_KONA
respected fault-proof program (Karst upgrade, 2026-06-17), Kona-in-Cannon
is authoritative for dispute resolution, so the divergent state could
finalize on-chain.

Fix: add SpanBatchError::BitfieldTooShort and return it when b.len() <
buffer_len, matching op-node's rejection semantics.

Regression tests cover: empty input at bit_length=1, and 1-byte input
at bit_length=16.

* fix(kona,security): bound gossipsub snappy pre-alloc by MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE

compute_message_id (registered as gossipsub message_id_fn) called
snap::raw::Decoder::decompress_vec on every inbound PUBLISH before any
signature or application-level validation. decompress_vec pre-allocates
a Vec<u8> whose size is read from the snappy frame header — an
attacker-controlled field bounded only by u32::MAX (~4 GiB).

A 7-byte snappy frame declaring u32::MAX decompressed length forces a
~4 GiB heap allocation. Amplification: 613,566,756x. On resource-limited
hosts the process aborts via handle_alloc_error; on Linux overcommit the
OOM killer fires. Attacker reconnects with fresh peer ID and re-publishes;
persistent restart-loop. Gossipsub mesh (mesh_D=8) fans out to every peer.

Op-node's parallel BuildMsgIdFn in op-node/p2p/gossip.go performs the
correct pre-check via snappy.DecodedLen(pmsg.Data) bounded to
maxGossipSize. This commit adds the same guard to Kona.

Regression test covers the exact 7-byte bomb payload and asserts that
compute_message_id returns the invalid-snappy hash branch without
allocating.

* fix(kona,security): gate admin RPC on --rpc.enable-admin; default bind to 127.0.0.1

Three related fixes to close an unauthenticated admin-RPC exposure:

1. rust/kona/crates/node/service/src/service/node.rs — gate the
   AdminRpc module merge on config.enable_admin(). Previously the admin
   namespace was registered unconditionally on every Kona node, on the
   default 0.0.0.0 listener, with no authentication middleware. The
   --rpc.enable-admin CLI flag was parsed but never consulted at the
   registration site.

2. rust/kona/bin/node/src/flags/rpc.rs — change default --rpc.addr from
   0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) to 127.0.0.1 (localhost). Operators who need
   remote RPC access must opt in explicitly. Matches op-geth's default
   posture.

3. rust/kona/crates/node/rpc/src/admin.rs — add the same
   sequencer_admin_client.is_some() gate to admin_post_unsafe_payload
   that every other admin method already has. Previously,
   admin_post_unsafe_payload was reachable on non-sequencer nodes,
   allowing a forged execution payload to be injected as the local
   unsafe head without going through P2P validation.

4. rust/kona/crates/node/rpc/src/config.rs — add the RpcBuilder::
   enable_admin() accessor used by (1).

Reference: op-node's admin API is opt-in via the same
--rpc.enable-admin flag and defaults to 127.0.0.1.

* fix(kona,security): bound gossip payload decode path against snappy bomb

The B2 fix bounded snappy pre-allocation only in `compute_message_id`
(the gossipsub `message_id_fn`). But that function only computes an id;
every inbound gossip message is then decoded via
`OpNetworkPayloadEnvelope::decode_v*`, which calls `decompress_vec` with
no bound. The identical tiny snappy frame declaring a huge decompressed
length still OOM-kills the node at that second, unbounded site.

Extract `snappy_decompressed_len_within_bound` and apply it in the block
handler before `decode_v*`, mirroring op-node, which bounds
`DecodedLen <= maxGossipSize` in both its `message_id_fn` and its gossip
topic validator.

Make the regression tests sound. The previous bomb test passed even
against unbounded code (`vec![0; u32::MAX]` is a lazily-committed calloc
under overcommit, so it never faulted 4 GiB). Add a test that a frame
which *validly* decompresses to more than `MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE` takes the
invalid-snappy domain — this fails against an unbounded implementation —
plus direct tests of the guard predicate.

* test(op-devstack): funder waits for balance >= target, not exact (#21790)

* test(op-devstack): funder waits for balance >= target, not exact

`Funder.Fund` / `FundAtLeast` waited for the EOA balance to become
*exactly* the expected post-funding value (`WaitForBalance`, `==`). This
hangs forever when the wallet is over-funded, which happens under faucet
retries.

`dsl.Faucet.Fund` retries `RequestETH` up to 3x. When the target chain's
sequencer stalls long enough for the client-side request to exceed its
deadline, the in-flight funding tx stays in the mempool while the retry
issues a *new* faucet tx at the next nonce. Once the sequencer recovers,
both the original and the retry tx are included, so the EOA receives the
funding amount twice. The exact-match wait can then never be satisfied
and the test fails with "Condition never satisfied: awaiting balance to
be updated" after TransactionTimeout.

Observed in CI on `TestPreNoInbox` (memory-all-opn-op-reth): faucet
account dev-faucet-902 published nonce 0 (03f306) and, after a ~22s
op-reth "Cannot seal block, payload ID is unknown" stall tripped the
faucet client deadline, nonce 1 (e915bb). Block 81 sealed with txs=2 —
both transfers landed — funding the EOA 0.02 ETH while the test waited
for exactly 0.01 ETH.

- Add `EOA.WaitForBalanceAtLeast` (lower-bound wait). Keep exact-match
  `WaitForBalance` for sender-side callers whose expected balance is
  below the starting balance (a >= wait would return immediately).
- `Fund` / `FundAtLeast` now use the lower-bound wait: a funder only
  cares that the wallet has enough.
- Drop the redundant exact `WaitForBalance` in RunOperatorFeeTest that
  followed `NewFundedEOA` and re-introduced the same hang.

post-deposit balance is a decreasing balance where an at-least wait
would return immediately and defeat the check.

* deps: bump andybalholm/brotli to v1.2.2 (#21799)

Upgrades the brotli decoder used by op-node derivation (BatchReader,
rollup/derive/channel.go) from v1.1.0. andybalholm v1.2.0 fixed its handling of
truncated streams: it now returns io.ErrUnexpectedEOF instead of a clean io.EOF
when input ends before the last meta-block completes, matching the C reference
(libbrotlidec) and RFC 7932 §9.3.

This bump is behaviorally inert for derivation on its own: op-node's
ChannelInReader.NextBatch collapses io.EOF and io.ErrUnexpectedEOF into the same
NextChannel + NotEnoughData outcome, and rlp.Stream already surfaces
ErrUnexpectedEOF for a mid-item EOF. Verified with a differential over the real
BatchReader (fixed channel decoded at v1.1.0 vs v1.2.2, full stream + all
truncation offsets + sampled corruptions): byte-identical batch output.

Its value is as an enabler for strict channel decompression
(ethereum-optimism/protocol-team#84): it gives op-node the signal to distinguish
a truncated channel, which the strict-decompression rule can act on. Context in
#21793.

* op-acceptance-tests: make intentbuilder deactivate forks correctly

op-deployer merges user configs with defaults, potentially overwriting
the user's configs in some cases.

The intentbuilder.WithForkAtOffset would incorrectly *delete* a key in
its hardfork mapping when the caller wanted to deactivate a fork. When
merged with op-deployer's default config, the default would take
precedence because there is no explicit override.

The fix in the intentbuilder is twofold:

1. Explicitly set the deactivated hardfork to `nil` in the
   intentbuilder's mapping.
2. Set all subsequent forks to `nil` in the intentbuilder's mapping,

forks.go and rollup/types.go--resolve those test failures.

* ci: fix rust shared-cache poisoning (#21832)

The shared rust dep-cache key is immutable, so after a Cargo.lock change
the first job to save wins. Fast jobs that download no crates (typos,
fmt, zepter, cargo-deny) or only one package's subset (compact-codec,
registry/superchain snapshots, Docker-built prestate publish) could
freeze an empty or partial registry that every later build restored.

- Drop rust-save-build-cache from jobs that don't populate the full
  cargo registry (restores kept); document the rule at the command.
- Bump the cache version 16 -> 18 to evict the poisoned keys.
- Add a pre-save guard that fails loudly on an empty registry.
- Remove the dead cache-key `prefix` parameter (unused since #21310)
  and its 18 call sites, which implied isolation that doesn't exist.

OpHandler::catch_error only reset the journal on the deposit error path, so a
non-deposit tx that failed validation left its sender EIP-2929-warm in the
shared journal. On the SDM Produce block-building path a later committed tx
could then be billed a warm access attributed to a tx that never entered the

builder-vs-validator gas mismatch that rejects the block.

errors, matching upstream revm's EthHandler::catch_error and mirroring Base's

* test(op-rbuilder): warm-leak regression for skipped failed candidate

Pin the SDM warm-set leak at the layer that ships in the sequencer. In
PostExecMode::Produce, op-rbuilder's execute_best_transactions loop attempts a
candidate, sees it rejected, and skips it (continue) while building the rest
of the block on the same EVM. Before the op-revm catch_error fix, the skipped
tx left its sender EIP-2929-warm, so a later included tx was billed a warm
access for a tx that never entered the block — diverging from a validator that
never ran the skipped tx.

Two variants cover the validation errors that reproduce it, mirroring the
alloy-op-evm suite: NonceTooLow and EIP-3607 (contract sender). Each injects
[A (fails, skipped), B] via PayloadTransactionsFixed (the tx pool would
pre-filter the invalid A), where B does a BALANCE on A's sender, and asserts
the block's pre-refund EVM gas is identical with and without the skipped A.
Both verified red (2500-gas divergence) against an op-revm that does not
discard the journal on non-deposit errors, green once it does.

Parameterizes the existing payload_builder_ctx test helper with post_exec_mode.

op-reth: remove unsupported --minimal option (breaking change)

--minimal configures maximum pruning, including pruning block bodies to
a fixed 10,064-block window. op-node reads the L1-info deposit
transaction from historical block bodies during derivation, so a
--minimal datadir breaks EL sync (l2 block is missing L1 info deposit
tx). The docs have long said not to use it; now the binary enforces it.

The flag lives in upstream reth arg structs that op-reth reuses, so it
cannot be removed at the type level. Instead the in-tree cli crate
grows a small deny-list (DENIED_ARGS) of (subcommand, arg id, error)
entries: denied args are hidden from all help output and rejected
after parsing with an error that points operators at the supported
pruning recipe and docs page. The shared parse entrypoints
(parse_args, try_parse_args_from, and the new parse_with_denied_args
used by the op-reth binary) all route through the deny-list, and
CliApp::run carries a backstop check so binaries that build their clap
command directly (the vendored op-rbuilder) reject --minimal at
startup too.

Nodes previously started with --minimal now exit at startup with the
guidance message; their datadirs were already unsupported and need a
resync regardless.

The CLI surface snapshot is updated to render --minimal with a
[hidden] marker, documenting the deny decision. The bin crate no
longer uses clap directly, so the dependency edge is dropped.

op-devstack: make the conductor preset produce one canonical chain

The MinimalWithConductors preset came up as a cluster whose chain never
advanced past genesis, which went unnoticed while the only conductor
acceptance test asserted Raft state alone (#21902). It could also start
from divergent unsafe forks because all three sequencers ran before the
Raft cluster and p2p mesh existed.

Make the preset a deterministic live HA cluster:

- Start every sequencer stopped, seed sequencing on the bootstrap node,
  then freeze the seeded head and require every follower to reach that
  exact head before conductor control loops resume. This both initializes
  the fresh Raft FSM and prevents failover to an incompatible follower.
- Mesh the nodes over CL p2p only. EL peering is unnecessary because unsafe
  blocks reach follower ELs through CL gossip and the engine API, and it is
  flaky against op-reth subprocesses (#18570). Register the same CL mesh
  with the frontend lifecycle so tests that restart nodes restore it.

op-ufm: fix memory leaks in provider tx pool and RPC clients (#685)

* op-ufm: fix memory leaks in provider tx pool and RPC clients

Long-running op-ufm pods grow memory monotonically (see PR description).
Three sources:

1. TransactionPool entries were only removed on the "seen by every provider"
   success path. Receipt-retrieval timeouts and non-NotFound receipt errors
   returned without deleting, and any provider that never observed a tx
   permanently pinned it. Add a defer-based cleanup on the RoundTrip failure
   paths plus an age-based GC pass at the top of each Heartbeat as a safety
   net for the "success but never propagated" case.
2. iclients.Dial was called on every Heartbeat and RoundTrip interval and
   the returned ethclient.Client was never closed, leaking connections,
   file descriptors, and transport goroutines. Cache the client on Provider,
   dial lazily on first use, and Close() on Shutdown. Expose Close() on
   InstrumentedEthClient to delegate.
3. Same pattern for the signer client (recreated per RoundTrip). Upstream
   SignerClient has no Close in the pinned version, so we just cache and
   reuse a single instance.

op-devstack: make the conductor preset produce one canonical chain

The MinimalWithConductors preset came up as a cluster whose chain never
advanced past genesis, which went unnoticed while the only conductor
acceptance test asserted Raft state alone (#21902). It could also start
from divergent unsafe forks because all three sequencers ran before the
Raft cluster and p2p mesh existed.

Make the preset a deterministic live HA cluster:

- Start every sequencer stopped, seed sequencing on the bootstrap node,
  then freeze the seeded head and require every follower to reach that
  exact head before conductor control loops resume. This both initializes
  the fresh Raft FSM and prevents failover to an incompatible follower.
- Mesh the nodes over CL p2p only. EL peering is unnecessary because unsafe
  blocks reach follower ELs through CL gossip and the engine API, and it is
  flaky against op-reth subprocesses (#18570). Register the same CL mesh
  with the frontend lifecycle so tests that restart nodes restore it.

op-node: run sequencer on its own goroutine

The sequencer no longer emits events on the block-production path: it
calls the engine controller directly (StartBuild/SealBuild/
ProcessPayload) and receives results as return values, and it paces
itself with its own timer in RunLoop, run on a dedicated goroutine
started by the driver.

External signals (forkchoice updates, resets, temporary errors,
derivation build activity) are ingested through an ordered mailbox:
OnEvent appends to a small log under a micro-mutex and fires a cap-1
wake channel, never blocking the event loop; the sequencer goroutine
replays entries in arrival order. Adjacent forkchoice updates coalesce
to the latest. Fan-out error events are still emitted (enqueue is
thread-safe).

The driver loses all sequencer timer plumbing (planSequencerAction,
sequencerTimer, sequencerCh, SequencerActionEvent) along with the
now-unused SequencerActionEvent type and SequencerIface.NextAction.

Closes #19263

op-node: add direct-call build methods to engine controller

Extract the build-start, build-seal, and payload-process event handlers
into unlocked cores shared between the event path and new exported
methods StartBuild, SealBuild, and ProcessPayload, which take the engine
mutex and are callable from any goroutine. The direct path returns
results and sentinel errors (ErrStaleBuild, ErrPayloadDenied,
ErrPayloadInvalid) instead of emitting BuildStarted/BuildSealed/
PayloadSuccess events; state notifications (ForkchoiceUpdateEvent,
UnsafeUpdateEvent) are emitted unchanged. The event path is a pure
delegation and behaves identically.

Also adds the SequencerEngine interface consumed by the sequencer.

op-alloy,op-reth: report zero DA footprint on PostExec receipts

Jovian repurposes the receipt's `blobGasUsed` field to carry the
transaction's DA footprint. The RPC receipt builder recomputed that value
from the tx bytes for every transaction once Jovian was active, with no
type gate, so a PostExec (`0x7D`) tx reported a non-zero footprint — the
Fjord minimum-size floor guarantees at least `100 * daFootprintGasScalar`,
never zero.

The block-level accumulator in alloy-op-evm already excludes the `0x7D`,
and `blobGasUsed` is not a consensus receipt field, so the executor's zero
never reaches the RPC layer. Gate the recomputation on the tx type instead,
restoring `sum(receipt.blobGasUsed) == header.blobGasUsed`.

Adds `OpTransaction::is_post_exec` as a provided method so callers behind
the generic bound can test the type without the inherent
`OpTxEnvelope::is_post_exec`, which the bound does not expose. All three
existing implementors, including the extended envelope used by downstream
chains, compile unchanged.

The block-level exclusion itself was correct but untested. op-geth
recomputed the footprint independently and so acted as a cross-check; it is
no longer a supported verifier, which leaves the accumulator unguarded. Add
a test asserting a `0x7D` leaves `da_footprint_used` unchanged, including a
check that a counted `0x7D` would have moved the total, so the assertion
cannot pass vacuously.

The two acceptance tests that recompute a block's footprint from its
transactions skipped deposits only, so they would disagree with the header
once a `0x7D` appears. Skip it in both, and assert the stronger property
while there: a PostExec receipt reports zero.

Follow-up to #22219, which closed the same gap in
`op-core/fees.CalcDAFootprint`.

Specification: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/specs/pull/926

Extract `da_footprint_gas(encoded, scalar)` in op-revm, next to
`estimate_tx_compressed_size`: the arithmetic was duplicated in the block
executor, the RPC receipt builder, and two tests. Which txs are charged stays at
the call sites, because the layers differ — the block total excludes deposits and
the `0x7D`, while a receipt reports zero only for the `0x7D`. A method on the tx
does not work here: op-revm depends on op-alloy-consensus (not the reverse), so
the trait cannot reach the FLZ estimator, and a `&self` method would force a
re-encode where the executor reuses `tx_env.encoded_bytes()`.

Revert the `0x7D` guards in the Jovian acceptance suites. Both callers pass
`sysgo.WithJovianAtGenesis`, which writes an explicit nil offset for every later
fork, so Lagoon — and therefore SDM — can never be active there and the branch
was unreachable. Assert the invariant where a `0x7D` does occur instead: the SDM
suite now checks that the `0x7D` receipt reports a zero footprint and that the
non-deposit receipts still sum to the header's `blobGasUsed`, with a positive
total so it cannot pass vacuously.

Order `OpTransaction::is_post_exec` before `as_post_exec`, matching the deposit
pair, and run the receipt test on a Lagoon-active schedule — a `0x7D` at a
Jovian-only timestamp is not a reachable state. No named chain schedules Lagoon
yet, hence the hand-built fork list.

op-reth: give Lagoon its own activation in the PostExec receipt test

Lagoon is a hardfork of its own, and the test schedule conflated it with Jovian:
it restated Jovian..Lagoon at `OP_MAINNET_JOVIAN_TIMESTAMP` on top of a schedule
that already carried Jovian and Karst. `OpChainHardforks` resolves an activation
positionally (`forks[fork.idx()]`), so those duplicate rows shifted every later
fork by one — `op_fork_activation(Lagoon)` was reading a *Karst* row, and only
returned a sane value because all three forks shared one timestamp. It also
placed Lagoon before Karst's real activation.

Append a single Lagoon entry two seconds after Karst instead, and run the test at
that timestamp. Two assertions pin the appended row and Karst's own row, so a
schedule that shifts again fails loudly: the gate under test is Jovian + tx type,
which would not have noticed either way.

op-node: gate local-safe derivation on cross-safe verification lag

When a SuperAuthority verifier is registered, derivation currently free-runs
arbitrarily far ahead of the cross-safe verified frontier. A late block
invalidation then rewinds everything derived past the invalidation point: on
interop-reorg-5 a resyncing supernode ran local-safe ~16.9k blocks ahead of
the verifier, and the resulting engine rewind walked back ~16.8k blocks over
~95 minutes of engine_newPayload timeouts.

Add verifier.max-cross-safe-lag (default 0 = disabled, no behavior change):
when local-safe exceeds cross-safe by more than the window, SyncStep backs
off before requesting pending-safe updates, pausing local-safe promotion
until the verifier catches up. The verifier consumes already-derived blocks
only, so it always makes progress while derivation holds, and OnL1Unsafe
re-requests a step every L1 block. Worst-case rewind depth becomes the
configured window instead of the full backfill sprint.

The supernode inherits the flag per-vnode automatically via FullDynamicFlags
(OP_SUPERNODE_VN_ALL_VERIFIER_MAX_CROSS_SAFE_LAG).

op-reth: report both gas senses to the commit hook

`on_commit` reported only the post-settlement canonical gas, while block-limit
admission in `is_tx_over_limits` measures the pre-settlement `cumulative_evm_gas_used`.
A `PayloadTransactionsWithCommitHook` implementor whose own admission check mirrors
the block-limit check therefore accumulated a different quantity than the builder
enforces against: with SDM refunds accruing, its total falls behind by the accrued
refund and it yields transactions the builder then refuses, dropping the sender's
descendants via `mark_invalid`.

Replace the `u64` with a `CommittedTxGas { canonical_gas_used, evm_gas_used }` so each
consumer picks the sense its own question needs. The field names match the two
identifiers already used where the values are produced in `alloy-op-evm`, and both
values are already locals at the call site.

needs to verify executing messages referencing initiating messages in that

databases are preserved for recovery (remove the interop data dir and restart

op-alloy,op-reth: report zero DA footprint on PostExec receipts

Jovian repurposes the receipt's `blobGasUsed` field to carry the transaction's
DA footprint. op-reth's RPC receipt builder recomputed that value from the tx
bytes for every transaction once Jovian was active, with no type gate, so a
PostExec (`0x7D`) tx reported a non-zero footprint — the Fjord minimum-size
floor guarantees at least `100 * daFootprintGasScalar`, never zero.

The block-level accumulator in alloy-op-evm already excludes the `0x7D`, and
`blobGasUsed` is not a consensus receipt field, so the executor's zero never
reaches the RPC layer. Gate the recomputation on the tx type instead, restoring
`sum(receipt.blobGasUsed) == header.blobGasUsed`.

Adds `OpTransaction::is_post_exec` as a provided method so callers behind the
generic bound can test the type without the inherent
`OpTxEnvelope::is_post_exec`, which the bound does not expose. All three
existing implementors, including the extended envelope used by downstream
chains, compile unchanged. It is ordered before `as_post_exec`, matching the
deposit pair.

Extract `da_footprint_gas(encoded, scalar)` in op-revm, next to
`estimate_tx_compressed_size`: the arithmetic was duplicated in the block
executor, the RPC receipt builder, and two tests. Which txs are charged stays at
the call sites, because the layers differ — the block total excludes deposits
and the `0x7D`, while a receipt reports zero only for the `0x7D`. A method on
the tx does not work here: op-revm depends on op-alloy-consensus (not the
reverse), so the trait cannot reach the FLZ estimator, and a `&self` method
would force a re-encode where the executor reuses `tx_env.encoded_bytes()`.

The block-level exclusion itself was correct but untested. op-geth recomputed
the footprint independently and so acted as a cross-check; it is no longer a
supported verifier, which leaves the accumulator unguarded. Add a test
asserting a `0x7D` leaves `da_footprint_used` unchanged, including a check that
a counted `0x7D` would have moved the total, so the assertion cannot pass
vacuously.

The receipt test runs on a Lagoon-active schedule, since a `0x7D` at a
Jovian-only timestamp is not a reachable state — SDM rides Lagoon. No named
chain schedules Lagoon yet, hence the hand-built fork list, which appends a
single entry two seconds after Karst rather than restating the tail of the
schedule: `OpChainHardforks` resolves an activation positionally
(`forks[fork.idx()]`), so a duplicate row shifts every later fork by one. Two
assertions pin the appended row and Karst's own row, so a schedule that shifts
again fails loudly — the gate under test is Jovian + tx type, which would not
have noticed either way.

End to end, the invariant is asserted in the SDM acceptance suite — Lagoon at
genesis with SDM opted in, the only in-tree chain whose blocks contain a
`0x7D`. It checks that the `0x7D` receipt reports zero and that the non-deposit
receipts still sum to the header's `blobGasUsed`, with a positive total so it
cannot pass vacuously. The Jovian suites pin Jovian at genesis
(`sysgo.WithJovianAtGenesis` writes an explicit nil offset for every later
fork), so Lagoon — and therefore SDM — can never be active there, which is why
the invariant is not asserted in those suites.

Deposit receipts also report a non-zero `blobGasUsed`, even though deposits
contribute zero to the block total. specs#926 does not cover it and changing it
is a user-visible RPC change, so it is left alone — it is also why
`da_footprint_gas` takes bytes and a scalar and leaves the exclusion to its
callers.

The receipt tests move to a file of their own, `eth/receipt/tests.rs`, the split
`builder.rs` and `maintain.rs` already use in this crate: `receipt.rs` was 1046
lines, two thirds of them tests. The module is renamed `test` -> `tests` to match
the crate convention, which every other module in it already follows. No test
body changes.

Follow-up to #22219, which closed the same gap in
`op-core/fees.CalcDAFootprint`.

Specification: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/specs/pull/926

op-node: encode post-exec span batch txs without go-ethereum

The span batch format transposes each transaction into its envelope
fields, so unlike the singular batch — which carries opaque transactions —
the encoder has to interpret every transaction. AddTxs did that through
go-ethereum's typed decoding, which only accepts the 0x7D post-exec class
while go-ethereum resolves to op-geth.

Post-exec transactions now take their own arm, dispatched on the type
byte: they are synthetic and unsigned, so all transposed envelope fields
are zero and only the opaque payload is carried. Deposits are never
batched, so what remains on the go-ethereum arm are signed, standard
transactions — the unreachable post-exec cases in newSpanBatchTx and
convertVToYParity are dropped, and a post-exec tx reaching either now
fails loudly instead of relying on op-geth.

The wire format is unchanged: TestSpanBatchTxsPostExecFieldsMatchGeth
pins the derived fields against op-geth's view of the same transaction.
TestSpanBatchTxsAddTxsPostExec covers the span-position bookkeeping
across blocks, and TestSpanChannelOutAddBlockPostExec takes a payload
through SpanChannelOut.AddBlock and back.

kona: prove pre-Lagoon PostExec batches drop cross-boundary spans

Follow-up to #22101, which moved PostExec transaction validation after span
decomposition but left the sad path uncovered.

A span batch that starts before the Lagoon activation block and crosses it must
be dropped in its entirety when one of its pre-Lagoon singular batches carries a
PostExec transaction, and the honest variant of the same span must derive
afterwards. The test builds both variants, posts the invalid one first, and then
proves the transition into the very block it poisoned, so op-node and
kona-client both have to reach that verdict on the same L1 data.

Two properties make the proof half meaningful rather than decorative, and both
are easy to get wrong:

  - The claim is the poisoned block, not the block before it. The driver stops
    at the claim height, so claiming earlier means the client never validates
    the invalid batch.
  - The claimed block carries a user transaction. Rejecting the transaction at
    the batch stage and rejecting it during execution yield the same safe chain
    when the block is empty, because Holocene's deposits-only replacement block
    is then byte-identical to the honest one.

Verified by disabling the rule in each client in turn: without op-node's check
the invalid span derives, and without kona's the proof claim mismatches. Both
traps are written up in docs/ai/fault-proofs.md for the next such test.

The rollup config is truncated at the claim fork for the proof run because
Lagoon is the interop feature gate and the single-chain client asserts that
interop is not scheduled.

op-node: run sequencer on its own goroutine

The sequencer no longer emits events on the block-production path: it
calls the engine controller directly (StartBuild/SealBuild/
ProcessPayload) and receives results as return values, and it paces
itself with its own timer in RunLoop, run on a dedicated goroutine
started by the driver.

External signals (forkchoice updates, resets, temporary errors,
derivation build activity) are ingested through an ordered mailbox:
OnEvent appends to a small log under a micro-mutex and fires a cap-1
wake channel, never blocking the event loop; the sequencer goroutine
replays entries in arrival order. Adjacent forkchoice updates coalesce
to the latest. Fan-out error events are still emitted (enqueue is
thread-safe).

The driver loses all sequencer timer plumbing (planSequencerAction,
sequencerTimer, sequencerCh, SequencerActionEvent) along with the
now-unused SequencerActionEvent type and SequencerIface.NextAction.

Pins the post-Holocene span batch overlap content rule end-to-end, in
both op-node (driving derivation) and kona-client (replaying the same
L1 data as the fault proof program): a span batch whose overlap
disagrees with the safe chain must be dropped as a whole, with a
channel flush, so the remainder of an invalidated lineage cannot be
spliced onto the canonical chain.

The scenario mirrors the interop block-replacement incident shape via
batcher equivocation: a span channel whose invalid element is replaced
with a deposits-only block, the same lineage batched again (must be
dropped whole, not tail-spliced), and the canonical continuation (must
win over the equivocating channel's tail). Honest-claim fault proof
runs at every height pin Go/Rust equivalence.

the safe head assertions (the invalidated lineage's tail splices onto
the replacement); kona-client rejects the honest claim at the height
where its derived chain diverges.

op-node: Validate span batch overlap content against the safe chain in Holocene

The Holocene batch stage validates span batches with prefix checks only
(checkSpanBatchPrefix): for a batch overlapping the safe chain, the 20-byte
parent_check of the pre-overlap ancestor is verified, but the overlapping
elements' contents never are - unlike the legacy full checks (checkSpanBatch),
which fetch every overlapped payload and compare transactions and L1 origins.
Dropping that comparison was sound under a pre-interop invariant: the safe
chain was derived from this same batch data, so overlap content provably
agrees with it.

Interop deposits-only block replacement breaks that invariant: the canonical
block at a replaced height no longer matches the batch element it was
originally derived from, and the prefix checks never notice.
GetSingularBatches past-skips every element at or below the safe head without
inspection, the deny check only fires when a payload at the denied height is
proposed, and the channel flush is a side effect of that deny event - so a
walk anchored at the replacement silently splices the remainder of an
invalidated lineage onto the canonical chain. The derived chain ends up
depending on where the pipeline (re-)anchored relative to the replacement,
observed on devnet interop-reorg-5 as nodes deriving different chains from
identical L1 data.

Reinstate the full overlap content validation in the Holocene batch stage: a
prefix-accepted span batch that overlaps the safe chain has every overlapped
element compared against the canonical block at the same height (transactions
and L1 origin number), reusing the exact legacy comparison, now factored into
checkSpanBatchOverlap and shared by both the pre-Holocene and Holocene paths.
A mismatch drops the batch and flushes the channel, like any other invalid
batch under Holocene; a payload fetch failure is Undecided (retried).

This restores the invariant that a batch overlapping the safe chain must
agree with the safe chain, making derivation anchor-invariant across
replacement boundaries: re-deriving from any anchor yields the same chain.

Alternative to #22214, which gates the same comparison to deny-listed heights
to avoid consensus-visible changes on non-interop chains and payload fetches
on reset walk-backs; this version needs no deny list plumbing at all.

op-deployer: estimate broadcast gas against the target chain

op-deployer currently sets broadcast gas limits from its Cancun-era script
simulator. Post-Cancun repricing such as EIP-8037 can make those limits too
low for the target L1.

Leave keyed broadcaster gas limits unset so txmgr estimates them against the
target chain. Send and confirm each transaction before estimating the next
one so dependent transactions are evaluated against the correct bundle-prefix
state. Stop after a failed transaction because later broadcasts may depend on
its state changes.

This relies on txmgr leaving the estimation gas ceiling unset, allowing the
target node to apply its active fork rules and block gas limit.

nuts: declare activation-block extra gas in the bundle schema

A fork's activation block reserves gas for upgrade deposits the consensus layer
emits outside the NUT bundle — for Lagoon, the setFeature(INTEROP) and
ETHLiquidity funding wrappers. Neither is expressible as a bundle transaction:
the funding deposit carries a non-zero mint, and both are emitted only by a
multi-chain dependency set.

That amount was hardcoded separately in op-node and kona, so UpgradeTransactions
and UpgradeGas returned different numbers for the same fork, and the two clients
could drift. Bundles now declare it themselves, as metadata.extraGas, and both
readers fold it into the bundle's total gas.

The generator already models which upgrade it produces (UPGRADE_NAME), so the
value is a constant beside it rather than a CLI argument — run() stays zero-arg,
and nut-bundle-check and nut-provenance-verify keep working unchanged, each
locked commit regenerating with its own generator.

Bundles carrying the field declare schema version 1.1.0. All three readers still
accept 1.0.0, which no generator can now emit but every already-locked bundle
uses, and reject a 1.0.0 bundle that declares extraGas — a reader predating the
field would silently under-reserve the activation block's gas limit.

fork_lock.toml mirrors the value so it is visible without opening a 350 KB JSON;
check-nut-locks enforces that the mirror and the bundle agree.

No bundle declares extraGas yet, so this commit changes no gas.

ci: front-load mise tool installs in the setup pipeline

mise install failures are the largest verified infra-failure class of 2026
(#22223). The setup job always completes before the continuation pipeline
exists, so installing the toolset there makes it the only job that hits the
network on a cold cache — every continuation job restores the cache it saved,
and the blast radius of an upstream event (GitHub rate limits, missing release
attestations) shrinks from every cache-missing job on every PR to one job per
pipeline. This replaces the setup job's unauthenticated yq wget from GitHub
releases; mise.toml pins the same yq version.

Both setup workflows attach the context holding MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN so cold
installs use authenticated GitHub API quota, and the same context is added to
circleci-schedule-trigger-check — the only mise-running job that lacked it.

Also documents mise.toml bump hygiene: release attestations propagate
asynchronously, so a bump to a brand-new release must verify a clean cold
install before merge.

The MinimalWithConductors preset came up as a cluster whose chain never
advanced past genesis, which went unnoticed while the only conductor
acceptance test asserted Raft state alone (#21902). It could also start
from divergent unsafe forks because all three sequencers ran before the

docs: clarify acceptance-test verification scope

Keep reusable domain operations, typed APIs, transport details, asynchronous waits, and stable domain invariants in the devstack DSL. Keep scenario-specific policy and expected outcomes visible in acceptance tests at the narrowest useful scope.

Choose the abstraction boundary based on cohesion and reuse rather than RPC count: a DSL workflow may span several calls when they form one safe operation, while one-off probe matrices and deliberately failing scenarios should compose lower-level DSL capabilities in the test.

op-node: run sequencer on its own goroutine

The sequencer no longer emits events on the block-production path: it
calls the engine controller directly (StartBuild/SealBuild/
ProcessPayload) and receives results as return values, and it paces
itself with its own timer in RunLoop, run on a dedicated goroutine
started by the driver.

External signals (forkchoice updates, resets, temporary errors,
derivation build activity) are ingested through an ordered mailbox:
OnEvent appends to a small log under a micro-mutex and fires a cap-1
wake channel, never blocking the event loop; the sequencer goroutine
replays entries in arrival order. Adjacent forkchoice updates coalesce
to the latest. Fan-out error events are still emitted (enqueue is
thread-safe).

The driver loses all sequencer timer plumbing (planSequencerAction,
sequencerTimer, sequencerCh, SequencerActionEvent) along with the
now-unused SequencerActionEvent type and SequencerIface.NextAction.

Closes #19263

op-revm,op-reth: report zero DA footprint on PostExec receipts

Jovian repurposes the receipt's `blobGasUsed` field to carry the transaction's
DA footprint. op-reth's RPC receipt builder recomputed that value from the tx
bytes for every transaction once Jovian was active, with no type gate, so a
PostExec (`0x7D`) tx reported a non-zero footprint — the Fjord minimum-size
floor guarantees at least `100 * daFootprintGasScalar`, never zero.

The block-level accumulator in alloy-op-evm already excludes the `0x7D`, and
`blobGasUsed` is not a consensus receipt field, so the executor's zero never
reaches the RPC layer. Gate the recomputation on the tx type instead, restoring
`sum(receipt.blobGasUsed) == header.blobGasUsed`.

Extract `da_footprint_gas(encoded, scalar)` in op-revm as
`encoded_tx_da_footprint` (plus a `tx_da_footprint` convenience wrapper that
encodes first), next to `estimate_tx_compressed_size`: the arithmetic was
duplicated in the block executor, the RPC receipt builder, and two tests. The
`0x7D` check lives in the helper and keys off the first byte of the EIP-2718
encoding, so it needs no trait bound beyond `Encodable2718` and no new method on
the transaction types. Free functions rather than methods — op-revm depends on
op-alloy-consensus (not the reverse), so a trait method could not reach the FLZ
estimator, and a `&self` method would force a re-encode where the block executor
reuses `tx_env.encoded_bytes()`.

Deposits are still excluded by their call sites, not by the helper: the block
total excludes deposits while their receipts report a non-zero footprint.
specs#926 does not cover that discrepancy and changing it is a user-visible RPC
change, so it is left alone.

The receipt test runs on a Lagoon-active schedule, since a `0x7D` at a
Jovian-only timestamp is not a reachable state — SDM rides Lagoon. No named
chain schedules Lagoon yet, hence the hand-built fork list, which appends a
single entry rather than restating the tail of the schedule: `OpChainHardforks`
resolves an activation positionally (`forks[fork.idx()]`), so a duplicate row
shifts every later fork by one. Two assertions pin that Karst's activation is
unchanged.

Also adds an end-to-end pin in alloy-op-evm that a `0x7D` leaves
`da_footprint_used` unchanged, and an SDM acceptance assertion that per-tx
receipt footprints sum to the header total on a real Lagoon block — the only
in-tree chain whose blocks contain a `0x7D`. The Jovian acceptance suites pin
Jovian at genesis, so Lagoon (and therefore SDM) can never be active there.

The `Encodable2718` bound means op-revm picks up a new `alloy-eips` dependency,
which accounts for the otherwise-unrelated build churn: the `serde` and `std`
features have to propagate to it (zepter), and the three satellite lockfiles
that path-depend on op-revm — `kona/sp1/programs`, `op-rbuilder`,
`rollup-boost` — each record its dependency list, so all three needed
refreshing. They were regenerated without `--locked`, so only the moved entry
changed and no unrelated dep was bumped.

Specification: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/specs/pull/926

justfile: Auto-select the native or Docker kona prestate build

`just build-deps` from op-acceptance-tests fails on macOS:

    error: linker `mips64-linux-gnuabi64-gcc` not found
    error: could not compile `kona-client` (bin "kona-client")
    error: Recipe `build-kona-client-elfs` failed with exit code 101

`cannon-prestates` always took the native cross-compile, which needs the
MIPS64 GCC toolchain. That toolchain is apt-only — no macOS package provides
it — so on a Mac the recipe could never succeed, and the failure surfaced as a
bare rustc linker error naming nothing to install.

Route `cannon-prestates` through a new `build-kona-prestates-auto`, which
picks the native build when the cross-linker is on PATH and the reproducible
Docker build otherwise. Both write the same per-variant artifacts dirs, so
consumers can't tell which ran; only the hashes differ. Linux keeps the fast
native path it has today, and no environment is forced to have Docker.

The Docker build exports only the prestate dirs — cannon is built as a stage
inside it — so the docker path also builds the host binary at cannon/bin/cannon,
which op-devstack points the challenger's VmBin at
(shared/challenger/challenger.go). Otherwise the fallback would produce
prestates whose tests then fail on a missing cannon.

When neither is available, both entry points now name what to install for each
path instead of deferring to rustc. `build-kona-client-elfs` also checks the
linker up front, so a missing toolchain reports itself before cargo compiles
the whole dependency graph rather than after.

The toolchain names move to MIPS64_CC / MIPS64_CXX / MIPS64_LINKER, each
defaulting to the previous literal and reading the same environment variable
the build exports, so a differently named toolchain is both probed for and
used. `KONA_PRESTATE_BUILD=native|docker` pins a path and skips detection.

CI is unaffected: it never runs `cannon-prestates`. The cannon-prestate jobs
run `just reproducible-prestate` / `just build-kona-reproducible-prestate`
directly, and op-acceptance-tests' `build-deps` exits early when $CIRCLECI is
set. Inside the prestate Dockerfile, `build-kona-client-elfs` runs on the
cannon-builder image, which apt-installs g++-mips64-linux-gnuabi64, so the new
preflight passes there.

Follow-up to #22340.

cci-stats: retry pipelines that were still running when indexed

The ingest high water mark is MAX(created_at) over the pipelines table, and
processPipeline wrote nothing at all for a pipeline with a workflow still in
progress. Because pipelines do not finish in creation order, a newer pipeline
that had finished pushed the mark past the skipped one, which was then never
looked at again.

Record such pipelines with complete = FALSE instead, and index them again on
later runs until every matched workflow reaches a terminal state. Only terminal
workflows contribute jobs and test results, so a slow workflow no longer
discards the data for the rest of its pipeline.

Also distinguish a pipeline whose workflows do not exist yet, which must be
retried, from one whose workflows match no pattern, which is done with.
Reindexing is bounded by FETCH_LIMIT_DAYS so a pipeline left awaiting approval
does not retry forever.

Requires pkg/db/migrate_v1_to_v2.sql to be applied before deploy.
cci-stats: retry pipelines that were still running when indexed

cci-stats: judge pipeline completeness on all workflows

Projects using dynamic config generation start a pipeline with only a setup
workflow; the workflows worth recording appear later, once setup produces the
continuation config. Judging completeness on matched workflows alone saw nothing
to record and marked such a pipeline complete, writing it off before its real
workflows existed.

Judge on every workflow instead. A pipeline is complete once all of its
workflows are terminal, which covers the setup window and still avoids retrying
a pipeline whose workflows will never match.
cci-stats: judge pipeline completeness on all workflows

cci-stats: gate pipeline completeness on the CircleCI pipeline state

Under dynamic config generation the setup workflow reaching success and the
continuation request creating the real workflows are near simultaneous and are
not ordered; measured over 20 monorepo pipelines the gap ran from -1s to +2s. A
poll landing in that window sees only a successful setup workflow, concludes
every workflow is terminal, and writes the pipeline off for good.

Require the pipeline state to be created, which the continuation request sets
once the workflow list is final, plus at least one workflow to guard the same
state being reported before setup has started. With the window handled properly,
completeness goes back to judging only matched workflows, so an unmatched slow
workflow no longer holds a pipeline on the retry list.

Pipelines reloaded from the database have no current state, so refresh it.
cci-stats: gate pipeline completeness on the CircleCI pipeline state

cci-stats: treat an errored pipeline as complete

An errored pipeline is terminal, so it will never create further workflows and
there is nothing to gain from reindexing it every run until it ages out of the
retry window.

Unlike created, errored is never the initial state, so it needs no workflow count
guard: a pipeline that failed before any workflow existed is still complete.
cci-stats: treat an errored pipeline as complete

- Paginate fetchWorkflows. The workflow count now feeds the permanence
  decision, so a truncated page could mark a pipeline complete on a partial set.
- Add an end-to-end test of record-incomplete -> reindex -> mark-complete using
  fakes for the client's Projects/Pipelines/Workflows/Jobs interfaces.
- Stop clearing a job's stored test results when the metadata fetch returns
  nothing, since a spurious not found is indistinguishable from a job with no
  tests and the wipe is permanent once the pipeline is marked complete.
- Skip, rather than fail the run on, a retried pipeline that cannot be fetched.
  It stays on the retry list, so failing would recur every run and stop anything

- Use UTC for the horizon; pgx reinterprets a non-UTC wall clock as UTC.

  slices, drop the redundant loop variable copy, make the deferred rollback

op-node: don't lose the sequencer deadline on an early timer fire

RunLoop recorded lastRan = armed before checking whether the fired
deadline was due. Sequencer deadlines are wall-clock values while the
timer sleeps monotonic time, so a backward wall-clock step (VM time
sync, NTP) delivers the fire early; the not-yet-due continue path then
left the deadline equal to lastRan, the planning pass refused to re-arm
it, and lastRan was only reset when the schedule emptied - never, while
a valid overdue action remained. One early delivery permanently froze
block production with no log, metric, or error, while
admin_sequencerActive kept returning true.

lastRan now records the post-drain deadline only when its action
actually runs, and any schedule mutation (inbox drain or the action
itself) invalidates it, so re-arming a byte-identical instant is
honored as a fresh deadline. The early fire is logged at debug level,
and the timer is armed via the injectable clock so the behavior is
testable.

justfile: Auto-select the native or Docker kona prestate build

`just build-deps` from op-acceptance-tests fails on macOS:

    error: linker `mips64-linux-gnuabi64-gcc` not found
    error: could not compile `kona-client` (bin "kona-client")
    error: Recipe `build-kona-client-elfs` failed with exit code 101

`cannon-prestates` always took the native cross-compile, which needs the
MIPS64 GCC toolchain. That toolchain is apt-only — no macOS package provides
it — so on a Mac the recipe could never succeed, and the failure surfaced as a
bare rustc linker error naming nothing to install.

Route `cannon-prestates` through a new `build-kona-prestates-auto`, which
picks the native build when the cross-linker is on PATH and the reproducible
Docker build otherwise. Both write the same per-variant artifacts dirs, so
consumers can't tell which ran; only the hashes differ. Linux keeps the fast
native path it has today, and no environment is forced to have Docker.

The Docker build exports only the prestate dirs — cannon is built as a stage
inside it — so the docker path also builds the host binary at cannon/bin/cannon,
which op-devstack points the challenger's VmBin at
(shared/challenger/challenger.go). Otherwise the fallback would produce
prestates whose tests then fail on a missing cannon.

When neither is available, both entry points now name what to install for each
path instead of deferring to rustc. `build-kona-client-elfs` also checks the
linker up front, so a missing toolchain reports itself before cargo compiles
the whole dependency graph rather than after.

The toolchain names move to MIPS64_CC / MIPS64_CXX / MIPS64_LINKER, each
defaulting to the previous literal and reading the same environment variable
the build exports, so a differently named toolchain is both probed for and
used. `KONA_PRESTATE_BUILD=native|docker` pins a path and skips detection.

CI is unaffected: it never runs `cannon-prestates`. The cannon-prestate jobs
run `just reproducible-prestate` / `just build-kona-reproducible-prestate`
directly, and op-acceptance-tests' `build-deps` exits early when $CIRCLECI is
set. Inside the prestate Dockerfile, `build-kona-client-elfs` runs on the
cannon-builder image, which apt-installs g++-mips64-linux-gnuabi64, so the new
preflight passes there.

Follow-up to #22340.

ci: front-load mise tool installs in the setup pipeline

mise install failures are the largest verified infra-failure class of 2026
(#22223). The setup job now installs the mise toolset: it always completes
before the continuation pipeline exists, so on a cold cache (mise.toml change
or eviction) it is the only job that hits the network — every continuation
job restores the cache it saved, and the blast radius of an upstream event
(GitHub rate limits, missing release attestations) shrinks from every
cache-missing job on every PR to one job per pipeline. This replaces the
setup job's unauthenticated yq wget from GitHub releases; mise.toml pins the
same yq version.

Because the routing scripts spawn yq/jq hundreds of times, the setup job puts
the resolved tool bin directories ahead of the mise shims, avoiding ~9s of
per-spawn shim resolution overhead.

Both setup workflows attach the context holding MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN so cold
installs use authenticated GitHub API quota, and the same context is added to
circleci-schedule-trigger-check — the only mise-running job that lacked it.

Measured: warm setup job 14.7s -> 38.6s (cache restore dominates); cold
2m46s paid once per mise.toml change instead of ~70 parallel cold installs.

kona: delegate precompile result conversion to revm

The FPVM precompile provider builds its own `InterpreterResult` from the
`PrecompileOutput` a precompile returns. That block is a hand-rolled copy of
revm's `precompile_output_to_interpreter_result` in three places:

- The result gas is built with `Gas::new`, which leaves the reservoir zeroed.
  revm builds it with `Gas::new_with_regular_gas_and_reservoir`, from the
  reservoir the output carries. The revm 38 bump (#20169, #20300) threaded the
  reservoir into the two calls whose signatures changed and left the result
  built from them alone.
- `state_gas_used` and `gas_refunded` never reach the gas tracker.
- A `Revert` status is handed back to the caller as `Return`.

Call revm's function instead of restating it. #21582 and #21634 each closed one
drift in this block by hand; delegating retires the copy, so there is nothing
left to keep in sync.

`test_non_accelerated_result_matches_wrapped_provider` runs the provider and the
`EthPrecompiles` it wraps over the same inputs at unaccelerated addresses and
compares the whole `InterpreterResult`, so a future local conversion has to
reproduce every field of it rather than the ones a test happens to read.

op-supernode: resume chains whose invalidation triggered no rewind

RewindEngine is the only path that resumes an invalidated chain, via its
internal Resume/WaitReady. But InvalidateBlock returns (false, nil)
without calling it when the engine reports a different block at the
invalidated height — so that chain kept a stopped virtual node for the
life of the process. Nothing retried, because the invalidation reported
success and the pending transition was cleared, and nothing logged above
Info.

Track which chains RewindEngine actually resumed and resume the rest.
This also covers failed invalidations, which are retried on the next
round rather than left wedged.

op-supernode: skip recovery for already-applied invalidations

An invalidation decision the previous recovery cycle already applied
restarted the whole recovery: every chain's virtual node was stopped and
restarted, which resets derivation and walks local-safe back a sequencing
window on chains that were never invalidated.

Add a read-only preflight before the freeze. When every pending
invalidation is already applied, clear the transition and do nothing. The
preflight distinguishes a completed rewind from one that crashed part-way
by checking the unsafe head against the WAL-captured rewind destination,
so a partial rewind is still driven to completion.

Also fix a wedge on the same path: only RewindEngine resumes an
invalidated chain, so a chain whose InvalidateBlock reported no rewind —
or failed before reaching the rewind — kept a stopped virtual node for
good. Resume every chain RewindEngine did not resume.

Part of #21948.

contracts-bedrock: Require a new anchor root when migrating to super root games

An upgrade that disables the output root games and enables a super root game
could omit the `overrides.cfg.startingAnchorRoot` instruction. OPCM then read
the anchor root back from the AnchorStateRegistry, so the root did not change,
the registry kept the legacy anchor game, and new super root games started from
an output root and an L2 block number that the super trace reads as a super
root and a timestamp. Honest challengers cannot build a trace for that
prestate, so invalid claims would go uncontested.

OPContractsManagerV2.upgrade now requires the instruction, and requires the
supplied root to be non-zero and in range. The requirement applies only when
the upgrade installs a super root game type while the registry still respects
an output root game type. Chains already on super root games and initial
deployments are unaffected.

The check lives in OPContractsManagerUtils because OPContractsManagerV2 has too
little EIP-170 headroom to hold it.

ci: feed reth build scripts git metadata so cold melange builds don't fail

reth-node-core's build script reads VERGEN_GIT_SHA/VERGEN_GIT_DIRTY/
VERGEN_GIT_DESCRIBE via env::var()? and aborts with Error: NotPresent when
they are absent. The melange sandbox has no .git, so vergen_git2 cannot
populate them (it only warns, fail-on-error is off), and the build script then
fails. maxperf builds only pass because that build-script output is served

feat(op-supernode): HTTP-backed remote interop nodes

Introduce a "remote node": a participant in the interop dependency set that the
supernode does not drive. Instead of running a consensus client for that chain,
the supernode polls a remote HTTP endpoint for its FINALIZED initiating
messages and seals them into that chain's LogsDB, so driven chains can
reference them as executing messages exactly as they reference messages from
driven chains. Finalized-only means there is no rewind path to implement.

This is a revival of the draft PR
https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/21479, whose author and
co-author are preserved here.

The wire protocol is the plugin boundary — point a remote node at any server,
in any language, that serves it:

  GET {url}/finalized?after={N}
  -> {"blockTime": <secs>, "block": <FinalizedBlock>|null}

- op-supernode/supernode/remote: the Adapter seam, the FinalizedBlock /
  InitiatingMessage wire types (normalized initiating messages), and
  HTTPAdapter, the production client.
- interop.remoteNode + Interop.AddRemoteNode: polls an adapter and seals
  finalized blocks into the per-chain LogsDB (mirrors processBlockLogs).
  Ingesters launch in Start.
- verifyExecutingMessage resolves the initiating chain's block time from either
  a driven chain or a remote node.
- --interop.remote-nodes <chainID>=<url> configures remote nodes; the supernode
  builds an HTTPAdapter per entry. Only a real HTTP client ships in the binary.
- remote/remotetest: a deterministic HTTP server implementing the protocol, for
  tests (a real HTTPAdapter is pointed at an httptest.Server) — no mock in the
  binary.

Engine-level e2e (remote_engine_test.go): a driven chain emits a real
CrossL2Inbox executing-message log referencing a remote-node-served initiating
message; the log is sealed through the production processBlockLogs path (real
decode) and validated by the real verifyInteropMessages engine — accepted when
valid, rejected when the reference is tampered.

New since #21479, from running this against a live public chain:

- Start-height anchoring. A remote node resumed from its LogsDB's latest sealed
  block and demanded strict contiguity from there, with an empty DB meaning
  "expect block 1" — unreachable for a live chain whose finalized head is tens
  of millions of blocks past genesis. An empty LogsDB now accepts whatever
  height the adapter serves for after=0 and seals it as the anchor of local
  history; strict contiguity is enforced from the anchor onward exactly as
  before. No change below the DB layer was needed: the raft-wal store already
  keys entries by block number and records its own first block, so a
  non-genesis-rooted history reads back correctly and Contains answers
  ErrSkipped below the anchor. This mirrors how a driven chain's logsDB already
  starts at an arbitrary height, where --interop.log-backfill-depth picks the
  start. The remotetest chain grows a FirstBlock knob so tests can simulate it,
  and the wire protocol documents after=0 as the anchor request.

- Ingestion drain with a per-cycle cap. Ingestion ran once per tick and the
  tick is the remote chain's block time, so it could only ever match the
  chain's production rate — a node that fell behind on a 2s chain could never
  catch up. The loop now drains until the adapter returns null, capped per
  cycle to keep shutdown responsive and bound adapter load.

- An env-gated live e2e (remote_node_live_test.go) that runs the whole chain of
  custody — a real server process against a real public chain, a real
  HTTPAdapter, the real ingester and a real LogsDB — and ends by asking
  Contains for a genuine on-chain log with the checksum an executing message
  would carry. Each link is somewhere the interop leg can break silently: an
  anchor at the wrong height, a logHash derived differently on the two sides, a
  log index shifted by a filtered log. None of them are visible in a test with
  fabricated blocks. Skipped unless ALTDA_SHIM_BIN points at a built server.

op-interop-filter: answer verdict reads without blocking on ingestion writes

The interop filter's verdict path (CheckAccessList -> Ready/Contains/
LatestTimestamp) took the chain ingester's RWMutex read-side while
processBlockLogs held the write-side across the entire logsDB block write,
and the logsDB itself held its own write lock across the fsyncing
StoreLog in SealBlock. A slow or starved block write therefore turned
into verdict-RPC silence: op-reth's one-shot 2s checkAccessList query
timed out, counted as a non-response, and the txpool failed closed —
even for verdicts that need no DB data at all (access-list parse
errors are rejected before any lookup, but Backend.Ready() blocked
first).

Serve reads from an atomically-published sealed-state snapshot plus
raft-wal's lock-free read path (raft-wal keeps immutable ref-counted
state snapshots precisely so readers never wait on the writer), and
downgrade processBlockLogs to the read lock: c.mu only guards the
logsDB handle, while the DB serializes its own writers. Rewind, Clear,
and Close still exclude readers. Verdicts now get a prompt definitive
or soft not-yet-available answer while a block write is in flight.

Fixes #21943

cci-stats: apply the schema with goose instead of by hand

The schema was two hand-maintained files: db.sql for a new database and a
separate script for an existing one. Nothing kept them in step, so a database
built from scratch and one carried forward could drift apart, and there was no
way to tell which version a database was at. Nothing read schema_version, so a
database behind the binary failed part way through a run.

The schema is now the migration chain in pkg/db/migrations, embedded in the
binary and applied at startup under a Postgres advisory lock. 00001 is a
baseline that reproduces the hand-applied schema and is written to be a no-op
against a database that already has it. Startup also stops when the database is
ahead of the binary, which a rolled-back deploy would otherwise leave unnoticed.

pkg/db now has tests, against the Postgres the go-test job already runs. They
cover a database built from nothing, a repeat run, adoption of the hand-applied
schema, and the refusal to run against a newer one. The adoption test compares
the adopted schema against a freshly built one, so the two paths cannot diverge
unnoticed. The tests skip when no database is reachable, but fail instead when
CI is set, so a missing database cannot pass silently.

DATABASE_URI now needs a role with DDL rights.

cci-stats: Retry pipelines that were still running when indexed

processPipeline wrote nothing for a pipeline that still had a workflow
running. The ingest high water mark is MAX(created_at) over pipelines, and
pipelines do not finish in creation order, so a later pipeline pushed the mark
past the skipped one. Those pipelines were lost permanently.

Unfinished pipelines are now recorded with complete = FALSE and reindexed each
run until done, so the mark can advance safely. Only terminal workflows
contribute jobs and test results, so one slow workflow no longer discards the
data for the rest of its pipeline. Newly listed pipelines are claimed as
incomplete before indexing starts, so a run that stops part way does not
strand them either.

A pipeline is complete once it will create no more workflows — state errored,
or created with at least one workflow — and every matched workflow is
terminal. The state check matters because dynamic config generation creates
the real workflows through the continuation request, and CircleCI's documented
flow holds the pipeline in setup or pending until that lands.

FETCH_LIMIT_DAYS bounds both how long a pipeline stays retryable and how far
back a run reaches, so nothing is claimed that could never be reindexed. A
retried pipeline that cannot be fetched is skipped rather than failing the
run. Reindexing never clears a job's stored test results unless it has new
ones to put back, because a spurious not found is indistinguishable from a job
with no tests.

The complete column arrives as 00002_pipeline_complete.sql, applied at startup
by the migration framework, so there is no step to run by hand.

op-devstack: make the conductor preset produce one canonical chain

The MinimalWithConductors preset came up as a cluster whose chain never
advanced past genesis, which went unnoticed while the only conductor
acceptance test asserted Raft state alone (#21902). It could also start
from divergent unsafe forks because all three sequencers ran before the
Raft cluster and p2p mesh existed.

Make the preset a deterministic live HA cluster:

- Start every sequencer stopped, seed sequencing on the bootstrap node,
  then freeze the seeded head and require every follower to reach that
  exact head before conductor control loops resume. This both initializes
  the fresh Raft FSM and prevents failover to an incompatible follower.
- Mesh the nodes over CL p2p only. EL peering is unnecessary because unsafe
  blocks reach follower ELs through CL gossip and the engine API, and it is
  flaky against op-reth subprocesses (#18570). Register the same CL mesh
  with the frontend lifecycle so tests that restart nodes restore it.

kona-proof: linear by-number header walks for span batch overlap validation

In the fault-proof provider, each block_by_number call resolved
header_by_number by walking parent hashes back from the L2 safe head,
so validating an overlap of length N performed N + (N-1) + ... + 1
header preimage reads and decodes (15 for N=5, per review measurement).

Give OracleL2ChainProvider the same by-number cache its L1 counterpart
already has: every header discovered on a walk is recorded by number
(with its hash), lookups start from the closest cached ancestor at or
above the target instead of the safe head, and exact hits return
without touching the oracle. The ascending per-block lookups of
check_batch_overlap now cost one walk over the overlap range in total;
descending patterns (pipeline reset walk-backs) resume from the lowest
cached header. Entries are canonical by construction — they are only
learned by walking back from the safe head, which advances along a
single lineage within a program run — so they never need invalidation.

Provider-level regression tests pin the complexity with a counting
mock oracle, mirroring the OracleL1ChainProvider tests: the five-deep
ascending overlap sweep is asserted at exactly 5 header reads (was 15),
plus resume-from-cached-ancestor, repeat-hit, and past-head cases.

Also hoist the transaction encoding buffer in check_batch_overlap out
of the comparison loops (review nit): one allocation per overlapping
span batch instead of one per compared transaction.

The interop consolidation provider (proof-interop/src/provider.rs) has
a similar per-chain backward walk, but it is not on the batch
validation path; left for a follow-up if needed.

cci-stats: Retry transient CircleCI API failures

A 5xx from CircleCI fails the whole run. The pipeline pool cancels its
siblings on the first error, so one 502 while listing pipelines costs the
rest of the run's work.

Every call now goes through pkg/cci, whose transport retries a rate limit,
a 5xx or a failed connection with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After. Retrying belongs in the transport for two reasons: it is the
last place that still has the status code, since the client reports a failed
response as its body's message and a 502 arrives indistinguishable from a
permanent failure; and every call inherits it, including any added later.
NewClient is the only way the program builds a client, so a new call site
cannot miss out.

A settled failure is not repeated: a 4xx, a name that does not resolve, a
certificate that does not verify, a cancelled request, or a method that may
already have applied. A request that exhausts its attempts is reported as
it was before, with the last response handed back untouched.

The transport also bounds one attempt with ResponseHeaderTimeout. Nothing
else does: the runner's context has no deadline, and the CronJob forbids
concurrent runs, so a connection that is accepted and never answered would
stop every later run too.

op-alloy: fix RPC effective gas price for txs below the base fee

`Transaction::from_transaction` derived `effectiveGasPrice` as
`effective_tip_per_gas(base_fee) + base_fee`. `effective_tip_per_gas`
returns `None` when `max_fee_per_gas < base_fee`, so `unwrap_or_default()`
collapsed the price to `base_fee` instead of `max_fee_per_gas`.

Use `Transaction::effective_gas_price` instead, which is
`min(max_fee_per_gas, max_priority_fee_per_gas + base_fee)` — the price the
executor charges and the one `build_receipt` already reports. Before this
change `eth_getTransactionByHash` and `eth_getTransactionReceipt` disagreed
for such transactions.

flashblocks-rpc had its own copy of the same derivation; it now delegates to
`Transaction::from_transaction` so the two cannot drift again.

cci-stats: Replace the test_results indexes

The dashboard reaches test_results through a set of jobs and then filters by
status. The two single-column indexes do not serve that shape: the planner ANDs
them into a bitmap and visits the heap for name, so a 14-day query over the
table takes 15 to 31 seconds. Forcing job-driven access instead returns the same
rows in 1.3 to 3.4 seconds, and pushing status into the index cuts the heap
visits down to the matching rows.

One composite index replaces both, and the surrogate primary key goes with them:
nothing reads test_results.id, no foreign key points at it, and writes address
rows by job_id. Net effect is about 2.4 GB reclaimed.

There is no natural key to promote in its place. CircleCI reports Solidity tests
without the contract that owns them, so (job_id, name) is not unique -- setUp()
appears 95 times in a single job.

fix(proxyd): evict out-of-order buckets in the sliding window

AvgSlidingWindow.advance() walks sw.buckets.Keys() and stops at the first
key inside the window:

    if k.(time.Time).After(windowStart) {
        break
    }

buckets is a linkedhashmap, so Keys() returns insertion order, not key
order. AddWithTime accepts an arbitrary timestamp, so a data point added
out of order leaves a newer key ahead of older ones — and the loop then
stops on that newer key without evicting anything behind it.

Expired buckets therefore stay in the window and keep contributing to
Avg(), Sum() and Count(), which is what proxyd uses to compare backend
latency and error rates.

Skip past in-window keys instead of stopping at them.

The size-dependent branch in the same loop goes too: it zeroed qty and
sum whenever the map happened to empty out, which double-counted the
last bucket's removal. Subtracting unconditionally is correct for both
cases, since removing every bucket subtracts every contribution.

Covered by TestSlidingWindow_AdvanceEvictsOutOfOrderBuckets, which fails
before this change with Avg() returning 5 instead of 6.

op-devstack: sequence ConnectP2P dials to avoid simultaneous-connect cross

ConnectP2P made both reth nodes dial each other at setup: admin_addPeer
starts the initiator's dial, and the acceptor's admin_addTrustedPeer makes
reth dial back immediately. When the two dials cross in flight, each side
rejects the other's connection with AlreadyConnected and both die; reth's
trusted-peer re-dial backoff then outlives the 30s verification budget.
The acceptor's trusted entry is now added only after the initiator's dial
is observed in admin_peers, so only one dial is ever in flight during
setup while drop-recovery still ends up mutually trusted.
