rust: tag upstream mirrors and extend reth bump-review guidance

Several op-crates carry code that mirrors upstream reth, revm or alloy —
ports, verbatim copies, overridden defaults, and re-declared surfaces. Nothing
marked them, so an upstream change that should force a matching edit here
produces no diff and no compile error, and the divergence is only found by
someone reading both sides.

Tag each site with `UPSTREAM-MIRROR(<kind>): <crate>@<version> <symbol>`,
recording the version the mirror was last verified against, and add
`rust/scripts/upstream-mirrors.py` (`just mirrors`) to list them and flag any
whose recorded version has fallen behind the pin. `--check` fails on a
malformed tag. The guide in `docs/ai/reth-upstream-mirrors.md` covers the
grammar, the kinds, and which repo to diff a `reth` mirror against.

Also extends the bump-review guidance in `docs/ai/reth-update-review.md` and
`rust/UPDATING-RETH.md`, including triaging the fork's cherry-picks on each
bump: drop the ones that landed upstream, replay the ones that did not.

kona-derive: Key the system config lookup by L2 block hash

op-node reads the system config by block hash at both sites kona read it by
number: the attributes builder (attributes.go:74) and the pipeline reset
(pipeline.go:259). A height alone does not identify a block across a reorg, so
a number-keyed lookup cannot be answered from a local cache without risking a
stale answer, and both kona callers already hold the hash they were discarding.

Renames L2ChainProvider::system_config_by_number and the matching Pipeline
method to system_config_by_l2_hash. The oracle-backed proof provider gains a
block_by_hash path, which also lets it address the header directly instead of
walking back from the safe head.

The alloy provider gains a hash-keyed block cache alongside its by-number one.
Both hold the same blocks behind an Arc, and a by-number fetch seeds both, so a
block fetched by number and later asked for by hash is neither fetched nor
stored twice. Seeding in the other direction would not be sound: a block found
by hash carries no claim to being canonical at its own height. Its one other
block-fetching method, block_info_by_id, bypassed the caches entirely and had
no callers anywhere in the workspace, so it goes.

The sequencer's attributes builder and the derivation pipeline each reconstruct
the SystemConfig of the block they are building on top of, once per block. That
block is one the node has just imported, yet both fetched it back from the
execution layer in full — the sequencer on the block-production path.

InsertTask already decodes every payload it inserts to derive the block's
L2BlockInfo, and SealTask and ConsolidateTask both route through it, so every
imported block passes one point holding exactly the (OpBlock, L2BlockInfo) pair

ImportedBlockSink, and put BufferedAlloyL2ChainProvider in front of the RPC
provider so those lookups read the buffer first.

Only the hash-keyed lookup is served locally. A height does not identify a block
across a reorg, so the by-number lookups stay on the RPC, and an entry for a
block that is later reorged out is never returned — it just ages out.

kona-providers-local: Take the block buffer off async locks

ChainStateBuffer guarded its two LRU caches with tokio::sync::RwLock, which made
every method async and forced ImportedBlockSink::block_imported to be async too,
so #[async_trait] boxed a future per imported block.

No guard was ever held across an await point. The one place it could have been,
get_block_by_number, dropped its guard by hand first. Async locks exist for the
case where a guard must survive an await; where it must not, the blocking locks
are both simpler and faster, and now the compiler enforces the rule rather than
a convention doing it.

Switching to std::sync::RwLock makes the buffer, the provider's write API, and
the sink synchronous, drops async_trait from ImportedBlockSink, and leaves
providers-local with no tokio runtime dependency. The L2ChainProvider and
BatchValidationProvider methods stay async, as their traits require.

Part of #22432.

derive: reserve Lagoon upgrade gas independently of the dependency set

A Lagoon activation block wraps the NUT bundle in setFeature(INTEROP) and
ETHLiquidity.fund() (150k gas) only when the chain has a multi-chain dependency
set. The gas was reserved conditionally to match, but the system config
reconstructed from the activation block must subtract the same amount again for
the next block — and that path sees only the rollup config and a timestamp,
never the dependency set. Each client hardcoded one branch and they picked
opposite ones: op-node always stripped the bundle-only amount, kona always
stripped bundle+150k. They disagreed by 150,000 gas in both configurations,
starting at the first block after activation.

Reserve the wrapper gas unconditionally. A single-chain activation carries it as
unused headroom in that one block; in exchange the amount no longer depends on
the dependency set, so both add and strip agree in both clients.

Only the tx set still varies with the dependency set.

cci-stats: Replace the test_results indexes (#721)

The dashboard reaches test_results through a set of jobs and then filters by
status. The two single-column indexes do not serve that shape: the planner ANDs
them into a bitmap and visits the heap for name, so a 14-day query over the
table takes 15 to 31 seconds. Forcing job-driven access instead returns the same
rows in 1.3 to 3.4 seconds, and pushing status into the index cuts the heap
visits down to the matching rows.

One composite index replaces both, and the surrogate primary key goes with them:
nothing reads test_results.id, no foreign key points at it, and writes address
rows by job_id. Net effect is about 2.4 GB reclaimed.

There is no natural key to promote in its place. CircleCI reports Solidity tests
without the contract that owns them, so (job_id, name) is not unique -- setUp()
appears 95 times in a single job.

release-notes: add skill for drafting house-style release notes

`just release-notes` emits a git-cliff changelog filtered by include-path.
Those paths are deliberately broad (go.*, op-core/**, op-service/**, and all
of rust/kona/**, rust/op-alloy/**, rust/alloy-op*/**), so a component's draft
lists many PRs that never reach that component's binary. Turning one into a
published note means pruning it and writing the operator-facing notices on
top, which so far has been undocumented per-release manual work.

The skill captures both halves. scripts/pr-facts.sh resolves linkage exactly
— `go list -deps` for the Go services, `cargo tree` for kona/reth — and tags
every PR in a draft LINKED (naming which linked packages it hit), DEPS, or
'--'. reference/triage.md covers the judgment pass that linkage alone cannot
settle, and reference/house-style.md documents the callout ladder and voice,
derived from the published op-node, op-batcher, kona-node and op-supernode
notes.

Checked against ground truth by regenerating raw drafts for two published
releases: op-node/v1.19.4 (32 PRs raw, 15 published) and op-batcher/v1.16.12
(23 raw, 1 published).

The go-tests job set test_timeout (40m, exported as go test -timeout) above
no_output_timeout (39m), so a silently hung test was always killed by
CircleCI's no-output watchdog before Go's deadline could dump goroutines,
making every hang undiagnosable. Lower test_timeout to 35m so Go's deadline
fires first.

The bootstrap live-RPC tests (TestImplementations, TestSuperchain) bound their
deploy calls with a 5m context, but hangs in paths that ignore context
deadlines (forked anvil against a dead upstream, cleanup) could still stall a
shard for the full job budget. Add a per-test watchdog (testutil.StartWatchdog,
10m vs a ~80s green runtime) that crashes the test binary with a full goroutine
dump, so an unresponsive archive RPC fails the test loudly instead of hanging
the shard.

against the pipeline's L1 origin when the engine confirms it, and trims the
record when the pipeline resets or EL sync completes.

advanced in between. Recording the safe head's own l1_origin would be wrong,
since a span batch can place a block's origin well before the L1 block whose

write with backoff so a transient disk failure does not cost an entry, and keep

rust: Fix the release recipe subdir guard

`just release` has been unusable since #20611. The recipe asserts that
the hardcoded ALL_SUBDIRS list equals every subdir under rust/ that
cargo metadata reports, but three workspace members joined later
without an update: revm-ee-tests (#20611), op-reth-test-engine (#21216),
and op-version (#21645). Any target aborted at the guard.

Those subdirs hold internal crates that no workspace release covers, so
they belong in a skip list rather than in the release order. Split the
one list in two, RELEASED_SUBDIRS and SKIPPED_SUBDIRS, and move op-reth
into the skip list in place of the `grep -vx op-reth` filter, which hid
the same intent.

The guard now reports only subdirs that neither list covers, so a new
subdir still has to be classified deliberately, while a stale entry is
harmless: its package list comes out empty and the release skips it.

op-devstack: fix L1 HTTP poll interval interpreted as nanoseconds

HttpPollInterval is a time.Duration, so the bare literal 100 is 100
nanoseconds instead of the intended 100 milliseconds. The polling
client schedules the next poll with time.AfterFunc(pollRate, ...),
so a 100ns interval causes near-continuous L1 RPC polling and can
exhaust local ports. Use 100 * time.Millisecond to match the
multichain devstack and other usages.

rust: update reth to v2.5.0 and drop the op-rs fork

Move the reth pin from the OP fork `op-rs/reth@aef8d3ef` back to upstream
`paradigmxyz/reth`, `tag = "v2.5.0"`. The fork's only cherry-pick
(`aef8d3ef92 feat(trie): expose payload state root receiver`) is byte-identical
to upstream `92cf59e2be`, which v2.5.0 contains, so the fork carries nothing
unique any more.

Shared crates.io versions synced to what v2.5.0 pins: revm 41.0.0 -> 42.0.1
(subcrates 42.0.0), revm-inspectors 0.41 -> 0.42, alloy-evm 0.37.0 -> 0.38.0,
alloy core 1.6.0 -> 1.6.1, the alloy main family 2.1.1 -> 2.3.0, and the
published reth-core crates 0.5.0 -> 0.6.0. All four lockfiles refreshed.

Upstream API adaptations:

- revm 42 reworks the `Handler` gas pipeline around `GasTracker` and the
  EIP-2780 runtime gas phase. `OpHandler::last_frame_result` is re-derived
  against the new default: the frame is settled with upstream's
  `handle_reservoir_remaining_gas`, and the pre-Regolith deposit rules are
  applied on top of the settled result. `refund` now returns `Result` and
  reads the refund quotient from `GasParams`.
- op-revm's `ExecuteEvm::replay` copy picked up upstream's new error path,
  which finalizes the journal so a failed transaction does not leak into the
  next one. This is the same class as the SDM warm-set leak (#21723).
- reth no longer derives `HashedStorage::wiped` from the account status in
  `from_bundle_state`; `HashedPostStateProvider::hashed_post_state` owns the
  destroyed-account handling and now returns `ProviderResult`. The Isthmus
  withdrawals-root path builds its `HashedStorage` directly, so it keeps
  propagating `wiped` explicitly; `OpProofsStateProviderRef` materializes the
  zeroed slots against the proofs storage at the parent block.
- `ExecutionWitnessRecord` became a borrow of `State<DB>` whose only public
  exit is `into_execution_witness`, which also fills in ancestor headers. Both
  op-reth witness paths use it; the payload-builder witness therefore gained a
  headers provider and now returns headers as `debug_executionWitness` already
  did.
- `ReceiptConverter` gained `RpcLog`/`convert_log` and the log-matching helpers
  now convert through it, so the flashblock log stream passes the converter and
  a header carrying the payload's number, hash and timestamp.
- Smaller: `reth_trie_db::from_reverts_auto` -> `HashedPostStateSorted::from_reverts`,
  `ChangesetCache` -> `reth_storage_overlay::OverlayManager`,
  `BuiltPayloadExecutedBlock::changed_paths` and
  `BuildNewPayload::{cache,state_root_handle}` removed,
  `validate_block_post_execution_with_hashed_state` gained a parent header,
  `calculate_initial_tx_gas` gained an EIP-2780 argument, and
  `alloy_genesis::ChainConfig` gained `bogota_time`.

op-reth,alloy-op-evm: zero overlay storage for destroyed accounts, cover the deposit gas-cap exemption

Two follow-ups from the `reth-update-reviewer` pass over the v2.5.0 bump.

`MemoryOverlayOpProofsStateProviderRef::hashed_post_state` only forwarded to the
inner provider, which zeroes a destroyed account's storage against the
*persisted* proofs storage. Slots written by blocks still in the in-memory
buffer live in the overlay, so a selfdestructed account stayed partially wiped
and the state root came out wrong. reth hit the same gap when it stopped
deriving `HashedStorage::wiped` from account status and extended
`MemoryOverlayStateProviderRef::hashed_post_state` to zero the unpersisted
slots too; this mirrors that. The path feeds `state_root_with_updates` in the
proofs engine, so the failure mode is a spurious state-root mismatch.

`alloy-op-evm` had no positive test for the EIP-7825 deposit gas-cap
exemption — only the negative case asserting non-deposits stay capped. The
exemption is not observable as an error, because deposits skip `validate_env`
where `TxGasLimitGreaterThanCap` is raised; it is only observable in how much
gas the first frame receives, via `initial_gas_and_reservoir`, which OP does
not override. The new tests measure that: a deposit above the cap runs a
payload costing more than the capped budget and must still complete, and the
saved cap round-trips through every resting state including `None`.

Both tests were checked red against deliberately broken variants — the first
against a disabled exemption, the second against a restore path that collapses
the inner `Option`.

kona-node: Serve the system config lookup from imported blocks

The sequencer's attributes builder and the derivation pipeline each reconstruct
the SystemConfig of the block they are building on top of, once per block. That
block is one the node has just imported, yet both fetched it back from the
execution layer in full — the sequencer on the block-production path.

InsertTask already decodes every payload it inserts to derive the block's
L2BlockInfo, and SealTask and ConsolidateTask both route through it, so every
imported block passes one point holding exactly the (OpBlock, L2BlockInfo) pair
kona-providers-local's BufferedL2Provider stores. Hand it over there via a new
ImportedBlockSink, and put BufferedAlloyL2ChainProvider in front of the RPC
provider so those lookups read the buffer first.

Only the hash-keyed lookup is served locally. A height does not identify a block
across a reorg, so the by-number lookups stay on the RPC, and an entry for a
block that is later reorged out is never returned — it just ages out.

Part of #22432.

kona-providers-local: Take the block buffer off async locks

ChainStateBuffer guarded its two LRU caches with tokio::sync::RwLock, which made
every method async and forced ImportedBlockSink::block_imported to be async too,
so #[async_trait] boxed a future per imported block.

No guard was ever held across an await point. The one place it could have been,
get_block_by_number, dropped its guard by hand first. Async locks exist for the
case where a guard must survive an await; where it must not, the blocking locks
are both simpler and faster, and now the compiler enforces the rule rather than
a convention doing it.

Switching to std::sync::RwLock makes the buffer, the provider's write API, and
the sink synchronous, drops async_trait from ImportedBlockSink, and leaves
providers-local with no tokio runtime dependency. The L2ChainProvider and
BatchValidationProvider methods stay async, as their traits require.

Part of #22432.

op-e2e/actions: emulate EL-sync p2p for the reth backend

The EL-sync tests rely on the sequencer and verifier engines peering over
devp2p so the verifier snap-syncs the chain from a single unsafe head. The
ephemeral reth engines are out-of-process subprocesses with no networking,
so Enode/AddPeers/PeerCount panicked 'not yet wired'.

Wire them against an in-process stand-in: a registry resolves a synthetic
enode back to the reth engine it identifies, peering is symmetric so both
PeerCount reads pass, and each peering starts a sync pump. The pump watches
optest_syncTarget (the head a forkchoice update reported SYNCING for) and,
while one is set, backfills the missing blocks from the peer engine one
validated optest_importBlock at a time — never moving safe/finalized, which
reproduces exactly the state op-geth reaches after backfilling under a
SYNCING forkchoice. It activates only once the engine has actually reported
SYNCING (which op-node triggers only during genuine EL sync, not for a
CL-mode gapped payload), so it fires exactly when a real EL would snap-sync.

The 'Forkchoice requested sync to new head' log the tests assert on is
emitted synchronously by the geth engine API inside forkchoiceUpdated, so
an async pump log would race the assertion. elSyncLogRPC wraps op-node's
engine RPC and reproduces it in op-node's own call path: it caches each
newPayload's block number and logs on a SYNCING forkchoice update to a head
it has seen.

complete execution payload into a committed canonical block, plus attrs-less
forkchoice.

Insertion uses reth's in-memory canonical state (the engine-tree path), not a DB
write: execute against the parent overlay, verify the post-state root, build an

  canonical/safe/finalized pointers: unknown head -> SYNCING (never silent VALID),
  unknown non-zero safe/finalized -> Error::UnknownForkchoiceBlock (resolved before
  any pointer moves). FCU with attributes returns Unsupported until the builder lands.
- `EphemeralChain`: store the chain spec; add state_at / commit_block /
  advance_forkchoice (+ test-only tip_header/latest_state).

op-reth-test-engine: stateful in-flight payload builder

Add the sequencer-flow block builder on top of the one-shot import path:
forkchoice_updated-with-attributes opens a payload (deposits applied and
validated, payload id derived via the production OpPayloadBuilderAttributes /
BuildNextEnv path), include_tx executes and appends a pool tx (with the op-geth
engine API's gas-limit and force-empty semantics), and get_payload seals it into
OpExecutionData that round-trips back through new_payload.

reth's block builder ties the executor, EVM state, and parent to a single
borrowed lifetime, so it can't be parked across calls; the in-flight payload
instead keeps the ordered tx list and re-runs a deterministic one-shot assembly
on demand.

Tests drive the full sequencer flow (FCU+attrs -> include_tx -> get_payload ->
new_payload -> FCU) into a valid two-block chain, plus gas-limit rejection,
force-empty skipping, and remaining-gas accounting.

feat(op-reth): add chain head gas and base fee metrics

op-geth exposes `chain/head/basefee`, `chain/head/gas_used` and
`chain/head/blob_gas_used` (plus the two gas histograms) from its
`updateOptimismBlockMetrics` hook. op-reth is meant to be a superset of
op-geth, but had no equivalent, so operators migrating off op-geth lose
head gas and fee visibility.

Add `OpChainHeadMetrics` under the `chain.head` scope, so the exported
names match op-geth's modulo the global `reth_` prefix that reth's
Prometheus recorder applies -- op-geth's `chain_head_basefee` becomes
`reth_chain_head_basefee`. The block height counterparts already exist
upstream as `reth_blockchain_tree_{canonical_chain_height,
safe_block_height,finalized_block_height}`.

The metrics are driven from the canonical state notification stream,
spawned in `OpAddOns::launch_add_ons` so every op-reth node gets them
without touching the launcher paths that `proof_history.rs` warns must be
kept in sync with the sdm-fixture node.

Attributes a header does not carry are left unrecorded rather than
reported as zero, matching op-geth's `TryUpdate` helpers: a pre-1559
chain does not publish a 0 base fee and a pre-4844 chain does not skew
the blob gas histogram with zeroes.

kona-engine: targeted reset via `Engine::reset_to`

`Engine::reset` always discovers where to land by walking the L2 back over
RPC. A caller that already knows the target heads gains nothing from that
search, and re-deriving risks picking a different block than the one it
means.

verbatim. `Engine::reset` is unchanged as the standalone default: it still
discovers a start point, and still re-runs the walkback on every retry,
because re-discovery is what makes retrying worthwhile there.

`reset_to` has no such escape hatch — the heads are fixed, so each attempt
sends the identical forkchoice update — so its retries are capped and the
error is handed back to the caller, the only party that can supply
different heads.

Neither reset mints a cross-safe promotion, so a reset cannot move the
cross-safe head forward. Bounding it against a rewinding target belongs to
the state transition, not here.

op-node: publish gossiped blocks off the sequencer's hot path

SimpleAsyncGossiper published inline in its select loop, so while the
publish was in flight the loop could receive nothing. With a remote
signer the publish is an HTTPS round-trip, and the sequencer reaches
Clear() 1-2ms after Gossip() - so it blocked for the rest of that
round-trip. The next block's build window is computed as a residual,
which subtracts that stall 1:1 from the next block's building time.

Publishing now runs on a dedicated goroutine and Gossip, Get and Clear
only take a mutex, so none of them waits for the network:

- Payloads are handed over through a pending slot. A payload that has
  not started publishing yet is superseded by a newer one: the tip is
  what peers need, and they reach the older block through sync.
- An epoch counter, advanced by both Gossip and Clear, decides whether
  a completed publish may still populate the reuse buffer. This keeps
  the invariant the blocking Clear() used to give for free: a publish
  that lands after Clear cannot resurrect a payload the sequencer has
  already inserted and moved past.
- Clear no longer cancels an in-flight publish - peers need the block
  either way - it only drops the payload held for reuse.

Get no longer waits for an in-flight publish, so it can return nil
where it previously blocked and returned the payload. The sequencer
then seals (or re-seals) its building job instead, which is strictly
cheaper than stalling the build window.

Also bounds a publish attempt with a deadline. Without one, a signer
connection that hangs rather than errors blocked publishing until TCP
gave up - and before this change, block production with it.

Fixes #22554

kona!: local/cross-safe head vocabulary and a single cross-safe promotion entry point

Splits the engine's single `safe_head` into an explicit local-safe head and
cross-safe head, and makes the cross-safe head — the forkchoice
`safeBlockHash` — writable through exactly one entry point.

The five existing writers (payload insert, three consolidation sites, and the
engine reset start point) now advance local-safe only. This is enforced
structurally rather than by convention: `EngineSyncStateUpdate` has no
cross-safe field, so a legacy writer cannot express a cross-safe move at all.
Moving it requires a `CrossSafePromotion`, which has no public constructor —
outside `kona-engine` only the holder of an engine's unique
`CrossSafePromoter`, handed out once by `Engine::with_external_cross_safe()`,
can mint one. Promotions accept backward moves and are clamped at the finalized
head.

Standalone kona-node keeps `Engine::new()`, whose cross-safe head is fed from
local-safe advancement. The trivial promotion is minted inside the same state
application, so the forkchoice update that reports the advance still carries
local-safe == cross-safe in a single call and the Engine API traffic is
unchanged.

The depth-1 lockstep confirmation back to derivation is now explicitly
local-safe-driven. It compiled fine either way, so it is covered by a
lagging-cross test alongside the engine-level ones: standalone always has
local-safe == cross-safe, so withholding promotion is the only shape that can
catch a head being classified as the wrong one.

Wire names are unchanged: `safe_l2`, `ws_subscribe_safe_head` and the `safe`
block-label metric value all keep their meaning as the forkchoice safe label.

BREAKING CHANGE: `kona-engine`'s `EngineSyncState::safe_head()` is now
`cross_safe_head()`, `EngineSyncStateUpdate` no longer has a `safe_head` field,
`L2ForkchoiceState::safe` is now `local_safe`, and `Metrics::SAFE_BLOCK_LABEL`
is now `Metrics::CROSS_SAFE_BLOCK_LABEL` (the label value is still `safe`).
`kona-node-service`'s `EngineActorRequest::ProcessSafeL2Signal`,
`DerivationActorRequest::ProcessEngineSafeHeadUpdateRequest` and
`EngineDerivationClient::send_new_engine_safe_head` gain `LocalSafe`/
`local_safe` in their names.

kona-engine: hold the cross-safe head down when local-safe rewinds

`EngineSyncStateUpdate` cannot express a cross-safe move, so `apply_update`
carried the cross-safe head through untouched. That is right when the other
heads advance, but two writers move the local-safe head *backwards*:

- `Engine::reset` installs the `find_starting_forkchoice` walkback point,
  deliberately at least a sequencing window behind the unsafe head.
- `ConsolidateTask::reconcile_to_local_safe_head` installs the injected
  local-safe block as both the local-safe and the unsafe head.

Neither carries a promotion, and under `CrossSafeSource::Promoted` no trivial
promotion is minted either, so nothing held the cross-safe head down. After any
interop reset the state routinely kept `cross_safe_head > local_safe_head`, and
since both writers lower the unsafe head to the same block,
`create_forkchoice_state` then reported `safeBlockHash` ahead of
`headBlockHash` — the `INVALID_FORK_CHOICE_STATE` rejection that arrives as
`SynchronizeTaskError::InvalidForkchoiceState` and costs a full engine reset.

`apply_update` now holds the cross-safe head at the local-safe head it is about
to install. This is the mirror of the clamp in `apply_cross_safe_promotion`,
placed at the single point where the sync state transitions rather than at the
point of damage, so every rewinding writer inherits it.

It logs at `info!` rather than `warn!`: unlike the promotion clamps this is not
a disagreement with the promotion source but ordinary node operation, and it
fires on every interop reset, so a warning here would devalue the promotion
clamp's warnings. A cross-safe head moving backwards is still a safety-level
regression worth seeing at default verbosity, so it is not `debug!` either.

Only the local-safe head is compared. The unsafe head is local-safe's own upper
bound, so a state where it alone drops below cross-safe already violates
`unsafe >= local-safe`, and the floor at the finalized head is already covered
by the `FinalizedAheadOfUnsafe` guard in `SynchronizeTask::execute`.

Regression test: `a_reset_below_the_cross_safe_head_holds_cross_safe_at_the_walkback_point`.
Against the old code the cross-safe head stays at the pre-reset block while the
heads rewind, and the forkchoice update carries safe ahead of head.

unsafe block signer sender, query receiver) moves into an
`L1WatcherChain`, of which the actor holds a non-empty vec; the L1
provider, the head and finalized streams, and the L1 head watch stay
shared. Every L1 update is fanned out to each chain, each chain's system
config logs are filtered by its own address, and each chain's queries are
answered from its own rollup config.

The `select!` arms now only classify the update, with handling after
their borrows end, so the query arm can hold the chain vec mutably while
the fan-out reads it. A standalone kona-node builds the same actor with a
one-element vec and is otherwise unchanged.

kona-node-service: fetch the L1 watcher's per-chain logs concurrently and name the chain in its logs

Addresses two review findings on the multi-chain L1 watcher.

The per-head system config log fetch ran one chain at a time and returned
on the first error, so the last chain's unsafe-signer update waited on
every earlier chain's RPC round-trip, and one chain's transient transport
error skipped the remaining chains' requests entirely. `try_join_all`
starts all N requests together: the latency is one round-trip rather than
N, and every chain's request is issued even when one of them fails. The
round is still not atomic - the first error aborts it, and the signer
updates already delivered stay delivered.

The four `L1WatcherChain` log sites and
`L1WatcherActorError::DerivationClientError` recorded nothing identifying
the chain, so with N chains an operator could not tell which chain's
derivation actor or signer channel broke. All four now carry a `chain_id`
field, and the error variant carries the chain id so the failure that
stops the whole watcher names its cause.

kona-node-service: stop one chain from blocking the others in the L1 watcher

Both of the watcher's fan-out loops awaited one chain at a time. Each
chain's derivation actor has its own bounded request queue, so a chain
that fell behind and filled it parked `step()` on that one send: while
parked no other chain received L1 heads or finalized blocks, and no
chain's queries were served. Start every chain's send together with
`try_join_all`, as the system config log fetch below already does.

The query fan-in had the same shape. `select_all` polls its futures in
the order it is given them and returns the first that is ready, and the
`select!` randomisation only covers the three top-level arms, not the
chains inside one of them, so a chain whose query channel was never
empty starved every chain after it. Rotate the polling order with a
cursor that advances past whichever chain was served, so each chain
takes its turn at the front.

Both are no-ops for a single chain: `try_join_all` over one future
awaits exactly that future, and rotating a one-element list by zero
leaves it alone.

The L1State query body was a module-level free function, against the
project's Rust style, which asks for methods on the struct even when the

op-reth: use the engine's sparse trie pipeline on the payload build path

`OpPayloadBuilder::build_payload` discarded `state_root_handle` through the `..`
pattern, so `--engine.share-sparse-trie-with-payload-builder` was inert for the
OP builder: every build walked the trie synchronously in `BlockBuilder::finish`,
and the sparse trie the engine preserved for the payload was taken by the
spawned task and stored back cleared.

Wire it the way reth's Ethereum builder does (`crates/ethereum/payload/src/lib.rs`):
install a state hook so state diffs stream to the trie task as they commit during
execution, then take the final root from the task and pass it to `finish`, falling
back to the synchronous walk if the pipeline fails.

`block_builder_with_mode` re-states the database bound its `ConfigurePostExecEvm`
counterpart already carries; without it the returned `impl BlockBuilder` hides the
`State` that owns the hook.

`OpBuilder` receives the handle through a setter rather than a `build` parameter,
so existing callers are unaffected.
op-reth: use the engine's sparse trie pipeline on the payload build path

op-reth: bound the wait for the shared sparse trie's state root

`OpBuilder::build` called `PayloadStateRootHandle::state_root()`, a blocking
`recv()` with no deadline. A trie task that never answers parked the build
forever: the payload job stayed pending, never spawned another attempt, and
`getPayload` never resolved, because the OP builder answers `AwaitInProgress`
when no payload has been built yet. One stalled task cost the slot and leaked a
payload-task permit and a blocking-pool thread.

Wait at most `OpBuilderConfig::state_root_wait` instead, and report a timeout as
an error so it takes the fallback the pipeline already had, the synchronous trie
walk. `None` keeps the unbounded wait; the default matches `TreeConfig`'s
`DEFAULT_STATE_ROOT_TASK_TIMEOUT`, which bounds the same computation on the
`newPayload` path.

Unlike the engine, the builder cannot race the fallback against the trie task:
`BlockBuilder::finish` consumes the builder, so a timed-out build pays both. The
bound is a hang-breaker, not a latency knob.

Drop the handle before the fallback walk, so the abandoned task is cancelled
rather than left competing for CPU with the walk that replaces it.

Count both outcomes, in `state_root_from_shared_trie_total` and
`state_root_fallback_total`. Together they answer the two questions an operator
enabling the flag has: is the pipeline being used at all, and is it working.

ci,rust: rebalance rust-cargo-hack with weighted package partitioning

The hack recipes shuffled the package list with a seeded shuf and passed it
as -p flags, but cargo-hack uses -p only as a membership filter and iterates
workspace members in cargo-metadata order, so the shuffle never changed the
run order. --partition then sliced that fixed order into contiguous chunks,
concentrating the adjacent heavy op-reth/kona blocks on the same nodes
(0.9-13.1 min per-node spread at parallelism 10).

Partition in the shell instead: scripts/hack-partition.sh deterministically
assigns packages to nodes by LPT bin-packing over a checked-in weight table
(scripts/hack-weights.txt, seconds measured from CI logs of build 5489984),
and each node passes only its own -p subset. Packages too heavy for one node
(op-reth, reth-optimism-cli) are sharded across nodes via per-package
--partition; the shard-1 node covers such a package in the test-targets
step. Both hack steps share one assignment so the per-node sum of both steps
is what gets balanced (predicted 5.5-5.7 min per node).

The placebo shuffle/seed parameters and their CI call-site arguments are
removed.

Closes #22103

kona-engine: skip unsafe-head staleness check for seals atomic with their build

The seal task's UnsafeHeadChangedSinceBuild check exists to catch a real
race in the sequencer flow, where Build and Seal run as separate engine
tasks and an Insert task can advance the unsafe head in between. In
build_and_seal (the consolidate reorg path and the Holocene deposits-only
fallback), build and seal run atomically inside a single engine task, so
the unsafe head cannot move between them — there, a build parent that
differs from the unsafe head is an intentional derivation-driven reorg,
not a stale build. Because that path has no result channel, the false
positive surfaced as a Critical error and crash-looped the node whenever
derivation reorged the unsafe chain while behind the tip.

Add an is_atomic_with_build flag to SealTask and gate the staleness check
on it: build_and_seal passes true, the engine actor's detached Seal
request keeps the check with its existing graceful handling.

release-notes: learn from published notes, retarget RC refs, comment out drops

Three gaps found by running the skill against the v1.19.5 train and then
reading what the release manager actually published.

Convention drift. Release managers edit these notes after they are drafted,
and those edits are the real house style — but nothing was reading them, so
each run would re-litigate the same corrections. scripts/recent-style.sh
dumps the hand-written parts of recent releases (headers and footers, PR list
omitted), and the skill now reads them before drafting and treats them as
authoritative over reference/house-style.md.

RC references. git-cliff drafts against the RC tag, so the heading, compare
link and image tag all read -rc.N. Publishing that finalized points operators
at an RC image. scripts/retarget-tag.sh rewrites them, and refuses — leaving
the file untouched — when the finalized tag is missing or sits on a different
commit than the RC.

Dropped PRs are now commented out rather than deleted, with a short reason,
so a reviewer can reinstate one in a single edit and can see what was
considered. This matches what the release manager was already doing by hand.

The same reading pass produced several corrections to the reference docs: the
verdict callout leads with the operator-visible symptom rather than the
mechanism; the breaking-changes section stays at one to three bullets and
drops importer-only entries; observability items merge into one callout; the
compare link's base is the previous finalized tag. triage.md gains the trap
that linkage alone cannot catch — op-core/fees is compiled into op-batcher,
but the DA-footprint work is reached only from op-chain-ops check tools, so
it was cut as "doesn't affect the batcher".

release-notes: curate the change list instead of annotating the raw one

The notes this skill produced kept git-cliff's flat list of PR titles and
stacked callouts on top to supply the context those titles lacked. Every
change was therefore mentioned twice, and the callouts competed with each
other for attention until none of them carried any.

Target the style of op-challenger/v1.9.4 and op-contracts/v8.0.0-rc.2
instead: replace the PR list with entries grouped under Features / Bug fixes
/ Other or a domain heading, fold PRs that are one logical change into one
entry, write each entry to stand alone, and reference PRs as bare (#NNNNN)
so GitHub autolinks them. Each PR is mentioned exactly once; the only
repeat allowed is a New Contributors row, which credits a person rather
than describing a change.

The upgrade recommendation moves to one standard sentence with fixed
vocabulary — optional / optional but recommended / recommended / required —
in a callout at the top of ## Overview. That callout is always [!NOTE],
except for a required upgrade, which uses [!CAUTION]. Holding the block type
constant is the point: severity comes from the sentence, and the block only
makes it findable. Flagging a routine recommended upgrade as a [!WARNING]
overstated it and made the recommendation harder to read. It is also the
note's only callout — anything reaching for a second is an entry in the list
or a breaking change.

Two proportionality rules, both from review of the v1.19.5 train. Check
whether a feature is live before drawing attention to a change to it:
interop/Lagoon, ZK dispute games and super dispute games are enabled
nowhere, so those changes sit under a "(not yet in production)" heading with
a standard Note in the Overview, however alarming they sound out of context.
And ask whether a reader would shrug — a new metric, a wrong version string
and a rare corner case are bullets, not callouts.

Go-API-only changes are not breaking changes: ## Breaking changes is for
things an operator must act on before upgrading.

release-notes: write impact, not implementation

Review of the v1.19.5 notes cut most of the technical explanation this skill
had written. The sequencer entry described goroutines, direct engine calls,
event-loop round trips and the latency mechanics, then noted which PR
introduced the bug another PR fixed. All of it went; what stayed was the
symptom — block production can slow right after a batcher transaction lands
on L1, most noticeably on low-throughput chains.

Add that as an explicit rule, with the before and after as the worked
example, because the PR descriptions read during triage are written the
opposite way round and pull hard in the wrong direction. Out: threads, event
loops, call paths, internal type and package names, refactor structure,
release-internal history. In: the symptom, the flag and metric names, the
values that shift, what the reader must do.

The line is not "no technical detail" — op-batcher's entry keeps
SuggestBlobTipCap sampling one block too many, because that is the observable
change and explains why suggested tips move. Detail describing a computation
whose result the operator sees stays; detail describing how the program is
put together goes. Pure churn gets one line saying it changed nothing
operator-facing, rather than a description.

Two smaller corrections from the same review. A dormant-feature change that
is a no-op for this component is now cut outright rather than sectioned —
kona-node's registry dependency-set change only ever mattered to kona-proofs.
And do not narrate an attack the live system cannot suffer: the span-batch
decoding fix was drafted with the chain-split scenario spelled out, which was
cut because the fix does not reach proofs until U20.

Recommendations can also be scoped to a role — "optional, but recommended
for sequencers" — rather than recommending a release to everyone on the
strength of something most operators never see.

op-acceptance-tests,ci: name the supernode a run selected, and the job honestly

A green acceptance run does not say which supernode it measured, and the job
name has been saying the wrong thing.

memory-all-kona-lokahi-op-reth-<fork> ran supernode_kind: op-supernode. The
flip to lokahi was made, measured and reverted -- job 5505219 at 7b4b313a,
190 passed, 130 failed, 25 skipped, 76 of them halting on "which L1 block
made timestamp N safe is no longer recorded on this node" -- and the name was
kept so ci-gate's requires list went on matching. That was a convenience at
the time and it outlived its context: three separate green runs of a job
named lokahi were then read as lokahi passing the acceptance tests, when
lokahi had not started in any of them. The most recent, 5508755, is a
complete 801-record run with no failures, and every record in it is the Go
op-supernode.

The name is now what it runs, kona-node for the per-chain CL and op-supernode
for the supernode, and ci-gate's requires is updated in the same commit --
that is the entire cost of renaming, since the gate is the only required
check and the ruleset names it rather than the jobs behind it. lokahi is left
reserved for a job that actually sets supernode_kind: lokahi. No
supernode_kind value changes here; which variant to run is a separate call.

Renaming alone would not have prevented this, because a name can drift from
its config again, so the selected kind is also reported into the test record.
It goes in as a subtest name rather than a log line on purpose: gotestsum's
JUnit output keeps names for passing tests but not their stdout, and the
green run is exactly the case where the question matters, because the green
run is what gets offered as evidence. A reader of the CircleCI test output
now sees TestSupernodeKindReported/selected=op-supernode without opening the
job's exported environment.

The reported kind is the requested one. The dispatch in
startTwoL2SharedSupernode and startSingleChainSharedSupernode branches
straight off ResolveSupernodeKind, so requested and started agree unless that
dispatch is bypassed; reporting the kind of the supernode object a preset
actually built would be stronger and needs plumbing the TwoL2 preset does not
have, which is left as a follow-up rather than done half-way.

every one of ci-gate's 19 requires entries resolves to a job the workflow
defines, with the fusaka matrix expanded. The new test has not been compiled
or run. This environment is out of disk (~2G free against a ~39G quota, 17G

kona-safedb,op-acceptance-tests: cover the safe-head floor moving under a reader

The safe-head database's floor can rise, and until now nothing covered the
sequence that raises it. `truncate_on_safe_head_reset_before_first_entry`
pins the wipe and `l1_at_safe_head`'s `target_below_first` case pins the
verdict below the floor, but not the two in sequence -- which is the only way
the floor ever moves up, since entries are otherwise only appended above it.

`a_wipe_and_refill_moves_the_floor_up_permanently` walks the whole sequence:
a database recording from L2 block 500, a reset at or before its earliest
entry that deletes everything and re-records nothing, the empty window where
every target is `L1AtSafeHeadNotFound` and so worth retrying, then a refill
from block 700 after which the same target is `L1AtSafeHeadUnavailable` and
permanent. The retry-to-permanent transition is the part that matters to a
reader: a lower bound resolved once and cached is wrong from there on through
no fault of its own, which is why the interop verifier re-reads it every
round rather than latching it at startup.

This is a characterization test. It passes on the parent commit, because it
pins behaviour the database always had -- the defect was in a reader's
assumption about that behaviour, not in the database.

caller of `with_safe_db` in the tree is lokahi

safe-head database and the `SafeDBPath` the test sets is not plumbed to it.

op-devstack,op-acceptance-tests: make the two-chain gate fail an inert supernode

People are leaning on the two-chain test as the lokahi gate, and it was a
weaker one than it reads. Two things it could not catch.

A supernode that crashed still reported as running. LokahiSupernode.Running
returned n.sub != nil, and n.sub is only cleared by a Stop this side asked
for, so a process that panicked or was killed left it set. The one assertion
that exists to say the supernode survived losing a chain's execution layer
could therefore not fail. It now reads SubProcess.Exited, which is closed
once cmd.Wait returns.

Nothing tied a route to the chain it serves. TestTwoChainProgress compared
the two endpoints' scheme, host and port for equality -- a claim that gets
easier to satisfy the more the routing collapses, since two identical
endpoints satisfy it perfectly -- and took the chain ids from ChainID(),
which is the id the devstack configured rather than anything the node said.
One chain served down both routes passed every check while both progress
loops measured that chain twice. The routes are now required to differ, and
each is asked for the rollup config it is running so the L2 genesis hash
says which chain answered.

The same test also let gossip stand in for derivation. An unsafe head
advancing says a payload arrived, which a supernode deriving nothing still
does; only the local safe head is set from L1 batch data. The two are now
stated as separate claims, the derivation check takes a fresh baseline
rather than reusing one captured up to 30s earlier -- against the old
baseline a head that moved during the gossip wait satisfied it on the first
tick -- and the chains must end past their genesis, which is what tells a
deriving chain from one sitting inert where it started.

Both fixes are pinned by unit tests that were watched failing first:
Running reported a process that exited on its own as running, and a route
builder that drops the chain id passes every host-and-port check while
handing out one endpoint twice.

The test-sequencer's standard builder fetches optimism_dependencySet from a
chain's CL whenever that chain schedules Lagoon
(op-test-sequencer/.../standardbuilder/config.go:68), and nothing in the Rust
tree answered it. op-node serves it from nodeAPI.DependencySet
(op-node/node/api.go:178), returning the configured set or ethereum.NotFound;
op-supernode inherits that on each of its per-chain routes, because every route
is an op-node handler.

Served from the same place: kona's `optimism` namespace, out of the dependency
set the node builder is already handed. That keeps it independent of where the
chain's RPC is bound.

The response is its own type rather than DependencySet itself. Go writes this
one through minStaticConfigDependencySet
(op-core/interop/depset/static_depset.go:52), which omits the expiry-window
override when it is zero; kona models it as an Option<u64>, which would put

lokahi: answer superroot_atTimestamp before interop activates

superroot_atTimestamp already had op-supernode's pre-activation branch: with no
verifier to ask, Branch::of(None) is Handoff, and the super root is composed
from the optimistic outputs, which are the canonical ones there. What it did not
have was the history that branch reads. The safe-head database was opened only
for an interop-scheduled chain set, so every other chain got DisabledDatabase,
and pairing a block behind the local-safe head with the L1 block that made it
safe returned SafeDbError::NotEnabled -> QueryError::HistoryUnavailable, failing
the whole call for exactly the timestamps a pre-interop proposer asks about.

op-supernode has no such gate: its chain container sets SafeDBPath on every
virtual node it starts
(op-supernode/supernode/chain_container/chain_container.go:236), so the history
is there whether or not interop is scheduled. Opened unconditionally here too.

Loading stays two-phase -- all checks, then all side effects -- so a chain set
that cannot run still leaves no rocksdb LOCK behind. The phases are now two
types rather than one type with an Option that meant both "not opened yet" and
"interop is off".

being removed; and they cannot be merged into one jsonrpsee module because
every chain has the same method names, so what routes them is the HTTP path
— structurally what Go's Router does. The router matches it behaviour for
behaviour: the first path segment is the chain id in decimal, an unknown
chain id is a 404, and a hosted chain that has not composed yet is polled
for 25ms at a time up to 60s and then refused with 503.

standalone kona-node — the module set is bound by `JsonrpseeServerLauncher`

lokahi: re-read the safe-head lower bound instead of latching it

Cold start read every chain's first safe head, clamped the verification
start to the latest of them, and latched it. op-supernode does not latch:
its backfill wait re-reads FirstSafeHeadTimestamp on every backoff pass
(op-node/rollup/interop/log_backfill.go:71,85-95). That asymmetry was a
permanent halt.

A derivation reset at or before the earliest recorded entry wipes the
safe-head database outright, and deliberately re-records nothing when the
boundary is the first entry (kona/crates/node/safedb/src/safe_db.rs:100-121,
covered by truncate_on_safe_head_reset_before_first_entry). The wipe alone
was survivable: an empty database answers L1AtSafeHeadNotFound, which is a
retry. The refill was not. The database comes back from wherever derivation
now is, its earliest record sits above the latched start, and every
subsequent round asks below it and gets L1AtSafeHeadUnavailable — the one
permanent verdict — from safe_db.rs:195-198.

The bound is now re-read each round, before anything is observed and after
any pending slot is applied. While nothing is committed the start follows
the history up and backfills the widened window; once a frontier is
committed it cannot move, so a bound above the next timestamp is a real gap
and still halts — but it halts at the bound with the gap named, rather than
several reads later as a chain that cannot answer.

That second arm is also the resume path's only safe-head check. Resuming
takes last_verified + 1 from the verified store and consults no safe-head
database, and log_history_gap reads only the log stores. The three
databases sit under two roots — a chain's log store and its safe-head
database in that chain's datadir, the verified store under the interop
datadir — so any one can be reseeded or lost without the others.

The all-chains-ready gate is unchanged; the bug was the latch, not the gate.

The round_loop fake answered Derived for any timestamp it held a block for,
which is why this read as healthy in tests and halted in production. It now
mirrors l1_at_safe_head: permanent below the earliest record, a retry when
the database holds nothing.

Also notes at the call site that L1AtSafeHeadUnavailable and NotEnabled
collapse into one verdict and one log line, so the halt message cannot
distinguish pruned records from a database that was never opened. Chain::open
opens it for every chain (lokahi/src/supernode.rs:366-375), which is what
makes NotEnabled unreachable and the message unambiguous in practice.

op-test-sequencer: fix nil ensemble panic in config Start cleanup

config.Ensemble.Start named its first result `ensemble` and installed a
deferred cleanup that closes it on error. Every error path returns
`nil, err`, which assigns nil to that named result before the defer runs,
so the cleanup called Close on a nil *work.Ensemble and panicked in
work.(*Ensemble).Close instead of closing the services already started.

acceptance run that hit it lost every result after the crash and buried
the underlying start failure.

Take the ensemble out of the result list so the error returns can no
longer clobber it, and let Close tolerate a nil receiver, since Starter
implementations may legitimately return a nil ensemble with an error and
callers may defer Close before checking it.

lokahi: serve supernode_syncStatus and superroot_atTimestamp

These are the two questions the rest of the stack asks a supernode, and until now
lokahi answered neither: op-proposer reads the super root it proposes from
superroot_atTimestamp, op-challenger reads it at every step of a dispute, and the
devstack DSL's Supernode wrapper calls QueryAPI() unconditionally.

The wire is op-supernode's, field for field. The chain ids are decimal strings, as
map keys and as array elements; super.timestamp is hexadecimal because eth.SuperV1
marshals it through hexutil.Uint64 while every other timestamp in these responses is
a plain number; super.chains carries the Go field names ChainID and Output because
eth.ChainIDAndOutput has no struct tags. The commitments are kona's own -
kona_interop::SuperRoot and kona_protocol::OutputRoot - whose encodings are byte for
byte eth.SuperV1.Marshal and eth.OutputV0.Marshal, so nothing here hashes anything
of its own.

The branch structure of superroot_atTimestamp is named rather than inlined, because
every branch produces a well-formed response and a wrong one is not a failure a
consumer can notice. Verified answers from the frontier the verifier committed to;
waiting answers with no super root at all; handoff composes the super root from the
optimistic outputs, which are canonical before interop activates, below the first
timestamp the verifier covers, and before the verifier has chosen a start.

Both methods answer from the chains' own queues and from the actor that owns the
verified store, not from a second view assembled beside them: a chain's sync status
is the one its own optimism_syncStatus serves, its optimistic pairing comes from one
borrow of its engine state, and the verified frontier is read in the same turn of the
verifier's loop as the L1 block it was derived from. op-supernode reaches that last
guarantee with an RWMutex across two reads and documents the window; there is no
window here.

Parity is asserted across the two languages through one fixture. The Rust tests
generate op-devstack/sysgo/testdata/lokahi_supernode_query.json and the Go test
decodes it with eth.SuperNodeSyncStatusResponse and eth.SuperRootAtTimestampResponse,
recomputing both commitments with eth.OutputRoot and eth.SuperRoot. Neither half says
much alone; together they say a super root lokahi publishes is the one op-supernode
would publish over the same chain outputs.

On the Go side this is plumbing only. op-service/sources.SuperNodeClient already
implements apis.SupernodeQueryAPI, so LokahiSupernode gains QueryAPI() over the
process-wide RPC and no second client exists to disagree with the first.

feat(lokahi): take an interop activation timestamp

lokahi reads interop activation from each chain's Lagoon time, which is
also where the message rules it applies read it -- a verifier activating
somewhere its chains' configs do not would put the verifier and the proof
on different rules. That stays the default and is unchanged for any node
not told otherwise.

The interop acceptance presets, though, describe activation as a
supernode parameter: they compute genesis L2 time plus a delay and hand
it to op-supernode, which takes it as its own configuration. The presets
built on NewSimpleInterop write rollup configs with no Lagoon at all, so
lokahi has nothing to read and leaves interop off -- 22 of 138 acceptance
failures.

So accept an explicit [interop] activation-timestamp. What it can do is
supply an activation for a chain whose config schedules no Lagoon, which
reading the fork cannot. What it deliberately cannot do is move a fork
that is scheduled: honouring a different number there would verify blocks
against rules the chain had not activated. A chain that does schedule
Lagoon must therefore agree with the override, compared by activation
point rather than by raw number -- WithForkAtGenesis writes Lagoon as 0
while the timestamp handed to a supernode is the genesis L2 time, and
those select the same blocks.

An overridden activation also has to carry a dependency set.
load_dependency_set requires one from lagoon_time.is_some() alone, which
an override bypasses, so a chain would have joined the cluster with
interop on and nothing for the verifier to read messages against -- a
missing-message error later rather than a configuration error at startup.
The requirement is restated in Supernode::load, the one place that knows
interop is on for the whole hosted set.

The devstack writes the table from the timestamp the preset already
computes. The Go-side assertion that the two agreed is gone: lokahi
enforces the rule now, in the one place that sees the whole set, and
duplicating it in two languages is how the two drift.

This is a bridge, not the destination -- the presets should schedule the
fork on the chains instead, tracked in #22625.

lokahi: sequence configured chains

A supernode that only validates cannot back the interop acceptance presets:
every one of them makes the hosted chains sequence and hangs the batchers and
proposers off the supernode route. The devstack component refused a sequencing
request outright, because lokahi's configuration had no key for a chain to sign
the blocks it gossips with.

Give a chain its sequencer settings in the configuration file, next to the
settings it already has, and compose kona's own sequencer path from them. A
chain's mode is now the presence of those settings rather than a separate flag,
so "sequences" and "has what sequencing needs" cannot disagree: a chain told to
sequence with no key, and a validating chain carrying sequencer settings, are
both startup errors that name the chain.

The key is read from the file the chain names rather than loaded through kona's
SecretKeyLoader, which writes a fresh key when the file is missing. That is
right for a P2P identity and wrong for a sequencer key: a mistyped path would
hand the chain a key no peer accepts, and every block it signed would be
dropped across the network while the chain itself looked healthy.

lokahi still cannot read a chain's unsafe block signer off its SystemConfig, so
the operator states both that address and the sequencer key. When they disagree
the chain starts and logs it: the blocks it gossips will be rejected, but a key
being rotated into the SystemConfig legitimately differs from the address
recorded there, so it is not lokahi's call to refuse.

kona-engine: pin the head-ordering invariant across reset and promotion

`unsafe >= local-safe >= cross-safe >= finalized` is held by four separate
mechanisms, each guarding a different writer: `FinalizeTask` drops a finality
signal for a block that is not yet cross-safe, `hold_cross_safe_at` drags the
cross-safe head down when a writer rewinds local-safe beneath it, and
`apply_cross_safe_promotion` clamps a promotion that runs ahead of local-safe
as well as one that falls below finalized.

Each has a unit test. None covers the *sequence* — a reset rewinds the heads
and then a promotion arrives that was decided against the pre-reset chain,
which is when the mechanisms interact and when a regression in one would be
masked by another. That sequence is also the one a chain reorging under a
running interop verifier actually produces, since the verifier's round and the
chain's reset are concurrent.

These tests assert the ordering after every individual transition rather than
only at the end, so a violation names the step that introduced it: a stale
promotion held at local-safe, a promotion below finalized held at finalized,
a repeated reset/promote interleaving at varying depths, and the ordinary case
where a promotion at exactly the local-safe head is applied unchanged, so the
clamps cannot pass by holding cross-safe back in normal operation.

Tests only; no behaviour change.

lokahi: run the interop verifier against real chains

The verification round loop existed but nothing ran it: `lokahi` did not
depend on `lokahi-interop`, `Verifier` was constructed only in that crate's
own tests, and kona's `CrossSafePromoter` was used only by kona's tests. A
lokahi supernode therefore composed N plain kona validators and answered
nothing about cross-chain safety.

This wires the loop up end to end, for the promotion half of the lifecycle.

The verifier reads each chain through three sources, each authoritative for
one thing. The chain controller's read-only queue answers about the live
chain — the local-safe head paired with its L1 origin, and output roots —
which is the same queue that chain's JSON-RPC server asks, so an operator
and the verifier cannot be told different things. The safe-head database
answers about history, which the live engine state cannot: it holds the L1
origin of exactly one L2 block, the head, and a lockstep verifier spends
most of its rounds behind that head. The execution layer answers about
block contents.

That second source needed a writer. `kona-safedb` was a complete, tested
crate that nothing used; the chain controller now records each paired
local-safe advance into it and rewinds it across a reset. It is the only
writer, which is what makes the database's ascending-L1 contract keepable
at all — the pairing comes out of the engine state that controller
exclusively owns. Hosts that do not need the history pass
`DisabledDatabase`, whose writes are no-ops, so standalone kona-node is
unchanged.

Promotions go through kona's existing single entry point rather than a new
one. A chain composed for interop gets its engine from
`Engine::with_external_cross_safe`, and composition hands the resulting
`CrossSafePromoter` back to the host. The interop actor holds it — one per
engine, not `Clone` — so the type system, not a comment, says that actor is
that chain's only cross-safe writer. Each verified frontier becomes one
`ChainControllerRequest::PromoteCrossSafe` per chain whose head moved.

Interop is on when every hosted chain schedules Lagoon at the same
timestamp and off when none does. Anything between is a startup error
rather than a partially-interop supernode: rounds are lockstep across the
whole set, so a chain outside the cluster would still be one the cluster
waited for.

Not included, and named in the module docs: finality is still driven
straight from L1 finality without consulting the verified frontier. If L1
finality ever overtakes the verifier — a cold start backfilling an expiry
window, not steady state — the engine's clamp holds the cross-safe head at
the finalized head and warns, so the reported `safe_l2` can run ahead of
what was verified. Gating finality on the frontier is the other half of
#22537 and is left to a follow-up rather than half-done here.

interop: state the message expiry check as a subtraction

The expiry invariant was written four different ways across the interop
implementations, three of them as `init + window`, which can overflow uint64.
op-core saturated the addition, so an overflowing sum made a message never
expire; op-supernode and op-interop-mon wrapped silently; op-interop-filter
rejected the message outright. kona already used a subtraction.

Every site now compares the message age instead: `exec - init > window`.
Each one already performs its ordering check first, so the subtraction cannot
underflow, and the form removes the overflow case rather than handling it four
ways. Behaviour at the boundary is unchanged: `exec == init + window` is valid.

The op-interop-filter timeout rule is converted the same way, comparing the
timeout against the remaining lifetime so no deadline addition can overflow.

op-core was the last user of op-service/safemath, so that package is deleted.

Also pin the expiry boundary in kona and op-interop-mon, and cover the
near-max-uint64 case at the sites that previously wrapped.

lokahi-interop: verification round loop

The interop verifier's lockstep round: observe every chain and the L1 once,
decide from that snapshot alone, write an effectful decision to the WAL slot,
then apply it. Cold-start initialization picks the first verifiable timestamp
from the chains' own safe-head history and backfills the log stores behind it;
a permanent condition halts the verifier instead of spinning.

Only Wait and Advance are applied. A round that reaches Invalidate or Rewind
records the decision and holds the verified frontier where it is, and writes
nothing to the WAL — a slot holding a transition this build cannot apply would
wedge the node on every restart.

The message-validity rules are kona-interop's `MessageRules`, shared with the
fault-proof consolidation path, so a node's verdict and a proof's verdict on
the same message cannot differ.

lokahi-interop: halt on missing local log history

An executing message whose initiating message the log store could not answer
for was charged against the message: `StoreError::Skipped` and
`StoreError::Future` both became `RuleViolation::NoSuchMessage`, on the premise
that every log store holds every timestamp below the round's. Nothing enforced
that premise. The log stores are separate databases from the verified store,
and `Verifier::new` skips backfill on resume, so a store that was truncated,
reseeded or lost made a valid message look like a protocol violation — the
round decided `Invalidate`, `hold` turned that into a `warn!` and `Pace::Idle`,
and cross-safety froze permanently with the verifier still reporting
`Running`. In the phase that applies `Invalidate`, the same input would
invalidate a valid block.

Below the round's timestamp the rules above the store lookup have already
established that a block must be there, so absence is evidence about this
node, not the message: it now maps to `RoundError::Permanent` and halts with
the chain and timestamp named, following the existing
`ChainAt::HistoryUnavailable` path. The arms that mean the store does cover the
position and disagrees — `Conflict` and `NotFound` — stay rule violations,
as does `Future` at the round's own timestamp, where the frontier view is
the whole answer because no store has sealed that block yet.

Resuming is also where the premise is checked rather than assumed:
`Verifier::new` verifies each chain's first sealed timestamp covers the
earliest timestamp a round from `start` can reference — the expiry window
behind `start`, floored by the interop activation time and by the chain's own
genesis, the bounds `backfill_window` and `chain_backfill_range` already apply
— and halts with a named, logged reason when it does not.

The round-loop test world backfilled 5 seconds behind a 20-second expiry
window, a store too shallow to answer every message a round may reference. It
now backfills the whole window, as the real default does, and the depth test
keeps a shallow depth of its own.

lokahi-interop: halt on store failures no retry can clear

`RoundError::is_transient` classified every `StoreError` except
`DataCorruption` as retryable, by negating a single variant rather than
naming the permanent ones. So each variant added since defaulted to
"retry": `UnsupportedVersion` — a record written by a build that disagrees
about the format — and `Closed` both returned `Pace::Retry` from every
round, forever, with a `warn!` per attempt and no halt. The round loop has
no path that reopens a closed store or teaches this build a format it does
not know, so neither cause outlives a retry; both spin.

Name the permanent set instead: damaged records, a format this build does
not read, and a gone handle. The rest stay retryable on purpose — a
rejected write or a position not sealed yet can clear, because the next
round observes the chains again and may ask something different. Halting on
those would stop a node that would have recovered, which is the costlier
direction of the two the method's doc names.

This is the same shape as the store-lookup mapping one commit earlier:
"the store cannot answer" was being read as a verdict about the chain
rather than about this node.

lokahi-interop: address store review findings

Seven should-fix findings from a review pass over the interop stores.

- `OutputArchive` now holds a lock across the read-modify-write in `record`
  and `prune_at_or_after`. Both read a height's outputs, edit the vector and
  write it back, so concurrently the later write dropped the earlier one.
  This is the store whose loss is silent -- a missing output root makes the
  optimistic superroot branch serve the replacement block's output, well
  formed and wrong -- and it was the only one of the three stores without a
  guard across that shape of update.

- `set_pending` refuses to overwrite an occupied WAL slot with a different
  transition, which would discard the record of side effects already applied:
  the loss the WAL exists to prevent. Re-writing the same transition still
  succeeds, so a replay path can set it unconditionally. The slot's
  read-check-write is serialised so that check cannot be raced.

- `commit` below retained history answers `Skipped`, rather than falling into
  the replay branch and surfacing a read's `NotFound` for a write.

- A format-version mismatch is `UnsupportedVersion` rather than
  `DataCorruption`. A downgraded binary is not a damaged store, and the
  distinction is what keeps an operator from chasing the wrong cause.

- Counts encode through `u32::try_from` rather than a truncating `as`,
  matching what `seal_block` already does for the same class of count.

- The documented crash-replay case -- the write landed, the WAL slot had not
  yet been cleared -- gets an on-disk test, and the record-layout test pins
  the executing-message sub-layout field by field against `encodeExecMsgInto`.
  Those offsets were covered only by round-trip, which cannot catch a
  consistent encode/decode swap that diverges from Go.

genesis, and lokahi made no engine call to either verifier execution layer for

share, and each `[[chains]]` entry states only what is specific to that
chain. Resolution is pure, so the mistakes N chains make possible — the
same chain twice, two chains on one port, two chains in one data
directory, chains on different L1s — are startup errors naming the chains
involved rather than symptoms later.

Per chain: its own data directory holding its P2P identity, bootstore and
persisted admin state; its own RPC socket, keeping the method names a
single-chain node has; and its own metric registration, which is what
makes the chain-labelled series of the kona crates separate by chain.

Process-wide fail-fast comes from running every chain's actors under one
`run_actors` call, with each chain's actors labelled so the error names
the chain that produced it.

kona-engine: answer local-safe-at-timestamp from one state read

Before: nothing served the query interop needs — "which L2 block was
local-safe at this timestamp, and which L1 block was it derived from?".
The pairing was recorded in the sync state but only readable as the
current head, and the L1 half had no read path at all.

After: `EngineQueries::LocalSafeSnapshotAt` answers it. The verdict, the
L1 origin and the sync status all come out of the single borrow of the
state watch that `EngineQueries::handle` already takes, so the two halves
of the answer cannot describe different instants. op-supernode's
`ChainContainer.OptimisticAt` assembles the same answer from two reads —
`LocalSafeBlockAtTimestamp`, then `safeDBAtL2`, each sampling the sync
status again — and its own comments name the TOCTOU gap between them;
there is no equivalent gap here.

How: `LocalSafeAtTimestamp` names where the requested timestamp fell.
Only the variant that landed on the local-safe head carries a pairing,
and it carries the whole `LocalSafeHead`, so an unpaired head stays
visibly unpaired instead of collapsing into a defaulted `BlockInfo` that
would read as "derived from block 0". The three cases that carry no
pairing stay distinct because a consumer treats them differently: ahead
of the head is a retry, behind it is a history lookup, and below L2
genesis is neither. `LocalSafeSnapshot` wraps the verdict with the sync
state and the EL sync flag it was read with; the L1 sync fields are not
in it, because they live in the L1 watcher and cannot be sampled with
this atomically.

kona-engine: record the L1 origin of the local-safe head

Before: the engine's sync state held a local-safe head with no record of
which L1 block it was derived from. Answering "which L1 block was the
chain safe at, at this L2 timestamp?" meant pairing the head with a
`derived_from` observed elsewhere, and the ChainController cannot do that
reliably: the engine task queue is a `BinaryHeap` that orders two
`Consolidate` tasks equal, so the last origin forwarded is not
necessarily the last one executed, and a drain that halts on an error
leaves later-forwarded origins unconsumed while an earlier task has
already written the head.

After: the pairing is recorded in the sync state by the writer of the
head, in the same step. `EngineSyncState::local_safe` reads both halves
out of one snapshot, so a consumer cannot observe a head from one update
beside an origin from another. Writers that hold no L1 key -- the
derivation-delegation path and engine resets -- record an explicit
"unpaired" rather than leaving a stale origin behind, and a reset thereby
invalidates the pairing it supersedes.

How: `LocalSafeOrigin` is `Unpaired | DerivedFrom(BlockInfo)`, so the
absent case is a distinct variant a consumer cannot mistake for a real
L1 block. `EngineSyncStateUpdate::local_safe_head` becomes an
`Option<LocalSafeHead>` -- head and origin together -- so no writer can
move the head without stating where it came from. `InsertTask` trades
`is_payload_local_safe: bool` for `local_safe_origin:
Option<LocalSafeOrigin>`, which carries the same "is this local-safe"
bit in its outer layer and the L1 key in its inner one; `SealTask`
supplies it from the attributes it already holds.

kona-engine: reject unsafe payloads that do not descend from local-safe

A gossiped payload is untrusted input, and inserting one moves the unsafe
head to it. The unsafe head is the top of the ordering
`unsafe >= local-safe >= cross-safe >= finalized`, so a payload at or
below the local-safe head rewinds the unsafe head under a head derived
from L1, and the next forkchoice update reports `safeBlockHash` ahead of
`headBlockHash` — the INVALID_FORK_CHOICE_STATE rejection that costs a
full engine reset. `EngineSyncState::apply_update` deliberately clamps
only the cross-safe head, on the grounds that no writer produces an
unsafe head below it; this check is what makes that true for the one
writer fed from outside the node. The execution layer's own
forkchoice-consistency check cannot be relied on for it.

Only two cases are decidable from state on hand, and only those two are
rejected: a payload at or below the local-safe head, and a payload
exactly one above it whose parent is not the local-safe head. Anything
further ahead is admitted — its ancestry is not on hand and derivation
settles it when local-safe catches up — as is a payload arriving before
the engine has a local-safe head at all, the execution-layer sync
bootstrap.

Untrusted input is rejected rather than clamped: the payload is dropped
at the queue boundary, next to the existing drop for an INVALID payload
status, and the heads stay put. The check reads the state the write
itself uses rather than the state at enqueue time, which the local-safe
head can outrun.

op-node: queue blocks awaiting publication instead of dropping them

Review feedback: replacing the pending payload with a newer one risked
stalling verifiers on a block they never received, and "they reach the
older one through sync" was not a claim that holds - payload-by-number
req/resp is disabled on some networks, sepolia-devnet-2 included.

Blocks now queue and publish in the order they were sealed. Two bounds
decide when a block is dropped instead:

- maxPublishAge (60s), mirroring the default of
  --p2p.gossip.timestamp.threshold. Peers REJECT a payload older than
  that, and an invalid delivery is scored against the sender, so
  publishing a block that has aged out spends a signing round-trip and
  peer score to have the block refused.
- maxPublishQueue (32 entries). Once full, the oldest entries are
  dropped rather than held, and the sequencer is never asked to wait
  for room: a block that goes ungossiped still reaches other nodes via
  L1 and derivation or other sync mechanisms, whereas a sequencer that
  stops building produces nothing for anyone. It doubles as a memory
  bound, since an envelope can be megabytes.

Both drops are logged and counted. New metrics make a filling queue
visible rather than something to infer:

- op_node_publish_queue_len (gauge)
- op_node_dropped_publishes (counter)

batch transaction by transaction. `BatchValidationProvider::block_by_number`

op-e2e/actions: emulate EL-sync p2p for the reth backend

The EL-sync tests rely on the sequencer and verifier engines peering over
devp2p so the verifier snap-syncs the chain from a single unsafe head. The
ephemeral reth engines are out-of-process subprocesses with no networking,
so Enode/AddPeers/PeerCount panicked 'not yet wired'.

Wire them against an in-process stand-in: a registry resolves a synthetic
enode back to the reth engine it identifies, peering is symmetric so both
PeerCount reads pass, and each peering starts a sync pump. The pump watches
optest_syncTarget (the head a forkchoice update reported SYNCING for) and,
while one is set, backfills the missing blocks from the peer engine one
validated optest_importBlock at a time — never moving safe/finalized, which
reproduces exactly the state op-geth reaches after backfilling under a
SYNCING forkchoice. It activates only once the engine has actually reported
SYNCING (which op-node triggers only during genuine EL sync, not for a
CL-mode gapped payload), so it fires exactly when a real EL would snap-sync.

The 'Forkchoice requested sync to new head' log the tests assert on is
emitted synchronously by the geth engine API inside forkchoiceUpdated, so
an async pump log would race the assertion. elSyncLogRPC wraps op-node's
engine RPC and reproduces it in op-node's own call path: it caches each
newPayload's block number and logs on a SYNCING forkchoice update to a head
it has seen.

op-reth-test-engine: stateful in-flight payload builder

Add the sequencer-flow block builder on top of the one-shot import path:
forkchoice_updated-with-attributes opens a payload (deposits applied and
validated, payload id derived via the production OpPayloadBuilderAttributes /
BuildNextEnv path), include_tx executes and appends a pool tx (with the op-geth
engine API's gas-limit and force-empty semantics), and get_payload seals it into
OpExecutionData that round-trips back through new_payload.

reth's block builder ties the executor, EVM state, and parent to a single
borrowed lifetime, so it can't be parked across calls; the in-flight payload
instead keeps the ordered tx list and re-runs a deterministic one-shot assembly
on demand.
