kona-engine: publish the state watch on reset and on failed tasks

A reset mutates the engine state outside drain, and a seal task can
import a deposits-only replacement (moving the local-safe head) and
then error with the flush signal. Neither path published the state
watch, so every reader served through it -- the RPC actor's queries,
and the interop verifier observing through them -- kept seeing heads
from before the mutation until some unrelated task succeeded.
op-supernode's readers take the chain container's live state under
lock (op-supernode/supernode/chain_container/chain_container.go) and
cannot lag a rewind; publishing on every state mutation, failed
attempts included, is the same guarantee for the watch.

lokahi-interop: apply Decision::Rewind when a committed frontier's L1 basis reorgs away

The response to a reorged committed L1 inclusion was deferred by #22645:
the round decided Rewind, logged it, and held the verified frontier
forever. This applies it, mirroring op-supernode:

- the verified results at or after the last verified timestamp are
  dropped (applyRewindPlan, op-supernode/supernode/activity/interop/
  interop.go:1032-1040; VerifiedDB.Rewind, verified_db.go:254);
- each chain's archived outputs recorded by decisions at or after that
  timestamp are pruned - the archive is the deny list, so this revokes
  denials whose basis was reorged out (interop.go:1057-1062;
  PruneDeniedAtOrAfterTimestamp, chain_container/invalidation.go:490);
- the log stores rewind onto the previous verified frontier, or clear
  entirely when none is retained (interop.go:1066-1094);
- only when an invalidation was revoked, every chain's engine is reset
  onto that frontier (shouldResetEnginesOnRewind, interop.go:1019-1030;
  resetChainEnginesIfNeeded, interop.go:1099-1122) - the deposits-only
  replacement a revoked invalidation forced is canonical and derivation
  alone will not remove it; without revoked entries the chains' own
  derivation absorbs the L1 reorg and the engines are left alone;
- the whole plan is decided up front and written to the WAL slot before
  any side effect (buildRewindPlan, interop.go:930-981), the L1 cursor
  is cleared (interop.go:783-785), failures preserve the slot for a
  whole-plan retry, and success reports no progress - the next round
  re-observes from the new frontier on the new L1.

The WAL replay now runs before cold start as well: a full rewind that
crashed after emptying the verified store must not have its store-clear
replayed on top of a fresh backfill.

The engine move rides the same chain-controller rewind request an
invalidation uses, through a new RewindableChain::reset_to on the
existing seam; a verifier built without replacement routes still holds
the decision, as it does for invalidations.

kona,lokahi: answer the fault-proof queries as op-supernode does

The fault-proof acceptance suites drive superroot_atTimestamp harder than
anything else: the proposer reads it per proposal, the challenger per claim,
and the DSL polls it for validation and L1 progress. Three behaviours of that
path diverged from op-supernode, and each one fails a slice of the family.

Timestamps floor onto the preceding block. op-node's TargetBlockNumber
(op-node/rollup/types.go:237) floors an unaligned timestamp, and
op-supernode's LocalSafeBlockAtTimestamp answers whenever the floored number
is at or below the local-safe head — super roots exist at every second, and a
chain without a block at that second contributes its preceding block. kona's
local_safe_snapshot_at classified by raw timestamp instead, so a boundary
timestamp one second past a frozen head answered NotLocalSafeYet forever: the
verifier stalled at every unaligned boundary ("super-root at timestamp N was
not validated in time", and downstream "supernode did not fully process L1
block N in time"), and the optimistic branch omitted the chain ("no
optimistic output for chain 901 at timestamp N" in the preinterop suites).

A reset landing at genesis seeds the safe-head database. op-node's
onEngineConfirmedReset (op-node/rollup/driver/sync_deriver.go:204-220)
records L2 genesis as safe from L1 block 0 whenever a reset walks back to
genesis — deliberately block 0 rather than cfg.Genesis.L1, because dispute
contracts may predate the L2 genesis's L1 origin. That entry is the
database's floor. Without it lokahi's earliest record was the first
post-reset advance, and l1_at_safe_head below it answered
L1AtSafeHeadUnavailable permanently — surfacing as "chain 901 no longer
records which L1 block made its block at timestamp N safe" ("Failed to get
absolute prestate") in TestFPP.

Genesis short-circuits the history lookup. op-supernode's virtual node
(op-supernode/supernode/chain_container/virtual_node/virtual_node.go:263-269)
answers L1AtSafeHead for the genesis block with {number: 0} before touching
the database. Mirrored in both readers of the safe-head history: the query
path's pairing resolution and the interop verifier's behind-head lookup,
which otherwise halts for good on a database that answers the permanent
error at the very timestamp verification starts from.

The optimistic branch consults the invalidated-output archive first.
op-supernode's OptimisticOutputAtTimestamp asks the deny list's
LastDeniedOutputV0 before the canonical read, so a height whose block was
invalidated and replaced reports the original block's output — what
"optimistically, had verification succeeded" means once a replacement
exists. lokahi's archive (the deny list) existed but the query path never
read it, so it served the replacement's output: the fpp subtests derived
transition states the proof program refutes ("Failed to validate progressed
transition state"), claims meant to be invalid verified clean, and the SP1
runner counted zero optimistic root replacements. The chain's own route
keeps answering without the archive, matching op-node's single-chain
superroot namespace, which consults no deny list.

lokahi-interop,kona: apply Decision::Invalidate as the deposits-only block replacement

The verifier's Invalidate decision was routed to hold() with "a decision
this phase does not apply", so an invalid cross-chain message stalled
cross-safety forever (the reorg acceptance family: TestReorgInitExecMsg,
TestReorgInvalidExecMsgs/*). This implements the application, mirroring
op-supernode's supervisor-driven invalidate-and-replace:

- verifier: an Invalidate decision is write-ahead logged and applied.
  Per invalid head, in op-supernode's order (invalidation.go:392-465):
  the block's output preimage is archived first - the archive doubles
  as the deny list, and the write is driven from the WAL slot on every
  replay so the "already replaced, just ack" branch (#22540) cannot
  lose the roots - then the chain is rewound onto the block's parent
  through a new RewindableChain seam. No frontier is committed: the
  next round re-verifies the timestamp against the replaced chain,
  as applyPendingTransition does for DecisionInvalidate.
- kona-engine: a DenyList trait the engine consults at op-node's three
  checkpoints with op-node's three postures. Seal-time (derived
  payloads; fails open, payload_process.go:56-85): a denied rebuild
  becomes a deposits-only build via the existing Holocene fallback,
  flushing the channel as DepositsOnlyAttributes does. Consolidation
  (fails closed, attributes.go:241-256): a denied matching block is
  reorged out, never adopted. Commit (opstack_commitBlockV1): denied
  payloads answer the caller, as ProcessPayload's ErrPayloadDenied.
- kona-node-service: ChainControllerRequest::Rewind applies a targeted
  Engine::reset_to onto the invalidated block's parent, rewinds the
  safe-head database and resets derivation; unsafe ingestion is gated
  from a denial until finality passes the highest denied height
  (engine_controller.go:776-799).
- SealTaskError::UnsafeHeadChangedSinceBuild is Reset, not Critical:
  during replacement the deposits-only block lands as the new unsafe
  head under a queued consolidate task, and the recovery is dropping
  the stale work and re-deriving - op-node's ResetEvent for queued
  attributes conflicting with a moved head (attributes.go:175-183).
  Critical killed the node (TestSequencingWindowExpiry).
- lokahi: each chain opens its invalidated-output archive next to its
  safe-head database; the chain controller reads it as the deny list
  and the verifier writes invalidations into it, one handle for both.

lokahi: serve the experimental opstack block-building namespace on chain routes

op-supernode's virtual op-nodes register the experimental opstack API on
every chain's route (op-node/node/node.go, registerAPIs, gated on
ExperimentalOPStackAPI, which the devstack's makeNodeCfg always sets), and
the op-test-sequencer's standard builder, committer and publisher drive
block building through it: opstack_openBlockV1, cancelBlockV1, sealBlockV1,
commitBlockV1, publishBlockV1. A lokahi chain route refused all of them
with "Method not found", so every acceptance test that sequences through
the test sequencer (op-devstack/dsl/sequencer.go) failed at its first
opstack_openBlockV1 -- the 18-test failure bucket of CircleCI job 5510201.

Each lokahi chain is a kona node and op-node is the spec, so the namespace
is implemented in kona and registered where op-node registers its own: in
the node's RPC module set, which lokahi's launcher routes under
/<chain-id>.

- kona-rpc: the opstack namespace, wire types matching the Go types field
  for field (serde tests pin Go-shaped JSON), and op-node's -401xx build
  error codes (op-service/apis/opstack.go). RpcBuilder gains
  experimental_opstack, default off.
- kona-node-service: OpStackRpc delegates as op-node's does. openBlockV1
  is EngineController.OpenBlock: a parent-exists check, then a direct
  engine_forkchoiceUpdated with head at the given parent and the given
  attributes, startPayload's error mapping code for code. sealBlockV1 and
  cancelBlockV1 are a direct engine_getPayload versioned by the job's
  timestamp; sealing does not canonicalize. commitBlockV1 moves the unsafe
  head the chain controller owns, so it goes through the controller's
  queue as a new CommitBlock request. publishBlockV1 hands the signed
  envelope to the network actor, whose publish channel now carries either
  an unsigned payload (signed at publish time with the node's own key, the
  sequencer's unchanged path) or a pre-signed one published with the
  signature it was given, as op-node's PublishBlock publishes it.
- kona-engine: CommitTask, an InsertTask with a result channel following
  SealTask's always-succeeds-with-channel pattern: the requester hears the
  newPayload verdict exactly once, instead of the queue retrying -- or
  silently dropping an invalid payload -- behind their back. A requester
  that disconnected before hearing it is logged, not escalated.
- kona-node: --rpc.experimental-opstack-api, op-node's
  --experimental.sequencer-api.
- lokahi: experimental-opstack-api in the TOML, resolved like the admin
  flag ([defaults] as the base, a chain's own entry overriding).
- op-devstack: the generated lokahi TOML enables it in [defaults],
  mirroring makeNodeCfg's ExperimentalOPStackAPI: true.

Documented divergences: publishBlockV1 schedules the gossip publish and
answers rather than awaiting it, and commitBlockV1 refuses a payload that
does not descend from the local-safe head (kona's unsafe-head admission
rule; op-node has no counterpart) instead of corrupting the head ordering.

Fail-first: with the namespace left unregistered, the new integration test
(rust/lokahi/tests/opstack_route.rs, two_chains.rs style) fails with
-32601 where op-node behaviour is expected; with it, both tests pass --
the gate stays -32601 without the flag, and with it the route answers
openBlockV1's parent refusal, sealBlockV1's -40199, commitBlockV1's insert
verdict through the controller, and publishBlockV1's scheduling, while the
supernode root serves none of it.

lokahi: gate interop history lower bound on stable safe-head entries

The interop verifier commits its verified frontier from each chain's
first safe-head DB entry. That first entry is recorded as soon as the
chain drains its first derivation step, keyed by an in-flight L1
traversal position — and an engine reset arriving moments later (as
happens on every cold start when the forkchoice snaps back) wipes the
DB and refills it from a later L1 block, raising the recorded history
floor above the already-committed frontier. The verifier then halts
permanently with "history begins at T+1 but verification must continue
from T", which is exactly the failure seen across 16 lokahi acceptance
tests (in every one, a reset request precedes the halt by ~12s).

Fix: first_safe_head_timestamp now reports an entry only once it is
stable — its L1 key is at or below the chain's current local-safe L1
origin, meaning derivation has fully traversed that L1 block and a
reset can no longer re-record the boundary above it. Until then the
chain reports NotReady and the verifier keeps waiting, so the frontier
is only ever committed against a history floor that cannot rise.

Unit tests cover the gate: no entry, in-flight (unstable) entry, no
local-safe cross-reference, and a stable entry reporting its timestamp.

lokahi: serve superroot_atTimestamp on each chain's route, as op-supernode does

Every route of the Go op-supernode answers superroot_atTimestamp, because
op-node registers the superroot namespace on its RPC unconditionally
(op-node/node/node.go, registerAPIs): the root answers over the whole chain
set, and each /<chainID> route answers op-node's single-chain implementation
(op-node/node/superroot_api.go). kona-node has no such namespace, so a lokahi
chain route built from kona's method set alone refused the call with "Method
not found".

The consumers that dial a chain route for it are real. The devstack's
per-chain proposers are pointed at the chain CL's own URL
(op-devstack/sysgo/singlechain_runtime.go, SuperRootRpcs = l2CL.UserRPC()),
and the anchor of a newly added game type is read the same way
(op-devstack/sysgo/add_game_type.go). In the first full lokahi acceptance run
(CircleCI job 5508932) this was the 19-test failure bucket: those proposers
retried superroot_atTimestamp against kona's per-chain module to end of log
while the challenger and the super proposer, dialling the same socket's root,
were answered.

The route's answer is composed exactly as the root composes its
pre-verification branch, specialised to one chain: the same QueryChain reads,
the same Aggregate arithmetic, the same from_handoff composition — so the
wire shape and the commitment are bit-identical to what the root states for a
set of one, which is also what op-node serves (it consults no verifier; a
single-chain node has none). supernode_syncStatus stays off the chain routes,
as it is off op-node's RPC.

kona registers a chain's route while the chain composes, so the route's extra
methods are deposited before composition and hold a OnceLock handle filled
once the chain exists — the same binding-before-composition the root's query
API uses; a call in that window is answered "still starting". A deposited
method that collides with one kona serves fails the chain's launch loudly
rather than shadowing either.

The two_chains integration test now asserts each chain's route answers
superroot_atTimestamp for exactly its own chain and refuses
supernode_syncStatus. It failed before this change with the same error the
acceptance run recorded, and passes after.

kona-node-service: survive transient L1 RPC failures in the L1 watcher

A failed eth_getLogs for one chain's system config made the L1
watcher's step return Err, which cancels every actor and exits the
host: one chain's transient L1 RPC error stopped every chain, and even
a single-chain kona-node died on an L1 blip.

Mirror op-node, which never treats a transient L1 RPC failure as
fatal: its runtime-config reloader logs a failed unsafe-block-signer
read and waits for the next interval, its L1 head subscription
resubscribes forever, and its safe/finalized polls warn and keep
polling. The per-chain system config log fetch is now infallible: a
failed fetch is logged and that head's logs are skipped for that
chain, while the other chains' fetches and the watcher itself keep
running. Channel-closed errors to a chain's derivation actor stay
fatal - a missing peer actor is shutdown, not a transient fault.

Tracks #22655.

op-devstack: bind lokahi's P2P listeners to ephemeral ports

The lokahi launcher reserved a concrete port per P2P listener by
listening on it and letting it go again before lokahi started
(reservePorts) -- so every launch had a window in which another
parallel test's component could take the port. The UDP discovery port
was doubly unprotected: it was reserved as a TCP listener, which says
nothing about the UDP socket discv5 actually binds. When the race was
lost, kona's discovery driver retried the bind at 1s/2s/4s, gave up,
and its task returned -- dropping the ENR channel and killing the
whole node with 'Critical error in sub-routine: chain N:
ChannelClosed' (the TestLokahiTwoChains /
TestFollowSource_HeadsDivergeThenConverge startup flake).

Every other component in the preset already binds ephemeral ports:
startMixedKonaNode runs kona-node with KONA_NODE_P2P_LISTEN_TCP_PORT=0
/ _UDP_PORT=0, newDevstackP2PConfig gives op-node listen ports 0, and
op-reth gets --port=0 --with-unused-ports. Do the same for lokahi:
write p2p-tcp-port = 0 / p2p-udp-port = 0 into the generated config
and drop reservePorts. Nothing needs the port ahead of time -- peering
reads the bound addresses back out of opp2p_self, which reports the
swarm's live listeners.

lokahi's config check treated the ports as literal addresses, so two
chains both asking for 0 were refused as a collision on
'127.0.0.1:0' -- an address neither chain will ever listen on. Exempt
port 0 from the uniqueness check: it is a request for a kernel-assigned
port, and every bind gets its own.

lokahi: mirror op-node's pre-activation and anchor cross-safe fall-throughs

lokahi's engines run with CrossSafeSource::Promoted, and the interop
actor's promote() minted promotions only from committed verified
frontiers -- so before interop activation the verifier has committed
nothing, cross-safe stayed pinned at genesis, and kona's FinalizeTask
(which drops finality signals for blocks that are not yet cross-safe)
pinned finalized there with it. op-node's SafeL2Head/FinalizedHead have
two fall-throughs lokahi lacked (engine_controller.go:219-241,327-355;
op-supernode super_authority.go:23-41): VerifierHeadPreActivation --
verifier not active at the local-safe timestamp, cross-safe follows the
local-safe head -- and VerifierHeadAnchor -- active but nothing verified
yet, cross-safe anchors at the canonical block at activation-1, clamped
to genesis and bounded by local-safe (resolveAnchorAsSafe).

Mirror both branches in InteropActor::promote, in op-supernode's order:
pre-activation first, then the verified frontier (unchanged), then the
anchor. The engine's apply_cross_safe_promotion clamps keep every target
inside the local-safe/finalized band, and finalization then unblocks
through the existing FinalizeTask gate. Fixes the pre-activation family
in the lokahi supernode acceptance matrix:
TestSupernodeResyncSchedulesAtActivation_PreActivation, TestPreNoInbox,
and TestFinalizedL2DoesNotRegressAcrossActivation (job 5518771's
finreg.log shows the smoking gun: 'Dropping a finality signal for a
block that is not yet cross-safe ... cross_safe=0' while L1 finality had
arrived).

kona-engine: walk the sync-start unsafe head back past reorged-out L1 origins

After an L1 reorg, `find_starting_forkchoice` kept the poisoned unsafe
head: it validated the head's L1 origin with a by-hash lookup
(eth_getBlockByHash), and execution layers keep serving reorged-out
side-chain blocks by hash, so mere hash existence passed the check on
the first iteration. The engine reset became a no-op for the unsafe
head, the sequencer kept extending L2 blocks whose epochs sit on the
dead L1 branch, and the batcher forever resubmitted batches that
derivation rightly rejected with "batch is for different L1 chain,
epoch hash does not match" -- wedging cross-safe below the pre-reorg
tip (TestL2ReorgAfterL1Reorg, both subtests).

Mirror op-node's FindL2Heads walkback (op-node/rollup/sync/start.go:
216-224, 262-276): fetch the origin BY NUMBER and compare hashes. A
mismatch means the origin was reorged out -- discard the candidate head
and keep walking to the L2 parent; a by-number miss means the origin is
ahead of our L1 view -- keep the candidate tentatively while still
verifying its ancestors' origins; a match means the origin (and, by L1
ancestry, every deeper origin) is canonical -- the candidate stands.
The walk is bounded, as in op-node, by the finalized block (erroring on
an L2 hash mismatch there, op-node's ReorgFinalizedErr) and by the L2
genesis block (erroring when the genesis origin is non-canonical,
op-node's WrongChainErr).

The function's own doc already promised these semantics ("not canonical
at another height ... and the same holds for all its ancestors"); the
implementation now delivers them. The new mock-EngineClient tests pin
the reorged-out case (origin resolves by hash, different block canonical
at its number), the ahead case, and ahead-then-reorged ancestors; the
reorged-out and ahead tests fail against the previous implementation.

kona gated derivation behind EL-sync completion, and nothing put a

EL right away.

whose forkchoice update doubles as the EL-sync probe -- a VALID answer
marks EL sync finished and derivation starts (op-node's CL-sync steady

bootstrap stays in charge (op-node's EL-sync regime). The reset is

kona-engine: keep the gossip EL-sync channel open past the initial sync; gate the startup probe on a finalized block

The rust-e2e-restart, rust-e2e-simple-kona, and kona-node CL-sync
acceptance failures on this branch all trace to the same two-part
regression in the earlier commits:

1. The unsafe-insert path refused SYNCING heads once el_sync_finished
was set, mirroring op-node's CL-sync regime. But op-node's CL-sync mode
has reqresp sync and an unsafe payload queue to catch up with; this
engine has neither, so pointing the execution layer at the gossiped tip
is its only unsafe-chain catch-up channel -- and a verifier that falls
behind (a restart, a dropped peer) re-enters it after the initial sync.
The gate stranded such verifiers behind a live sequencer forever
(TestUnsafeChainNotStalling_*, TestSequencerRestart,
TestSyncUnsafeBecomesSafe). Revert to op-node's EL-sync regime
(engine_controller.go:587-594, sync_deriver.go:102-115) in both phases;
the sync-tester livelock this gate was protecting against is instead
broken where op-node breaks it, at the consolidation fetch miss
(attributes.go:204-221) -- whose not-found hardening now also covers the
bare "not found" error op-service's sync tester emits
(sync_tester.go:183-187), a documented superset of MaybeAsNotFoundErr:
unlike op-node, this engine fetches ahead of the EL by design, so it
meets that answer where op-node's payload queue never would.

2. The startup walkback reset probed every reachable execution layer,
and a fresh EL at genesis answers VALID for its own genesis -- wrongly
marking EL sync finished before the gossip bootstrap ever ran. Gate the
probe on the EL reporting a finalized block, op-node's own EL-sync
discriminator ("the engine has no finalized block until its initial
snap-sync completes", engine_controller.go:597-624, and EL sync is only
entered "if there is no finalized block", engine_controller.go:29): an
EL with no finalized block is left to the gossip bootstrap exactly as
before, while one with chain state (the sync-tester EL always reports
its finalized label) is probed so derivation starts without waiting for
a gossiped payload it may never be able to validate.

op-sync-tester: relay eth_getBlockReceipts raw instead of round-tripping geth's consensus receipt type

The sync tester served eth_getBlockReceipts by decoding the upstream
EL's response into geth []*types.Receipt and re-marshaling it. The
consensus receipt type carries no from/to fields, so the round-trip
silently stripped the fields the execution-apis spec requires and every
real EL serves. Go clients never noticed -- they decode into the same
lossy type (op-service/sources/receipts_rpc.go:96) -- but alloy's
TransactionReceipt requires from (alloy-rpc-types-eth
src/transaction/receipt.rs:64), so lokahi's interop verifier failed
deserialization on the very first block's receipts, retried the
transient-classified error every ~2s for the full 720s budget, and
cross-safe never left 0: the round-2 wedge behind all five sync_tester
acceptance tests.

Relay the raw payload instead, exactly as the block accessors already do
(GetBlockByNumberJSON/GetBlockByHashJSON); the session ahead-of-state
gate reads only blockNumber out of the raw payload. The regression test
pins that from/to survive through both the backend and the RPC frontend.

op-sync-tester: serve spec-shaped engine_getPayload responses

The sync tester answered every getPayload version with its stored
eth.ExecutionPayloadEnvelope -- the gossip envelope shape, carrying only
the payload and the parent beacon block root. The execution-apis spec
requires blockValue (V2+), blobsBundle/shouldOverrideBuilder/
parentBeaconBlockRoot (V3+) and executionRequests (V4+); Go clients
decode into the same envelope and never noticed, but alloy's payload
envelopes require the fields, so a kona-node sealing a block against the
tester failed the fetch outright ("missing field blockValue"), retried
at the backoff ceiling forever, and could never advance a chain it had
to build -- the round-3 wedge of TestSupernodeVerifier{CatchesUpFromCold,
ELSyncsFromCold} (session reset to Latest:0, every block force-built).

Wrap the stored envelope into the spec response per version at the RPC
frontend: blockValue zero (the tester relays canonical blocks, there is
no fee value to report), an empty-but-present blobs bundle, and an empty
executionRequests list, with the payload itself served untouched. Go
clients ignore the additions.

kona-gossip: allowlist gossip subscription topics

Kona built the gossipsub behaviour with the default AllowAllSubscriptionFilter.
libp2p therefore accepted a subscription for any topic a peer announced.

A peer could exploit this in two ways. It grew its uncapped PeerDetails.topics
set in the swarm peer table. It also minted an unbounded number of `topic`
label values on the kona_node_gossip_events metric, which the Prometheus
recorder never evicts.

Install a WhitelistSubscriptionFilter built from the topics the handlers serve.
op-node applies the same allowlist in BuildSubscriptionFilter. Neither node
conditions the topic set on scheduled forks, so all four block topics stay
allowed at all times.

op-node: allow the L1 data source to be injected, and an embedder to publish its APIs

This is the entire consensus-layer change Silhouette needs: 71 lines across
three files, both of them seams in the pattern of the ones already there.

DataSourceOverride joins InitializationOverrides beside L1Source/Beacon/
SuperAuthority and is threaded to NewDerivationPipeline as a variadic
PipelineOption. A nil override yields the stock DataSourceFactory, so every
existing caller is untouched and the default path is byte-for-byte what it was.
It is the same kind of seam the altDA parameter already is: retrieval's source
changes and every stage downstream of it stays stock. It exists for a chain
whose derivation input is not batcher transactions at all -- the frames
entering FrameQueue may be transcoded from some other L1 object -- and the
pipeline neither knows nor needs to.

ExtraAPIs is the second half, and it exists because embedding an execution
client REMOVES a service the network otherwise has: on a chain with a real EL,
eth_getBlockByNumber is answered by that client at its own endpoint, so an
embedder that replaces the L2 endpoint with a service of its own has to be able
to put that service back. Namespaces mount on the node's own handler after the
node's own, so a collision is the embedder's problem and never a silent
replacement of `optimism`. The Engine API is deliberately not published: it is
the private channel between a chain's node and its execution client.

Variadic options rather than a new positional parameter so the two existing
NewDerivationPipeline call sites and the op-e2e action-test helper keep
compiling unchanged.

op-supernode: the proof-batch wire codec (v3), and the corpus that pins it

The wire IS the interface between a silhouette chain and the public network,
and this is the whole of it: a KCPB envelope (magic, version, public-values
length, proof length), an ABI-encoded body of per-block exports, and the
acceptance structure the verifier checks before anything else looks at it.

Version 3 is the consolidation wire: a block says what it IMPORTED as well as
what it exported. `BlockExport.execMsgs[]` is a decode-enforced DEDUPLICATED
SET of {Identifier, msgHash} -- the executing messages the block consumed --
and deliberately carries no executing-side position: no tx hash, no tx index,
no sender, no count. The disclosure is the edge (P-block, A-message) at block
granularity, which is also all the judge needs. Exactly one version is
accepted; a v2 envelope is REFUSED as retired rather than best-effort decoded.

The load-bearing discovery this shape rests on: `calculateChecksum` computes
keccak256(origin ‖ msgHash) internally, which is exactly a v2 LogExport's
logHash -- so ONE comparison discharges both the stock per-message check and
consolidation's, and needs no preimages and no MPT. v3 is one field, not two.

The corpus lands with the codec because neither is worth anything alone. 35 v3
fixtures (each a .bin plus a .json stating what it is, indexed by index.json)
plus generative cases and vector files; and the FROZEN v2 corpus of 25 real
envelopes, whose whole job is to prove the version gate against genuine v2
bodies rather than against a v3 body wearing a v2 version byte. It lives at
the Rust crate's canonical path because it is ONE corpus read by both
implementations -- the Rust codec lands later in this series and reads the same
bytes, which is what makes "byte-identical across two languages" a checked
property rather than a claim. 129 Go tests green.

One deliberate edit to the imported corpus: the fixture `mock-proof-empty` is
renamed `empty-proof-slot`, and the two prose sites that called an empty proof
slot "mock mode" now call it attested. The .bin bytes are untouched -- what
the corpus asserts is unchanged -- but the name was wrong in the direction
that matters: an empty proof slot is not a stand-in for v1's proving system,
it is what v1's proving system looks like on the wire.

op-supernode: the silhouette chain -- decode source, fact store, shim EL, log sink

The chain itself. A stock op-node derives a silhouette chain through its
completely standard pipeline; everything here is what sits on the two ends of
that pipeline, and nothing here forks derivation.

THE DECODE SOURCE AND TRANSCODER (source.go, tracker.go). Injected at the
DataSourceOverride seam. It filters the inbox transactions, checks the five
acceptance rules against the node's own L1 view, chains the batch against the
proven head, and re-encodes the proven blocks as stock singular batches in
stock channel frames. From FrameQueue onward this is unmodified derivation
running for real. Rule 1 is the load-bearing one in v1: `tx.from ==
submitterEOA`, which is what makes the batch transaction's own signature the
attestation. Rule 5 is the only rule that a stronger proving system would
change, and it is one call behind the Verifier interface.

THE FACT STORE AND THE FORCED-EXTENSION CONVENTION (facts.go, forced.go,
forced_at.go, rendered.go, store_shim.go). Proof-committed facts are served
verbatim and never fabricated: number, timestamp, blockHash, stateRoot,
messagePasserStorageRoot, exported log hashes and indices. When P's L1 origin
advances a full sequencing window past the last proven block's origin, stock
derivation force-generates empty blocks -- DESIGNED liveness, so a dead prover
can never stall the depset's cross-safe frontier. The store PRE-COMPUTES those
forced facts, which is what keeps the shim's fail-stop intact: getPayload
serves proven-or-forced facts and nothing else.

extraData is NOT free residue, and this is the trap worth naming: op-node
reconstructs SystemConfig by parsing eip-1559 params out of the parent's
extraData, so a header carrying a human-readable marker there would silently
reset fee params and divide by zero. Self-declaration lives at the service
layer instead; the header stays consensus-shaped.

THE SHIM EXECUTION CLIENT (shim_*.go, sequencer_api.go). A purpose-built
service speaking the Engine API and the eth_ query surface that never executes
anything: it "builds" blocks by serving the proof-committed facts. Because
op-node treats the engine as the hash authority and re-hashes no payload on the
derivation path, the public network operates on the private chain's REAL
identity -- stock code computes P's real output roots from these headers,
byte-identical to settlement claims. Declared fake execution, with the guards
that make it honest: newPayload refuses any hash outside proven-or-forced
facts, getPayload fails on missing facts, and no path reaches invalidation or
replacement-block synthesis. shim_declare.go is the service-layer
self-declaration; getProof is a hard error rather than a lie.

THE WIRE-FED LOGSDB SINK (logsink.go). LogsDB is fed from the wire -- explicit
indices, poison gaps for unexported logs -- and NEVER from the rendering
device's receipts. Positional receipt ingestion would need filler logs with
public preimages, which are forgeable initiating messages; real-hash gaps would
let a P insider reference an unexported log and bypass the export policy. The
poison gaps are load-bearing for the export policy itself.

The one change outside op-supernode is op-service/sources/eth_client.go:
InfoByNumber/InfoByLabel trust the reported block hash. That is the compliance
oracle these methods are checked against, and re-deriving a hash the engine is
authoritative for is what the shim exists to avoid.

ATTESTED-ONLY, as ratified. `proofType` is a required config field with no
default -- both a node that checks something and a node that checks nothing
must never be one unstated field apart -- and `attested` is the one value this
build implements. `groth16` is recognised BY NAME and refused with an error
saying the config is ahead of the binary rather than malformed, because the
slot is real: the wire carries a proof field and rule 5 is the rung that reads
it. `mockProofs` is refused too, with instructions; it is decoded only so the
error can teach, since "unknown field" would say the key is wrong without
saying the mode it named is alive and renamed.

53 tests green, including the 12-law virtual-node conformance suite retargeted
to a shim-backed chain, the forced-extension determinism gates, and the shim's
per-method compliance-oracle checks against op-service/sources.

op-supernode: the interop seams a proof-carried chain needs, all chain-agnostic

Four changes to the shared interop machinery, and the point of every one is
that a silhouette chain is judged by the STOCK judge. None of them is behind a
chain-kind branch, because none of the seams is actually specific to a proven
chain -- they are seams the shared code was missing.

THE JUDGE FLIP (algo.go, interop.go, types.go). A proven chain's dependencies
are CHECKED, not trusted. The wire carries each block's import list, so P's
executing messages are handed to the stock cross-safety algorithm exactly like
a driven chain's: checksum, hazards, expiry, fixpoint. The retired posture --
"execMsgs empty, proof-trusted" -- is gone. This is what licenses the honest
half of v1's trust model: an attester can invent what its own chain said, but
it cannot invent what someone else's chain said, and this is the code that
makes the second half true.

THE THIRD VERDICT (types.go, algo.go, cycle.go). A chain's block at a
timestamp is verified, invalid, or NOT YET DECIDABLE -- because absence of data
is not evidence of a conflict. A verifier reading an initiating message it does
not have yet learns only that it cannot see it from here, now. Treating that as
invalid is how a live-edge verifier forks itself off a perfectly valid chain:
deny-list the executing block, rewind, re-derive it, deny-list it again, while
the network that HAD the message advances past it. `Result.NotReady` is never
persisted -- a round holding one of these waits, and only advance/invalidate
transitions reach the WAL. A proof-carried chain makes this routine rather than
exotic (its initiating messages appear when a batch lands on L1, minutes after
the blocks exist), but any lagging verifier meets the same seam.

REFUSE EVERY PROVEN CHAIN'S INVALIDATION, DETERMINISTICALLY (algo.go,
verification_view.go). There is no legitimate path to invalidating or
replacing a block of a chain nobody may extend, so the attempt is refused
rather than attempted -- for EVERY such chain, in a deterministic order, so the
refusal cannot depend on map iteration.

THE CAPABILITY SEAMS (logdb.go, log_backfill.go, chain_container.go). Message
ingestion becomes a declared capability rather than an assumption about how a
chain's logs arrive, so a chain fed from the wire mounts where a chain fed from
its own receipts does. Three small branches; they survive by design.

Two new suites: proven_imports_test.go drives the flip against a proven
chain's import list, and wait_on_lagging_source_test.go drives the
wait-then-advance thesis -- a late message pins the frontier and then releases
it, which is the property that distinguishes waiting from forking. Both build
on the package's own existing chain fakes rather than introducing new ones.
Full op-supernode/supernode suites green.

op-supernode: assembly, the chain container and its two postures

What turns the pieces into a running chain, and the seam by which a supernode
mounts one.

ASSEMBLY (assembly.go). A silhouette chain is a stock op-node with the decode
source injected at the DataSourceOverride seam, the shim as its execution
client, and the shim's query surface published through ExtraAPIs -- because
embedding the EL removed a service the network otherwise has. It takes no
gossip (there is no peer to gossip with; the proof stream on L1 is the only
input) and it names its L1 explicitly.

THE CHAIN CONTAINER AND ITS TWO POSTURES (container.go). A silhouette chain
mounts as a chain container beside driven ones, with the message-ingestion
capability wired to the wire-fed sink. Two postures, and the difference is
which head the labels come from: a VERIFIER's proven head advances only when a
batch lands on L1, while a SEQUENCER's local-safe head is its own. The
sequencer posture is mandatory rather than an optimisation -- a frozen P
local-safe would freeze chain A cluster-wide, so the two are not symmetric and
the asymmetry has to be configured, not inferred. The cluster-freeze gate and
the frozen-safe-head disarm are both here, and both have tests that fail
loudly if the disarm ever stops being needed.

THE MANIFEST (manifest.go, example/v1/). The chain declaration: what a
silhouette chain is, in JSON, with the rollup config generated from it rather
than hand-maintained. example/v1/ is a WORKING minimal v1 declaration --
verifier config plus manifest -- and example_test.go asserts it is attested and
pins a wire version that carries the import list, so the example cannot drift
away from the document it illustrates.

THE SUPERNODE WIRING (supernode/silhouette.go, supernode.go, config, flags,
resources). One factory switch: a chain in the supernode's config can be a
silhouette chain, and everything else about the supernode is unchanged. The
startup log states the trust model in words -- proofType, wire version, whether
dependencies are verified -- because those are the three facts that decide what
this node's acceptance of a batch MEANS, and a node should say them out loud
rather than leave them to be inferred from an empty proof slot.

THE TRUST MODEL IS A PASSING TEST (attested_test.go). Alongside the ordinary
gates, attested_test.go asserts what attestation does NOT buy: the fabricated
export is ACCEPTED. That is deliberate and it is the point -- a weakness
documented only in prose is a weakness the next reader will not find, and this
one sits directly beside the false-import test that pins the frontier. The
contrast is the documentation. It also doubles as a tripwire: it is written so
that it fails at the acceptance step under any proving system that actually
checks P's state, so if it ever goes red somebody changed the trust model
deliberately, which is the only acceptable way.

bomb_test.go is the deliberate failure: a test that arms a condition which must
never hold and goes off if it does. 90 tests green in the package.

op-supernode: the proof-batch submitter, and the two ops tools

THE SUBMITTER (cmd/proofbatch-submitter) is v1's producer side in full. Its
attested mode builds batches on a cadence from the chain's own outputs with an
empty proof slot, and that is not a bring-up stand-in for a prover: the SEND is
the attestation. The transaction is signed by the submitter key, acceptance
rule 1 binds every accepted batch to that key, so posting a batch is the
operator putting their name on the state it claims. Flags, env vars and
function names all say `attested` with no aliases -- a CLI flag that still said
"mock" would be the primary path describing v1's real proving system as a fake
one.

It batches on the chain's UNSAFE head, which is the correct choice and worth
one line: a silhouette chain's safe head is defined by its own proof stream, so
waiting for safety before posting a batch is waiting for the batch.

TWO TOOLS. cmd/silhouette-config generates the rollup config from the chain
manifest, so the artifact that must agree with the guest's pinned
rollupConfigHash is generated from one source rather than hand-maintained in
two. cmd/proofbatch-inspect decodes an envelope off L1 or off disk and prints
what it says -- the tool you want at 3am when a batch was refused and the
question is which rule.

Both tools take the wire version EXPLICITLY rather than inheriting the codec's
current version, because a tool that silently followed the codec would write or
read the wrong version through a rotation and look correct doing it.

.gitignore covers the locally-built binaries so they cannot be committed.

op-devstack, op-acceptance-tests: a silhouette chain in the devstack, and the v1 gate

The multi-process end-to-end system, which is where every claim on this branch
is actually checked. A chain in the devstack can be a silhouette chain: its
node is assembled with the shim as its EL and the decode source injected, a
second supernode verifies it from L1, and a submitter posts proof batches into
a real inbox in real blobs. Both postures run, and both cross-chain directions
run, in one system.

sysgo/silhouette_runtime.go builds the chain; sysgo/silhouette_submitter.go is
the producer, driven on a cadence exactly as the real one is. The preset carries
the option so that a two-L2 system can have one driven chain and one proven
chain -- which is the whole configuration under test, because a silhouette
chain is only interesting next to a public chain it interoperates with.

THE SUITE, and what each part of it is for:

Liveness and configuration. TestSilhouetteVerifierStarts; and
TestSilhouetteRefusesWrongL1ChainConfig, because a verifier pointed at the
wrong L1 must refuse to start rather than derive a chain that looks fine.

The proof stream. TestSilhouetteProofBatchAdvancesVerifier: a batch, in a blob,
on L1, moves the verifier's proven head -- with the assertion made AT THE
HEIGHT rather than off the head's hash, in the negative test too, so a test
cannot pass by comparing something to itself.

Interop, both directions. TestSilhouetteImportsAMessageAndTheDependencyIsVerified
and TestSilhouetteCrossChainPinsThenAdvances (a dependency that is not yet
knowable PINS the frontier and then releases it -- the wait-then-advance thesis
on a real system), against TestSilhouetteImportThatIsFalseIsRefused (one false
declared import pins it permanently). The pair is the non-vacuity control:
without the negative, "the frontier advanced" proves nothing about checking.

The postures. TestSequencerPostureKeepsSequencingAndTakesLabelsFromProofs and
TestSequencerPostureUnfreezesTheClusterFrontier -- the second is the hazard the
sequencer posture exists for, asserted as a system property rather than a unit.

The trust model, twice. TestAttestedIsTheConfiguredProvingSystem states the
label by reading the verifier's OWN config, because a submitter posting no
proof looks identical to a proof-verifying verifier about to reject everything.
TestAttestedRefusesABatchCarryingProofBytes asserts the spec rule holds in the
running system: a proof this node cannot check must not be allowed to look like
one it did. And TestAttestedFabricatedExportIsAccepted posts an export P never
emitted and asserts it is ACCEPTED and CROSS-SAFED -- the documented weakness,
as an executable fact, sitting beside the false-import test that refuses.

SuperchainETHBridge: per-counterparty net-flow solvency cap

A chain in the dependency set can only ever mint ETH here up to what this
chain voluntarily sent it. `sendETH` credits `netSent[dest]`; `relayETH`
requires and debits `netSent[source]`, where `source` comes from the
messenger's `crossDomainMessageContext()` (transient message context) and
not from the caller.

Under an attested private chain, a lying attester can fabricate exported
messages that stock interop validation accepts, minting unbounded ETH on
public chains. This bounds the worst case to exactly the deposits made to
that chain. It applies uniformly to every counterparty: no config, no
owner, no special cases. A chain nobody sent ETH to has a cap of zero at
genesis and can extract nothing.

Also converts `version` to a virtual function and `sendETH`/`relayETH` to
`public virtual`, ABI-compatibly, so a genesis variant can extend them
(next commit) instead of duplicating the accounting.

SuperchainETHBridgePinned: one home chain, both directions

Genesis variant of SuperchainETHBridge for a private chain whose genesis we
control: `sendETH` may only target the configured home chain and `relayETH`
may only accept it as source. Because that chain is then the sole mint/burn
venue for this chain's ETH, the home chain's `netSent[thisChain]` is the one
global running figure for all ETH this chain holds, instead of a figure
fragmented across every counterparty.

Inherits the net-flow cap rather than restating it, following the
L2ToL1MessagePasserCGT variant precedent (including the `+suffix` version
and its valid-semver-check exclusion).

`homeChainId` has no setter and no owner: only a genesis allocation can
write it. Storage rather than an immutable because predeploy implementations
are installed as deployed bytecode. Unconfigured (zero) is inert -- every
send and every relay reverts -- so a genesis mistake fails closed.

Sends out of this chain revert before the burn, so a misroute originating
here is impossible. Inbound ETH sent from a non-home chain still burns at
its source and is refused here; those funds need message expiry + refund
(karl/interop-expiry-refunds), noted in the spec, not handled here.

feat(kona-derive): expose the op-stack blob payload decoder

`decode` on the blob-data source is the inverse of what the batcher writes into
a blob: strip the field-element encoding, check the version byte and the
declared length, and hand back the payload. It was private because the only
caller was the stage above it.

That coupling is the problem. The decoding is a consensus-critical detail of the
op-stack blob format, and any component that reads op-stack blobs out of L1
without also wanting channel-frame framing on top -- a single object spanning a
transaction's blobs, say -- currently has to reimplement it. A second
implementation of a decoding that independent readers must agree about is
exactly the thing not to have, so the existing one is published rather than
copied.

contracts: OptimismPortalNoDeposit, silhouette's gated portal

`OptimismPortal2` with the deposit path closed. A silhouette chain takes NO user
deposits, ever -- an open portal would let a stranger force a transaction into a
private chain, and the settlement guest's no-deposit soundness rule (no 0x7E
transaction other than the L1-info tx may appear in any block, which is the
inflation gate) is enforced in-circuit by ASSUMPTION. This contract is what
makes that assumption true on L1 rather than promised.

WHY INHERIT-AND-OVERRIDE rather than a purpose-built always-revert contract:
the portal still OWES its callers a working view surface. `SystemConfig.paused()`
reads `portal.ethLockbox()`; `SystemConfig.disputeGameFactory()` reads the DGF
THROUGH the portal; `ETHLockbox._authorizePortal` reads `superchainConfig()` and
`proxyAdminOwner()`; `L1CrossDomainMessenger` reads `l2Sender()`; and the anchor
state registry's `paused()` gates every dispute game and DelayedWETH. A blanket
revert would take the whole settlement stack down with it. Inheriting keeps all
of it untouched and changes exactly one function.

WHY NOT `pause()`: it does not gate deposits at all. `_assertNotPaused()` is
called from exactly three sites, all on the WITHDRAWAL side. Pausing would block
withdrawals and leave deposits wide open -- the exact inverse of what is needed
-- and it expires by itself after PAUSE_EXPIRY.

Two paths close for free, and both matter: `receive()` makes an INTERNAL call to
`depositTransaction`, and Solidity dispatches internal calls to `virtual`
functions through the override; and `TransactionDeposited` is emitted at exactly
ONE place in the whole src/ tree, which is what makes a one-function override a
COMPLETE gate. Both are tested, so if the base's `virtual` keyword is ever
dropped, a test says so.

Storage layout is byte-identical to the base -- nothing added, reordered or
removed -- asserted slot by slot against a fresh stock portal. That matters
concretely for a chain whose proxy carries orphaned storage from an earlier
implementation: appending even one slot would land on top of it.

The base needed one keyword, `virtual`, which is the entire diff to shared code.

FOUR DEFECTS FIXED, all found by a later sweep and none of them cosmetic:

* `valid-semver-check` failed. The version is `5.8.0+silhouette.nodeposit.1`,
  and that check requires a bare X.Y.Z -- which is why the CGT predeploy
  variants are on its exclusion list. This one now is too, following that
  precedent exactly.
* `interfaces-check` failed: there was no interface. `interfaces/silhouette/`
  now carries one, generated from `IOptimismPortal2` plus the single new error,
  because the gate is a BEHAVIOUR-only override -- `depositTransaction` keeps its
  selector and its signature and reverts. Nothing enters the ABI surface and
  nothing leaves it, and that is now a checked property rather than a claim.
* Snapshots had never been generated. `snapshots/abi/` and
  `snapshots/storageLayout/` now carry the contract, and `semver-lock.json` is
  regenerated -- which also picks up `OptimismPortal2`'s own source hash, stale
  since the `virtual` keyword landed.
* `test_viewSurfaceIntact_succeeds` FAILED, and it was a test-authoring bug
  rather than a contract bug. It called `superchainConfig()` on a freshly
  constructed instance; that getter does not read storage, it delegates to
  `systemConfig`, which is the zero address before initialization -- so it
  reverted on a call to nothing. The property under test is ANSWERABILITY of the
  getters that read this contract's own storage; the two pass-through getters are
  now excluded, with the reasoning recorded at the test, because asserting them
  here would be testing the deployment fixture rather than the gate.

The test suite is also restructured to this tree's sanctioned naming
(`_TestInit` / `_DepositTransaction_Test` / `_Uncategorized_Test`), which
`lint-forge-tests-check` requires and which the previous single `_Test` contract
failed.

Gates: 8/8 in `test/silhouette/`; 32/32 across the two ETH-bridge suites;
`valid-semver-check`, `interfaces-check`, `lint-forge-tests-check`,
`unused-imports-check`, `strict-pragma-check` and `reinitializer-check` all
clean; snapshots regenerated and stable on a second run.

Pre-existing and deliberately untouched: `interfaces-check` also reports
`ISuperPermissionedDisputeGame` and `IZKDisputeGame`, neither of which this
branch touches.

silhouette: the documents, and every in-code reference made resolvable

Five documents. README.md is the branch overview -- what this is, what it rests
on, what the diff costs, and what is deliberately absent. TRUST-MODEL.md states
on what authority the public network believes any of it, without softening, with
every claim named as a test -- including the one that asserts a weakness and
passes. RUNNING-V1.md is the runbook: build, configure, run, and the four traps
that have actually bitten. SPEC-WIRE-V3.md is the wire contract and
SPEC-ETH-NETFLOW-CAP.md the L1-side blast-radius bound.

The settlement story these state is v1's real one: **there is no on-chain
settlement path.** No proposer, no dispute game, no output-root claim, nothing on
L1 adjudicating whether the private chain told the truth. The L1 contracts here
gate the portal shut and bound ETH flow; they do not settle. The cross-chain
consistency that would otherwise need settling is enforced live, in the node, by
the stock cross-safety judge, on every block. The proof-shaped upgrade path --
attested to proven, same wire, same slot, same rules -- is real, and the seam is
built for it, but it lives on the shelf branches.

The rest of the diff is every in-code reference made resolvable, which was owed.
These comments were written while the settlement guest was in the tree, so they
name it -- and a comment pointing at code that is not on this branch is worse
than no comment, because it sends a reader looking for a file that is not there.
Where a reference was to a real cross-implementation invariant -- a convention
several implementations must compute byte-identically -- the invariant survives
verbatim and only the pointer moves, to the proving side and the shelf. Where it
was to a mechanism v1 does not have -- a verifying key pinning a wire version --
the claim is restated in the terms v1 actually uses: a config pinning a version.
The absence claims are deliberately left saying what they say. v1's whole thesis
is that a deployment holds no proving artefact, and the tests asserting it have
to name what is absent to assert it.

The fixture corpus moves with its reader, from the departed Rust crate's
testdata to op-supernode/proofbatch/testdata, bytes untouched. A wire record is
language-agnostic; it belongs beside a codec that reads it rather than inside a
crate that no longer exists, and it has to survive either implementation being
absent -- which one now is.

Three things fixed while here, all found by the branch's own grep gates. The
envelope table described an empty proof slot as "mock mode", the one phrase the
rest of this branch spent commits removing. RUNNING-V1 quoted its size figures
as "with the groth16 shelf excluded", which describes a tree that had a shelf to
exclude; they are now measured on this branch -- 5,858 non-test lines in the
verifier core, 7,045 with the tools, 8,017 lines of tests. And a comment pointed
at `checkLogs`, which does not exist: the function is `checkPreimages`.

op-supernode: an image for the proof-batch submitter

The verifier side already had an image: `op-supernode` is an upstream component
and its bake target predates this branch, and because the silhouette stack
compiles into that same `./cmd` binary, the target needed nothing. The build log
is the proof -- `op-supernode/silhouette` is one of the packages that stage
compiles. What had no image was the producer: v1's whole publishing path is
`proofbatch-submitter`, and a system whose public footprint is one blob per
cadence is not deployable while the thing that posts the blob has to be built
from source on the host.

So: one bake target, following the op-batcher/op-proposer shape exactly -- same
shared Dockerfile, same `$TARGET_BASE_IMAGE`, same builder stage keyed on a
`_VERSION` arg, same bare-name `CMD`. Three files, and no new Dockerfile: the
submitter lives in the op-supernode module, so it builds through that
component's justfile, and `!/op-supernode` already puts its source in the build
context.

`proofbatch-inspect` rides in the same image, which is a deliberate break from
one-binary-per-image and the reason is a runbook step rather than convenience.
When a verifier rejects every batch because its configured `rollupConfigHash`
disagrees with the posted one -- trap-shaped, because the system looks healthy
and simply accepts nothing -- the answer is a decode of an envelope the
submitter itself wrote, and those envelopes are on the submitter's filesystem.
Needing a second image pulled mid-incident to read a file that is already local
is how a five-minute answer becomes an hour. It reads files and never L1, it
holds no credentials, and it costs 18MB on a 31MB image. `silhouette-config`
does NOT ride along, on the same test applied honestly: it is run once, before
the chain exists, to generate a rollup config -- there is nothing for it to do
inside a running submitter, and it would add 59MB to say so.

`proofbatch-inspect` also takes no ldflags, unlike every other recipe in that
justfile. It declares no version symbols, and `-X` against a symbol that does
not exist is silently a no-op -- so stamping it would read, in a diff, like a
version was being applied when none is.

Both images were built and run. The supernode image loads `example/v1` and
prints the line the runbook tells an operator to check --
`assembled silhouette chain ... wireVersion=3 dependenciesVerified=true
proofType=attested` -- and the same image with `proofType: groth16` refuses to
start, which is what makes the first result a parse and not a read. The
submitter image reaches `wire_version=3 declares_imports=true` and then fails on
its L2 endpoint. Neither smoke touches a real network.

What is deliberately not here is the apko/melange release wiring. That is the
path that publishes, it is enrolled per-image in `.github/images.apko.json`, and
where these images should live is an open question rather than one this commit
should answer quietly. Local `docker buildx bake proofbatch-submitter` is
complete without it.

The overview's diff table is updated in the same commit rather than left to go
stale by one row: it claims a file count, and three modified files move it. 246
files, +26,912, -67, and the rows still sum to the total. Measured after the edit
that changed it, and re-measured until two readings agreed -- the table's own
last commit was tripped by exactly that, and the fix is stable here because
README.md is a new file, so editing a number in place cannot move a line count.

`ensure_create2_deployer` decided whether a block triggered the Canyon irregular
state transition by probing `timestamp - 2`, hardcoding a 2-second block time.
OP chains run at 1, 2, 5 and 10 seconds. On a 1-second chain that force-deploys

two blocks it deploys on a block op-geth leaves alone.

OP chain schedules Canyon on a block boundary, so this is the activation block,
and the rule no longer depends on the chain's block time.

chains that ever ran this transition all have a 2-second block time and a Canyon
timestamp that lands on a block.

op-reth: date the pending block env one second after its parent

`build_pending_env` dated the `pending` environment `parent.timestamp + 12`,
Ethereum's L1 slot time, inherited verbatim from upstream reth. On a 2-second OP
chain that is up to five blocks ahead of the block the sequencer will actually
produce, so `eth_call`, `eth_estimateGas`, `eth_createAccessList`, the tracing
call variants and `eth_simulateV1` could execute under a hardfork the real next
block has not activated -- which also changes which `L1Block` slots op-revm
reads and which L1-fee formula it applies.

The EL chain spec carries no block time, so use `parent + 1`: the lower bound of
the next block's timestamp for every OP block time, and the same floor op-geth
clamps to in `miner/worker.go`. Geth reaches that floor from `max(now, parent+1)`,
which is not an option here -- wall-clock time is nondeterministic and can itself
jump a fork boundary, which is the failure this removes.

kona-node: recover from a stale sequencer build instead of hot-looping FCUs

A sequencer build carries the parent the sequencer read from its snapshot of
the unsafe head. When derivation reorgs the unsafe chain in between - which
force-inclusion after a batcher outage does deterministically - that parent no
longer descends from the safe head, and the pre-build forkchoice update is
rejected with -38002. That error was classified Temporary, and the task queue
retried temporary errors in an unbounded loop with no backoff, wedging the
engine actor and the sequencer with it.

- Map -38002 on the build forkchoice update to a reset, mirroring
  SynchronizeTask and op-node's startPayload.
- Reject a detached build whose parent is no longer the unsafe head before
  calling the engine, mirroring op-node's startBuild, and report it to the
  caller over the result channel.
- Let the sequencer re-build on the new head next tick rather than treating a
  rejected or dropped build as a fatal actor error.
- Back off between retries of a temporarily failing task, so an engine API call
  that keeps failing - an execution layer restarting, say - can no longer spin
  the engine actor at the rate the transport answers.
- Publish the unsafe head after an engine reset too, so a caller cannot build
  against a pre-reset snapshot.

kona-derive,kona-protocol: derive multi-block sibling groups

Batch validity for span batch v2 and sibling blocks:

- span prefix checks locate the span's parent by parent_check hash (the
  last block before ts_0, or the matching block in the <= M-long run at
  ts_0 when bit 0 is set) instead of timestamp arithmetic; elements the
  safe chain already holds are skipped by number, so a span is Past when
  its last element is at or below the safe head
- group length is derived from the chain by walking back while
  timestamps are equal (never a counter); groups > max_multi_blocks, a
  sibling at a timestamp where siblings are not allowed, an origin change
  inside a group, or a v2 span included before activation are dropped
- BatchStream vouches for span-derived siblings through StagedBatch, so

superchain-ops: remove the OPCMMigrateV800 template

U20 and the op-contracts/v8.0.0 series do not call OPCM.migrate. The
production v8.0.0 OPCM cannot run migrate either, because migrate requires
the OPTIMISM_PORTAL_INTEROP dev feature and the production deployment has
devFeatureBitmap == 0.

The template therefore targeted an interop-enabled dev OPCM, which no task
will use. This change removes the template, its integration test, the 036
example task and the CI skip that the example task needed.

OPCMUpgradeV800: remove the unused cannonPrestate input

The template never uses cannonPrestate. It builds six game configs, and
only SUPER_PERMISSIONED (5) and SUPER_CANNON_KONA (9) can be enabled. Game
type 5 encodes the proposer, and game type 9 encodes the Kona prestate. The
retired Cannon game types stay disabled, and the OPCM ignores the game args
of a disabled config.

The StandardValidator also ignores the value. This template always leaves
the chain on a super respected game type, so the validator takes its super
path, where cannonPrestate reaches assertValidSuperPermissionedDisputeGame,
which takes no prestate.

A required non-zero field that nothing reads makes operators source a real
Cannon prestate for U20 that has no effect.

op-service: move PathFlag to a leaf package so oppprof is importable

op-service/oppprof needs exactly one thing from op-service/flags: the
PathFlag value type, for --pprof.path. But op-service/flags also defines
the --network flag, whose usage string interpolates
chaincfg.AvailableNetworks():

    Usage: fmt.Sprintf("Predefined network selection. Available networks: %s",
        strings.Join(chaincfg.AvailableNetworks(), ", ")),

Go compiles at package granularity, so that one help-string reference put
op-node/chaincfg — and with it op-core/superchain and its embedded
superchain-configs.zip — into the build closure of every consumer of a
pprof flag.

superchain-configs.zip is generated by sync-superchain.sh and gitignored,
so it is absent from the published module. Anything reaching
op-core/superchain therefore cannot be built by a downstream module at all:

    op-core/superchain/chain.go:21:12: pattern superchain-configs.zip:
        no matching files found

That made op-service/oppprof — and so any service wiring up pprof flags —
unimportable outside this repo from v1.19.1 onward, which is when the
registry moved into op-core. Before that the data came from op-geth's own
superchain package, which ships intact, so a downstream op-geth replace
covered it.

PathFlag moves verbatim to the new leaf package op-service/cliflags, which
imports only the standard library. op-service/flags keeps the
chain-selection flags and its chaincfg dependency, which is legitimate.

Adds op-service/deps_test.go, guarding the consumer-facing op-service
packages against a transitive op-core/superchain import via the existing
depguard helper, in the same spirit as op-node/rollup/deps_test.go. The
guard was confirmed to fail on the pre-fix code, reporting the chain
oppprof -> flags -> chaincfg -> op-core/superchain.

Verified: with the bundle deleted, op-service/oppprof compiles, and a
throwaway external module importing op-service/oppprof and
op-service/cliflags builds against this tree. All 15 guarded packages are
bundle-free; `go build ./...` and the touched packages' tests pass.

op-service: invert the bundle guard to an allowlist over ./...

Review feedback: a list of guarded packages goes stale exactly when it
matters, because a newly added package is silently unguarded.

Adds depguard.RequireNoTransitiveImportExcept, which walks every package
matched by a broad pattern and permits only an explicit allowlist. The
op-service guard now covers all 76 packages under ./... instead of the 15
that were named, so the invariant holds by default.

The allowlist is checked in both directions: an entry that no longer
reaches a forbidden import fails the test, so entries cannot outlive the
dependency that justified them.

Enumerating the exceptions surfaced that op-service/flags is not the only
way into the bundle. op-service/{apis,dial,sources,testutils,txintent,...}
reach it through op-core/interop/depset, whose FromRegistry loader sits
alongside the DependencySet types those packages actually use. That is the
same shape as the PathFlag problem and would yield to the same fix, which
would make op-service/sources importable downstream. Left for a follow-up
and recorded against each allowlist entry; see #22678.

depguard gains positive controls for both new failure modes — a non-allowed
package reaching a forbidden import, and a stale allowlist entry — since a
guard that can only pass is worthless. The op-service guard was also
re-confirmed to fail on the pre-fix code.

kona!: add a chain_id label to every metric, from an ambient scope

kona resolves every metric through the process-wide `metrics` recorder, so a
metric's chain is not knowable at the emit site. In a single-chain kona-node
that costs nothing. In a process that runs several chains it does: every
chain's series collapse into one.

Rather than pass the chain id to each of kona's ~320 emit sites, the new
`kona-metrics` crate carries it in an ambient scope and adds it as a label in
a wrapping `metrics::Recorder`. Every `counter!`/`gauge!`/`histogram!`
resolves its key through the recorder on every emit, and no kona emit site
hoists a handle, so the wrapper sees all of them. No emit site changes.

Four places bind a chain, because a `tokio::task_local` does not propagate
into a spawned task:

- `spawn_and_wait!`, which spawns all seven per-chain actors from one line.
- `Discv5Driver::start`, whose event loop is its own detached task.
- the jsonrpsee servers, through a `ChainScope` RPC middleware, because
  jsonrpsee serves each call on a task it spawns itself. Both the node's
  launcher and the `net` subcommand's server install it.
- the `net` subcommand's network actor, which it spawns directly.

`ChainLabelRecorder`'s fallback covers what no chain owns: the process
collector thread, the build-info gauge, and the start-up zero-fill. kona-node
serves one chain, so it passes that chain and every series is labelled. A
multi-chain process passes `None`, so a process-wide emit stays unlabelled
rather than claiming a chain it does not have.

The fallback comes from the resolved rollup config, not from `--chain`:
`node --l2-config-file` overrides the flag, and the actors scope themselves
with the chain from that file, so the recorder has to agree or a devnet gets
two chain ids in one process.

An emit that already carries a `chain_id` is passed through untouched, which
leaves an explicit label available to a component that serves several chains
from one task.

than `Result<(), BuildError>`, and `CliError` gains two variants. `CliError`
is `#[non_exhaustive]` now, so later variants are additive.

kona: make the pre-created metric series match what the code emits

`Metrics::zero()` pre-creates a series per expected label tuple so that
Prometheus exposes it before the first event. Nothing links that list to the
emit sites, and the two had drifted apart in both directions: series that no
code can ever produce sit at 0 forever beside the real ones, and emitted
series are missing until their first event, which is what `zero()` exists to
prevent.

Each label list is now derived from the emit sites, and expressed as a loop
over the emitted values rather than one call per series.

Corrected in `zero()`:

- `kona_node_dial_peer_error` pre-created one unlabelled series; all nine
  emits carry `type`. Three shipped dashboard panels select on that label.
- `kona_node_find_node_requests` pre-created one unlabelled series; the emit
  carries a constant `find_node` label that the dashboard selects on.
- `kona_node_rpc_calls` omitted the emitted `opp2p_unblockPeer` and
  `admin_postUnsafePayload`.
- `kona_node_block_validation_failed` pre-created `parent_beacon_root`, which
  no `BlockInvalidError` variant produces.
- `kona_node_gossip_events` pre-created five `type` values, but `message`,
  `subscribed` and `unsubscribed` also carry `topic`. Only the two topic-free
  types are pre-created now; for the other two the topic comes from remote
  peers, so the value set is not knowable.
- `kona_node_banned_peers` is no longer pre-created: its emit carries
  `peer_id` and `score`, so there is no finite series set.
- `kona_providers_chain_rpc_calls`/`_errors` omitted the emitted
  `block_by_number`.
- `kona_providers_beacon_requests`/`_errors` pre-created `blob_sidecars`; the
  emit says `blobs`.
- `kona_providers_l2_chain_requests`/`_errors` pre-created

  code path, and omitted the emitted `l2_block_by_hash`.

  which no emit uses, and omitted the emitted `l2_block_info_by_hash`.

`opp2p_peerStats` was pre-created but `P2pRpc::opp2p_peer_stats` was the one

`SEQUENCER_STATE` was described with `describe_counter!` but is emitted with
`metrics::gauge!`, so the description never attached. It is a gauge now.

Five metrics were declared and described but emitted by nothing. They are
removed rather than left reporting a permanent 0:
`kona_node_gossipsub_events`, `kona_providers_cache_memory_bytes`,
`kona_providers_request_duration`, `kona_providers_local_cache_capacity` and

sites, so that is the only place the two halves can be compared, and it makes

kona-client: skip consolidation when interop is inactive

The consolidation step dispatched purely on the transition state's step
counter, so it ran the full superchain consolidation on every chain
regardless of whether the Lagoon hardfork was active.

Below the activation timestamp op-supernode composes the super root from
the unmodified optimistic outputs: it performs no cross-chain validation
and no block replacement. kona did not match. MessageGraph::derive parses
logs regardless of fork state, so a pre-activation executing message was
found, rejected as ExecutedTooEarly, and the block replaced with a
deposit-only one, changing the resulting super root.

Gate consolidation on interop activation at the timestamp being
finalized. When no covered chain is active, accept the optimistic outputs
and finalize the super root directly.

The gate uses is_interop_active rather than the stricter
interop_active_for_full_block, so the activation timestamp itself still
consolidates and the per-message rules keep rejecting via
is_first_interop_block.

Reuse transition_and_check for the post-state check instead of the copy
that consolidate_dependencies carried, so the two paths cannot drift.
