op-private-interop/render: the rendering transformation, as one shared primitive

The rendering's log positions ARE the identity of the private chain's messages,
symmetrically, for every component: the counterparty's judge, the interop
filter, relayers, and the operator's own supernode. One index of disagreement
between the builder that writes the rendering and the readers that seed message
databases from private blocks makes the operator invalidate counterparties'
valid executing messages. So there is exactly one implementation --
`RenderedLogs` / `RenderBlock`, pure and consensus-critical -- and every side
imports it rather than restating it.

Order is the ORIGINAL interleaved log order, not exports-then-imports. The
standing invariant is that `RenderedLogs` equals the derived rendering block's
log sequence, and sorting by kind breaks it for any block that interleaves the
two.

The emitter set is (address, topic0) pairs, and it selects CLAIMS only. The
messenger's bookkeeping events are not claims, and a rendered `RelayedMessage`
at the replayer's address would be consumable at the wrong address under stock
interop's any-log-initiates rule. `RelayedMessageEventTopic` is exported with no
production caller precisely to pin that exclusion.

Replay transaction construction sits behind `ReplayTxBuilder`, with every
contract binding in one file. Imports reuse `txintent.ExecTrigger` rather than
re-deriving the checksum access list: a second checksum implementation is a
second one that drifts.

Origins are COPIED, not chosen. A rendering block's L1 epoch is the private
block's OWN origin, read from its L1-info deposit and carried through with its
sequence number, so `RenderedBlock` carries the whole private `L2BlockRef`. The
private sequencer already chose origins under identical stock rules at identical
timestamps, so re-deriving them could only agree with the private chain or be
wrong -- and doing it would need a live L1 view, a confirmation-depth buffer and
a past-range view. Three things follow: span validity holds by construction,
since the copied origins are ones a stock sequencer already produced; the
rendering's sequence numbers equal the private chain's, which is what lets the
public supernode serve follow refs; and the batch becomes a pure function of
private-chain data with NO live L1 input at all, so two honest operators can no
longer diverge by observing L1 at different moments.

There is no service in front of this. An earlier design wrapped `RenderedLogs`
in an RPC "rendering view" that the interop filter would dial instead of the raw
private node; the in-process transformation ruling superseded it, and the filter
now reads the real private node and applies this function itself between fetch
and LogsDB insertion. One pure function, called in-process by the builder and by
the filter, is the whole packaging story.

`replay.go` turns those replay actions into the operator's signed transactions,
behind an interface because the operator's key lives with whatever signer the
deployment uses and a pure package must not know about it. Its determinism
contract is explicit: an implementation must be a pure function of the starting
nonce and the calls made since -- no clock, no fee oracle, no discovered nonce.
The rendering's transactions are consensus data, so a builder that prices a
transaction from a live gas oracle produces a different chain every time it
runs; fees come from the frozen configuration the rendering's genesis already
encodes. WHICH transactions exist, and in what order, is decided by RenderBlock
and is not negotiable there.

op-private-interop/builder: the range builder, and byte-determinism as a gate

The rendering has no sequencer, so the operator must produce exactly the bytes a
stock batcher would have produced for it: one span batch per cadence, stock
frames, stock blob packing, derivation version 0x00, and nothing a public
verifier could tell apart from any other chain's output.

The channel ID is the one place stock behaviour cannot be reused. The batcher
randomizes it, which is right for a chain with one writer and wrong for a
payload that must be reproducible by anyone holding the same private data -- so
it is keccak(prevTerminalRenderingHash || firstBlock)[:16], and this package
drives the encoding pipeline itself while reusing every encoder in it
(RawSpanBatch RLP, the channel compressor, Frame, eth.Blob).

Because origins are copied from the private blocks rather than chosen here,
the builder is what the design says it is: an effectively stock batch submitter
that strips private transactions, inserts the claim transaction and the replay
transactions, and alters nothing about block progression. Span validity then
holds by construction, since the copied origins are ones a stock sequencer
already produced. `l1Head` in the claim is DERIVED rather than supplied -- it is
the terminal block's own origin, which since origin-copy is the newest L1 block
the range actually depends on. That is the honest reading of the field, it costs
no L1 access, and unlike a supplied value a verifier can CHECK it, because the
rendering's terminal block carries that origin.

`privatedata.go` is the range's FULL PRIVATE DERIVATION INPUT -- the object whose
keccak the claim carries as `privateDataHash`. It is a COMMITMENT, not a
payload: nothing publishes these bytes. Private data reaches the operator's own
followers over the firewalled p2p network, and the claim binds, for anyone who
later holds the bytes, exactly which object is the range's real derivation
input. So the ENCODING is consensus-relevant even though its output never leaves
the batcher -- change it and every past claim commits to something nobody can
reproduce. The object is exactly what a STOCK batcher for the private chain
would have posted for these blocks: version byte, then stock channel frames over
one span batch, with the private chain's own transactions in them. Not a bespoke
archive format -- the private chain is a real OP Stack chain, so the one
description of it that stock software can consume is the one stock software
writes, and a reader holding this object plus the private genesis can reproduce
the private chain with no code of ours at all.

The gates are the point of the package: the same range built twice from fresh
state gives identical span bytes, frames and blobs; the span passes real
`derive.CheckBatch` for a full 300-block cadence, for a claim-less range and for
a single block; a parent check the rendering does not match is a plain
BatchDrop; and the claim transaction is the FIRST transaction of the
range-opening block, with every message in that block keeping its `RenderedLogs`
rank -- which holds only because the registry is log-less.

op-deployer: the privateInterop stanza, an intent-level resource config, and the deposit gate

Deploying a private interop pair needs two things the intent could not say.

ONE STANZA PER CHAIN names which half a chain's genesis renders, who the
operator is, what the operator opens with, and -- for the private half -- which
chain holds the lock vault its mint bridge mints against. It is absent on every
ordinary chain, which is what keeps an ordinary chain's genesis untouched. The
dev feature bits are DERIVED from the stanza rather than written by hand into
devFeatureBitmap, so the intent stays the single place a half is chosen and the
bitmap cannot disagree with it. While here, buildDevFeatureBitmap learned to
read a chain's own deployOverrides before falling back to the global ones: the
bitmap was global-only, which is wrong for a knob that is per-chain by nature.

Validation lives with the config it validates. The rendering must not be a
custom gas token chain -- its replay transactions pay gas in the rendering's own
ETH -- and must open with a positive operator balance, since that balance is the
only gas the chain will ever have. The private half must be a custom gas token
chain, must name a counterparty and vault, and cannot mint the operator more
than the reserve holds. The operator EOA is premined by the genesis script
itself rather than through the dev-genesis prefund stage, because a production
rendering needs the balance too and that stage only runs against a genesis
target; that puts a bare EOA in the allocs, so the structural check is told to
expect it.

AN OPTIONAL RESOURCE CONFIG on the chain intent buys the deposit gate with no
contract change. A chain becomes undepositable on a completely stock portal when
its SystemConfig is initialized with maxResourceLimit = 0: every
depositTransaction is metered against that limit with a gas limit of at least
21000, so every deposit reverts on L1 and no user deposit ever exists for
derivation or attribute handling to see. That is exactly what the pair needs --
the rendering's ETH solvency story rests on nothing minting ETH into it from a
deposit -- and it wanted only somewhere to say it. There was nowhere: the
resource config was derived from the gas limit and nothing else, behind a
`require(maxResourceLimit > 0)` that no gas limit can get past, and it appeared
in no Go struct in the deploy path. Now an optional resourceConfig threads
through DeployOPChainInput to the FullConfig field OPCM already had; absent
means the gas-limit-derived default, so an ordinary deployment is unchanged by
this existing. Three fields, not six: maxResourceLimit, elasticityMultiplier and
systemTxMaxGas are the ones `SystemConfig._setResourceConfig` constrains against
each other and against the gas limit, and the EIP-1559 parameters and base fee
bounds keep their defaults because nothing about a deposit gate wants them
moved. The same constraints are checked on the intent, so a bad value is caught
while it is still a file. The resource config is set ONLY through
`initialize` -- there is no owner-callable setter -- so a live SystemConfig
owner can rotate the batcher key without being able to reopen deposits.

Audited for the assumption this breaks, and nothing in the pipeline requires
maxResourceLimit > 0. The Go tree has no ResourceConfig type at all; its one
related assumption is a gas-limit floor in `L2GenesisBlockDeployConfig.Check`
computed from default constants, which a private interop chain's normal gas
limit clears regardless. In Solidity the divisions are by elasticityMultiplier,
never by maxResourceLimit, and `_setResourceConfig` accepts zero against all five
of its checks. Two things are reported rather than papered over:
OPContractsManagerStandardValidator hardcodes the six default values
(SYSCON-50..100), so a gated chain fails `op-deployer validate` -- already true
of it for custom gas token -- and continue_verify does not diff the resource
config against the chain.

The oracles are integration tests that run the real apply pipeline, which is
where the coverage for the two dev features lives (they gate genesis
GENERATION, so the contract suite's fixed input never reaches them): genesis
allocs for both halves, the pair's two rollup configs rendered and asserted, and
an assertion that the deposit gate actually reaches the deployed SystemConfig.

`intentbuilder` gains the per-chain door, and `interopgen` is told explicitly
that it never renders a half -- neither PRIVATE_INTEROP_* bit is ever set in its
bitmap, so the script never reads the two fields it now has to pass.

op-batcher: the private interop terminal seam and its flag group

The ratified operator topology has no new batching binary: the range builder is
op-batcher with `--private-interop` flags. The whole batcher lifecycle is worth
reusing unchanged -- unsafe-head polling, reorg detection against the PRIVATE
chain (the only chain anything can reorg), channel retry, txmgr, blob
submission, throttling. Only the last stage differs: the blocks loaded are
private, the bytes posted describe the rendering.

So the seam is the ChannelOutFactory hook that already existed, plus one
addition to the loading path: receipts are what the transformation needs and
what an execution payload does not carry, and fetching them in the loader means
a failure fails the load -- which the batcher already retries -- instead of
surfacing under the channel-manager mutex.

`renderChannelOut` implements `derive.ChannelOut` rather than wrapping
`SpanChannelOut` for one reason: the channel ID must be a function of the range,
and SpanChannelOut randomizes it with no seam to inject one. Every encoder is
still stock; only the drive moved. Nothing foreign is posted -- these are stock
frames with a derived channel ID, and stock `txData.Blobs()` puts the 0x00 in
front exactly as it does for any chain, which the test asserts blob-for-blob. So
stock op-batcher files stay untouched apart from the hook.

The RangeSource is stateless, and that is a property worth keeping. It dials a
node following the rendering and reads all of a range's starting facts off the
rendering's previous block -- including the operator's nonce, from the chain and
never from memory, so a restarted batcher rebuilds the same range. It holds no
L1 client and no view: since origins are copied from the private blocks, the
batch is a pure function of private-chain data with no live L1 input at all, so
two honest operators cannot diverge by observing L1 at different moments.

Close encodes the range's private derivation input and hashes it before a single
frame exists, so until Build returns ReadyBytes is zero and OutputFrame is
io.EOF: there is nothing to get wrong at the transaction layer because there is
nothing to send. The object is not a bespoke archive -- it is exactly what a
stock batcher for the PRIVATE chain would have posted for these blocks, built
from the same `derive.PayloadToSingularBatch` conversion the seam already
performed and was throwing away, which is the only way the object and the
rendering are guaranteed to describe the same range. Its channel ID is derived
for the same reason the rendering's is: the object's NAME is the hash of its
bytes, and a random channel ID would give the same range a new content address
every build. Nothing publishes those bytes; the hash in the claim is a
commitment, and the bytes reach the operator's own followers over the firewalled
p2p network.

The flag group is registered in the optional set and is inert unless
`--private-interop.enabled`. Enabled, it is all-or-nothing, and Check is where
that is decided: every address and hash is validated for syntax AND for the zero
value, matching the posture render/abi.go takes, because the rendering's
contracts are placed by its genesis builder so there is no defensible default,
and `common.HexToAddress` is silently lenient enough to turn a typo into a
plausible address no contract sits at. Gas limits are floored at the intrinsic
21000; the numbers stay flagged and labelled UNMEASURED.
`--private-interop.replay-messenger` has a default, and it is the only value
that renders valid exports -- a re-emitted `SentMessage` must carry the emitter
every stock consumer expects -- but it is a flag so that a deployment which
moved the implementation fails at its own hands rather than ours.

The operator key is deliberately a local hex key. The rendering's transactions
are consensus data and must be a pure function of the range, which go-ethereum's
RFC 6979 signing is and a remote signer that adds entropy is not.

Two bugs a live pair caught, fixed here: the rendering follower decoded
fullTx=true responses as raw bytes and failed on every non-empty block, so range
2 onward never built (it now asks with fullTx=FALSE and never decodes a
transaction at all); and the default gas fee cap was 1000x under a fresh
genesis base fee and failed silently.

op-supernode: the private interop claim follow module

A private chain's stock LightCL has to be told what its own safe head is. The
supernode is where that answer belongs, and the answer comes ENTIRELY from
public data the supernode already derives -- no private EL, no private
credential, no endpoint of its own to dial. There is no follower binary and no
sidecar.

Two ratified amendments make that possible. ORIGIN-COPY means a private block
and its rendering share an L1 origin, and therefore a sequence number, by
construction rather than by hope; and the claim publishes
`privateTerminalParentHash`. So of the six fields the follow consumer compares,
two come from the claim and four are read off the supernode's OWN rendering
block at the same height.

Access is in-process: the module reads through the chain container's existing
accessors -- SyncStatus, PayloadByNumber, FetchReceipts -- and never dials, not
even a loopback. PayloadByNumber is the load-bearing one, since a single call
yields the block's identity, its timestamp, its transactions AND, through its
L1-attributes deposit via `derive.PayloadToBlockRef`, its origin and sequence
number. No interface on the container or the engine controller needed widening.

Serving is SNAP-TO-COMMITMENT. Claims are served verbatim: there is no private
chain to check them against and, under the ratified posture, no check to make --
the claim is the operator's binding statement, and a claim naming a block that
exists nowhere fail-stops in the consumer as an unfindable-hash stall. The one
rule this actively changes rather than merely drops is that a REVERTED postClaim
is a skip with a metric, not the deleted sidecar's withhold latch. Every served
label is a high-water mark, because a sequencing follower force-resets onto
whatever local-safe ref it is told. Completion is a separate step from reading,
because a claim LEADS its range: it rides in the range's first block while the
ref it resolves to lives at the last, a whole cadence later.

Finality gates on the claim's TERMINAL block, not its carrier. Four of a served
finalized ref's six fields are borrowed from the rendering block at lastBlock, a
whole cadence above the carrier, so gating on the carrier published a ref two of
whose fields came from a finalized block and four from one that was only safe --
an L1 reorg above the finalized height could then change the borrowed four while
the claim-borne hash stayed put, producing a CHANGED FINALIZED REF AT AN
UNCHANGED HEIGHT. The consumer treats a finalized head as immutable at a height
(`applyFinalizedHeadCacheChecks` returns the stale cached value on an ID match
and PANICS on a same-height hash conflict), so a finalized output must be a pure
function of finalized-depth inputs. Requiring `lastBlock <= renderFinalized`
makes all six fields exactly that, and costs nothing in ordering: a claim leads
its own range, so the new gate strictly implies the old one.

Before the first claim the module serves the PRIVATE GENESIS REF, from one flag,
and the reason is a bootstrap deadlock that a live pair actually hit. Erroring
until the first claim was right about the consumer it considered -- a follow-mode
sequencer's initial engine reset comes from `sync.FindL2Heads` over real L1 and
its own EL, never from the follow source, retried and never fatal -- but the
sequencer is not the only consumer of the op-node it feeds. The operator's
BATCHER polls the same op-node, whose CurrentL1 in follow mode has exactly one
writer: the driver forwards this module's `current_l1` verbatim. An erroring
module left it zero, op-batcher's first sync check rejects a zero CurrentL1
outright and loads no blocks, and then no blocks means no batch, no batch means
no claim, and the not-yet state never ends. Measured: a pair sequenced its
private chain to block 126 while its batcher logged "empty BlockRef in sync
status" 486 times and the rendering never left block 0.

The fix is ONE flag, not the two an earlier draft declined. Only the HASH of the
private genesis is unknowable from public data: number, timestamp and l1origin
follow from the pair's block-for-block construction and the rendering's own
rollup config, and parentHash and sequenceNumber are zero by the definition of a
genesis block -- exactly what `derive.PayloadToBlockRef` produces on its genesis
branch, so the served ref compares equal to the one the private EL derives for
itself. `--private-interop.genesis-hash` is REQUIRED whenever the module is
enabled, so a missing one is a startup failure instead of a bootstrap that hangs
with every component looking healthy, and it is length-checked because
`common.HexToHash` silently pads and truncates. The package comment carries the
lesson rather than the old conclusion: reasoning about a follow source one
consumer at a time is not enough, because everything downstream of the op-node
it feeds inherits whatever it does or does not say.

The module answers at a SIBLING ROUTE, `<base>/<chainID>/<name>`. The shared
router keys on the first path segment only, so anything under a chain's prefix
must be mounted on that chain's own `oprpc.Handler` -- the monorepo's established
sub-route idiom (op-faucet, op-sync-tester, op-test-sequencer all use AddRPC +
AddAPIToRPC). Mounting there rather than adding a namespace to the virtual node's
own route means a mispointed consumer gets a loud 404 instead of plausible-looking
answers about the wrong chain. The option is variadic, so a container built with
no options is byte-identical to one built before options existed; registration
re-runs on every virtual-node restart, so the service behind a route outlives the
handler and must be safe for concurrent use. The routes inherit the chain's
readiness gate, which is correct rather than incidental: a module whose only
inputs are one chain's derived data has nothing new to say while that chain is
down, and hold-then-503 reaches a follow consumer as a skipped tick.

Flags follow the op-batcher dormant-flag standard: an `--private-interop.enabled`
gate, an all-or-nothing Check behind it, and registration through
RegisterActivityFlags so op-supernode/config never imports this package.
`initClaimFollow` is the whole of the wiring and its dormant path is the point --
unset, it returns a nil activity and an empty route map, every chain container is
built with an empty option list, no activity is added, no goroutine starts, no
metric is registered, and a stock supernode is unchanged. Enabled, it makes the
two validations only the supernode can make (that the configured chain is one
this process actually runs, and that its rollup config loaded) and fails startup
rather than serving an error forever. The module and the container are built in
that order of necessity -- the container needs the module's API among its routes,
the module needs the container as its data source -- so Attach closes the loop
right after the chain loop, and an unattached module is a skipped tick rather
than a nil dereference.

The tests drive a rendering chain whose blocks carry REAL L1-attributes
deposits, so ref completion is exercised through `derive.PayloadToBlockRef`
rather than around it, and a wire test puts the module behind the real handler
and the real router and reads it with the stock `sources.FollowClient`, at the
sibling route and not at the chain's own.

op-interop-filter: render a flagged chain's logs before storage

A private chain in a public dependency set publishes its messages as a separate
public rendering chain, and a message's identity is its position THERE. A filter
that stores raw private positions files every message under a number no
counterparty will ever cite.

`--render-transform-chains` marks a chain whose logs are stored at their RENDERED
positions, with `--render-extra-emitters` for the non-standard half of that
chain's emitter set. The option is chain-ID keyed rather than URL keyed, so it
says "this chain's positions are rendered" instead of depending on exact URL
spelling. Check rejects a listed chain with no rollup config, and extra emitters
with no listed chain: both are typos, and the first is the one that would
otherwise be silent. Addresses go through `common.IsHexAddress` rather than
`common.HexToAddress`, which quietly turns anything unparseable into the zero
address -- as an emitter that would silently change the numbering.

For a listed chain, blocks and receipts are fetched and verified exactly as for
every other chain -- the source is an ordinary execution client serving
self-consistent blocks -- and `render.RenderedLogs` is applied to the
already-verified logs between the fetch and the logs DB. Logs outside the
emitter set are dropped, the survivors keep their interleaved order and are
renumbered densely from zero, and the block is still sealed under its real hash,
number and timestamp. Only the log sequence is transformed.

`RenderedLogs` is IMPORTED from op-private-interop/render, never reimplemented.
It is the same call the rendering builder makes when constructing replay
transactions, and the filter's admission decisions only mean anything if the two
agree about every index.

This replaces an earlier detour in which the filter dialled a transforming RPC
service instead of the real private node. TrustRPC stays false for every chain
and no verification is relaxed anywhere, and a doc comment preserves the finding
that killed the detour: TrustRPC in op-service/sources gates verification but NOT
identity derivation. `EthClient.InfoByNumber` and `InfoByLabel` wrap their header
in `eth.HeaderBlockInfo`, which derives the block hash from the header fields
unconditionally, so against a source whose header is not self-consistent a
TrustRPC client does not merely skip a check -- it silently adopts a block hash
that is no block's. Reading a real node makes the question moot, which is the
point.

The end-to-end test drives the real ingestion path -- production constructor,
real HTTP JSON-RPC listener, real op-service/sources client with verification
fully on -- against an ordinary private execution client. The fixture block
carries four logs, two in the emitter set, at raw indexes 1 and 3, so the raw
and rendered numberings disagree for both: transform off stores all four at
their raw indexes, transform on stores two with the import at RENDERED index 1
and the block sealed under its REAL hash, and configuring the private address as
an extra emitter shifts the import back to 3 -- which pins that the flag reaches
the same predicate the builder uses, and therefore that an emitter set which
disagrees with the builder silently renumbers messages.

op-devstack, op-acceptance-tests: the pair as a preset option, and its e2e

A test holds three surfaces -- a transaction surface, a derivation/judge surface,
and a batcher control surface -- and the devstack builds all three from URLs.
That is why a private interop pair can be an OPTION on the two-L2
light-sequencer preset rather than a preset family of its own: the pair changes
which processes those URLs point at, and changes nothing about what a test
holds. The option is registered in all three places option_validation.go keeps
-- the kind, the allOptionKinds mask, and the label table -- because a kind
missing from the mask is reported as unknown(0x...) and a kind missing from a
preset's set is rejected with a blank name. The cadence default is four blocks
rather than production's ~300: the rendering only advances when a range lands,
so the cadence is how long a test waits for its message to become public, and
ten minutes is not a test.

BOTH HALVES COME FROM ONE WORLD. A pair is two genesis states under one chain
ID, and the production runbook makes them with two op-deployer runs that must
both pin the same l1StartBlockHash -- or the halves take their genesis
timestamps from different L1 blocks and the builder can never emit a block at
both the private chain's number and its timestamp. A devstack cannot follow that
runbook, because l1StartBlockHash is resolved by reading a block off a live L1
and a genesis-target run seals its own; two runs would be two L1s and two
timestamps, exactly the failure the constraint warns about. So this does
something stronger than pinning: one world is built with chain B as the PRIVATE
half, then that one chain's L2 genesis is re-rendered with the stanza flipped to
`rendering`, against the same state, the same L1 genesis, and above all the same
chainState.StartBlock -- which is where both halves' timestamps come from. The
halves cannot disagree about their start block because there is only one. The
re-render runs the real pipeline stage plus the real inspect call, on a copy.

EVERY PROCESS IS A STOCK BINARY. The private chain is a stock op-reth and a
stock op-node in light-sequencer mode whose `--l2.follow.source` points at the
supernode's `<base>/<chainID>/claimed` sibling route; the rendering is a stock
op-reth and the supernode's own verifier route; the publisher is op-batcher with
its `--private-interop` flag group, configured through the CLI path an operator
uses rather than through the programmatic seam, so the devstack exercises the
wiring a deployment actually has. The follow module is enabled by handing the
supernode a parsed flag group as a `*cli.Context`, because that is its only
config door -- a second door would leave the operator's path untested and test
one nothing runs. Every other preset passes nil, which reads as disabled.

Three construction edges are forced and the order encodes them, and one sharp
edge is handled as an ordering plus a check: a disabled module's sibling route is
not a 404, because the chain container mounts its root JSON-RPC at "/", so
`/claimed` falls through and answers `optimism_syncStatus` for the RENDERING,
which a sequencing LightCL would force-reset onto. So the supernode is
constructed and started with the module enabled before that URL is used for
anything, and `assertClaimedRouteIsTheModule` proves which of the two is
answering before the sequencer consumes it: `optimism_rollupConfig` must fail
(the module is one method wide, the rendering's handler is not) and
`optimism_syncStatus` must succeed naming the PRIVATE chain's genesis hash --
the fall-through would answer with the rendering's own status, whose safe head is
the rendering's genesis, which is the one field that tells the two chains apart.

That genesis hash is read from the PRIVATE network's own rollup config, the one
place it can come from: the halves share a chain ID, a genesis timestamp and a
genesis L1 block and differ in exactly this field, so reading it off the
RENDERING's config would be the classic mistake and would produce a module that
vouched confidently for the wrong chain.

P2P SEVERANCE IS NOT A MECHANISM. `connectL2CLPeers` and `connectL2ELPeers` are
explicit calls, and this runtime makes them only within the public side. That
absence is the whole implementation, which is why it is written down. Relatedly
the private sequencer runs CLSync, not the light-sequencer path's ELSync: ELSync
is that path's answer to reorging onto a supernode replacement over EL p2p, a
peering this topology forbids and a replacement a private chain never gets. The
preset's VN-sequencer handoff is unusable here for its own reason -- it would
have to enable sequencing on the supernode's routes, and one of those is the
rendering, a chain that must never sequence anything.

Three batcher settings are stated rather than inherited. The gas fee cap is the
sharp one: the flag default is 1,000,000 wei and an OP genesis opens its base
fee at 1 gwei, so every replay and every claim offered to a freshly deployed
rendering is unpayable by three orders of magnitude -- and the failure is quiet
in the worst way, because the batch still posts, the rendering still derives
blocks at the right numbers and timestamps, and the pair looks alive while
carrying no claims at all. The channel duration is disabled and the span-batch
cap is raised to the cadence, because the cadence owns where a range ends: one
span batch per cadence is the ratified shape, and a range that ends somewhere
its claim did not say it would is a range whose parent check the next one gets
wrong.

The standing checker asserts only what cannot flake: block-for-block
correspondence (timestamps, never hashes -- the chains differ by design),
monotone safe heads on both sides, and that the safe head the module serves
names a block the private chain actually has. Under snap-to-commitment there is
no withhold latch, so what that third assertion catches is the condition itself:
the operator's chain and the operator's own public claims having parted company.
Progress is deliberately not asserted in the background, since a deadline
invented once for every suite is a flake; tests that care call
RequireRenderingProgress with their own budget, and the waits are "reached block
N" rather than "advanced by N", because a delta measured from whenever the call
was made is a race with the pair's own progress.

THE IDENTIFIER RESOLVER lives here, where both halves of a pair are in hand. It
computes the rendered index through `render.RenderedLogs` -- imported, never
restated -- then reads the log the rendering actually carries there, taking the
origin from the real public log and cross-checking its payload hash. And it
waits, once, keyed off the preset: a message has no public position until the
rendering has derived the block that carries it.

`DEVSTACK_PRIVATE_INTEROP` is what makes "existing suites run UNCHANGED against a
pair" literally true. A test that had `WithPrivateInteropChain()` added to its
constructor call is a test that was changed, and it proves only that the option
compiles. A test names its preset in its own body and passes its own options, so
the only place left to say "build this world as a pair" is outside the test --
in the shape `DEVSTACK_L2EL_KIND` and `DEVSTACK_L2CL_KIND` already established.
Unset, it does nothing. `NewTwoL2SupernodeInterop` dispatches to the pair's
runtime, and a preset asked for something a pair cannot provide (the in-process
interop filter, which reads a chain's own blocks, and a pair's public blocks are
its rendering's) skips with a reason rather than quietly running a weaker test.

The two acceptance tests are the gate. The pair's smoke test comes first because
almost everything that can go wrong with a pair goes wrong before any message is
sent -- a genesis mismatch, a follow source that never answers, a builder that
cannot resolve its parent check -- and a failure there says which, where a
failure in a cross-chain test would only say "the message never arrived". The
round trip is deliberately asymmetric: INTO the private chain is written with
the stock devstack helpers and no resolution step anywhere, because the
initiating message is on an ordinary public chain and its identifier is an
ordinary receipt position; OUT of the private chain goes through the resolver,
and the test CHECKS the resolver by sending the message behind a log the export
policy drops, so the SentMessage sits at private index 1 and public index 0 and
an identifier that did not move is one the judge must reject. The assertions are
the whole answer rather than the fast one: the counterparty's CROSS-SAFE frontier
passing the block that executed the message, and the super-root at its timestamp
-- the range built, its claim landed, the rendering derived it, the message
database indexed the replayed SentMessage where the identifier said, and the
judge agreed.

op-up, interopsmoke: `op-up --private-interop --smoke` stands the pair up and checks it

The devstack option already exists and is already legal for this preset, so
hosting a private interop pair is one flag: the same `NewTwoL2SupernodeInterop`
call plus `WithPrivateInteropChain`, returning the same type, so
`runSupernodeSystem` is reused verbatim.

Two things op-up has to do that a test does not. It checks the environment
BEFORE building anything, because the preset skips on op-geth and op-up's
testing handle treats a skip as fatal -- so the operator would otherwise read a
message about a skip rather than about the `DEVSTACK_L2EL_KIND` that caused it,
and a missing op-reth binary is reported the same way, naming the variable that
fixes it. And it turns the standing rendering-invariant checker off: that checker
asserts at t.Cleanup, which for op-up is Ctrl-C, so a devnet stopped mid-range
would panic out of its own shutdown.

The pair activates INTEROP AT GENESIS, found by booting it. The pair's genesis is
generated by a contracts-bedrock dev feature that refuses to build with interop
activating later ("private interop private chain requires interop at genesis",
L2Genesis.s.sol), so op-up's two-second activation delay -- and the suggested
Lagoon offset that says the same thing through the deployer -- failed during
genesis generation, before any node started. The acceptance tests construct their
presets at delay zero for the same reason; op-up now does too, and the public
devnet keeps its delay.

The endpoint printout gains the pair's other half -- rendering EL and CL, the
private op-node's follow source, the operator address -- and, for both
topologies, the ELs' DIRECT URLs: the 8545/8546 endpoints are op-up's logging
proxy, which speaks one JSON-RPC object per request and cannot serve a client
that batches.

INTEROPSMOKE GAINS AN IN-PROCESS ENTRYPOINT. It was a CLI with its behaviour
inside the command actions, so the only way to run it was as a second process
against two URLs. `interopsmoke.Run(ctx, stderr, Config)` is now the whole of it
and the CLI is an adapter: one flag-reading function per subcommand, a named test
registry the subcommand names come from, and a plan that decides what a run is
called and whether it reports per-test results. Suite defaults moved from the
`all` action into the plan and are applied ONLY to a suite -- the caller with no
per-test flags to speak with -- so a single test is still handed its
configuration verbatim and `--blocks=0` still reaches the test that rejects it.

That door is what `op-up --smoke` uses, in-process once the devnet is up, exiting
with its result, against the ELs' own RPCs rather than op-up's proxy. In-process
is not a convenience: the private pair's identifier resolver is registered in the
process that BUILT the pair, in a process-global registry, so out of process
there is no resolver and the identifiers would be raw private positions -- some
legs would pass without ever exercising the naming. The CLI therefore refuses the
private-pair profile outright and names the in-process door.

The private-pair profile says which test each of three properties moves:

  - Messages initiated on the private chain are named by their positions on the
    RENDERING. valid-message gains the mirror leg -- initiated on the private
    chain, executed on the public counterparty -- which is the only leg that
    makes that naming load-bearing. It sends through the
    L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger, whose SentMessage the rendering republishes,
    because an EventLogger log is not public on a private chain: the export
    policy publishes the messenger's SentMessage and the inbox's
    ExecutingMessage and nothing else, so a log the rendering does not carry has
    no public position at all and its identifier stays an honest private receipt
    position the judge correctly rejects. As first written the mirror leg was a
    fabricated-import test wearing a valid-message name.
  - The private chain has no judge and its blocks are never replaced.
    invalid-message is held to the direction that can report the right thing,
    and chained-invalid-message -- whose cascade begins with chain B's block
    being replaced -- is refused outright.
  - The chain is custom gas token, so the ETH bridge path is closed on it:
    bridge skips, naming the NativeMintBridge path that is sanctioned and not
    yet exercised, and transfer keeps running and says what unit it moved.

Nothing is skipped silently. A test that cannot apply prints its reason where its
result would be and the run carries on; a test asked for BY NAME is refused with
the reason and reported as SKIP, because that skip is the whole result of that
run and reporting it as PASS claimed a check that never happened. The head and
balance waits are raised on both chains of a pair, because a leg that starts on
the private chain has no identifier until the rendering catches up and the
resolver bounds that wait at five minutes -- a sixty-second wait around it would
report the wrong failure.

docs(private-interop): DESIGN.md, the one design document

One document, ratified, describing the design that exists rather than the ones
it passed through. It records what the code cannot: why each decision is the way
it is, which alternatives were tried and retired, and what is deliberately not
built.

The sections that carry weight beyond the code:

  - Canonical message positions -- the standing invariant that RenderedLogs
    equals the derived rendering block's log sequence, which is why every
    component imports one implementation rather than restating it.
  - The claim-chain framing and the range claim -- leading placement,
    log-lessness, forward-gap contiguity, and the canonical-form decode rule
    that log-lessness makes load-bearing.
  - Operator topology, and Division of checks -- four components, every one of
    them a stock binary, which of them follows whose identity, and who is
    responsible for checking what.
  - Proven mode (v2, unbuilt) -- the ratified decisions only: the gate is an
    op-node derivation rule at the DATA SOURCE, verification is NATIVE rather
    than eth_call with the three costs that ruled eth_call out, the proof rides
    in the leading claim transaction, unproven-past-the-window collapses the
    range to deposit-only forever, and a mandatory kona twin.
  - Testing -- the plug-in thesis and the identifier seam, the preset entry
    points (WithPrivateInteropChain / DEVSTACK_PRIVATE_INTEROP), the
    `op-up --private-interop --smoke` one-command gate, what the two acceptance
    tests cover, the excluded-suite table with reasons, and the traps that still
    bite.

What it deliberately does not describe: the alt-DA era's permissioned inbox and
PIP1 commitment, the trailing envelope, the object store, the standalone
claim-follower sidecar and its withhold latch, and the rendering-view RPC
service. All were designed, some were built, and all were retired -- the code
carries none of them, and neither does this.

kona!: add a chain_id label to every metric, from an ambient scope

kona resolves every metric through the process-wide `metrics` recorder, so a
metric's chain is not knowable at the emit site. In a single-chain kona-node
that costs nothing. In a process that runs several chains it does: every
chain's series collapse into one.

Rather than pass the chain id to each of kona's ~320 emit sites, the new
`kona-metrics` crate carries it in an ambient scope and adds it as a label in
a wrapping `metrics::Recorder`. Every `counter!`/`gauge!`/`histogram!`
resolves its key through the recorder on every emit, and no kona emit site
hoists a handle, so the wrapper sees all of them. No emit site changes.

Four places bind a chain, because a `tokio::task_local` does not propagate
into a spawned task:

- `spawn_and_wait!`, which spawns all seven per-chain actors from one line.
- `Discv5Driver::start`, whose event loop is its own detached task.
- the jsonrpsee servers, through a `ChainScope` RPC middleware, because
  jsonrpsee serves each call on a task it spawns itself. Both the node's
  launcher and the `net` subcommand's server install it.
- the `net` subcommand's network actor, which it spawns directly.

`ChainLabelRecorder`'s fallback covers what no chain owns: the process
collector thread, the build-info gauge, and the start-up zero-fill. kona-node
serves one chain, so it passes that chain and every series is labelled. A
multi-chain process passes `None`, so a process-wide emit stays unlabelled
rather than claiming a chain it does not have.

The fallback comes from the resolved rollup config, not from `--chain`:
`node --l2-config-file` overrides the flag, and the actors scope themselves
with the chain from that file, so the recorder has to agree or a devnet gets
two chain ids in one process.

An emit that already carries a `chain_id` is passed through untouched, which
leaves an explicit label available to a component that serves several chains
from one task.

than `Result<(), BuildError>`, and `CliError` gains two variants. `CliError`
is `#[non_exhaustive]` now, so later variants are additive.

kona: make the pre-created metric series match what the code emits

`Metrics::zero()` pre-creates a series per expected label tuple so that
Prometheus exposes it before the first event. Nothing links that list to the
emit sites, and the two had drifted apart in both directions: series that no
code can ever produce sit at 0 forever beside the real ones, and emitted
series are missing until their first event, which is what `zero()` exists to
prevent.

Each label list is now derived from the emit sites, and expressed as a loop
over the emitted values rather than one call per series.

Corrected in `zero()`:

- `kona_node_dial_peer_error` pre-created one unlabelled series; all nine
  emits carry `type`. Three shipped dashboard panels select on that label.
- `kona_node_find_node_requests` pre-created one unlabelled series; the emit

derive: reserve Lagoon upgrade gas independently of the dependency set

A Lagoon activation block wraps the NUT bundle in setFeature(INTEROP) and
ETHLiquidity.fund() (150k gas) only when the chain has a multi-chain dependency
set. The gas was reserved conditionally to match, but the system config
reconstructed from the activation block must subtract the same amount again for
the next block — and that path sees only the rollup config and a timestamp,
never the dependency set. Each client hardcoded one branch and they picked
opposite ones: op-node always stripped the bundle-only amount, kona always
stripped bundle+150k. They disagreed by 150,000 gas in both configurations,
starting at the first block after activation.

Reserve the wrapper gas unconditionally. A single-chain activation carries it as
unused headroom in that one block; in exchange the amount no longer depends on
the dependency set, so both add and strip agree in both clients.

Only the tx set still varies with the dependency set.

Fixes #22166

which ends at the activation block. The upgrade-gas strip only takes effect when
the reconstructed system config is used to build the *next* block, so a gas leak
past the activation block could not fail this test.

UpgradeTransactions and UpgradeGas returned different numbers for Lagoon — the
bundle's own total versus the reservation that also covers the setFeature and

the system config reconstructed from the activation block would then subtract

deposits' own limits, since it also covers wrappers only a multi-chain
activation emits; that is the invariant, and it is now the only number either
getter can report.

The wrapper reservation is summed from the wrapper deposits themselves rather
than restated as a constant, in op-node and kona alike, so it cannot drift from
what they actually cost.

The activation block emitted both the fork's NUT bundle and the interop wrapper
deposits under one interop-activation check. IsInterop / is_interop_active is an
ephemeral development toggle (rollup/toggles.go, RollupConfig::is_interop_active);
flipping it off would have stopped the Lagoon bundle executing at all, including

two emit different activation blocks the moment the toggle is flipped.

equivalent until someone toggles interop off.

op-supernode: bound interop L1 consistency checks

The interop verification loop passed the activity context to SameL1Chain.
That context has no deadline, and LimitRPC acquires the shared L1 client's
semaphore with the caller's context, before the RPC client's own 10s call
timeout applies, so an unbounded call can queue on a saturated client until
the process exits. Interop verification then stops advancing and every
superroot_atTimestamp served off the same chain containers stalls with it.

Seen on develop in CircleCI job 5536079 (memory-all-opn-op-reth-fusaka,
container 3, 2026-09-02): from 21:20:35 the supernode's L1-facing work
stopped dead and the loop only unwound 15s later at shutdown with
"L1 consistency check: failed to fetch header by num 6: context canceled",
failing TestProposerIgnoresInvalidChallengedGame on the stalled super-root
RPC.

The check now runs under a per-round deadline, so a slow L1 fails that round
and the loop retries on its next tick.

kona-chainview: add a SQL chain view compiled by Feldera at build time

Adds `kona-chainview`, an incrementally maintained view of chain facts for
kona-node. The view is a SQL program (`src/chainview.sql`) compiled at build
time by upstream Feldera's `sql-to-dbsp` (v0.342.0, a sha256-pinned release
JAR that `build.rs` locates but never downloads) into an in-process `dbsp`
circuit that runs on its own thread. Actors push facts (inserts and
retractions) through typed input handles; the circuit maintains the views;
the host integrates per-step deltas into a snapshot and a bounded safe-head
history.

Tables: the L1 blocks the derivation pipeline traverses (one per height; a
block arriving at a held height with another hash replaces it, blocks below
finalized L1 are dropped), L1/L2 status rows, engine-confirmed derived L2
blocks paired with the L1 block they were derived from, and the unsafe-block
signer read at an L1 head. Views: canonical derived blocks, safe head per
derived-from L1 block, the next block to finalize (guarded to be above the
engine's finalized head and at or below its safe head), and the current
unsafe-block signer. A reorg is a retraction, never a reset.

Also pins the Feldera crates in the workspace, adds `just chainview-*`
recipes (fetch and verify the compiler JAR, doctor, smoke, check, test; the
pin is read from build.rs on demand), and ships circuit-level tests for
finality, L1 reorg replacement, pipeline reset retraction,
nearest-at-or-below lookup, signer rotation and rollback, finalized pruning,
and LATENESS handling.

kona-node: serve finality, sync status and safeHeadAtL1Block from the chain view

The chain view replaces, rather than shadows, the paths it supersedes, and
its L1 facts come from the derivation pipeline's own traversal:

- The derivation actor pushes every L1 origin its pipeline advances through
  (including the heights it re-walks after a reset), pairs each
  engine-confirmed safe head with the pending attributes' derived-from
  block, retracts derived blocks above the safe head (and at its height with
  another hash) on `Signal::Reset`, and finalizes by hash when the view's
  `finalized_l2` names a new block at or below the confirmed safe head with
  the safe head's hash at that height. `L2Finalizer`, the finalized-L1
  request to derivation, and finalize-by-number are removed. Reorgs need no
  code of their own: a block that arrives at a held height with another
  hash replaces it.
- A `ChainViewActor` mirrors the L1 tags the watcher publishes and the
  engine's heads into the circuit, reads the unsafe-block signer from the
  SystemConfig contract at every new L1 head (one storage read per head,
  replacing the watcher's head-only log scan that lost rotations in skipped
  blocks), forwards the derived signer to the network actor, and turns the
  circuit thread's exit into an actor error.
- The L1 watcher only polls the head, safe and finalized tags, publishes
  them on watch channels, and fans heads out to derivation. Its per-chain
  signer scan and its three-RPC `L1State` query are removed, along with the
  provider it needed for them.
- `RollupRpc` serves `optimism_syncStatus` L1 fields from the snapshot with
  no L1 RPC on the request path, and implements
  `optimism_safeHeadAtL1Block` with op-node SafeDB semantics (nearest entry
  at or below; "not found" wording the Go client maps to safedb.ErrNotFound).
- The node refuses to start for a chain whose `seq_window_size +
  channel_timeout` reaches the circuit's LATENESS. No new flags.

fix(op-challenger): record a stuck VM run as a timeout, not a setup failure

The VM timeout is enforced by cancelling the run's context, which kills the
VM's process group. exec then reports an *exec.ExitError ("signal: killed")
and Cmd.Wait discards the context error, so the `errors.Is(err,
context.DeadlineExceeded)` check in runOnce never matched. A stuck run fell
through to the catch-all branch in recordError and was counted as a setup
failure instead of a VM failure.

That matters for alerting: challenger-runner-vm-failure fires on any increase
in vm_failures_total, while challenger-runner-setup-failure needs more than 10
consecutive failures sustained for 30m. With the default 3h VM timeout, a
permanently stuck runner takes well over a day to page anyone.

Classify on the context's deadline state rather than the returned error's
identity, and apply the same check to trace provider creation so a hang while
fetching the prestate is also reported as a timeout.

The existing test passed only because its stub returned ctx.Err() directly,
which no real provider does; it now returns the error a killed VM produces.

test(kona): prove proof transitions with the interop client program

The kona-client single-chain variant is going away after U20, and it cannot
prove a Lagoon span at all: its pipeline is built without a DependencySet,
which StatefulAttributesBuilder needs to decide whether an activation block
carries the multi-chain wrapper deposits. Move the action-test suite in
rust/kona/tests/proofs onto `kona-host super` (the interop client program),
which works pre-Lagoon too — the exec-message verification step is a no-op.

The switch is contained in the helpers, so no test had to change how it asks
for a proof:

  - WithSuperDefaults builds the interop inputs for the transition into
    l2ClaimBlockNum: the agreed prestate is the single-chain super root at
    claimTimestamp-1 (which resolves to block l2ClaimBlockNum-1, since
    TargetBlockNumber rounds down), and the claim is the commitment to the
    transition state after step 0 appended the claimed block. A super-root
    sub-transition advances the active chain by exactly one L2 block, so this
    is the same granularity RunFaultProofProgram already had.
  - RunKonaSuperNative drives `kona-host super --native` and synthesizes the
    one-chain dependency set from the rollup configs, matching the set
    NewL2FaultProofEnv hands the sequencer so op-node and kona agree on the
    activation block's contents.
  - No supernode is needed: InteropHost derives everything from the L1, beacon
    and L2 endpoints the suite already provides.

Two tests encoded single-chain-only semantics and are deleted rather than
ported. Their interop analogues already exist in op-acceptance-tests'
superfaultproofs suite:

  - end_of_source_test.go (honest actor repeats the safe-head output root when
    the data source is exhausted) -> ChainReachesL1Head and
    SuperRootInvalidIfUnsupportedByL1Data
  - trace_extension_test.go (claim maliciously repeats the agreed root) ->
    ChainOptimisticBlock-InvalidNoChange

Under interop that behaviour is the InvalidTransition cascade, not root
repetition, so there is nothing to translate one-to-one.

RunFaultProofProgramFromGenesis now starts at genesis+1: the program proves
the advance between two consecutive super-root timestamps, and there is no
super root before the L2 genesis timestamp.

The kona-sp1 range guest still runs on the single-chain path
(WithPreInteropDefaults is kept for it). Migrating it needs the action-test
verifier's superroot_atTimestamp API exposed over HTTP so the super-range
executor can reach it; left as a follow-up.

single-chain client, so move the last action test off the range guest.

and drives kona-sp1-super-range-executor over the same 0 -> 1 transition,
exercising both the range and the consolidation mode of the super-range
guest.

The executor is not handed an agreed pre-state and a claim: it resolves
both from superroot_atTimestamp and collects its own witnesses. So the
harness serves op-node's superroot API over a loopback HTTP listener
(L2Verifier.StartSuperRootHTTPRPC) and passes it as --supernode-address --

answers with a one-chain response, which is what the action-test chain is.

no claim to pass in, and a witness that would fail host-side if collected
against a bad one, corruption has to happen inside the executor. Add
--corrupt-claimed-root there, mirroring the single-chain range executor: it
flips a bit in the claimed optimistic output root after witness collection,
so the guest re-derives the real root and aborts. If the guest instead runs
the tampered claim to completion and agrees with the honest outputs, the
executor exits 2 rather than reporting the claim valid.

helpers' RunKonaNative and RunRangeExecutor, rustbin.RunKonaSP1Range, and

The consolidation step dispatched purely on the transition state's step

trie through the preimage oracle even when the Lagoon hardfork was not

kona-node-service: don't let a signer failure kill the node

`NetworkActor::step` propagated every block-signing error, which `NodeActor`
defines as fatal. `spawn_and_wait!`'s drop guard then cancels the umbrella
token and the supervisor tears down derivation, the engine and the RPC with it,
so one transient error on the signing endpoint took the whole node down. The
sibling failure paths in the same arm, a missing signer and a failed publish,
were already handled gracefully.

Transient signing failures are now warned, counted and dropped. The call also
carries a deadline, so a signer connection that hangs rather than errors no
longer wedges the actor until TCP gives up.

One failure stays fatal, deliberately. `RemoteSignerError::InvalidAddress`
means the configured signer is not the chain's unsafe block signer, so this
node cannot produce a block any peer will accept, and no retry fixes it.
Nothing else stops it sequencing: the sequencer canonicalises the block and
commits it to the conductor before the payload reaches this actor, so the
unsafe head keeps advancing and conductor health checks keep passing while
nothing is ever published. `NetworkActorError::FailedToSignPayload` is kept for
exactly that case, so this change is not breaking.

- Warn, count and drop on a transient signer failure; keep stepping.
- Bound the signing call at 10s, at the call site rather than on the HTTP
  client, so the signer's lock acquisition is covered too. Generous against
  real signer latency: it exists for the hang, not the delay.
- Add `kona_node_block_signing_errors`, labelled
  `kind=timeout|signer_error|signer_mismatch`, pre-registered at zero per kind.
  The kind is on the log line too, so log-based alerting can match the label
  rather than parse the message.
- Add a network actor test fixture: a mock op-signer at the JSON-RPC boundary,
  with the handler assembled from an unstarted swarm so no port is bound.

`a_signer_error_is_not_fatal` fails on the parent commit with the reported
symptom. `a_signer_address_mismatch_is_fatal` fails if the mismatch is folded
back in with the transient failures, and `signing_is_bounded_by_the_deadline`
asserts the call waited the full deadline rather than merely returning.

The supervisor teardown chain above was established by reading
`spawn_and_wait!`, not by exercising it. Since an `Err` from `step()` is what
makes the task exit and drop its guard, asserting on the step's return is the
actor's half of that claim, and is what the tests assert.

Operators should alert on `kind=signer_mismatch`; it fires at most once per
process, immediately before the node exits.

This bounds the swarm starvation at 10s rather than fixing it. Getting the
await out of the select loop follows separately.

the discriminator for "this genesis is the private half". A private chain

release, or one already projected. Which chain is private is explicit

contracts-bedrock: pin the compile-time EVM version to cancun

Amsterdam changes execution semantics, not the bytecode our contracts emit, but
forge derives both the solc target and the EVM executor from a single
`evm_version`. Running the L1 half of the suite with `--evm-version amsterdam`
therefore recompiled the whole tree against a target no contract needs: solc
clamps 0.8.15 to london and 0.8.25 to cancun regardless, and only the 0.8.31
floating-pragma files could go higher.

Pin `evm_version = 'cancun'` in every compiler profile and compilation
restriction so the requested EVM version drives the executor alone. Each
optimizer tier gains a cancun-pinned variant and a catch-all covers everything
outside the tiers, since a restriction must be satisfied by a profile matching
all of its constraints.

semver-lock is unchanged: initCodeHash is identical for every contract.

op-e2e/actions: emulate EL-sync p2p for the reth backend

The EL-sync tests rely on the sequencer and verifier engines peering over
devp2p so the verifier snap-syncs the chain from a single unsafe head. The
ephemeral reth engines are out-of-process subprocesses with no networking,
so Enode/AddPeers/PeerCount panicked 'not yet wired'.

Wire them against an in-process stand-in: a registry resolves a synthetic
enode back to the reth engine it identifies, peering is symmetric so both
PeerCount reads pass, and each peering starts a sync pump. The pump watches
optest_syncTarget (the head a forkchoice update reported SYNCING for) and,
while one is set, backfills the missing blocks from the peer engine one
validated optest_importBlock at a time — never moving safe/finalized, which
reproduces exactly the state op-geth reaches after backfilling under a
SYNCING forkchoice. It activates only once the engine has actually reported
SYNCING (which op-node triggers only during genuine EL sync, not for a
CL-mode gapped payload), so it fires exactly when a real EL would snap-sync.

The 'Forkchoice requested sync to new head' log the tests assert on is
emitted synchronously by the geth engine API inside forkchoiceUpdated, so
an async pump log would race the assertion. elSyncLogRPC wraps op-node's
engine RPC and reproduces it in op-node's own call path: it caches each
newPayload's block number and logs on a SYNCING forkchoice update to a head
it has seen.

complete execution payload into a committed canonical block, plus attrs-less

write: execute against the parent overlay, verify the post-state root, build an

engine API's gas-limit and force-empty semantics), and get_payload seals it into
OpExecutionData that round-trips back through new_payload.

reth's block builder ties the executor, EVM state, and parent to a single
borrowed lifetime, so it can't be parked across calls; the in-flight payload
instead keeps the ordered tx list and re-runs a deterministic one-shot assembly
on demand.

Tests drive the full sequencer flow (FCU+attrs -> include_tx -> get_payload ->
new_payload -> FCU) into a valid two-block chain, plus gas-limit rejection,
force-empty skipping, and remaining-gas accounting.

op-interop-mon: propagate the caller's context into job updates

RPCUpdater.Run takes a context and starts from Start(ctx), but the receipts
fetch it ultimately performs ignored it:

    func (t *RPCUpdater) UpdateJobStatus(job *Job) {
        blockInfo, receipts, err := t.client.FetchReceiptsByNumber(context.Background(), ...)

Nothing between Run and that call carried the context: processJobs, UpdateJob
and UpdateJobStatus all took no ctx, so the one Run was handed was dropped and a
fresh background context substituted at the RPC boundary.

The fetch is therefore uncancellable. That matters because processJobs runs
inline in Run's select loop, not in its own goroutine:

    case <-processTicker.C:
        t.processJobs()

so a fetch that hangs against an unresponsive L2 RPC blocks Run from ever
reaching its <-t.closed case. Stop() closes that channel and returns nil
immediately, so shutdown reports success while the updater goroutine is still
parked in a fetch that nothing can interrupt.

RPCFinder, the sibling component in this package, already does this correctly.
It has the same shape -- Start(ctx) -> go Run(ctx), a ticker loop selecting on
t.closed -- and threads the context into the identical client call:

    blockInfo, receipts, err := t.client.FetchReceiptsByNumber(ctx, t.next)

Both are constructed over the same *sources.EthClient in service.go, so the two
components behaved differently against the same connection.

Thread the context Run already has down through processJobs, UpdateJob and
UpdateJobStatus to the fetch, matching RPCFinder. No behaviour changes on the
success path; a cancelled context now aborts the fetch instead of being ignored.

UpdateJob and UpdateJobStatus are exported, so their signatures change. They are
not part of the Updater interface and have no callers outside this file and its
test, so nothing else in the tree is affected -- flagging it in case that
surface is considered load-bearing.

Tests: TestUpdaterPropagatesContext fetches with an already-cancelled context
and asserts the client observes context.Canceled. It fails against the
unmodified UpdateJobStatus and passes with the change.

op-node: dedupe, discard and retry in the async gossiper

Addresses review feedback on #22585.

Dedupe re-sealed blocks. Get() no longer waits for an in-flight publish, so
the sequencer re-seals its build job and hands the identical block over again,
once per retry, while an insert keeps failing temporarily. The epoch counter
treated each of those as a new block: it queued a duplicate and invalidated the
copy already being sent, so Get() kept returning nil and the sequencer kept
re-sealing, filling the queue with copies of one block. The queue is now keyed
on block hash, and a block already queued or in flight is not queued again.

Add Discard(hash) and DiscardAll(). Clear() is called both when a block is
successfully inserted, where the queue must keep publishing, and when a block
is rejected, where it must not - with a queue those cases are no longer
indistinguishable. Clear() now means only "drop the reuse buffer"; Discard(hash)
drops one rejected block from the queue and suppresses its retry and reuse; and
DiscardAll() drops everything when the sequencer abandons the chain the queued
blocks extend, on a derivation reset or a start from an unknown pre-state. A
publish already in flight cannot be recalled, but it is not retried and its
result is not stored.

Retry a failed publish ahead of the blocks behind it, bounded by
maxPublishAttempts. Dropping a failed block and carrying on with its
descendants leaves peers a gap they cannot follow the chain past - the same
reason blocks go out in seal order rather than skipping to the tip.

Update the queue gauge under the same lock as the queue mutation, in enqueue
and dequeue, so the reported depth cannot be reordered against the queue it
describes. Narrow the dropped_publishes help text to queue overflow, which is
the only thing that increments it; publish failures are counted by
publishing_errors.

Tests: TestAsyncGossiperDedupesResealedBlock, TestAsyncGossiperRetriesFailedPublish
and TestAsyncGossiperGivesUpOnFailedPublish all fail on the previous revision
with the reported symptoms, and pass here. TestAsyncGossiperDiscardDropsQueuedBlock,
TestAsyncGossiperClearKeepsQueue, TestAsyncGossiperDiscardInFlightBlock and
TestAsyncGossiperDiscardAll cover the new API, and the sequencer tests pin that a
rejection discards by hash while a temporary error and a successful insert do not.

op-node: dedupe, discard and retry in the async gossiper

op-node: pin the PM-44 invariant in the sequencer's gossip handling

PM-44 (Mainnet Unsafe Head Stall, 2024-02-15, ~49 minutes) was caused by this
exact feature: the async-gossip buffer and the sequencer's building state
disagreed, the sequencer took a code path that depended on the state that had
been cleared, and it looped emitting errors without producing a block. Each
recovery also reorged, because a gossiped block was lost on restart and a
different block was built at that height.

This PR reopens the same surface from the other side. Get() no longer waits for
an in-flight publish, so it returns nil while building state IS set - the same
disagreement, opposite polarity. TestSequencerProgressesWhilePublishInFlight
pins that the sequencer falls through to re-sealing and makes progress rather
than spinning, and that re-sealing yields the same block, so peers are never
offered two blocks at one height.

TestSequencerResetClearsGossipAndBuilding pins the invariant the incident turned
on: gossip state and building state are cleared together. onReset was already
asymmetric before this PR - it cleared building but never touched the gossip
buffer - so a payload from the pre-reset chain could survive a reset. The queue
would have widened that from one block to maxPublishQueue, and DiscardAll on
onReset closes both.

op-node: pin the PM-44 invariant in the sequencer's gossip handling

op-node: bound publish retries by queue pressure, not an attempt count

maxPublishAttempts = 2 was an arbitrary number doing a job the queue already
does better. A retried block sits at queue[0], and enqueue evicts queue[0] on
overflow, so queue pressure already decides how long a failing head is worth
holding - and it scales with block production instead of being a fixed count.

It also had a real defect: a signer outage lasting 30-60s made the gossiper give
up on a block after ~20s and move on to its descendants, creating precisely the
gossip gap that in-order publishing and retry exist to prevent.

Retries now need pacing, for a reason that was not obvious. Topic.Publish runs
op-node's own block validator inline and synchronously on the publishing node
(ValidateLocal -> validate(local=true); go-libp2p-pubsub validation.go:337), so a
publish can fail in about a millisecond with no I/O at all - and gossip.go:356
rejects a payload older than the gossip timestamp threshold, on our own publish.
A block retried long enough therefore ages into permanent local rejection.
Measured unpaced: 257,261 publish attempts in 500ms. Hence retryInterval, which
is a spin guard rather than a policy knob.

The wake-up for the rest of the queue moved from before the network call to
after it. A signal queued up front would have been consumed immediately after a
requeue, skipping the pacing in exactly the sustained-outage case it is for.

An attempt backstop remains, set to maxPublishQueue rather than a new constant,
for the case queue pressure cannot reach: with production stopped nothing is ever
enqueued, so nothing evicts the head, and an unpublishable block would be offered
and logged once per interval until the process exits.

Also fixes a Stop hang found in review, on the seal-time ErrStaleBuild path: that
branch drops a block that a previous action already sealed and gossiped, but did
not reconcile lastSealed, which Stop waits on. Pre-existing, but newly reachable
because Get no longer waits for the publish, making re-seal the normal retry.
TestSequencerStopAfterStaleReSealDropsSealed fails on the previous revision with
"context deadline exceeded".

Amsterdam changes execution semantics, not the bytecode our contracts emit, but
forge derives both the solc target and the EVM executor from a single
`evm_version`. Running the L1 half of the suite with `--evm-version amsterdam`
therefore recompiled the whole tree against a target no contract needs: solc
clamps 0.8.15 to london and 0.8.25 to cancun regardless, and only the 0.8.31
floating-pragma files could go higher.

restriction so the requested EVM version drives the executor alone. Each
optimizer tier gains a cancun-pinned variant and a catch-all covers everything
outside the tiers, since a restriction must be satisfied by a profile matching
all of its constraints.

semver-lock is unchanged: initCodeHash is identical for every contract.

release-notes: sharpen triage tags, drop semver framing, restructure sections

Changes derived from writing the op-node/v1.19.6 and op-reth/v2.4.3 notes.

House style:
- The Overview classifies the release as optional / recommended / strongly
  recommended / required, never as a semver release type — our tags are not
  strict semver, so "minor release" carries no information. Callout type now
  follows the recommendation: NOTE / IMPORTANT / CAUTION.
- New `## Chain Configuration` section after `## Breaking changes` for a release
  that moves a chain's embedded config, with the World Chain Karst activation
  entry as the worked example. It stands alone because a registry pin bump
  frequently ships without a breaking change.
- `## What's Changed` becomes `## Other changes` — the two sections above it are
  also changes, and the old heading was git-cliff's, not ours. Its catch-all
  subheading becomes `### Miscellaneous` to avoid Other inside Other.
- Derivation changes get their own `### Derivation` heading, listed first.
- A change with no user-visible impact is cut outright, not demoted to a
  catch-all. Importability of the monorepo as a Go module is not user impact:
  we do not maintain releases of it as a Go module.
- A change confined to an unreleased feature is cut entirely, rather than
  getting a `(not yet in production)` heading and an Overview note. It keeps its
  place in the note for the release that activates the feature. The test is
  whether the change reaches a live path, not what motivated it.

pr-facts.sh, all three from rows it got wrong on this release train:
- A superchain-registry pin bump now tags CONFIG instead of `--`. Its diff is a
  submodule gitlink plus a generated-archive checksum, so no source file changes
  and nothing resolves as linked — yet a new activation time is routinely the
  most consequential change in the release.
- A manifest change tags DEPS whenever no compiled package moved, not only when
  the manifests are the sole changed files. One unrelated file alongside a
  lockfile bump used to demote the row to `--`, which claims the binary compiles
  nothing that changed — it hid a hickory-resolver advisory fix for op-reth.
- Rust linkage counts only src/, build.rs and Cargo.toml under a crate
  directory, so a script or README beside the crate no longer reads as LINKED.

Procedure:
- Ask whether to finalize an RC with `just release` before writing notes against
  an RC tag.
- `just release-notes` needs `mise exec --`; git-cliff is mise-pinned and the
  failure names neither git-cliff nor mise.

op-reth: bound the flashblocks websocket, drop superseded pending blocks

A flashblocks upstream that stops sending without closing its connection left
`WsFlashBlockStream::poll_next` parked in `Poll::Pending` forever: the read
registered no timer, so nothing ever woke the task again. Six op-reth nodes on
OP Mainnet served a frozen `pending` block that way, the longest for 16 days,
while importing canonical blocks normally, logging nothing and moving no metric.

Two independent bounds, either of which alone contains the failure:

- The stream arms an idle deadline before any poll that can return `Pending`,
  covering the websocket read, the queued-pong flush and the connect handshake.
  On expiry it drops both halves of the connection and yields an error, so the
  existing reconnect path runs and the stall is logged and counted through the
  new `flashblock_service_stream_errors` metric. Configurable via
  `--flashblocks-idle-timeout`, default 5s, `0` disables.

- `pending` reads no longer answer from a flashblock whose height the canonical
  chain has already reached. That is what made the freeze harmful: archive nodes
  returned an `eth_getTransactionCount(addr, "pending")` below the same call
  against `latest` -- not a legal result, and enough to build a transaction on
  an already-consumed nonce -- while pruned nodes failed with `state at block #N
  is pruned`.

The second guard tests against the canonical tip rather than the flashblock's
age. An age-based expiry re-introduces the same defect in a smaller window: a
flashblock that is merely old but still ahead of the tip is the best answer
available, and discarding it lowers a nonce that `pending` had already reported.

`just release` has been unusable since #20611. The recipe asserts that
the hardcoded ALL_SUBDIRS list equals every subdir under rust/ that
cargo metadata reports, but three workspace members joined later

into the skip list in place of the `grep -vx op-reth` filter, which hid
the same intent.

subdir still has to be classified deliberately, while a stale entry is
harmless: its package list comes out empty and the release skips it.

docs(superchain-upgrades): disallow simultaneous upgrade activations

Two network upgrades activating in the same block is not a supported
configuration: each upgrade's activation-block behavior is only defined
against a chain where all prior upgrades are active and no later one is,
so overlapping activations would require specifying every combination of
upgrades that could activate together.

The restriction was implicit until now. Spell it out as a general
activation rule rather than in each fork's own specification.

Holocene and Isthmus in the same block. Their history cannot be changed,
so state that the rule applies to newly scheduled activations.

fix(op-node): reject simultaneous fork activations after genesis

Config.Check hand-rolled a checkFork chain that stopped at Isthmus and
explicitly permitted two forks sharing an activation time. Drive the
check off forks.All instead, so Jovian, Karst, Lagoon and every future
fork are ordered too, and reject two forks activating at the same
timestamp after genesis.

Simultaneous activation is unsupported: each fork's activation-block
behavior is only defined against a chain where every earlier fork is
already active, which is how ethereum-optimism/optimism#22828 slipped
through. Forks that activate at or before genesis all activate in the
genesis block, so they may keep sharing a timestamp.

Enforcement starts at Jovian. Six registered chains already share a
post-genesis activation timestamp — Celo mainnet activated Holocene and
Isthmus in the same block, and five Sepolia chains did the same for
earlier pairs — and op-node must keep syncing them.

Also document the rule in the network upgrades page.
