op-node: retain the sealed block, and stop retrying what cannot publish

Addresses bitwiseguy's review on #22585. Five findings, all confirmed against
the code; four were correctness bugs. Net -35 lines.

Retain the committed envelope instead of re-sealing. building.Ref is set only
after CommitUnsafePayload and Gossip, so once it is non-zero the conductor
quorum has already committed that block. Recovery re-sealed the job, which
staked it on the engine still holding the payload - and ErrSealExpired then
routed to handleInvalid, discarding a committed block and rebuilding at the
same height. This was a regression from making Get() non-blocking: before, that
state always took the insert-only path. BuildingState now carries the envelope
and the retry re-inserts exactly it.

That removes the reason the gossiper held a block at all. Get, Clear, the reuse
buffer and the wanted-hash tracking are gone, along with the toBlockRef hook and
its failure branch; the interface is Gossip/Discard/DiscardAll/Stop/Start. It
also makes the seal-time ErrStaleBuild discard added earlier unreachable - a job
that produced a block is now retried, never re-sealed - so that goes too.

Discard on two more abandon paths. onForkchoiceUpdate adopting a competing head,
and StopSequencer wiping the building state, both dropped a block that had been
committed and gossiped without discarding it or reconciling lastSealed: it could
still publish as a sibling of the branch everyone else is on, and Stop could wait
for it until the context expired.

forceStart discards unconditionally. The old check read the reuse buffer, so it
could not see queued or in-flight payloads - which are exactly the ones that
would still go out. Reconciling against lastSealed does not work either, since
Stop overwrites it. Dropping the backlog can lose a canonical block, which costs
gossip only; publishing one from an abandoned branch does not.

Classify permanent publish failures. Deferring this was wrong: with a full queue
spanning ~64s against a 60s threshold, every head is already too old, the
requeued head is exactly what the next arrival evicts, so each block gets one
attempt and the attempt bound never fires. Nothing drains, so the queue stays
full - an absorbing state entered by a merely transient ~64s outage, leaving
gossip dead until restart. async.ErrPermanentPublish is wrapped in p2p and node
and matched with errors.Is, as an allowlist: Topic.Publish also surfaces the
caller's context error, and a timed-out publish must stay retryable.

Close the shutdown window. OpNode.Stop closed p2p and the signer before
Driver.Close, which is the only thing that stops the publisher. With Clear no
longer waiting, a publish can be in flight - plus up to 32 queued - when
StopSequencer returns. p2p and the signer now close after the driver.

Also from review: dropped_publishes now counts every block that never reaches
peers, not only queue overflow, since giving up is indistinguishable from a
retried failure on publishing_errors alone; handleInvalid's discard parameter
was unreachable at every call site; and the attempt-bound comment claimed an
equivalence to queue pressure that the constants do not support.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
op-node: retain the sealed block, and stop retrying what cannot publish

op-node: keep a block that is still ahead of the clock retryable

The one validator rejection a retry actually fixes. Everything else the
inline validator rejects is a function of the envelope and the config, and
the staleness threshold only moves further out of reach, because a retry
makes a block older, never younger - but a block ahead of the local clock
validates once the clock catches up.

Reaching it needs the clock to have stepped backwards: block timestamps are
chain-derived, sealing happens 50ms before payloadTime, and the sequencer
waits rather than sealing early. A steady lag does not do it, since the
scheduler and the validator run in the same process off the same clock.
Classifying it permanent would nonetheless turn such a step into sustained
gossip loss rather than a few seconds of it.

The 5s allowance is now a named constant shared with the validator, and the
publisher judges it against the same clock, so the two cannot drift apart.

op-devstack: make the conductor preset produce one canonical chain

The MinimalWithConductors preset came up as a cluster whose chain never
advanced past genesis, which went unnoticed while the only conductor
acceptance test asserted Raft state alone (#21902). It could also start
from divergent unsafe forks because all three sequencers ran before the
Raft cluster and p2p mesh existed.

Make the preset a deterministic live HA cluster:

- Start every sequencer stopped, seed sequencing on the bootstrap node,
  then freeze the seeded head and require every follower to reach that
  exact head before conductor control loops resume. This both initializes
  the fresh Raft FSM and prevents failover to an incompatible follower.
- Mesh the nodes over CL p2p only. EL peering is unnecessary because unsafe
  blocks reach follower ELs through CL gossip and the engine API, and it is
  flaky against op-reth subprocesses (#18570). Register the same CL mesh
  with the frontend lifecycle so tests that restart nodes restore it.

kona-sp1: embed the build commit in the guest ELFs

Given a super-range or super-aggregation ELF and nothing else, there was no way
to tell which monorepo commit produced it. The new kona-sp1-build-info crate
resolves the commit at build time and both guests carry it as a single .rodata
literal, so it can be read straight out of the artifact:

  grep -aoE 'KONA_SP1_BUILD\{git_sha=[^}]*\}' elf/super-aggregation-elf

Both guests also print the marker at startup, which surfaces wherever the
executor runs it locally; on the Succinct network guest output goes to the
remote prover, so the ELF scan is the path that always works.

The commit reaches the compiler on two channels because cargo prove build
--docker forwards neither the host environment nor .git: an environment
variable natively, and a --cfg rustflag under Docker. That mirrors how
kona_custom_configs_dir already reaches kona-registry. Native builds keep the
env channel so a new commit rebuilds only build-info and the two guests rather
than invalidating the whole graph through RUSTFLAGS.

The marker is part of the compiled image, so it is part of the vkey. Two builds
from different commits now produce different vkeys even when the program logic
is identical, and because super-aggregation embeds SUPER_RANGE_VKEY, a range
prover and an aggregator must come from the same commit rather than merely the
same code. The proposer fetches guest ELFs from PRESTATES_URL keyed by vkey, so
every merge produces a new prestate pair that has to be published before a game
bearing it can be defended. Nothing pins a vkey today - elf/ and vkeys.toml are
gitignored and every consumer reads them dynamically - but the plan to pin
per-version vkeys into standard-prestates.toml inherits per-commit churn.

The marker is recoverable, not attested: it records what an honest build
embedded and proves nothing against a rewritten artifact. Binding it
cryptographically is the same mechanism, so that option stays open.

The commit is resolved once per build and inherited by both guests, carrying
-dirty when tracked files are modified and -custom for a KONA_CUSTOM_CONFIGS_DIR
build, whose guest is compiled from configs the commit does not describe. Each
build recipe verifies its own ELF after cargo prove build, so every path is
covered rather than only the one CI exercises; CI additionally pins the natively
built ELFs to the commit under test. vkeys.toml records the commit alongside the
toolchain tag, since it now determines every hash in that file.

Verified by building the real zkVM ELFs and reading the marker back out of them,
including the two-channel injection and the negative cases (missing literal,
unknown fallback) that the checks must reject.

kona-sp1: harden the guest build marker checks

Two review findings on the build-commit marker.

The documented KONA_SP1_GIT_SHA override bypassed _git-sha, so setting it alongside
KONA_CUSTOM_CONFIGS_DIR dropped the -custom suffix and skipped the -dirty check, and the
ELF and manifest checks compared against the overridden value and accepted the misleading
marker. Nothing set the override, so it is removed rather than taught the suffix rules;
build-elfs and build-elfs-native always resolve through _git-sha. The variable remains as
the internal transport between the recipes and build.rs.

The scanners took the first match of a permissive pattern, so an ELF carrying the expected
marker followed by a conflicting one passed, and the pattern could capture control bytes
that the README command would print to a terminal. They now collect every match, sort -u,
and require exactly one distinct marker, over a character class that excludes control
bytes. Kept permissive enough that a marker reading `unknown` still reports as `unknown`
rather than as an empty match.

op-node: leave the shutdown ordering alone, and record why

Reverts the shutdown reordering from the last two commits. Both attempts at
"stop the publisher before the dependencies it uses" broke something, each in
a different job:

  - closing p2p after Driver.Close also put it after resourcesClose, which
    cancels the context the pubsub instance was built on, so Topic.Close
    returned that cancellation. Broke TestSequencerFailover_ActiveSequencerDown.
  - closing the driver early left the rest of the node running against a
    cancelled driver context, which spun the derivation system resetting and
    buried the acceptance-test job in >50MB of logs. Broke
    memory-all-opn-op-reth-fusaka, which had passed on the commit before.

The ordering is now identical to develop again. The residual issue is real but
unchanged from today: a publish in flight, or one queued behind it, can run
against a closed topic and a closed signer at shutdown and log an error on the
way out. Fixing it properly means stopping just the publisher, ahead of both,
which needs a hook that does not exist yet - so it is a follow-up rather than
something to keep destabilising this PR with. The reasoning is recorded in a
comment at the call site so the next person does not retry either ordering.

fix(viem): unbreak the interop relay tests against supersim alpha.60

Two separate causes, both surfaced by the supersim bump.

relayMessage now reverts with CrossL2Inbox_NoExecutingDeposits (0xdc9f4daa)
when estimating or simulating. CrossL2Inbox rejects the call if tx.gasprice is
0 while basefee is not, to stop deposits executing messages, and both default
the price to 0. The write path was unaffected because the wallet client fills a
real price, which is why only two of the three tests failed.

simulateRelayCrossDomainMessage could not be given a price at all: it read only
account, id, payload and accessList and dropped the rest, unlike its estimate
counterpart which spreads them. That is a bug for consumers, not just tests, so
it now spreads too and carries a changeset.

The simulate test also asserted with expect(() => promise).not.throw(), which
never awaits, so it passed regardless and leaked the rejection as one of the
unhandled errors in CI. It now awaits and checks the result.

sendSuperchainERC20 is skipped rather than fixed. It drives sendERC20 on the
SuperchainTokenBridge predeploy, removed in ethereum-optimism/optimism#19999.
Verified on a running alpha.60 chain: the proxy is still in genesis at 2059
bytes but its implementation at 0xc0D3C0d3...0028 is empty, hence "Proxy:
implementation not initialized". Nothing replaced the bridge, so these cannot
pass. The action remains public API on both viem and wagmi, so whether to
deprecate it is a separate decision.

Full viem suite: 23 passed, 3 skipped, no unhandled errors.

Two independent apt dependencies in CI, both of which fail the job when an
Ubuntu mirror is unreachable — as happened during Canonical's archive.ubuntu.com
outage.

`todo-issues` apt-installed ripgrep on every run. mise already manages ~40
tools for this repo from GitHub releases, with a warm cache in CI, and ripgrep
is in the registry (aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep) — so pin it there and drop the
step. ops/scripts/todo-checker.sh only needs `rg` on PATH, which mise now
supplies.

apt-install.sh deliberately rewrites the machine image's single-region EC2
mirror to archive.ubuntu.com, on the reasoning that geo-routing and redundancy
are better handled by Cloudflare anycast than by one set of AWS hosts. That
still holds, but it leaves the CDN as a single point of failure: when Canonical
had an outage, every job installing a package went down with it. Keep a copy of
the lists as the image shipped them and, if apt fails against the CDN, restore
them and retry once — the EC2 mirror is usually still serving. A marker file
keeps later calls in the same job from rewriting back onto a CDN already known
to be failing.

The remaining apt packages (zstd, clang/llvm-dev/libclang-dev, eatmydata) have
no GitHub-release or mise path, so they still need apt or a prebuilt image.

contracts-bedrock: pin the compile-time EVM version to cancun

Amsterdam changes execution semantics, not the bytecode our contracts emit, but
forge derives both the solc target and the EVM executor from a single
`evm_version`. Running the L1 half of the suite with `--evm-version amsterdam`
therefore recompiled the whole tree against a target no contract needs: solc
clamps 0.8.15 to london and 0.8.25 to cancun regardless, and only the 0.8.31
floating-pragma files could go higher.

Pin `evm_version = 'cancun'` in every compiler profile and compilation
restriction so the requested EVM version drives the executor alone. Each
optimizer tier gains a cancun-pinned variant and a catch-all covers everything
outside the tiers, since a restriction must be satisfied by a profile matching
all of its constraints.

The amsterdam pass now reuses the cancun artifacts instead of rebuilding, and
semver-lock is unchanged: initCodeHash is identical for every contract.

fix(op-node): retain undecided Holocene span batches for retry

The Holocene BatchStage consumed a span batch from the previous stage
and, when validation returned BatchUndecided (transient L2 parent-block
or overlap-payload fetch failure), skipped the batch entirely instead of
retrying it. A temporary local fetch failure could therefore make one
node skip a valid span batch while others accept it, splitting the
local safe chain until a pipeline replay or restart recovered the batch
from L1.

Retain the consumed span batch in a pending slot on an undecided result
and re-check the same batch on the next derivation step; clear the slot
on accept, drop, past, channel flush and reset. BatchDrop, BatchPast
and accepted-span behavior are unchanged.

Fault-injection tests pin the lifecycle: transient parent lookup
failure, transient overlap payload failure, and permanent invalidity
discovered after an undecided attempt still dropping the span/channel.

Fixes #22629 (op-node portion; kona follows)

docs: add the OP Stack architecture page

The Protocol tab had no single page explaining how the system fits together.
Six pages each partially claimed the job — introduction/op-stack,
protocol/index, protocol/overview, protocol/components, components/index and
learn/index — and a reader who wanted one architecture page had to assemble
it from all of them. A reader evaluating the OP Stack would leave instead.

Adds op-stack/architecture.mdx as the canonical system view: the big picture,
the actors and who runs each, one transaction walked through every component,
where data lives and how the trust boundary moves as a transaction ages,
topology options, and what is permissionless versus privileged.

Two diagrams, because the tab had almost none: across 101 Protocol-tab files
only 11 used mermaid and the pages that most needed a picture had none.

The page routes rather than restates, per the content guide's dual-sourcing
ban. Finality semantics stay in transaction-finality, which already owns that
sequence diagram; mechanical batching detail stays in transaction-flow; the
layer taxonomy stays in protocol/components; roles stay in privileged-roles.

Content is verified against monorepo source. Four claims in particular were
checked because they are easy to get wrong and this page is meant to be
canonical:

- Proposing and challenging are permissionless only when the chain's
  respected game type is the permissionless FaultDisputeGame. Under
  PermissionedDisputeGame, the fallback and the starting configuration for
  many new chains, both are gated to two named EOAs
  (PermissionedDisputeGame.sol:20-26 gates move and step; :72-73 requires
  tx.origin == proposer on creation). The page turns on game type rather than
  claiming blanket permissionlessness, which would have contradicted
  privileged-roles, and names the Guardian's setRespectedGameType control
  (AnchorStateRegistry.sol:152-159).
- The execution client holds the mempool and orders transactions; the rollup
  node fixes the block's L1 origin and deposit prefix and leaves the rest
  (op-node/rollup/derive/attributes.go:64-65).
- op-deployer deploys contracts but no longer upgrades them; its upgrade
  command is deprecated past op-contracts/v5.0.0.
- Derivation and forced inclusion bind the sequencer, not only verifiers,
  which is the whole censorship-resistance argument.

Data availability claims are scoped, since Alt-DA puts only a commitment on
L1; challenging is marked as requiring bonded capital; the dispute game is
not presented as self-executing; kona-node is named for client diversity.

lagoon: specify the span batch encoding of post-exec transactions

The post-exec transaction type 0x7D is fully specified as an EIP-2718
envelope in specs/protocol/lagoon/post-exec.md, but its span batch
representation was specified nowhere. Delta lists tx_datas encodings for
legacy, type 1 and type 2; Isthmus adds type 4 with an exact field order.
No document added 0x7D, and the word "span" did not appear anywhere under
specs/protocol/lagoon/.

Delta's generic sentence -- that tx_datas matches "the encoding of the
fields as in the EIP-2718 format of the TransactionType" -- does not close
the gap. It settles only tx_datas, and the document does not treat it as
sufficient for a new type anyway, since Isthmus still added an explicit
row. It settles none of the other slots. contract_creation_bits in
particular is defined as marking a contract creation, which a post-exec
transaction is not, yet both clients set the bit to 1 so that no tx_tos
entry is consumed.

Backfill a Lagoon derivation document from the implementations, which
agree byte for byte. It records the tx_datas row (0x7D followed by the
payload RLP list, verbatim, so the element is the transaction's whole
EIP-2718 encoding rather than a reduced one), the value of every
transposed envelope slot, and the reconstruction rules.

Two points are stated with deliberate asymmetry. A batcher MUST zero the
unused signature, nonce and gas slots, so a given sequence of blocks has
one encoding. A decoder MUST ignore them, and MUST NOT reject a batch
because of the values they carry -- reconstruction discards them, so a
batch with non-zero values derives identical blocks, and a verifier that
rejected it would drop batches both clients accept. The same holds for a
contract_creation_bits bit of 0: both clients consume a tx_tos entry and
discard it rather than failing.

Verified against op-node (span_batch_txs.go addPostExecTx and fullTxs,
span_batch_tx.go spanBatchPostExecTxData and convertToFullTx,
op-core/types/post_exec_tx.go) and kona (batch/tx_data/wrapper.rs,
batch/transactions.rs), plus the batch/safe-block overlap check in
batches.go, which stays deterministic for these blocks because
reconstruction discards every unused slot.

The batch queue drop rule for future types above 2 still needs a Lagoon
amendment. That applies to singular batches too, where no encoding
question arises, so it is left to its own change; this document marks the
boundary rather than assuming the rule.

Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/318

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

lagoon: require decoders to reject non-conforming post-exec slots

Per review: make the decoder strict rather than permissive. A decoder MUST
reject a batch whose contract_creation_bits bit is 0 for a post-exec
transaction, and MUST verify that y_parity_bits, tx_sigs, tx_nonces and
tx_gases are zero, rejecting the batch otherwise.

The previous wording had the decoder tolerate any value in these slots on
the grounds that reconstruction discards them, so no value can change the
derived blocks. That is true but it is the weaker property. Tolerating
them makes a span batch's encoding malleable: one sequence of L2 blocks
would have unboundedly many valid encodings, differing in bytes a batcher
picks freely, and tx_sigs alone reserves 64 unused bytes per transaction
to pick them in. Strict decoding keeps the encoding canonical and leaves
nothing for a later upgrade to tighten retroactively.

Tightening costs nothing here because 0x7D is new: no chain in the
superchain-registry sets lagoon_time, and a post-exec transaction cannot
legally appear in a batch before Lagoon, so no already-posted batch is
reinterpreted. Nor does it break any honest batcher -- op-batcher reaches
addPostExecTx through AppendSingularBatch and already zero-fills every one
of these slots.

Both clients currently accept what this now rejects, so op-node and kona
each need a matching change before Lagoon activates.

chore(ci): drop duplicated release build and SP1 ELF jobs

Two jobs are byte-for-byte duplicates of a job in a sibling workflow that
always runs alongside them, so every pipeline builds the same artifact
twice.

rust-build-release and rust-e2e-ci's rust-workspace-release are the same
`rust-build-binary` invocation — same directory, profile, features, no
package or binary filter, same contexts. rust-workspace-release adds
persist_to_workspace, making it a strict superset.
rust-build-release has no downstream consumer; it only feeds
required-rust-ci. compute-workflow-conditions.sh emits `run rust_ci` and
`run rust_e2e_ci` as a pair in all three branches (PR, merge queue,
develop), so there is no case where the rust-ci copy is the only release
build. Recent pipelines spend ~22 minutes on each of them.

kona-build-sp1-elfs runs in both main and rust-e2e-ci with no parameters
and identical contexts, gate-only in both (ci-gate and required-rust-e2e
respectively). main runs in every case rust-e2e-ci does, so dropping the
rust-e2e-ci copy cannot lose coverage. ~4.5 minutes each.

required-rust-e2e now requires rust-workspace-release directly rather
than only through the e2e jobs: a failed build leaves those unrun rather
than failed, and this workflow is now the only place the release build
happens.

Co-authored-by: wwared <wwared@users.noreply.github.com>
chore(ci): drop duplicated release build and SP1 ELF jobs

chore(ci): cap Rust build parallelism at nproc-1

`rust-build-release` has been OOM-killed since 2026-09-14 — the kernel
SIGKILLs a rustc process and cargo reports `sccache: Compile terminated
by signal 9`. It is intermittent: 5 failures in 26 runs on 09-14, and 0
in the 71 runs from 09-10 through 09-13.

The peak is the tail of the release build. `rust-build-binary` runs on
`xlarge.gen2` (8 vCPU / 16 GiB) and builds the workspace with
`lto = "thin"` and no `-j` cap, so cargo runs 8 units at once. Since
kona-zkvm-canary landed in #22791 the final window links op-reth,
kona-zkvm-canary, kona-sp1-proposer, op-reth-sdm-fixture and the op-reth
examples together; before it, the sp1-sdk binaries finished ~30 units
earlier. Nothing reduced the resource class — it has been xlarge.gen2
since #20917 in May, a same-size Gen1 to Gen2 migration.

Cap parallelism one below the vCPU count. nproc reflects the resource
class on these executors, so this is 7 on xlarge.gen2.

windows-targets 0.48.5); both crates declare open ranges (`>=1, <3` and

op-reth: report the real cause of a failed interop failsafe poll

The failsafe poll collected endpoint results with `if let Ok(Ok(v))`, so
every TLS, DNS, connect, HTTP and JSON-RPC failure was discarded and
reported as a 2-second timeout. A sub-5ms connector error therefore read
as a deadline expiry, sending operators after load and endpoint health.

is returned, so `Timeout` means the deadline actually expired. The error
is built with `other`, not the access-list classifier `from_json_rpc`,

op-reth,alloy-op-evm: zero overlay storage for destroyed accounts, cover the deposit gas-cap exemption

Two follow-ups from the `reth-update-reviewer` pass over the v2.5.0 bump.

`MemoryOverlayOpProofsStateProviderRef::hashed_post_state` only forwarded to the
inner provider, which zeroes a destroyed account's storage against the
*persisted* proofs storage. Slots written by blocks still in the in-memory
buffer live in the overlay, so a selfdestructed account stayed partially wiped
and the state root came out wrong. reth hit the same gap when it stopped
deriving `HashedStorage::wiped` from account status and extended
`MemoryOverlayStateProviderRef::hashed_post_state` to zero the unpersisted
slots too; this mirrors that. The path feeds `state_root_with_updates` in the
proofs engine, so the failure mode is a spurious state-root mismatch.

`alloy-op-evm` had no positive test for the EIP-7825 deposit gas-cap
exemption — only the negative case asserting non-deposits stay capped. The
exemption is not observable as an error, because deposits skip `validate_env`
where `TxGasLimitGreaterThanCap` is raised; it is only observable in how much
gas the first frame receives, via `initial_gas_and_reservoir`, which OP does
not override. The new tests measure that: a deposit above the cap runs a
payload costing more than the capped budget and must still complete, and the
saved cap round-trips through every resting state including `None`.

Both tests were checked red against deliberately broken variants — the first
against a disabled exemption, the second against a restore path that collapses
the inner `Option`.

op-revm: apply the pre-Regolith deposit gas rule after the EIP-2780 refund

`last_frame_result` settles the frame, then applies the Bedrock deposit rule
(gas used equals the limit, no refund), then applies upstream's EIP-2780
refundable-state-gas refill. A refill after the deposit rule would hand

the refill needs a `charged_*` flag that only EIP-2780 (Amsterdam) sets and
Bedrock maps to `SpecId::MERGE`, so no test can fail on the baseline; the
reorder makes the rule unconditional so that no upstream credit, present or
future, can undo it.

delta: rename contract_creation_bits to zero_to_bits

The bitlist is named for a condition it does not test. What it governs is
whether a transaction consumes an entry from tx_tos: a 0 bit consumes the
next address, a 1 bit consumes none. For every transaction type that has a
to field, "is a contract creation" and "has no to" coincide, so the name
was accurate by luck rather than by construction.

The Lagoon post-exec transaction (0x7D) is the first type where they come
apart. It has no to field and is not a contract creation, so it sets a bit
whose documented meaning is false of it. Specifying that took a paragraph
of apology in lagoon/derivation.md; renaming the field removes the need for
it, and that paragraph goes away here.

zero_to_bits keeps the polarity: the bit is 1 when the transaction's to is
absent. Note that nonzero_to_bits, the first name suggested, would read as
the inverse and silently flip the meaning for a fresh reader.

This is editorial. Nothing in a span batch is self-describing -- txs is a
positional concatenation with no tags or field names on the wire -- so the
encoding, the bit polarity and every derived chain are untouched, and no
fork gate is involved. The Delta text keeps a note recording the former
name so searches and third-party implementations still land. Client
identifiers (contractCreationBits in op-node, contract_creation_bits in
kona) can follow whenever convenient; nothing breaks while they differ.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

derivation: state that transaction_list carries EIP-2718 bytes verbatim

The v0 batch format already settles how a post-exec transaction appears in
a singular batch: transaction_list is "an RLP-encoded list of EIP-2718
encoded transactions", and 0x7D ++ rlp_encoded_payload is one such
encoding. No new rule is needed, and both clients agree -- op-node holds
SingularBatch.Transactions as []hexutil.Bytes and kona holds
SingleBatch.transactions as Vec<Bytes>, neither decoding nor transposing
anything.

What the format does not say is the consequence: that the element is
opaque, so a new transaction type needs no change to it. That is the step a
reader has to supply, and it is the same gap in reasoning that made the
span-batch case look settled when it was not. Say it, and separate it from
the acceptance question, which is where new types actually do need a rule.

The Lagoon document gains the matching statement, so a reader is not left
inferring that singular batches were overlooked rather than genuinely
unaffected.

No normative change in either file.

op-conductor: persist an empty Raft snapshot when no unsafe head is committed

snapshot.Persist dereferenced the FSM's unsafe head without a nil check.
Raft decides to snapshot from log growth, so a cluster that has not
committed any unsafe head yet (fresh bootstrap, sequencers stopped during
a single-to-HA migration) crashed on its first snapshot and re-crashed on
restart.

Persist now writes a zero-length snapshot for a nil head and Restore
treats a zero-length snapshot as "no unsafe head", so Raft keeps
snapshotting and compacting while the cluster is idle. Snapshot also sets
the snapshot logger that the existing error path dereferenced.

Supersedes #19149, which returned an error from Snapshot() and left Raft
logging a failed snapshot every SnapshotInterval until the first commit.

kona-zkvm-canary: report the underlying cause of RPC failures

Every parent RPC call discarded its jsonrpsee error with map_err(|_| ...),
so a request timeout, a refused connection, an HTTP 5xx and a JSON-RPC
error object all logged the same opaque "request failed" detail. No log
level could recover a value that was dropped at the call site.

Append the error and its source chain at each site. The chain matters
because jsonrpsee marks both ClientError::Transport and the HTTP transport
error #[error(transparent)], which forwards Display to the innermost layer
while leaving the actionable cause reachable only through source(); a
refused connection renders as "client error (Connect)" until the chain is
walked. anyhow's alternate Display already implements exactly that walk,
so rpc_detail delegates to it and keeps the 1 KiB parent-detail cap its
sibling call sites use.

This is safe to log because no jsonrpsee error variant renders the request
URL: Rejected carries only a status code, Http delegates to hyper, and the
Url variant carries a ParseError rather than the target. Note that
config.rs forbids credentials, queries and fragments in RPC URLs but
permits an API key embedded in the path, so that validation is not what
makes this safe.

Also render attempt detail with the alternate formatter so anyhow context
chains reach the log field instead of collapsing to their outermost
message. This widens every attempt detail, not just RPC failures; the
artifact refresh path benefits most, having previously logged only
"failed to refresh range artifact" while discarding the URL and the
reqwest cause beneath it.

contracts-bedrock: pin the compile-time EVM version to cancun

Amsterdam changes execution semantics, not the bytecode our contracts emit, but
forge derives both the solc target and the EVM executor from a single
`evm_version`. Running the L1 half of the suite with `--evm-version amsterdam`
therefore recompiled the whole tree against a target no contract needs: solc
clamps 0.8.15 to london and 0.8.25 to cancun regardless, and only the 0.8.31
floating-pragma files could go higher.

Pin `evm_version = 'cancun'` in every compiler profile and compilation
restriction so the requested EVM version drives the executor alone. Each
optimizer tier gains a cancun-pinned variant and a catch-all covers everything
outside the tiers, since a restriction must be satisfied by a profile matching
all of its constraints.

The amsterdam pass now reuses the cancun artifacts instead of rebuilding, and
semver-lock is unchanged: initCodeHash is identical for every contract.

lagoon: finish the batch queue amendment for post-exec transactions

Two gaps left after #944, both raised by protocol-team#319.

The drop rule appears twice. #944 amended the copy in derivation.md to
admit 0x7D but left the one in delta/span-batches.md, which repeats it
verbatim for span batch validity and still names only the Isthmus type 4
exception. A literal reading of the span batch rules therefore still drops
every span batch carrying a post-exec transaction. Isthmus amended both
sites for the same reason.

The activation paragraph stated the drop obligation for the wrong fork:
"if a singular batch contains a transaction of type 4 before Isthmus is
active". It reads as adapted from the Isthmus paragraph and left the
Lagoon rule it was meant to state unwritten, immediately after the sentence
that says 0x7D is accepted only when Lagoon is active. Now says type 0x7D
and Lagoon.

Both clients already behave as the corrected text describes: op-node's
checkSequencerTxData drops a PostExec tx when !isSDM, computing isSDM from
each block's own timestamp inside the per-block loop of the span batch
check, and kona drops with PostExecPreLagoon per SingleBatch timestamp. So
the activation granularity the paragraph specifies -- per individual batch,
letting a span straddle activation -- is what ships.

Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/319

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
lagoon: finish the batch queue amendment for post-exec transactions

delta: rename contract_creation_bits to zero_to_bits

The bitlist is named for a condition it does not test. What the bit governs
is whether a transaction consumes an entry from tx_tos: a 0 bit consumes the
next address, a 1 bit consumes none. For every transaction type that has a
to field, "is a contract creation" and "has no to" coincide, so the name was
accurate by luck rather than by construction.

The Lagoon post-exec transaction (0x7D) is the first type where they come
apart. It has no to field and is not a contract creation, so it sets a bit
whose documented meaning is false of it. Specifying that took a paragraph of
apology in lagoon/derivation.md; renaming the field removes the need for it,
and that paragraph goes away here.

zero_to_bits keeps the polarity: the bit is 1 when the transaction's to is
absent. Note that nonzero_to_bits, the first name suggested, would read as
the inverse and silently flip the meaning for a fresh reader.

This is editorial. Nothing in a span batch is self-describing -- txs is a
positional concatenation with no tags or field names on the wire -- so the
encoding, the bit polarity and every derived chain are untouched, and no
fork gate is involved. The Delta text keeps a note recording the former name
so searches and third-party implementations still land.

Also phrases the decoder rule at span batch granularity, matching the slot
rule below it rather than leaving two rules in one document worded
differently.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

lagoon: say that the span batch encoding assumes block validity

Review question: the encoder assumes a post-exec transaction is unique and
last in its block, but it will happily encode input that is neither. Should
the batch layer verify, or should the assumption be written down?

Written down. The span batch format transposes and reconstructs a
transaction list and has no notion of block validity, so it can faithfully
encode a block carrying two 0x7D transactions, or one where the 0x7D is not
last. Such a batch is well formed as a batch. The structural rules are
enforced where post-exec.md states them, on the block: op-alloy's
parse_post_exec_payload_from_transactions rejects MultiplePostExecTxs,
PostExecTxNotLast, BlockNumberMismatch and a pre-Lagoon UnexpectedPostExecTx,
and op-reth calls it while executing the block. A hand-crafted batch
encoding such a block therefore decodes, produces payload attributes, and is
rejected by the engine; Holocene's Steady Block Derivation replaces the
payload with a deposit-only one and drops the remaining span batch and
channel.

Deliberately not duplicating that check into the codec. It would give one
rule two enforcement points with different outcomes -- batch drop at decode
time against invalid block plus channel drop -- which derive different
chains, the divergence class already open as protocol-team#222.

Encoder-side validation is also not required: a batcher only encodes blocks
the engine has already accepted, so a check there would guard against a
local bug rather than a protocol condition.

No normative change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
lagoon: say that the span batch encoding assumes block validity

lagoon: pin decode-rejection granularity and where payload checking stops

Review findings from an Opus 5 pass, three of which were unaddressed.

Rejection granularity. The zero-slot rules said "reject a batch" without
saying which. The slots are positional across the whole span, so a
violation cannot be attributed to the single block whose transaction
carries it: the span batch is what becomes invalid. Say so. How far that
invalidity propagates -- whether the remaining channel goes with it -- is
deliberately left alone: op-node and kona disagree today
(protocol-team#222), it is a property of malformed span batches generally
rather than of post-exec transactions, and settling it here would fix for
one trigger what stays contested for every other decode failure.

Where payload checking stops. The document required the element to be a
single RLP list and then said nothing, which reads like the start of a
contract. Both clients treat everything below that framing check as opaque
-- op-node captures it with s.Raw(), kona copies the header-delimited
bytes -- and neither reads the version byte at batch decode. State that a
decoder MUST NOT, so payload validity stays block-level.

Activation granularity. Isthmus specifies, for type 4, that activation is
checked per individual batch derived from the span rather than per span
batch, so a span may straddle activation. Both clients already do exactly
this for 0x7D -- op-node computes isSDM from each block's timestamp inside
the per-block loop, kona from the SingleBatch timestamp -- but no document
says it. It qualifies the acceptance rule rather than the encoding, so it
is recorded here as something the Batch Queue amendment owes rather than
specified here. The contradiction that amendment resolves is now stated
outright instead of implied.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
lagoon: pin decode-rejection granularity and where payload checking s…

lagoon: cite the rule the strictness argument rests on

The argument for a strict decoder said a post-exec transaction "cannot
legally appear in a batch before Lagoon" without saying what makes that
true, which reads as an appeal to the batch queue drop rule -- the one rule
that does not yet say it. The support is elsewhere and is already
normative: post-exec.md requires that a block before the Lagoon activation
timestamp contain no 0x7D transaction, so no posted batch carries one.
Cite that instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
lagoon: cite the rule the strictness argument rests on

lagoon: forbid decode-time rejection of the block-level structural rules

The document said the structural rules are caught on the block and that
encoders need not check them, but left the decoder's obligation implied.
It is stronger than "not required": a decoder MUST NOT check them, because
doing so changes the chain.

The two paths do not converge. A block-validity failure returns INVALID
from the engine, and Steady Block Derivation replaces the payload with a
deposit-only block at that height before discarding the rest of the span
batch and channel. A decode-time rejection returns NotEnoughData, produces
no block at that height, and leaves it to be filled by a later batch. One
forces a deposit-only block into the chain; the other does not. From the
same L1 data they derive different chains, so this is not a choice a
decoder may make locally.

mandating rejection of a nonzero tx_nonces byte while leaving a misplaced

value that cannot reach the derived block is checked nowhere else, so the
decoder must check it; a property of the block is already checked, so the
decoder must not. Both halves are now stated where a reader meets them.

delta: rename contract_creation_bits to zero_to_bits (#945)

The bitlist is named for a condition it does not test. What the bit governs
is whether a transaction consumes an entry from tx_tos: a 0 bit consumes the
next address, a 1 bit consumes none. For every transaction type that has a
to field, "is a contract creation" and "has no to" coincide, so the name was
accurate by luck rather than by construction.

The Lagoon post-exec transaction (0x7D) is the first type where they come
apart. It has no to field and is not a contract creation, so it sets a bit
whose documented meaning is false of it. Specifying that took a paragraph of
apology in lagoon/derivation.md; renaming the field removes the need for it,
and that paragraph goes away here.

absent. Note that nonzero_to_bits, the first name suggested, would read as
the inverse and silently flip the meaning for a fresh reader.

This is editorial. Nothing in a span batch is self-describing -- txs is a
positional concatenation with no tags or field names on the wire -- so the
encoding, the bit polarity and every derived chain are untouched, and no
fork gate is involved. The Delta text keeps a note recording the former name
so searches and third-party implementations still land.

Also phrases the decoder rule at span batch granularity, matching the slot
rule below it rather than leaving two rules in one document worded
differently.

* lagoon: specify the span batch encoding of post-exec transactions

The post-exec transaction type 0x7D is fully specified as an EIP-2718
envelope in specs/protocol/lagoon/post-exec.md, but its span batch
representation was specified nowhere. Delta lists tx_datas encodings for
legacy, type 1 and type 2; Isthmus adds type 4 with an exact field order.
No document added 0x7D, and the word "span" did not appear anywhere under
specs/protocol/lagoon/.

Delta's generic sentence -- that tx_datas matches "the encoding of the
fields as in the EIP-2718 format of the TransactionType" -- does not close
the gap. It settles only tx_datas, and the document does not treat it as
sufficient for a new type anyway, since Isthmus still added an explicit
row. It settles none of the other slots. contract_creation_bits in
particular is defined as marking a contract creation, which a post-exec
transaction is not, yet both clients set the bit to 1 so that no tx_tos
entry is consumed.

Backfill a Lagoon derivation document from the implementations, which
agree byte for byte. It records the tx_datas row (0x7D followed by the
payload RLP list, verbatim, so the element is the transaction's whole
EIP-2718 encoding rather than a reduced one), the value of every
transposed envelope slot, and the reconstruction rules.

Two points are stated with deliberate asymmetry. A batcher MUST zero the
unused signature, nonce and gas slots, so a given sequence of blocks has
one encoding. A decoder MUST ignore them, and MUST NOT reject a batch
because of the values they carry -- reconstruction discards them, so a
batch with non-zero values derives identical blocks, and a verifier that
rejected it would drop batches both clients accept. The same holds for a
contract_creation_bits bit of 0: both clients consume a tx_tos entry and
discard it rather than failing.

Verified against op-node (span_batch_txs.go addPostExecTx and fullTxs,
span_batch_tx.go spanBatchPostExecTxData and convertToFullTx,
op-core/types/post_exec_tx.go) and kona (batch/tx_data/wrapper.rs,
batch/transactions.rs), plus the batch/safe-block overlap check in
batches.go, which stays deterministic for these blocks because
reconstruction discards every unused slot.

The batch queue drop rule for future types above 2 still needs a Lagoon
amendment. That applies to singular batches too, where no encoding
question arises, so it is left to its own change; this document marks the
boundary rather than assuming the rule.

Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/318

* lagoon: require decoders to reject non-conforming post-exec slots

Per review: make the decoder strict rather than permissive. A decoder MUST
reject a batch whose contract_creation_bits bit is 0 for a post-exec
transaction, and MUST verify that y_parity_bits, tx_sigs, tx_nonces and
tx_gases are zero, rejecting the batch otherwise.

The previous wording had the decoder tolerate any value in these slots on
the grounds that reconstruction discards them, so no value can change the
derived blocks. That is true but it is the weaker property. Tolerating
them makes a span batch's encoding malleable: one sequence of L2 blocks
would have unboundedly many valid encodings, differing in bytes a batcher
picks freely, and tx_sigs alone reserves 64 unused bytes per transaction
to pick them in. Strict decoding keeps the encoding canonical and leaves
nothing for a later upgrade to tighten retroactively.

Tightening costs nothing here because 0x7D is new: no chain in the
superchain-registry sets lagoon_time, and a post-exec transaction cannot
legally appear in a batch before Lagoon, so no already-posted batch is
reinterpreted. Nor does it break any honest batcher -- op-batcher reaches
addPostExecTx through AppendSingularBatch and already zero-fills every one
of these slots.

Both clients currently accept what this now rejects, so op-node and kona
each need a matching change before Lagoon activates.

* lagoon: say that the span batch encoding assumes block validity

Review question: the encoder assumes a post-exec transaction is unique and
last in its block, but it will happily encode input that is neither. Should
the batch layer verify, or should the assumption be written down?

Written down. The span batch format transposes and reconstructs a
transaction list and has no notion of block validity, so it can faithfully
encode a block carrying two 0x7D transactions, or one where the 0x7D is not
last. Such a batch is well formed as a batch. The structural rules are
enforced where post-exec.md states them, on the block: op-alloy's
parse_post_exec_payload_from_transactions rejects MultiplePostExecTxs,
PostExecTxNotLast, BlockNumberMismatch and a pre-Lagoon UnexpectedPostExecTx,
and op-reth calls it while executing the block. A hand-crafted batch
encoding such a block therefore decodes, produces payload attributes, and is
rejected by the engine; Holocene's Steady Block Derivation replaces the
payload with a deposit-only one and drops the remaining span batch and
channel.

Deliberately not duplicating that check into the codec. It would give one
rule two enforcement points with different outcomes -- batch drop at decode
time against invalid block plus channel drop -- which derive different
chains, the divergence class already open as protocol-team#222.

Encoder-side validation is also not required: a batcher only encodes blocks
the engine has already accepted, so a check there would guard against a
local bug rather than a protocol condition.

No normative change.

* lagoon: pin decode-rejection granularity and where payload checking stops

Review findings from an Opus 5 pass, three of which were unaddressed.

Rejection granularity. The zero-slot rules said "reject a batch" without
saying which. The slots are positional across the whole span, so a
violation cannot be attributed to the single block whose transaction
carries it: the span batch is what becomes invalid. Say so. How far that
invalidity propagates -- whether the remaining channel goes with it -- is
deliberately left alone: op-node and kona disagree today
(protocol-team#222), it is a property of malformed span batches generally
rather than of post-exec transactions, and settling it here would fix for
one trigger what stays contested for every other decode failure.

Where payload checking stops. The document required the element to be a
single RLP list and then said nothing, which reads like the start of a
contract. Both clients treat everything below that framing check as opaque
-- op-node captures it with s.Raw(), kona copies the header-delimited
bytes -- and neither reads the version byte at batch decode. State that a
decoder MUST NOT, so payload validity stays block-level.

Activation granularity. Isthmus specifies, for type 4, that activation is
checked per individual batch derived from the span rather than per span
batch, so a span may straddle activation. Both clients already do exactly
this for 0x7D -- op-node computes isSDM from each block's timestamp inside
the per-block loop, kona from the SingleBatch timestamp -- but no document
says it. It qualifies the acceptance rule rather than the encoding, so it
is recorded here as something the Batch Queue amendment owes rather than
specified here. The contradiction that amendment resolves is now stated
outright instead of implied.

fix(SuperchainAddressRegistry): discover the v8.0.0 super-root games

Upgrade 20 (op-contracts/v8.0.0) clears a chain's CANNON (0),
PERMISSIONED_CANNON (1) and CANNON_KONA (8) implementations and installs
SUPER_CANNON_KONA (9) and SUPER_PERMISSIONED (5) instead. Discovery read
the permissioned game unconditionally, so on every upgraded chain it
reverted with `SuperchainAddressRegistry: zero address for
PermissionedDisputeGame`, which broke `stacked_simulation_sep` and
`forge_test` on `main` once sep/108 executed for OP, Ink, Soneium and
Unichain Sepolia.

Guard the permissioned game the way the fault game is already guarded and
fall back to the super games:

- `SuperFaultDisputeGame` and `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` are registered
  when the legacy games are cleared, matching the naming already used in
  the U20 validation files.
- `AnchorStateRegistryProxy`, `MIPS`, `PreimageOracle`, `PermissionlessWETH`
  and `Proposer` resolve through the super games' `gameArgs`. The
  permissioned game is still preferred, so pre-U20 chains are unaffected.
- `Challenger` and `PermissionedWETH` are only registered when the legacy
  permissioned game exists: the simplified super permissioned game carries
  only an AnchorStateRegistry and a proposer, so neither role exists
  on-chain after the upgrade.

The SUPER_PERMISSIONED `gameArgs` are 40 bytes (asr | proposer) rather than
the 124/164-byte layout, so they need their own decoder; both decoders were
checked against OP Sepolia's live `gameArgs(5)` and `gameArgs(9)`.

op-devstack: retry conductor leadership-transfer requests

TransferLeadershipTo asserted on the first response from
conductor_transferLeaderToServer, but that RPC is a request rather than a
result: hashicorp/raft hands the target a TimeoutNow and then gives it
exactly one ElectionTimeout to win the election that triggers.
op-conductor never overrides ElectionTimeout, so it stays at
raft.DefaultConfig()'s 1s while the devstack preset runs heartbeats at 1s
and the leader lease at 500ms. One election round costs the candidate and
every granting voter three separate fsync'd BoltDB transactions each,
plus the RequestVote round trips, so under CI CPU contention it can
exceed that second; the old leader then reports "leadership transfer
timeout" even though the target goes on to win the election a few hundred
milliseconds later.

Fold the transfer request into the same bounded settle loop this file
already uses for every other cluster-wide invariant, so an advisory
response can no longer fail a test on its own. The untargeted
TransferLeadership path had the same defect and gets the same treatment.

The verdict stays a cluster-wide observation, and deliberately not in
this helper: awaitLeadershipTransferRequestTo only gets a request
accepted, while TransferLeadershipTo still requires the target to take
leadership (waitForLeadership) and the cluster to settle on it as sole
active sequencer (AwaitOneActiveSequencer). A transfer that never moves
anything therefore still fails, just later. It also refuses to report
success if the target gained leadership before this loop ever asked,
which would otherwise let a coincidence satisfy the assertions without
the transfer under test happening at all.

Reproduced at the consensus layer, since the acceptance test itself fails
about once in 245 and is useless as a local signal: three RaftConsensus
nodes on the preset's exact timeouts, transferring leadership around the
ring, under 18 shards each pinned to one CPU. 24 of 726 transfers failed
(3.3%), 23 with exactly "leadership transfer timeout" and 1 with "node is
not the leader"; in every instrumented case the target became sole leader
40-400ms later, so the operation had succeeded and was misreported. With
the convergence loop, 0 of 755 failed. Two runs per arm were excluded as
UNSETTLED -- at this starvation the harness can drive the cluster into
election thrash with no single leader, which measures neither arm; the
exclusions are symmetric and the result survives assuming both post-fix
exclusions were hidden failures.

Caveat: the harness drives the production RaftConsensus type, so the
baseline arm and the error it reproduces are the real code path, but the
fix lives in unexported dsl.Conductor methods the harness cannot call, so
the post-fix arm re-implements the retry at harness level. It validates
the diagnosis, not this patch. CI is the only thing that exercises the
shipped code.

Fixes #22924

op-node,kona: reject post-exec span batch slots that are not the fixed values

ethereum-optimism/specs#944 specified the span batch encoding of a post-exec
(0x7D) transaction, which until now no document stated. Both clients already
produced the encoding it describes; neither enforced it on decode.

The spec requires a decoder to reject the span batch when a post-exec
transaction does not carry the fixed slot values: the contract creation bit
set, so no tx_tos entry is consumed, and zero for the y parity bit, the
signature, the nonce and the gas limit.

The check has to be here. These slots are discarded when the transaction is
reconstructed, so no later stage can notice a batcher that filled them with
anything else, and the same blocks would have more than one valid span batch
encoding. tx_sigs alone reserves 64 bytes per transaction that a post-exec
transaction does not use.

Deliberately not checked here: the block-level structural rules -- at most
one post-exec transaction, last in its block, anchored to the block number.
Those are already enforced in op-alloy's parse_post_exec_payload_from_transactions
when the derived block is validated, and checking them at decode time would
change the chain rather than harden it. An invalid block is replaced by a
deposit-only block at that height under Steady Block Derivation; a decode
rejection produces no block there at all. The two derive differently, so the
decoder must leave them alone.

A violation invalidates the whole span batch rather than one block, because
the slots are positional across the span.

Tests cover each slot in both clients, plus an end-to-end op-node case
asserting that derive now rejects a tampered batch. That case fails on the
parent commit, where derive accepts it and reconstructs the same blocks.

Note for review: this adds a new decode-time rejection, which is the path
where op-node drops only the batch and kona drops the remaining channel
(ethereum-optimism/protocol-team#222). It adds a trigger to that existing
divergence rather than a new class of it; the spec deliberately leaves the
propagation unsettled, and it should be fixed once for all decode failures.

op-node,kona: rename the span batch contract creation bits to zero-to bits

Carries ethereum-optimism/specs#945 into both clients, ahead of it merging.
The rename is editorial on the spec side and it is editorial here too:
nothing in a span batch is self-describing, so no encoding, bit polarity or
derived chain changes.

The bitlist was named for a condition it does not test. What the bit governs
is whether a transaction consumes an entry from tx_tos. For every type that
has a to field, "is a contract creation" and "has no to" coincide, so the
name held by luck. The post-exec transaction is the first type where they
part: it has no to field and is not a contract creation, so it sets a bit
whose old name is false of it -- as the check added in the previous commit
has to assert.

zero_to_bits keeps the polarity: set when the transaction's to is absent.

  contractCreationBits  -> zeroToBits          (op-node)
  contractCreationCount -> zeroToCount
  contract_creation_bits -> zero_to_bits       (kona)
  contract_creation_count -> zero_to_count

Error strings and doc comments follow the identifiers, so nothing still
describes the bit as marking a contract creation. zeroToCount is documented
as the count of transactions with no to field, which is what it returns.

If #945 lands under a different name, this commit is a rerun of the same
substitution.

op-reth: warn on every log filter that straddles bedrock

A missing or tip-tracking bound resolves to the chain tip, not genesis,
in both reth and l2geth. Treating an absent fromBlock as genesis warned
about ranges that don't straddle anything and metered a span nobody
asked for, and bailing on an unresolvable toBlock skipped the warning
for fromBlock=<pre-bedrock> with toBlock=latest or absent -- the
everyday "all logs for this contract" query, and the one that actually
loses logs.

Decide on the resolved bounds instead, so the warning covers every
straddling filter and an open-ended range is forwarded unmetered: the
historical endpoint resolves the missing bound to its own tip, the last
pre-bedrock block, so there is no span to meter.

Also stop claiming local handling rejects an over-wide range with the
span limit specifically; with pre-bedrock history pruned it reports
unavailable history first.

lagoon: specify post-exec receipt JSON-RPC fee fields

The post-exec (`0x7D`) receipt section pinned only the consensus RLP
fields, so the OP-specific fee fields a client surfaces over JSON-RPC
were unspecified. op-reth consequently reports a non-zero `l1Fee` and
`l1GasUsed` on a transaction that pays no fees, which is misleading for
anything that sums L1 fees from receipts.

Split the section into consensus and JSON-RPC fields, and specify the
JSON-RPC fee fields in the two groups they naturally fall into:

- Transaction-scoped (`gasUsed`, `effectiveGasPrice`, `l1Fee`,
  `l1GasUsed`, `blobGasUsed`) MUST be present and zero, since a
  post-exec transaction is charged nothing.
- Block-scoped (`l1GasPrice`, the base/blob fee scalars,
  `operatorFee*`, `daFootprintGasScalar`) MUST match every other
  receipt in the same block in both value and presence.

`l1Fee` and `l1GasUsed` are zeroed rather than omitted. Keeping them
present makes a post-exec receipt the same shape as a regular
transaction's receipt and matches `gasUsed` and `effectiveGasPrice`,
which are already reported as zero rather than omitted, so a consumer
summing `l1Fee` over a block needs no special case either way.

fix(SuperchainAddressRegistry): discover the v8.0.0 super-root games (#1554)

* fix(SuperchainAddressRegistry): discover the v8.0.0 super-root games

Upgrade 20 (op-contracts/v8.0.0) clears a chain's CANNON (0),
PERMISSIONED_CANNON (1) and CANNON_KONA (8) implementations and installs
SUPER_CANNON_KONA (9) and SUPER_PERMISSIONED (5) instead. Discovery read
the permissioned game unconditionally, so on every upgraded chain it
reverted with `SuperchainAddressRegistry: zero address for
PermissionedDisputeGame`, which broke `stacked_simulation_sep` and
`forge_test` on `main` once sep/108 executed for OP, Ink, Soneium and
Unichain Sepolia.

Guard the permissioned game the way the fault game is already guarded and
fall back to the super games:

- `SuperFaultDisputeGame` and `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` are registered
  when the legacy games are cleared, matching the naming already used in
  the U20 validation files.
- `AnchorStateRegistryProxy`, `MIPS`, `PreimageOracle`, `PermissionlessWETH`
  and `Proposer` resolve through the super games' `gameArgs`. The
  permissioned game is still preferred, so pre-U20 chains are unaffected.
- `Challenger` and `PermissionedWETH` are only registered when the legacy
  permissioned game exists: the simplified super permissioned game carries
  only an AnchorStateRegistry and a proposer, so neither role exists
  on-chain after the upgrade.

The SUPER_PERMISSIONED `gameArgs` are 40 bytes (asr | proposer) rather than
the 124/164-byte layout, so they need their own decoder; both decoders were
checked against OP Sepolia's live `gameArgs(5)` and `gameArgs(9)`.

Co-authored-by: Wazabie <48911235+Wazabie@users.noreply.github.com>

* docs(sep-108): mark U20 op-ink-soneium-uni executed

The task executed on Sepolia in
0x788dfac2ac1b025b31a95b72336e7435fd192a352af8aec302a7d3907a603c4a
(block 11724769) from the standard L1PAO
0x1Eb2fFc903729a0F03966B917003800b145F56E2. That is the same block in which
the four chains' PERMISSIONED_CANNON implementations were cleared, which is
what the registry change in this PR handles.

Co-authored-by: Wazabie <48911235+Wazabie@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(SuperchainAddressRegistry): skip MIPS on a chain with no fault game

Upgrade 20 leaves SUPER_CANNON_KONA (9) disabled on a chain that had no
CANNON_KONA impl to carry over, so the chain is left with SUPER_PERMISSIONED
(5) as its only game. That game runs no fault proof and therefore has no VM:
sepolia-devnet-3 is in this state today after sep/107, and Soneium will be
once eth/071 executes.

Registering `MIPS` unconditionally reverted such a chain's discovery with
`SuperchainAddressRegistry: zero address for MIPS`, so only register `MIPS`
and its `PreimageOracle` when a game that carries a VM exists — the legacy
permissioned game, the legacy fault game or the super fault game.

contracts-bedrock: probe CrossDomainMessenger gas under Amsterdam

Exploratory. Adds CrossDomainMessenger_StateGas_Test, which sizes two
independent ways EIP-8037 / Amsterdam repricing breaks the messenger's gas
accounting. Run every test under both --evm-version cancun and amsterdam: the
cancun run is the control, since these constants are correct under EIP-7623 and
a test that fails there is measuring its own harness.

  cancun    2 passed, 0 failed
  amsterdam 0 passed, 2 failed

RELAY_RESERVED_GAS is withheld from the target call so relayMessage can always
record an outcome afterwards. Under EIP-8037 the status write is a priced state
creation, and the sequence measures 123,694 gas against a 40,000 reserve.

baseGas() is the relay transaction's whole budget, and delivering its calldata
is charged before execution starts. For a 13,920-byte message baseGas() returns
588,200 where 920,472 is charged, so the relay cannot begin — which is why
raising the reserve alone relocates the existing
testFuzz_relayMessage_baseGasSufficient_succeeds counterexample to larger
messages instead of fixing it.

Deliberately not asserted: whether MIN_GAS_CALLDATA_OVERHEAD (16) and
FLOOR_CALLDATA_OVERHEAD (40) are individually stale. Three attempts to price a
calldata token failed their cancun control; vm.lastCallGas() reports
execution-path gas and does not apply the EIP-7623 floor, so decomposing the
price needs a different instrument. The test above avoids the problem by never
decomposing one.

contracts-bedrock: probe SafeCall min-gas buffer under Amsterdam

Exploratory. Covers the Portal side of the Amsterdam repricing problem, which
the CrossDomainMessenger probes do not reach.

callWithMinGas promises a withdrawal's target at least tx.gasLimit, and guards
that promise with a flat 40,000 gas buffer sized, per SafeCall's own natspec, as
address_access_cost 2,600 + positive_value_cost 6,700 + value_to_empty_account
25,000 = 34,300 plus 5,700 slack. EIP-8037 turns the last term into a priced
state creation, so the buffer stops being an upper bound.

  cancun     1 passed, 0 failed
  amsterdam  0 passed, 1 failed -- 195,900 > 40,000

195,900 matches the expected decomposition: 2,600 + 6,700 + 183,600 state gas
for the account creation, plus roughly 3,000 of EIP-8038 execution gas.

This matters because OptimismPortal2.finalizeWithdrawalTransaction marks a
withdrawal finalized before calling the target and ignores the call's return
value by design, so the minimum-gas promise is the only thing standing between
an underforwarded target and a finalized withdrawal whose message never ran.

Scope: this sizes the guard, it does not demonstrate the end-to-end outcome. A
sweep through prove/resolve/warp/finalize is still needed to show a withdrawal
finalizing while its target was shortchanged. Note also that underforwarding
alone is broad, while bricking is narrow: the target must both be a
non-existent account and fail, and an account with no code cannot fail.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
contracts-bedrock: probe SafeCall min-gas buffer under Amsterdam

contracts-bedrock: reproduce bricked withdrawal end to end under Amsterdam

Exploratory. The component probes size RELAY_RESERVED_GAS and the SafeCall
min-gas buffer in isolation. This drives the real path a user's withdrawal
takes -- prove, resolve, wait, finalize -- and asserts the property that
actually matters: a finalized withdrawal must leave its message either executed
or replayable.

  cancun     1 passed, 0 failed
  amsterdam  0 passed, 1 failed

Under Amsterdam the withdrawal finalizes while successfulMessages and
failedMessages are both unset, so finalizeWithdrawalTransaction reverts with
OptimismPortal_AlreadyFinalized and relayMessage reverts on
require(failedMessages[versionedHash]). Both doors shut in one transaction,
which itself succeeds. Under cancun the identical path records failedMessages
and the message stays replayable, so the repricing is the only difference.

The messenger runs as the Portal's child here. Its frame unwinds on the failed
status write while the Portal's flag, written in the Portal's own frame before
the call, survives -- and callWithMinGas is raw assembly, so the Portal sees
only a false return it was designed to ignore.

The target must consume everything forwarded to it. Gas a target does not spend
is returned to the messenger, so only an exhausting target leaves the messenger
on its reserve; an earlier revision of this test used a cheap target and passed
under Amsterdam for that reason. GasBurner is the mock the repo's own baseGas
fuzz test uses, for the same reason.

Scope: this reproduces Type 2, where the messenger cannot record an outcome. It
does not cover Type 1, where the Portal underforwards its target -- that needs a
target that both is a non-existent account and can fail, and an account with no
code cannot fail. FINALIZE_GAS sits in a window bounded on both sides; see the
constant's natspec.

op-devstack: retry conductor leadership-transfer requests

TransferLeadershipTo asserted on the first response from
conductor_transferLeaderToServer, but that RPC is a request, not a result:
a nil error only means Raft accepted it. Raft then gives the handover a
single ElectionTimeout, which op-conductor leaves at the 1s default while
the devstack preset runs heartbeats at 1s, so a loaded CI box can exceed it
and report "leadership transfer timeout" even though the target wins the
election a few hundred milliseconds later.

Move the request inside the settle loop this file already uses for every
other cluster-wide invariant. The verdict stays where it was --
waitForLeadership and AwaitOneActiveSequencer -- so a transfer that never
moves anything still fails, just later. The untargeted TransferLeadership
path had the same defect and gets the same treatment.

Reproduced at the consensus layer, since the acceptance test itself fails
about once in 245 runs: three RaftConsensus nodes on the preset's timeouts
under CPU starvation failed 24 of 726 transfers, 23 of them with exactly
this error, and in every instrumented case the target became sole leader
40-400ms later. 0 of 755 failed with the retry. The harness cannot call the
unexported DSL methods the fix lives in, so that validates the diagnosis,
not this patch -- CI is what exercises the shipped code.

Fixes #22924

contracts-bedrock: pin the compile-time EVM version to cancun

Amsterdam changes execution semantics, not the bytecode our contracts emit, but
forge derives both the solc target and the EVM executor from a single
`evm_version`. Running the L1 half of the suite with `--evm-version amsterdam`
therefore recompiled the whole tree against a target no contract needs: solc
clamps 0.8.15 to london and 0.8.25 to cancun regardless, and only the 0.8.31
floating-pragma files could go higher.

Pin `evm_version = 'cancun'` in every compiler profile and compilation
restriction so the requested EVM version drives the executor alone. Each
optimizer tier gains a cancun-pinned variant and a catch-all covers everything
outside the tiers, since a restriction must be satisfied by a profile matching
all of its constraints.

The amsterdam pass now reuses the cancun artifacts instead of rebuilding, and
semver-lock is unchanged: initCodeHash is identical for every contract.

narrowed to the window around the transition -- and with
--rpc.max-blocks-per-filter unset it swallows an earliest -> latest
query whole.

Split such a filter instead: ask the historical endpoint for the blocks
below the bedrock block and the local node for the rest, then
concatenate, which keeps the response ordered by block number the way a
single-backend answer is. The split needs both the inner service and the
historical client, so the dispatch moves into HistoricalRpcService::call
and the getLogs decision becomes a three-way LogFilterRoute.

A failure on either side fails the whole request; returning the
surviving half would be a well-formed answer to a narrower query than
the caller asked for.

--rpc.max-blocks-per-filter still applies to the range sent upstream, so
a split can't be used to aim an unmetered scan at the operator's l2geth
either: a pre-bedrock half wider than the limit isn't split, and the
whole range is left to local handling, which rejects it because the
range asked for is wider still. That case keeps the warning.

Metering each half of a split separately let a filter centred on the
transition scan up to twice --rpc.max-blocks-per-filter: both halves
pass their own check while the range asked for is refused by local
handling. Meter that range instead when its upper bound resolves, and
fall back to the pre-bedrock half only when the bound tracks the chain
tip and there is nothing wider to measure.

payload costing more than the capped budget and must still complete, and the

lagoon: specify how the post-exec transaction appears on the subblock stream

The subblock stream carries the post-exec (0x7D) transaction as
`diff.post_exec_tx`. The field was added without stating where it lives,
why, or what consumers may assume about it, leaving open questions about
whether it belongs in `transactions` and whether `metadata.receipts`
should cover it.

Add a Subblocks section to the Lagoon post-exec spec that locks the
current behaviour as five normative decisions, each paired with a
rationale (marked non-normative and subject to change) and a consumer
implication:

1. it is carried in `diff`, not `transactions`, because it is recomputed
   as subblocks are added;
2. it never appears in `transactions`, in any subblock, at any index;
3. only the last subblock's value is canonical, and the stream marks no
   subblock as the last;
4. `transactions` may be empty;
5. `metadata.receipts` carries no receipt for it.

Also close the cross-reference loop: subblocks.md pointed at
lagoon/post-exec.md but nothing pointed back. subblocks.md gains a
Post-execution transactions section summarising the rules and linking to
the normative statement, and its field list and consumer guarantees now
say that `transactions` excludes the post-exec transaction and that
`metadata.receipts` never covers it.

Behaviour is unchanged; this records what op-rbuilder already does.

Refs: ethereum-optimism/protocol-team#334

op-node: publish blocks after inserting them, not before

The sequencer published each sealed block to peers before inserting it into
its own chain. That ordering came from #8905 (Jan 2024, "op-node: Gossip
Before Import"), whose entire stated rationale was "to avoid waiting any
longer than needed before gossiping" - no measurement, no linked issue. It
reversed the original insert-then-gossip order. #14580 has since recorded
that it "never won us that much time" and "did however add fragility", and
both op-test-sequencer (Seal -> Sign -> Commit -> Publish, where Commit is
the local insert) and kona's sequencer publish after inserting.

Publishing before adopting means op-node can hand peers a block it never
makes canonical. Verifiers adopt a gossiped unsafe payload as their head on
arrival, so if the insert then fails and the sequencer seals a sibling at
that height, every verifier reorgs. The denylist case is the sharpest:
ErrPayloadDenied is checked inside ProcessPayload, so a block on the
SuperAuthority denylist was broadcast before the sequencer consulted the
denylist.

Gossip now happens once ProcessPayload has returned nil, so the invariant
becomes: anything peers receive is already the sequencer's canonical head.
A queued block can be late, but never one the sequencer has to take back.

That is what makes the queue safe. SimpleAsyncGossiper now holds a bounded
queue drained by a dedicated goroutine, and Gossip and Clear only take a
mutex - neither waits for the network. Previously the publish ran inline in
the gossiper's select loop over unbuffered channels, so with a remote signer
the sequencer's Clear() blocked for the rest of an HTTPS round-trip, 1-2ms
after Gossip(), and that stall came 1:1 out of the next block's build window
(#22554). A publish also now carries a deadline of its own, which the signer
round-trip did not.

The interface loses Get(). It existed only to let the sequencer re-insert a
block it had already gossiped, and with it go the reuse buffer, the
resume-from-buffer branch in RunAction, the toBlockRef hook, and four of the
six Clear() call sites. handleInvalid, onPayloadSuccess and both stale paths
no longer need to unpublish anything, because nothing was published.

The insert-retry store moves into the sequencer instead: BuildingState.Envelope
holds the sealed block from the moment it is committed to the conductor. This
is kept deliberately - it guards the conductor invariant, not the gossip one.
Re-sealing after a temporary insert failure would stake recovery on the engine
still holding the build job, and losing it would abandon a block the conductor
has committed and build a different one at that height. Because the envelope
now lives in the build state, a forkchoice update onto a competing branch
drops it automatically, with no explicit discard.

A failed publish is retried at the front of the queue: peers follow the chain
block by block, so a gap they cannot cross is worse than a delay. Retries are
paced at 1s, because Topic.Publish runs op-node's own block validator inline
and synchronously on the publishing node and so can fail in about a
millisecond. maxPublishAttempts bounds head-of-line blocking without needing
permanent-vs-transient error classification, and queue overflow evicts the
oldest block. op_node_dropped_publishes counts every sealed block that never
reaches peers, since on publishing_errors alone a final failure is
indistinguishable from a retried one.

Each behaviour has a test verified by reverting the code rather than assumed:
inlining the publish fails DoesNotBlockOnPublish, dropping instead of retrying
fails RetriesAtFront, unbounded attempts fails GivesUpAfterMaxAttempts, and
moving Gossip back before ProcessPayload fails four sequencer tests.

op-node: measure the latencies the publish ordering trades off

Reordering the publish past the insert trades sequencer-side latency for a
guarantee about what peers hold, and none of that trade was measurable.
There was no metric for the insert at all - despite its name,
logBlockProcessingMetrics only logs, and sequencer_sealing_seconds covers
engine_getPayload, not the insert. The only figure available was an
insert_time log field that fuses newPayload and the forkchoice update into
one number, so the two candidate publish points could not be priced apart.

Adds five metrics, one per question the change raises.

sequencer_insert_seconds{stage} splits the insert by engine call. Stages
are observed separately and "total" in its own right, because summing
buckets across label values pools observations rather than convolving
distributions, so it would not give the p99 of the sum. Buckets start at
50us: a sub-millisecond insert sits entirely inside the first bucket of
sequencer_sealing_seconds, which cannot tell "nearly free" from "5ms" -
exactly the distinction at issue. This needed processNewPayload to also
return the instant engine_newPayload came back; it is recorded only from
ProcessPayload, whose sole production caller is the sequencer, so the
derivation and follower paths are untouched and the name stays honest.

sequencer_publish_handoff_seconds is the regression guard for #22554: time
the sequencer's own goroutine spends handing a block to the publisher,
which comes straight out of the next block's build window. It should stay
near zero now that the call only takes a mutex.

publish_queue_len and publish_delay_seconds cover the queue: depth, and
queued-to-published, which added to the insert time is what the ordering
actually costs peers. Queue entries carry their enqueue instant, so the
delay is measured rather than inferred.

unsafe_payload_arrival_delay_seconds is the one that matters most, and the
only one measured on the receiving side: how far behind its own timestamp a
gossiped block arrives. It is the sole metric that shows what peers
experience end to end, which is the thing #8905 claimed to be optimising
without ever measuring. It depends on clock skew between sequencer and
receiver, so it is meaningful in aggregate and for before/after on one
node, not as an absolute. No new call site - it folds into the existing
RecordReceivedUnsafePayload hook on the gossip receipt path.

No op-reth change: its engine API comes from the external op-rs/reth
dependency, not this repo, and reth already exposes per-method engine.rpc
latency histograms including new_payload_v*. Subtracting those from
sequencer_insert_seconds{stage="newpayload"} isolates the RPC overhead from
EL execution.
