op-service/log: own the Logger and its slog implementation

op-service/log.Logger was an alias of the op-geth fork's log.Logger, whose
context methods (SetContext, WriteCtx, LogAttrs, Trace..ErrorContext) do not
exist upstream, so logcli, logfilter and testlog could not build against
upstream go-ethereum. The package now owns the Logger interface, an
slog-backed implementation, the global logger and the package-level log
functions. It compiles against both op-geth and upstream go-ethereum. The
implementation is written from scratch over log/slog; the go-ethereum
handlers and level helpers stay re-exported.

The owned Logger is immutable. WithContext returns a logger whose records
default to the given context, in place of the fork's mutating SetContext;
every caller already derived a fresh logger and set its context right away,
so each becomes a WithContext call. testlog implements WithContext for real
instead of ignoring the context, so devtest's test-scope and chain-ID context
now reaches its handlers: records logged without an explicit context gain the
scope= (and chainID=) attributes, and context-based filters apply to them.

The Logger has no Write or WriteCtx, which attributed records to the caller's
caller; Log and the *Context methods cover them. Every method, and every
package-level function, attributes its record to its direct caller through
one emit function at a fixed stack depth.

Go has no covariant return types: With and New return a Logger, so a Logger
is not a go-ethereum log.Logger. ToGeth converts one for the go-ethereum APIs
that take a logger. The only such call site is discv5's discover.Config.Log.
The converted logger forwards to the Logger, so it shares its handler,
attributes and context, and implements go-ethereum's Write with caller's
caller attribution, which go-ethereum's package-level functions rely on.
SetDefault also installs the logger as go-ethereum's global logger, so geth
code running in-process logs through the same handler.

geth.go is now the package's only importer of go-ethereum/log, and the
depguard allow-list moves from logger.go to geth.go and its test.

op-revm,alloy-op-evm: exempt deposits from the gas cap in OpHandler::tx_gas

Deposits are force-included from L1 and are exempt from the EIP-7825
per-transaction gas limit cap, but that exemption lived only in
`alloy_op_evm::OpEvm::transact_raw`, which replaced `cfg.tx_gas_limit_cap`
with `u64::MAX` around a deposit. `OpHandler` did not override revm 42's
defaulted `Handler::tx_gas`, so a consumer driving the published `op-revm`
crate directly (`ExecuteEvm::transact`/`replay`/`transact_commit`, or the
inspector path) handed an oversized deposit only `cap - intrinsic` regular
gas and parked the rest in the EIP-8037 reservoir, which no OP fork draws
on: a spuriously out-of-gas deposit.

The handler is where the rest of a deposit's divergence from upstream lives
(`validate_env`, `validate_against_state_and_deduct_caller`, `catch_error`),
and `Handler::tx_gas` is the single point from which every execution path -
`run_without_catch_error`, `runtime_oog_result` and the inspector's
`inspect_run_without_catch_error` - builds the transaction-level gas. So
override it there: a deposit's split is computed with the cap lifted and
everything else delegates to the upstream default. `run_system_call` goes
through it too, but is unaffected either way: system calls pass an all-zero
`InitialAndFloorGas`, which `initial_gas_and_reservoir` already treats as
uncapped.

The save/restore in `transact_raw` is deleted, so the exemption has one
home. The two deposit-cap tests in alloy-op-evm keep passing unchanged,
now against the handler-level exemption.

One behavioral difference is deliberate: the old cfg replacement also hid
the cap from `validate_initial_tx_gas`, which OP does not override. That
check reads the cap only when EIP-8037 (Amsterdam) is enabled, and no OP
fork enables it.

Fixes #22971

Two follow-ups from the `reth-update-reviewer` pass over the v2.5.0 bump.

`MemoryOverlayOpProofsStateProviderRef::hashed_post_state` only forwarded to the
inner provider, which zeroes a destroyed account's storage against the
*persisted* proofs storage. Slots written by blocks still in the in-memory
buffer live in the overlay, so a selfdestructed account stayed partially wiped
and the state root came out wrong. reth hit the same gap when it stopped

slots too; this mirrors that. The path feeds `state_root_with_updates` in the
proofs engine, so the failure mode is a spurious state-root mismatch.

`alloy-op-evm` had no positive test for the EIP-7825 deposit gas-cap
exemption — only the negative case asserting non-deposits stay capped. The
exemption is not observable as an error, because deposits skip `validate_env`
where `TxGasLimitGreaterThanCap` is raised; it is only observable in how much
gas the first frame receives, via `initial_gas_and_reservoir`, which OP does
not override. The new tests measure that: a deposit above the cap runs a
payload costing more than the capped budget and must still complete, and the
saved cap round-trips through every resting state including `None`.

Both tests were checked red against deliberately broken variants — the first
against a disabled exemption, the second against a restore path that collapses
the inner `Option`.

exist upstream, so logcli, logfilter and testlog could not build against
upstream go-ethereum. The package now owns the Logger interface, an
slog-backed implementation, the global logger and the package-level log
functions. It compiles against both op-geth and upstream go-ethereum. The
implementation is written from scratch over log/slog; the go-ethereum
handlers and level helpers stay re-exported.

The owned Logger is immutable. WithContext returns a logger whose records
default to the given context, in place of the fork's mutating SetContext;
every caller already derived a fresh logger and set its context right away,
so each becomes a WithContext call. testlog implements WithContext for real
instead of ignoring the context, so devtest's test-scope and chain-ID context
now reaches its handlers: records logged without an explicit context gain the
scope= (and chainID=) attributes, and context-based filters apply to them.

The Logger has no Write or WriteCtx, which attributed records to the caller's
caller; Log and the *Context methods cover them. Every method, and every
package-level function, attributes its record to its direct caller through
one emit function at a fixed stack depth.

Go has no covariant return types: With and New return a Logger, so a Logger
is not a go-ethereum log.Logger. ToGeth converts one for the go-ethereum APIs
that take a logger. The only such call site is discv5's discover.Config.Log.
The converted logger forwards to the Logger, so it shares its handler,
attributes and context, and implements go-ethereum's Write with caller's
caller attribution, which go-ethereum's package-level functions rely on.
SetDefault also installs the logger as go-ethereum's global logger, so geth
code running in-process logs through the same handler.

geth.go is now the package's only importer of go-ethereum/log, and the
depguard allow-list moves from logger.go to geth.go and its test.

internally when a subscription ends.

op-reth: re-price pending txs' OP fees on every new block

#23076 reserves the L1 data fee and operator fee in `cost()` at admission,
but nothing refreshes them. reth only re-checks a sender's cumulative
`cost()` when its account changes, so if the L1 fee rises after admission a
later nonce can stay pending while execution rejects it for insufficient
funds, retried by every payload build and never lifetime-evicted.

Add a txpool maintenance task that, on every canonical block, prices each
pending transaction's OP fees at the tip's L1 block info and removes the
first transaction per sender whose cumulative worst-case cost exceeds the
sender's balance, along with its descendants. This is the pool-side
counterpart of op-geth's `demoteUnexecutables`. Share the fee calculation
with the validator via `op_fee_reservation`.

Spawned from `OpPoolBuilder::build_pool` for every non-dev node, so
wrappers such as op-reth-premium inherit it without changes.

op-reth: include OP fees in txpool cost for sender affordability

`OpTransactionValidator` checks L2 cost + L1 data fee + operator fee
against the sender's balance, but only per transaction. reth's pool then
decides which of a sender's consecutive nonces are pending by summing
`PoolTransaction::cost()`, which for `OpPooledTransaction` was the L2 cost
alone. A sender whose balance covers one transaction's L1 data fee but
not two had every nonce marked pending; the payload builder then rejected
the later ones for insufficient funds each block, and since lifetime
eviction only applies to queued/basefee transactions they never left the
pool (observed as a growing stuck-pending cohort on ink-mainnet).

Reserve the OP fees on the pooled transaction during validation so
`cost()` reports the worst-case total, matching op-geth's pool which
counts `TotalTxCost` in its per-account cost. Unaffordable descendants
now park in queued and age out.

op-supernode: ignore reorged L1 inclusions in the finality lookup

VerifiedBlockAtL1 picked the newest verified result whose L1 inclusion
number was at or below the finalized L1 block, comparing numbers only.
After an L1 reorg, verified results from the abandoned branch can stay in
verifiedDB until the rewind removes them. Once finalized L1 moves past
that height, their numbers qualify and the lookup could finalize an L2
head whose L1 inclusion is no longer canonical.

Check that the finality L1 boundary and each candidate's L1 inclusion
are on the canonical L1 chain, and skip results that are not. Failing to
read L1 ancestry fails closed.

cannon: fail on a misaligned clock_gettime pointer

The clock_gettime handler masked a1 with ADDRESS_MASK before validating the
memory proof, so a misaligned pointer was silently aligned instead of
rejected. ADDRESS_MASK clears exactly the low 3 bits that the alignment check
in MIPS64Memory inspects, so the check could never fire for this path and the
timespec was written at a different address than the guest requested.

Use the address as supplied. The timespec is two consecutive 64-bit words, so
a misaligned pointer is invalid, and MIPS64Memory already reverts on one.

The other three uses of ADDRESS_MASK are left alone: loadSubWord, storeSubWord
and syscallGetRandom need the aligned address for MIPS64 sub-word and
getrandom semantics.

Closes #13442

Server-side RPC metrics no longer depend on op-geth's fork-only
Server.SetRecorder hook, so op-service/rpc builds against upstream
go-ethereum. An HTTP middleware inside the CORS/vhost/JWT stack parses
the JSON-RPC envelopes of each request and its response, and reports
them to the handler's jsonrpc.Recorder. Metric names and labels are
unchanged.

Websocket traffic is no longer recorded server-side, and each element
of a batch request is timed as the whole HTTP request. No service that
records RPC metrics serves websockets. A handler with both websockets and a
recorder logs a warning at construction.

op-service/rpc: hold the response back until it is recorded

The recording middleware now holds the response body back until the
response is recorded, then writes it to the client. Recorded server
request durations end when the response is built, as with op-geth's
hook, instead of when the client has received it, so a slow client no
longer inflates them. It also keeps one copy of the body instead of
passing it through while copying it. Responses over the 5 MiB recording
cap still pass through unrecorded.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
op-service/rpc: hold the response back until it is recorded

op-service/rpc: record the response on its first write

The recording middleware no longer holds the response back. The
go-ethereum server writes each HTTP response in a single call, so the
middleware parses and records that first write, then passes it straight
through. Recorded durations still end when the response is built, but
no response is buffered, and responses of any size are recorded. The
5 MiB limit now only applies to requests. TestServerRPCMetrics pins the
single-write behaviour this relies on.

post_exec_tx_not_last and too_many_gas_refund_entries with string

op-node drives — three of the failure reasons never reached the series

decode failure is not an SDM signal and is only logged).

kona-sources: share a reloading mTLS RPC client that survives repeated rotations

Move the remote signer's TLS handling into a public
`kona_sources::ReloadingRpcClient` so kona-sp1 can reuse it, and fix the
problems in the previous implementation:

- Watch the directories containing the CA, certificate and key instead
  of the files, and reload on events for those names or for the
  Kubernetes `..data` symlink, 2s after the last event. This ports
  op-service's certman. Watching the file paths followed the symlink
  into the timestamped secret directory; kubelet deletes that directory
  on rotation, so the watch was dropped after the first rotation and
  every later rotation was missed.
- Watch the CA file too, as the docs already claimed.
- Keep the current client when a reload fails and retry every 2s until
  it succeeds, and reload on an inotify overflow. Before, a failed
  reload or dropped events left the old certificate in use until the
  next rotation.
- Use the aws-lc-rs provider explicitly. With both the ring and aws_lc_rs
  rustls features enabled, `ClientConfig::builder()` panics unless a
  default provider was installed.
- Trust platform roots when no CA is configured, instead of an empty
  root store.
- Reject CA and client certificate files that contain no certificates.

authenticated each request. Rotate the client certificate the way
kubelet updates a Secret volume: write a new `..<generation>` directory,
swap the `..data` symlink, delete the old generation. Check that the
client presents the new certificate after each rotation.

file-path watch, the test fails there: the watch is dropped when kubelet
deletes the first generation, so the client keeps presenting

keep its current certificate, then pick up the repaired key through the
retry: repairing the key inside the generation directory produces no
watched event. Unit tests cover the reload trigger and the watched
directories.

127.0.0.1/localhost, and two client certificates. The CA key was not
kept.

op-interop-filter: serialize cross-unsafe validation with reorg recovery

A validation pass captures the minimum ingested timestamp and current
watermark once, then advances. If reorg recovery rewound the logs DB and
reset the watermark mid-pass, the pass kept advancing from its stale
locals, treated post-rewind timestamps as message-free, and stored a
watermark past the rewind that was never revalidated.

Hold a mutex across each advanceValidation pass and across
ResetCrossValidatedTimestamp, so a reset always lands after any pass
that may have read pre-rewind state.

Fixes #22848

op-service/engineipc: bound the stderr drain when reaping the engine

op-e2e/actions: emulate EL-sync p2p for the reth backend

The EL-sync tests rely on the sequencer and verifier engines peering over
devp2p so the verifier snap-syncs the chain from a single unsafe head. The
ephemeral reth engines are out-of-process subprocesses with no networking,
so Enode/AddPeers/PeerCount panicked 'not yet wired'.

Wire them against an in-process stand-in: a registry resolves a synthetic
enode back to the reth engine it identifies, peering is symmetric so both
PeerCount reads pass, and each peering starts a sync pump. The pump watches
optest_syncTarget (the head a forkchoice update reported SYNCING for) and,
while one is set, backfills the missing blocks from the peer engine one
validated optest_importBlock at a time — never moving safe/finalized, which
reproduces exactly the state op-geth reaches after backfilling under a
SYNCING forkchoice. It activates only once the engine has actually reported
SYNCING (which op-node triggers only during genuine EL sync, not for a
CL-mode gapped payload), so it fires exactly when a real EL would snap-sync.

The 'Forkchoice requested sync to new head' log the tests assert on is
emitted synchronously by the geth engine API inside forkchoiceUpdated, so
an async pump log would race the assertion. elSyncLogRPC wraps op-node's
engine RPC and reproduces it in op-node's own call path: it caches each
newPayload's block number and logs on a SYNCING forkchoice update to a head
it has seen.

op-node: seed SuperAuthority finalized cache on engine reset

After op-supernode invalidates a block it rewinds the engine and restarts
the chain's virtual node. The new EngineController starts with an empty
superAuthorityFinalizedHead cache, and the verifier (just Reset()) has no
entry at FinalizedL1, so SuperAuthority.FinalizedL2Head answers
Anchor{ts=genesis}. resolveAnchorAsFinalized only bounds the anchor from
above (local finalized), and the only regression guard is the in-memory
cache that the restart wiped, so FinalizedHead() publishes genesis and the
reset forkchoice update carries finalized=genesis.

On interop-sdm-v2 (2026-10-01) that genesis finalized head was served by
proxyd-cl as the sequencers' follow-source finalized head, which made every
sequencer force-reset onto a regressed view and reorg ~590 unsafe blocks.

forceReset already seeds the cross-safe cache from the reset heads. Do the
same for the SuperAuthority finalized cache: the reset finalized head is
what this node last published (sync-start reads the engine's finalized
label), and finalized is monotonic, so only ever raise the cache.

The new test drives ForceReset on a fresh controller with an Anchor-at-
genesis SuperAuthority and asserts the reset FCU and FinalizedHead() keep
the persisted finalized head. Without the fix it fails with the FCU
carrying finalized=genesis, matching the incident logs.
op-node: seed SuperAuthority finalized cache on engine reset

op-node: only seed SuperAuthority finalized cache from the engine label

The reset-time seed of superAuthorityFinalizedHead assumed the reset
finalized head is always the engine's own finalized label. The two
EL-sync recovery branches of FindL2Heads break that: they return
L2HeadsForELSyncWithOffset, which synthesizes Finalized from the unsafe
tip minus OffsetELSafe (the tip itself at offset 0). The cache is trusted
without re-validation and beats lower SuperAuthority answers, so seeding
it there published, and FCU'd, a block the verifier never approved as
finalized (e.g. head=400 safe=0 finalized=400 with an Anchor-at-genesis
verifier).

FindHeadsResult now records whether Finalized came from the engine's
label, and the seed moves out of forceReset into the FindL2Heads callers
(onResetEngineRequest, TryInitialResetEngineForSequencer), gated on it.
The incident path (normal walk-back after a supernode rewind) still
seeds; the recovery branches no longer do.

op-node: treat SYNCING on a follow-source target as temporary in CL sync mode

In consensus-layer sync, FollowSource retargets the unsafe head to the
upstream local-safe block when the local node lags, and relies on the EL
to fetch that block over devp2p. The FCU for that head returns SYNCING
until it does. Since #20310, CL mode turns any SYNCING forkchoice status
into a reset. Each reset re-runs FindL2Heads, which walks back to
genesis while the EL's safe/finalized are still at genesis, and by then
upstream is further ahead. On anything but a tiny chain the node loops
forever and never promotes safe or finalized.

Remember the head FollowSource set ahead of the EL. A SYNCING status for
exactly that head is now a temporary error, so lastForkchoice stays
unset and the next follow-source tick retries. SYNCING for any other
head still resets, which keeps the EL-restart recovery from #20310.

Fixes #23167

op-reth: execute streamed post-exec tx in flashblocks consumer

The flashblocks consumer built pending blocks with PostExecMode::Disabled and
never read diff.post_exec_tx, so pending receipts and balances omitted SDM
refunds, and --flashblock-consensus overwrote block_hash/state_root with
refund-less local values while the payload carried the 0x7D, submitting an
invalid payload for every refunded block.

- Recover diff.post_exec_tx per flashblock (rejecting non-0x7D bytes) and
  append the latest flashblock's 0x7D to the sequence's block transactions,
  which also feeds the tracked reorg fingerprint.
- Build in PostExecMode::Verify when the transactions end in a 0x7D, via

lagoon: specify block-level warming as a producer policy with a net refund

Split the SDM refund policy out of the consensus Gas Refund Semantics
text into its own subsections, and state plainly that a refund policy
is not a consensus rule: verifiers do not run it, and a block whose
refunds differ from it is still valid.

The block-level warming subsection now defines the three warmth states
(cold, block-warm, transaction-warm), the per-access surcharges, and
the refund amount. The refund is the net saving, evmGasUsed minus the
gas used with the surcharges removed and the EIP-3529 cap and EIP-7623
floor recomputed, so a refund never charges a transaction less than it
would have used had its block-warm accesses been priced

kona-engine: bound engine client requests at the transport

Replace the per-call `rpc_timeout` wrappers, the timeout inside
`record_call_time`, and the outer timeout around the reset forkchoice update
with one deadline on each of the engine client's RPC clients: a tower
`MapFutureLayer` on the alloy transport that times out each request. Every
request the engine client sends is now bounded, including ones that were not
wrapped, and a new call site cannot miss the deadline.

The deadline wraps alloy's transport future rather than the hyper client below
it: hyper's future completes when the response headers arrive, and alloy reads
the body afterwards. The new test covers both a request that is never answered
and a response whose body stalls after its headers.

The deadline is still per request, so a long reset traversal is not cut off,
and a timeout is still a transport error, so the engine retries it as before.

kona-node!: make the L1 watcher the source of the unsafe block signer

The L1 watcher sent each signer it read to the network actor over a bounded
channel, and the network actor relayed it into a watch channel that the gossip
crate created for block validation. Each L1 watcher chain now owns that watch
channel, seeded with the signer read at startup, and gossip validation
subscribes to it directly. The network actor's relay arm and its
closed-channel error are removed. Publishing a signer can no longer block, so
the refresh loop no longer reserves channel capacity and re-checks the head
before sending, and subscribers are only notified when the signer changes.

The gossip builder accepts an external signer receiver. Callers without an L1
watcher, such as `kona-node net` and the gossip example, still pass a fixed
address.

BREAKING CHANGE: affects code built on the `kona-gossip` and
`kona-node-service` crates. `GossipDriverBuilder::build` returns only the
driver, `GossipDriverBuilder::with_unsafe_block_signer_receiver` takes a
`watch::Receiver<Address>` instead of an `Address`, and
`GossipDriverBuilder::new` and `GossipDriver::builder` are no longer `const`.
`NetworkHandler` and `NetworkDriver` lose `unsafe_block_signer_sender`,
`NetworkActor::new` loses its signer-update receiver, and
`L1WatcherChain::new` takes a `watch::Sender<Address>`. To follow a changing
signer, create a watch channel, give its sender to the L1 watcher chain, and
pass its receiver to `NetworkBuilder::with_unsafe_block_signer`. To use a fixed
signer, keep passing an `Address` to `NetworkBuilder::new`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
kona-node!: make the L1 watcher the source of the unsafe block signer

kona-node!: move block signing into a SignerActor

Signing moves out of the network actor into a new `SignerActor` between the
sequencer and the network actor. It signs payloads in order and retries
transient signer failures (remote signer transport errors and per-attempt
timeouts) with capped backoff until they succeed, so no payload is skipped or
reordered. A long outage fills the sequencer's 256-payload queue and halts
block production. Other signing errors are fatal, as before. The expected
signer is read from the L1 watcher's watch channel on each attempt. If the
signer rotates between signing and publishing, the network actor publishes
the payload anyway and peers reject it.

This replaces the signing task inside the network actor, which gave each
payload three 2s attempts and then skipped it, leaving a gap in gossip.

The block signer is started only in sequencer mode, before the network binds
its ports. A sequencer without a signer drops its payloads with a warning, as
before. A validator with a signer configured logs that it is ignored, and no
longer health-checks a remote signer at startup.

BREAKING CHANGE: affects code built on the `kona-node-service` crate.
`NetworkBuilder::new` loses its `signer` parameter and
`NetworkBuilder::with_signer` is removed. `NetworkDriver` and
`NetworkHandler` lose `signer`. `NetworkDriverError::BlockSignerStartError`
and `NetworkActorError::{FailedToSignPayload, SigningTask,
MissingUnsafeBlockSigner}` are removed. `NetworkActor::new` takes a receiver
of `SignedPayload` instead of unsigned payloads. To gossip a sequencer's
blocks, start the `BlockSigner` and run a `SignerActor` between the
sequencer's payload channel and the network actor's publish channel.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

kona-node!: require a block signer in sequencer mode

The `SignerActor` now always holds a signer. A sequencer without one has
nothing to sign its blocks with, and its 256-payload queue would never be
read, so a node in sequencer mode now fails at startup when no block signer
is configured. Before, it started and dropped every payload with a warning,
so its blocks were never gossiped.

The kona-node sequencer docs and the CLI reference now list the signer flags,
and every sequencer example sets one.

BREAKING CHANGE: a kona-node started with `--mode sequencer` and none of
`--p2p.sequencer.key`, `--p2p.sequencer.key.path`, or
`--p2p.signer.endpoint` with `--p2p.signer.address` (or their
`KONA_NODE_P2P_*` environment variables) now fails to start. Configure one of
them. op-node still allows a sequencer without a signer. For code built on
`kona-node-service`, `SignerActor::new` takes a `BlockSignerHandler` instead
of an `Option`.

kona-node: keep the sequencer responsive while gossip is backed up

During a long signer outage the gossip queue fills. The sequencer sealed the
next block, committed it to op-conductor, and then waited for queue space
inside its step, so it stopped answering admin RPC, including op-conductor's
`StopSequencer`. A remote signer is typically shared by every sequencer in a
cluster, so failing over does not help, but the sequencer still has to answer
the conductor.

The sequencer now checks for queue space before it seals, and while the queue
is full it builds nothing and keeps answering admin queries. It is the queue's
only sender, so once there is room the hand-off after sealing cannot wait. No
block is skipped: building resumes on the next tick after the queue drains,
and the backlog is gossiped in order. The pause and resume are each logged
once.

op-reth-test-engine: reorgs, side-chain state and EL-sync import

Make the engine follow op-node's forkchoice the way a real EL does, so
the action tests' reorg, reset and EL-sync scenarios can run on it.

- new_payload validates and records a block without canonicalizing it.
  Every validated block is retained and executes on its parent's state,
  canonical or side block; a forkchoice update reorgs onto it, onto an
  alternate fork, or back onto an abandoned one.
- Forkchoice safe/finalized must be the head or one of its ancestors
  (-38002 otherwise). An unknown head reports SYNCING with or without
  attributes, and a build on a side head opens on that head's state
  before anything moves.
- Payload attributes that cannot open a block, including an unappliable
  forced transaction, are -38003; malformed ones get op-reth's
  engine-API codes, and an evicted payload id is -38001.
- eth_sendRawTransaction parks transactions per sender and nonce for
  optest_includeNextTx to include, with a pending nonce over the parked
  run.
- optest_syncTarget, optest_blockPayloadByNumber and optest_importBlock
  let a harness backfill the engine from a peer engine in place of
  devp2p sync.

op-core/genesis: add the OP Stack genesis JSON type

Genesis encodes an L2 genesis file in go-ethereum's core.Genesis layout,
with the "config" object in op-core/params.ChainConfig's JSON encoding.
GethGenesis bridges to core.Genesis for ToBlock and state commitment.

ChainConfig gets its own JSON codec: it encodes the go-ethereum config
GethChainConfig derives, embedded, with the OP fields declared directly so
that they dominate op-geth's same-named fields. Keys follow go-ethereum's
declaration order, with the OP keys last. Decoding keeps only the OP fields
and rejects an Ethereum fork key that contradicts the derived schedule.

The encoding is pinned against the genesis.json op-chain-ops writes through
op-geth (identical except osakaTime, which op-geth's config omits for Karst),
and GethGenesis().ToBlock() against op-geth's genesis block, including the
Isthmus withdrawals root.

/blob_sidecars/ fallback slightly differed: in the former case,
returned blobs were ordered based their index in the blob, while in the
latter case they were ordered based on the provided hashes.

This bug was not caught in testing because all calls to BeaconBlobs
provide a slice of hashes sorted by index.

alloy-op-evm: clip SDM producer refunds to their net saving

The block-level warming policy rebates the gross EIP-2929 surcharge on
block-warm accesses. The EIP-3529 refund cap and the EIP-7623 floor are
both functions of gas spent, so when either binds, part of that
surcharge never reached gas used: a cap-bound transaction got back up
to a fifth of the rebate for nothing, and a floor-bound one all of it
(SDM-M5, SDM-L10).

sanitize_producer_refund now treats a policy refund as a discount on
gas spent and clips it to what the discount saves: evmGasUsed minus the
gas used with spend reduced by the refund and the cap and floor
recomputed. Canonical gas therefore never drops below what the
transaction would have used had its block-warm accesses been priced
transaction-warm. Producer-only; verifiers still apply whatever refund
the payload carries.

The SDM fixture probe was a plain transfer, which sits exactly on the
floor and so now gets no refund; it calls the StateBloat workload
contract instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

op-interop-filter: report not-yet-available data as ErrFuture

ValidateAccessEntry wrapped ErrOutOfScope (-321100) when the referenced
timestamp was not ingested yet, when no cross-validated timestamp existed
yet, and when the message was newer than the cross-validated timestamp.
op-reth maps -321100 to a definitive invalid verdict, so a filter that was
only lagging got interop transactions rejected at admission.

All three cases mean the data is not available yet, which is what
ErrFuture (-321401) stands for, and op-reth already treats that code as a
non-response.

Fixes #21944

op-reth-test-engine: UDS JSON-RPC server, op-service/ipc and Go test-engine client

Serve the test engine over a Unix socket from a companion binary, and add
the Go side that spawns and drives it.

- rpc.rs: a jsonrpsee module over the shared engine with the engine_
  newPayload/forkchoiceUpdated/getPayload methods (V1 to V4), read-only
  eth_ queries, and optest_ sequencing hooks that stand in for direct
  engine-API calls in the action tests. Engine errors map to the engine
  API's error codes.
- bin/op-reth-test-engine: --socket and --genesis; the op-geth genesis JSON
  configures the chain fully (fork schedule, chain id, predeploy state).
- op-service/ipc: spawns a child process that serves JSON-RPC on a Unix
  socket passed under a caller-chosen flag, with a parent-death signal,
  forwards its stderr, fails as soon as the child exits, and dials the
  socket. Its tests run the test binary itself as the child, a JSON-RPC
  server that misbehaves on demand, so they need no shell.
- op-e2e/e2eutils/testengine: resolves the engine binary (an explicit
  path, else a built one, never an implicit build), spawns it over a
  genesis, and builds test chains from the op-core chain config. A smoke
  test builds one block over the socket through the engine API and reads
  it back.
- CI builds and persists the engine binary and has go-tests require it, so

op-reth: reuse flashblocks prefix cache for post-exec Verify builds

When a streamed subblock carries a 0x7D, the follower builds in
PostExecMode::Verify and, since #23157, skips the prefix tx cache, so
every subblock re-executes the whole block so far (~N(S+1)/2 EVM
executions per block instead of N).

Restore the cache for Verify builds:

- alloy-op-evm: OpBlockExecutor::resume_at_tx_index(k), also on
  PostExecExecutorExt. It runs the payload checks pre-execution would,
  numbers transactions from k so refund entries land on block indexes,
  and skips entries below k, which the prefix already settled. Refunds
  settle per transaction, so a Verify-built prefix is a valid prestate.
  Refuses Produce mode, whose state can't be rebuilt from a prestate.
- flashblocks tx cache: record the refund entries the cached prefix ran
  with, and resume only when the incoming build's entries for those
  indexes are identical. Under today's block-level-warming policy they
  always are (entries only append), but the spec allows the sequencer
  to restate them, so a revision falls back to full re-execution.
- worker: cache the user-tx prefix only (never the provisional 0x7D,
  which executes as a zero-gas no-op), and resume both Disabled and
  Verify builds through post_exec_builder_for_next_block().into_executor()
  plus resume_at_tx_index.

directory; the entries it holds were not derived from L1 and are not
meaningful. Point dispute tooling that needs superroot_atTimestamp or

operator_fee_charge returns zero for a transaction whose enveloped bytes are empty (or a deposit), but operator_fee_refund never looked at the envelope and refunded fee(gas_limit) - fee(gas_used) regardless. kona-engine: bound engine client requests at the transport

Replace the per-call `rpc_timeout` wrappers, the timeout inside
`record_call_time`, and the outer timeout around the reset forkchoice update
with one deadline on each of the engine client's RPC clients: a tower
`MapFutureLayer` on the alloy transport that times out each request. Every
request the engine client sends is now bounded, including ones that were not
wrapped, and a new call site cannot miss the deadline.

The deadline wraps alloy's transport future rather than the hyper client below
it: hyper's future completes when the response headers arrive, and alloy reads
the body afterwards. The new test covers both a request that is never answered
and a response whose body stalls after its headers.

The deadline is still per request, so a long reset traversal is not cut off,
and a timeout is still a transport error, so the engine retries it as before.

kona-node!: make the L1 watcher the source of the unsafe block signer

The L1 watcher sent each signer it read to the network actor over a bounded
channel, and the network actor relayed it into a watch channel that the gossip
crate created for block validation. Each L1 watcher chain now owns that watch
channel, seeded with the signer read at startup, and gossip validation
subscribes to it directly. The network actor's relay arm and its
closed-channel error are removed. Publishing a signer can no longer block, so

kona-node!: move block signing into a SignerActor

Signing moves out of the network actor into a new `SignerActor` between the
sequencer and the network actor. It signs payloads in order and retries
transient signer failures (remote signer transport errors and per-attempt
timeouts) with capped backoff until they succeed, so no payload is skipped or
reordered. A long outage fills the sequencer's 256-payload queue and halts
block production. Other signing errors are fatal, as before. The expected
signer is read from the L1 watcher's watch channel on each attempt. If the
signer rotates between signing and publishing, the network actor publishes
the payload anyway and peers reject it.

This replaces the signing task inside the network actor, which gave each
payload three 2s attempts and then skipped it, leaving a gap in gossip.

The block signer is started only in sequencer mode, before the network binds
its ports. A sequencer without a signer drops its payloads with a warning, as
before. A validator with a signer configured logs that it is ignored, and no
longer health-checks a remote signer at startup.

`NetworkBuilder::new` loses its `signer` parameter and
`NetworkBuilder::with_signer` is removed. `NetworkDriver` and
`NetworkHandler` lose `signer`. `NetworkDriverError::BlockSignerStartError`
and `NetworkActorError::{FailedToSignPayload, SigningTask,

kona-node: keep the sequencer responsive while gossip is backed up

During a long signer outage the gossip queue fills. The sequencer sealed the
next block, committed it to op-conductor, and then waited for queue space
inside its step, so it stopped answering admin RPC, including op-conductor's
`StopSequencer`. A remote signer is typically shared by every sequencer in a
cluster, so failing over does not help, but the sequencer still has to answer
the conductor.

The sequencer now checks for queue space before it seals, and while the queue
is full it builds nothing and keeps answering admin queries. It is the queue's
only sender, so once there is room the hand-off after sealing cannot wait. No
block is skipped: building resumes on the next tick after the queue drains,
and the backlog is gossiped in order. The pause and resume are each logged
once.

remote signer, so the actor only sees errors that retrying cannot fix.

The remote signer's HTTP client now has a request timeout, which also bounds
the startup health check and clients rebuilt for new certificates. The shared
ReloadingRpcClient takes the timeout as an optional parameter for this;
kona-sp1 passes none, so its client is unchanged. Its signing
request is retried with exponential backoff until it succeeds when the signer
is unreachable, does not answer in time, or answers with an error. A request
or response that cannot be encoded or decoded is not retried. The retry is in
the signing call rather than in transport middleware because the same client
makes the startup health check, which should fail fast.

The signer address is now checked once per payload instead of once per
attempt. If the unsafe block signer rotates while a request is being retried,
the signature returned is for the retired address and the next payload fails

interop: specify per-message expiry and SuperchainETHBridge refunds

A destination sequencer can refuse to relay an interop message forever, and
executing messages cannot be deposited. Once the expiry window passes, the
message can never be relayed. This specifies how the source chain learns that
through a withdrawal and a deposit:

- L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger records send timestamps, exposes
  expiredMessages and expireMessage, rejects the L2CrossDomainMessenger and
  L2ToL1MessagePasser as targets, and no longer has resendMessage.
- A new UndeliveredMessageExporter predeploy at 0x...30 exports that a message
  was not relayed on its destination.
- L1CrossDomainMessenger.relayUndeliveredMessage forwards the fact to the
  source chain for chains in its ETHLockbox.
- SuperchainETHBridge.refundETH returns the ETH of an expired send.
- Dependency sets must not configure an expiry window above 7 days.

kona-node!: instrument RPC requests in middleware and always build metrics

The engine client timed Engine API calls by wrapping each method by
hand, which also forced OpEngineClient to forward every Engine API
method to its L2 provider. It skipped failed calls and calls outside
newPayload, forkchoiceUpdated and getPayload. A tower layer on the L2
transport now records every request's duration, including failures,
and OpEngineClient gets its Engine API methods from the provider
implementation instead of forwarding them.

The engine tasks also timed their steps only to add durations to log
lines. Those timers are removed: the request histogram covers the RPC
calls they measured.

The JSON-RPC server now instruments requests through jsonrpsee
middleware instead of counters scattered across rollup, P2P and admin
handlers. The middleware records calls, failures by JSON-RPC error
code, and call durations by result using the registered wire method
names. It covers HTTP, WebSocket subscription setup and individual
batch entries while preserving batch response limits. Notifications
are counted separately from calls, and unregistered method names share
an unknown label. The actor and server lifecycle stay unchanged.

The node crates (kona-engine, kona-node-service, kona-gossip, kona-disc
and kona-rpc) compiled their metrics only behind a `metrics` feature,
although only kona-node uses them and it always enables it. Metrics
now compile unconditionally, removing every `cfg(feature = "metrics")`
from those crates along with code that went unused when the feature
was off. kona-rpc no longer needs a metrics dependency because the
server middleware records its request metrics. kona-derive keeps its
feature: the fault proof programs build it without std, which
`metrics` requires.

BREAKING CHANGE: kona_node_engine_method_request_duration now labels
each request with its full JSON-RPC method name, such as
engine_newPayloadV3 instead of engine_newPayload, and also covers
failed requests and every other L2 execution layer method. Dashboards
that select a method by its version-less name must match on the
versioned names instead; the bundled Grafana dashboards are updated.
Engine log lines no longer carry *_duration fields. The node crates no
longer have a `metrics` feature, so dependents that enable it must drop
it from their feature lists.

BREAKING CHANGE: The rollup_rpc and kona_node_rpc_calls gauges are
replaced by kona_node_rpc_requests_total, kona_node_rpc_errors_total
and kona_node_rpc_request_duration_seconds. Dashboards must use full
registered method names, such as optimism_outputAtBlock instead of
op_outputAtBlock. The request counter labels kind as call or
notification; error counters label the JSON-RPC code and durations
label result as success or error. Unknown methods share method=unknown.
The old kona_gossip::Metrics::RPC_CALLS and RollupRpc::RPC_IDENT
constants are removed.

op-challenger!: label L2 sequence numbers and root claims correctly

`list-games` and `list-claims` labelled two values as L2 block numbers and
output roots. Both are only accurate for output-root games. `l2SequenceNumber()`
returns an L2 timestamp for the four game types where `UsesSuperRoots()` is true
(5, 7, 9, 10), and a game's root claim is a super root for those same types.

The root-claim mislabel is the more dangerous of the two: a super root and an
output root are both bytes32 and indistinguishable by inspection, so comparing
the reported "output root" against `optimism_outputAtBlock` yields a guaranteed
mismatch -- the signature the forgery runbooks treat as a suspected forgery.

BREAKING CHANGE: Affects anyone scripting `op-challenger list-games` or
`list-claims`, or passing `--sort-by` / `OP_CHALLENGER_SORT_BY`.

  list-games  --sort-by l2BlockNum  -> l2SequenceNum
  list-games  JSON l2BlockNumber    -> l2SequenceNumber
  list-games  JSON outputRoot       -> rootClaim
  list-claims JSON l2StartBlock     -> l2StartSequenceNumber
  list-claims JSON l2BlockNumber    -> l2EndSequenceNumber

Text output changes too: the `list-games` columns are now "L2 Sequence" and
"Root Claim", and `list-claims` prints "L2 Sequence: X to Y • Block Num
Challenge: ..." in place of "L2 Blocks: X to Y (...)".

An old `--sort-by` value fails loudly with `invalid sort-by value`. An old JSON
key resolves to null, so check scripts that read these fields.

`create-game --l2-block-num` is deliberately unchanged: its usage string already
documents the super-root timestamp case, and renaming the flag and its env var
is a larger break than this change warrants.

feat(contracts-bedrock): expire undelivered interop messages in L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger

Interop executing messages cannot be forced in as deposits, so a destination
sequencer can refuse to relay a message forever. The protocol's message
expiry window makes that permanent once it passes: no valid block can relay
the message any more. This turns that fact into state an application on the
source chain can act on, using only the withdrawal and deposit paths:

- sendMessage records each message's send timestamp.
- resendMessage restarts it, since the re-emitted event can be relayed until
  its own timestamp plus the window. Only the sender can resend, so no one
  else can keep a message from ever expiring, and an expired message cannot
  be resent.
- exportUndeliveredMessage, on the destination, hashes the message with this
  chain as the destination, checks successfulMessages, and sends "not relayed
  by now" to the MessageExpiryHub on L1 through the L2CrossDomainMessenger.
  It is a plain call, so it can be forced in as a deposit.
- expireMessage, on the source, accepts the fact only from the hub through
  the L2CrossDomainMessenger, and only if it is dated past the send time plus
  MESSAGE_EXPIRY_WINDOW (7 days, the protocol window), then sets
  expiredMessages[hash] for applications to read.
- The hub trusts withdrawals this contract sends through the
  L2CrossDomainMessenger, so no message may target the L2CrossDomainMessenger:
  sendMessage and relayMessage both reject it.
- setExpiryHub is gated to the L2 ProxyAdmin owner.

The implementation's deploy gas limit is raised to the measured 1.5x.

refactor(contracts-bedrock)!: remove L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger.resendMessage

Resending and expiry are opposites: a resend revives a message that can no
longer be relayed, expiry declares it can never be. Keeping both needed a
timer restart on every resend (or the sender could resend, get a refund, then
relay the resent event), a sender-only rule (or anyone could keep a message
from ever expiring), and a ban on resending an expired message. Without
resend, a message's send time is written once and can never move.

A message that is not relayed within the expiry window now expires, and its
source chain reports it in expiredMessages so the sending application can
undo the send. The messenger's version moves to 2.0.0, since a function is
removed. The docs page on message expiration says so.

the deposit runs out of gas, the call lands in the destination messenger's

every chain in it can already withdraw its ETH, so trusting its word adds no

  either a block number range (hex quantities) or a timestamp range
  (JSON numbers), the two being mutually exclusive;
- without `maxBlockNumber` the bundle expires 10 blocks after
  submission; a timestamp-ranged bundle expires at `maxTimestamp`, at
  most 10 minutes ahead; ranges whose maximum is already in the past
  are rejected;
- unless its hash is listed in `revertingTxHashes`, the transaction is
  revert protected: the payload builder only commits it when it
  succeeds, so a revert costs the sender nothing;
- the response carries the transaction hash as `bundleHash`, and once
  the bundle's window has passed without inclusion,
  `eth_getTransactionReceipt` for it answers with `-32602: the
  transaction was dropped from the pool`, also on a replica that
  forwarded the bundle to its sequencer.

The window is carried by the pool transaction's existing conditional.
Two gaps in conditional handling are closed because bundles rely on
them: the payload builder now skips a conditional transaction whose
window does not cover the block being built (the minimum bounds were
never enforced before), and the conditional expiry sweep now covers
`Private`-origin transactions, which is how conditional transactions
and bundles enter the pool (they never expired before).

Revert protection is a new flag on `OpPooledTransaction`
(`MaybeRevertProtectedTransaction`, now part of `OpPooledTx`) which
`execute_best_transactions` honours via the executor's commit condition.

BREAKING CHANGE: `OpPooledTx` gains the `MaybeRevertProtectedTransaction`
supertrait. Downstream crates with their own pool transaction type
implementing `OpPooledTx` must implement it too, delegating to the
wrapped `OpPooledTransaction`. Node operators are unaffected.

kona-node: track the sequencer's in-flight block as one state machine

The sequencer tracked its in-flight block with two independent Options,
next_payload_to_seal and pending_canonicalization_payload. Only three
of their four combinations were valid, and the code relied on unstated
invariants: the committed envelope's parent came from the handle,
error paths had to clear both fields together, and expect() guarded
the canonicalization step.

Replace them with a single Option<InFlightBlock>, whose Building and
Committed variants each hold only that state's data. seal_and_commit
moves a block from Building to Committed, and canonicalize_and_gossip
publishes a committed block. Both take &self, so step() alone decides
whether to advance, retry from the state the block failed in, or drop
it. Retry, drop and timing behavior is unchanged.

kona-node: handle sequencer publish errors where they occur

CanonicalizeTask reported SealTaskError, so the sequencer received one
error type from two steps that can fail in different ways, and handled
both with one shared classifier at the end of the tick. Errors and the
block's state were carried there in (error, InFlightBlock) tuples.

Give CanonicalizeTask its own CanonicalizeTaskError, holding only what
it can produce, and surface it as EngineClientError::CanonicalizeError.
The sequencer now handles each step's errors where they occur, with an
exhaustive match on that step's error type, so a new variant still
fails compilation until it is classified. is_seal_task_err_fatal
narrows to is_insert_task_err_fatal.

Reachable behavior is unchanged. Seal-path variants that only the
derived path or the engine itself produce are now treated as fatal by
the sequencer; none of them reach it today.

op-reth-test-engine: block execution and stateful payload builder

Grow the ephemeral test chain into an OP execution engine driven through
engine-API-shaped calls, on reth's in-memory canonical state (nothing past
genesis touches the database):

- new_payload imports a complete execution payload: structural validation
  through op-reth's payload validator, execution with OpEvmConfig against
  the parent's state, OP consensus checks on the result and state-root
  verification. A known block is answered without re-executing; an unknown
  parent yields SYNCING, a bad block INVALID with the parent as latest
  valid hash.
- forkchoice_updated moves the head, safe and finalized pointers, and with
  payload attributes opens an in-flight build. It takes the message version
  of the engine_forkchoiceUpdated method called; the attributes are checked
  against it with op-reth's ensure_well_formed_payload_attributes and must
  be later than the head they build on. Failures keep reth's typed errors.
- The in-flight payload applies the attributes' forced transactions
  (deposits first, then a batch's user transactions), accepts pool
  transactions one at a time with the action-test engine's gas-limit and
  force-empty semantics, and get_payload seals it into an execution payload
  that round-trips through new_payload. reth's block builder cannot be
  parked across calls, so the build keeps the ordered transaction list and
  re-runs a deterministic assembly on demand.

contracts-bedrock!: expire undelivered interop messages in the L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger

The messenger records each message's send timestamp and marks a message
expired when its own L1CrossDomainMessenger brings word that the
destination had not relayed it more than EXPIRY_PERIOD (the 7-day protocol
window plus a day) after it was sent. Applications read expiredMessages to
undo a send. resendMessage is removed: a resend gives a message a new relay
window, which conflicts with expiry. As defense in depth, the messenger no
longer sends or relays messages to the L2CrossDomainMessenger or the
L2ToL1MessagePasser, so it never starts a withdrawal.

BREAKING CHANGE: L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger.resendMessage is removed, and
messages targeting the L2CrossDomainMessenger or the L2ToL1MessagePasser
revert on send and on relay. Applications should undo an unrelayed send once
expiredMessages(messageHash) is set instead of resending it.

op-node: prefetch one L1 origin ahead so adoption keeps pace with L1

Since the sequencer runs on its own goroutine (#22241), it starts the next
build right after inserting a block, usually before the forkchoice update of
that insertion reaches the L1 origin selector. That update is what prefetches
the next origin, so the build finds no next origin cached and keeps the one
just adopted: the origin advances at most every other L2 block. With L2 blocks
longer than half the L1 block time that cannot keep up with L1, and the origin
lags until the max sequencer drift forces it along.

The forkchoice handler now also prefetches the successor of the cached next
origin, and promoting the next origin promotes that lookahead with it, if it
still extends the new current origin. The fetch happens a whole block build
before it is needed, and stays off the sequencer's build path.

Fixes #23271

kona-node!: instrument RPC requests in middleware and always build metrics

The engine client timed Engine API calls by wrapping each method by
hand, which also forced OpEngineClient to forward every Engine API
method to its L2 provider. It skipped failed calls and calls outside
newPayload, forkchoiceUpdated and getPayload. A tower layer on the L2
transport now records every request's duration, including failures,
and OpEngineClient gets its Engine API methods from the provider
implementation instead of forwarding them.

The engine tasks also timed their steps only to add durations to log
lines. Those timers are removed: the request histogram covers the RPC
calls they measured.

The JSON-RPC server now instruments requests through jsonrpsee
middleware instead of counters scattered across rollup, P2P and admin
handlers. The middleware records calls, failures by JSON-RPC error
code, and call durations by result using the registered wire method
names. It covers HTTP, WebSocket subscription setup and individual
batch entries while preserving batch response limits. Notifications
are counted separately from calls, and unregistered method names share
an unknown label. The actor and server lifecycle stay unchanged.

The node crates (kona-engine, kona-node-service, kona-gossip, kona-disc
and kona-rpc) compiled their metrics only behind a `metrics` feature,
although only kona-node uses them and it always enables it. Metrics
now compile unconditionally, removing every `cfg(feature = "metrics")`
from those crates along with code that went unused when the feature
was off. kona-rpc no longer needs a metrics dependency because the
server middleware records its request metrics. kona-derive keeps its
feature: the fault proof programs build it without std, which
`metrics` requires.

BREAKING CHANGE: kona_node_engine_method_request_duration now labels
each request with its full JSON-RPC method name, such as
engine_newPayloadV3 instead of engine_newPayload, and also covers
failed requests and every other L2 execution layer method. Dashboards
that select a method by its version-less name must match on the
versioned names instead; the bundled Grafana dashboards are updated.
Engine log lines no longer carry *_duration fields. The node crates no
longer have a `metrics` feature, so dependents that enable it must drop
it from their feature lists.

BREAKING CHANGE: The rollup_rpc and kona_node_rpc_calls gauges are
replaced by kona_node_rpc_requests_total, kona_node_rpc_errors_total
and kona_node_rpc_request_duration_seconds. Dashboards must use full
registered method names, such as optimism_outputAtBlock instead of
op_outputAtBlock. The request counter labels kind as call or
notification; error counters label the JSON-RPC code and durations
label result as success or error. Unknown methods share method=unknown.
The old kona_gossip::Metrics::RPC_CALLS and RollupRpc::RPC_IDENT
constants are removed.

The sequencer tracked its in-flight block with two independent Options,
next_payload_to_seal and pending_canonicalization_payload. Only three
of their four combinations were valid, and the code relied on unstated

op-reth-test-engine: serve the eth_ reads op-node and the action tests need

op-node's EthClient rebuilds payloads from full-transaction blocks,
validates fetched receipts against the header's receipts root and
verifies withdrawals proofs against a past block's state; the action
tests read accounts and storage and call and estimate against
contracts.

The eth_ reads are served by op-reth's OpEthApi, mounted over the
engine's provider with a noop pool and network. Only two eth_ methods
are the crate's own: eth_sendRawTransaction parks transactions in the
engine's buffer, and eth_getTransactionCount answers "pending" from the
committed nonce plus the parked run. Since the reads bypass the engine
lock, the binary serves requests through a request-serializing RPC
layer, so a read interleaves safely with engine writes and never
observes a half-applied reorg.

Two deliberate differences from op-geth:

- eth_estimateGas is reth's estimator, not op-geth's bisection; no
  action test depends on the estimated values.
- The eth_getProof window is maxed: reth's default of 0 rejects proofs
  for any past block, which breaks op-node's output-root proofs.

enginetest proves op-node's client stack decodes the engine's blocks and
verifies its historical proofs.

the action tests' reorg, reset and EL-sync scenarios can run on it.

- new_payload validates and records a block without canonicalizing it.
  Every validated block is retained and executes on its parent's state,
  canonical or side block; a forkchoice update reorgs onto it, onto an
  alternate fork, or back onto an abandoned one.

  of crate-local block maps; side-chain state reads its in-memory blocks
  over the provider.
- Forkchoice safe/finalized must be the head or one of its ancestors
  (-38002 otherwise). An unknown head reports SYNCING with or without
  attributes, and a build on a side head opens on that head's state
  before anything moves.
- Payload attributes that cannot open a block, including an unappliable
  forced transaction, are -38003; malformed ones get op-reth's
  engine-API codes, and an evicted payload id is -38001.
- eth_sendRawTransaction parks transactions per sender and nonce for
  optest_includeNextTx to include, with a pending nonce over the parked
  run.
- optest_syncTarget, optest_blockPayloadByNumber and optest_importBlock
  let a harness backfill the engine from a peer engine in place of
  devp2p sync.

op-conductor: persist an empty Raft snapshot when no unsafe head is committed

snapshot.Persist dereferenced the FSM's unsafe head without a nil check.
Raft decides to snapshot from log growth, so a cluster that has not
committed any unsafe head yet (fresh bootstrap, sequencers stopped during
a single-to-HA migration) crashed on its first snapshot and re-crashed on
restart.

Persist now writes a zero-length snapshot for a nil head and Restore
treats a zero-length snapshot as "no unsafe head", so Raft keeps
snapshotting and compacting while the cluster is idle. Snapshot also sets
the snapshot logger that the existing error path dereferenced.

Supersedes #19149, which returned an error from Snapshot() and left Raft
logging a failed snapshot every SnapshotInterval until the first commit.

Fixes #13363

op-supernode!: remove the interop activation timestamp override

The supernode now takes interop activation only from the chains' rollup
configs. `--interop.activation-timestamp` (OP_SUPERNODE_INTEROP_ACTIVATION_TIMESTAMP)
changed the activation time of the interop activity but not of the chains, so
any value other than the rollup configs' Lagoon time made the verifier and the
chains disagree about when interop starts.

The override's one remaining job was Lagoon at genesis: op-deployer writes that
as a Lagoon time of 0, and the activity needs the timestamp of the first block
with interop active. The resolver now raises each chain's Lagoon time to the
earliest chain genesis before comparing the chains. For devstack's own fork
schedules that is the value devstack passed. Tests that move Lagoon away from
genesis through deployer options used to keep the activity at genesis, and now
activate it at the chains' fork.

The ZK presets were one such case: WithZK pinned the fork schedule to Jovian,
which unschedules Karst and Lagoon, while the override kept the interop
activity running from genesis. WithZK now keeps the preset's fork schedule, so
the ZK interop presets run Lagoon like the other interop presets.

BREAKING CHANGE: op-supernode no longer accepts --interop.activation-timestamp
and fails at startup when it is set. A leftover
OP_SUPERNODE_INTEROP_ACTIVATION_TIMESTAMP is ignored with an "Unknown env var"
warning. Schedule interop with the Lagoon activation time in the rollup configs
instead, which the execution clients must share. A node that ran with an
override different from the rollup configs' Lagoon time must start from a
fresh interop data directory. When SafeDB history is unavailable, the
remaining remediations are reseeding the data directory or rederiving from L1.

alloy-op-evm,op-reth,kona!: checkpoint refund policies instead of snapshotting them

In Produce mode the block executor rolls back the producer refund policy
for every candidate transaction it does not commit. The seam modelled that
rollback as a snapshot that copies the policy's block-scoped state, so a
stateful policy paid a cost proportional to everything the block had
accumulated, once per candidate. That makes block building quadratic in the
block's transaction count.

The snapshot was also meant to carry refund state across subblock
executors. Nothing does that; the only production caller is the
per-candidate rollback.

Replace snapshot/restore with checkpoint/revert_to_checkpoint and state the
cost contract on the seam: a checkpoint must be O(1), and a revert may cost
no more than undoing the changes made since its checkpoint. Delete the
cross-executor carry-forward API rather than renaming it.

Refs ethereum-optimism/protocol-team#373.

BREAKING CHANGE: refund-policy implementors and anyone driving the post-exec
seam directly must migrate:

| Before                                  | After                                          |
|-----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| PostExecRefundInspector::Snapshot       | PostExecRefundInspector::Checkpoint            |
| PostExecRefundInspector::snapshot       | PostExecRefundInspector::checkpoint            |
| PostExecRefundInspector::restore        | PostExecRefundInspector::revert_to_checkpoint  |
| PostExecEvm/PostExecEvmFactoryHooks::Snapshot | ::Checkpoint                             |
| refund_snapshot                         | refund_checkpoint                              |
| seed_refund_snapshot                    | revert_refund_checkpoint                       |
| PostExecExecutorExt::{Snapshot, refund_snapshot, seed_refund_snapshot} | removed |
| OpBlockExecutor::{refund_snapshot, seed_refund_snapshot} | removed; use executor.evm().refund_checkpoint() |
| ConfigurePostExecEvm::Snapshot          | removed                                        |

A checkpoint no longer has to be Clone. It is only valid on the policy that
issued it, and only until that policy reverts to an earlier checkpoint, so it
cannot seed a fresh policy. A policy whose checkpoint copies its state must be
rewritten to record changes and undo them on revert.

op-revm, alloy-op-evm: support revm's feature-gated asyncdb fields

revm 43 adds `Evm::async_stack` behind the `asyncdb` feature. `OpEvm::new`
and alloy-op-evm's inspector wrapping built/destructured `revm::context::Evm`
exhaustively, so any downstream that enabled `revm/asyncdb` (directly or via
Cargo feature unification) failed to compile with E0063.

Construct through `Evm::new_with_inspector` instead. Where alloy-op-evm must
derive the new inspector from the old one, destructure with `..` and carry the
frame stack over; feature-gated fields are reset to their defaults, which for
`async_stack` is a lazily allocated fiber stack (matching upstream's `Clone`).

fields. `from_env*` wraps the inspector before building so the per-EVM frame
stack is still allocated only once.

existing `cargo hack --each-feature` and `--all-features` CI runs compile this

rust: pin reth fork with overlay storage-root, trie and forkchoice backports

Pin reth to a fork commit that adds upstream fixes on top of the
CanonicalInMemoryStateProvider pin:

- reth#27129: the `OverlayStateProvider` storage root and storage proofs
  read trie nodes through the overlay, and historical proofs complete the
  overlay to the Finish checkpoint. With state masking, the database
  storage trie omits nodes overwritten by the masking suffix, so the
  Isthmus withdrawals root (the L2ToL1MessagePasser storage root) was
  computed from stale cached child hashes, both when building blocks and
  when validating them. A regression test covers masked and unmasked
  tries over both storage versions.
- reth#27634, the follow-up to #27129: use trie changesets for every
  overlay. Without it, #27129 makes historical proofs and witnesses for
  blocks below the in-memory window rehash from the leaves, which takes
  minutes and hits the read-transaction timeout.
- reth#27247 and reth#27429: validate safe and finalized before applying
  a forkchoice reorg, and stop reporting VALID for a reorged-out
  persisted head.
- reth#27252: the state root task persisted accounts emptied under
  EIP-161 as all-zero `HashedAccounts` rows instead of deleting them. The
  block's root is still right, but a later full recomputation of that
  trie branch diverges and halts the node.
- reth#27832: the walker used by the startup Merkle unwind, which repairs
  a masked state trie after an unclean shutdown, could leave stored
  branch nodes that their parent no longer references. The regular walker
  skips them, so the repair's root check passes, but proof_v2 reads them
  and the engine can then compute a wrong state root.

The fork branch follows the maintenance procedure: the upstream release,
the retained patches oldest first, then the CI commit. The backports
change no symbol a mirror covers, so every reth mirror tag advances to
the new pin unchanged.

op-reth: retry proofs execution failures in the sync loop

The proofs engine reads bytecode and block hashes from reth. If reth has
left a block's fork, code that fork deployed before persistence can be
missing, so execution fails the state-root check. On develop such blocks
were skipped when reth could not provide parent state; after decoupling
execution from that provider, the failure propagated out of the ExEx and
shut the node down.

Classify only the error. Block-execution errors and state-root mismatches
are retryable: the ExEx logs them and hands the range to the sync loop,
which retries with reth's canonical block at each height, so a block from
an abandoned fork is replaced and a real failure keeps retrying without
stopping the node. Storage, persistence, and provider errors still
propagate, including a provider error the EVM raises while reading state.

The sync loop created a fresh backoff timer for every event, so once the
backoff exceeded the interval between notifications, incoming actions
postponed the retry indefinitely. Track the next retry as a deadline, and
clear it when an action moves the proofs tip, such as a reorg replacing
the block that kept failing.

Tests cover the error classification, the ExEx surviving a retryable
failure, and the sync loop retrying a failed block until it succeeds while
engine actions keep arriving.

op-reth: halt the proofs ExEx when verification fails

At the verification interval the ExEx re-executes a block instead of
indexing reth's trie data, to check that proofs-history execution agrees
with reth. Retrying such a failure in the sync loop would turn a
correctness problem into a silent stall, so propagate it and stop the
ExEx, as before retryable failures were introduced. Execution failures
outside verification still retry.

op-reth: acknowledge only persisted proofs heights

The proofs ExEx emitted FinishedHeight for each committed notification's
tip as soon as it handled the notification, even when it had only
scheduled catch-up, buffered the blocks in memory, or handed a failed
block to the sync loop. reth skips commits at or below the finished
height, finalizes its WAL, and lets pruning advance to it, so it could
prune block bodies the sync loop still needed, and a crash could lose
buffered blocks the ExEx had already acknowledged.

Have the engine publish its persisted tip on a watch channel and emit
FinishedHeight from the ExEx's main loop when it changes. Buffered blocks
are not acknowledged until they are persisted.

op-reth: fix filtered flashblock log streams

reth #26946 made `matching_block_logs_with_tx_hashes` return early when the
filter does not match the header's logs bloom. The synthetic header that
`flashblock_receipts_stream` builds left the bloom zeroed, so every filter
with an address or topic yielded no logs.

Set the bloom to all ones so the prefilter never rejects the flashblock.
Its receipts are scanned right after, so a bloom computed from them would
save no work and only cost hashing every log for every subscriber. Also
extract the per-flashblock matching into a function so it can be unit
tested.
